The activation and output interpretation must be specified: class probabilities, numerical forecasts, and intermediate representations need not use the same output function.

The hidden state is a computed representation of the sequence processed so far. It is not a verbatim transcript of every earlier input, and its size does not automatically grow with sequence length. It can retain useful information, discard information, or be dominated by recent observations. What it actually retains depends on the transition, parameters, inputs, and training objective.

[figure: sg-unroll]

**Unrolling** draws the repeated computation as a chain of positions. The states $h_1, h_2, h_3$ are distinct values, but the matrices $U,V,W$ and their biases are shared. Unrolling three steps does not create three independently fitted recurrent models. A shared weight contributes wherever the repeated function uses it.

The initial state $h_0$ also needs a convention. It may be zero, supplied by another computation, or fitted as part of a model. Changing it can change the whole forward sequence even with identical inputs and weights. When a sequence represents a separate example, retaining the previous example's state would introduce a dependency that the task might not permit.

For a small scalar example, use $h_t=\tanh(0.6x_t+1.4h_{t-1})$, $h_0=0$, and inputs $[1,-1,1,-1]$. The first state is $\tanh(0.6)\approx0.53705$. The second pre-activation is $-0.6+1.4(0.53705)\approx0.15187$, so its state is approximately 0.15071. Applying the same rule gives states approximately 0.67014 and 0.32587 at the next positions.

These numbers define an **added numerical example**, not hidden weights inferred from a diagram. They show that an input of −1 can still leave a positive state because the previous state contributes. The network does not merely apply an independent function to each token. The training experiment later uses this same transition and exposes all of its forward and backward values.

reading.takeaway: Unrolling repeats one shared state-transition function, producing distinct hidden states.

sections.title: Match the architecture to sequence lengths
sections.body:
Input and output schedules are part of an architecture. A **one-to-one** mapping takes one input and returns one output; it does not require recurrence simply because it appears beside recurrent examples. A **one-to-many** mapping uses a conditioning input to produce several outputs, as in a captioning system. A **many-to-one** mapping combines several observations into a final prediction, such as classifying an entire sequence.

A **many-to-many** mapping returns a sequence from a sequence. There are at least two important forms. An aligned model produces an output at each input position. An encoder–decoder can process an input sequence and produce an output sequence whose length differs. Both are sequence models, but their dependence and output schedules differ.

[figure: sg-patterns]

Consider an unrolled recurrent architecture in which every step receives one $x_t$ and emits one $\hat y_t$. The first input has the first output above it, the second has the second, and so on through the final step. For this particular aligned architecture, the appropriate condition is **$T_x=T_y$**. Choosing a different number of outputs requires a change in when the model emits outputs or how decoding is organized.

This is a statement about the shown alignment, not a claim that every RNN requires equal lengths. A many-to-one classifier emits only after the final input. A translation encoder–decoder can generate a target until an end token appears, even when its input and output token counts differ. A token is also not necessarily a whole word, so comparing lengths requires identifying the tokenization convention.

The scalar browser trainer uses an explicitly different **many-to-one memory task**. It receives four inputs, then predicts whether the first input was positive. Only the final output supplies that example's loss. Intermediate hidden states still matter because they form the path connecting the first observation to the final prediction.

**Check an application:** an activity label for every video frame suggests aligned outputs; a single sentiment label for a sentence suggests a final sequence output. Translating a sentence should permit different token counts. Explain each choice using the required output, rather than merely naming a familiar model family.

reading.takeaway: Aligned per-position outputs require equal sequence lengths; other schedules require a different stated architecture.

sections.title: Learn through time with shared gradients
sections.body:
Backpropagation through time applies the chain rule to the unrolled recurrent graph. It uses the actual forward states, propagates derivatives backward through the transitions, and adds contributions for each shared parameter. The optimizer then updates the shared parameters once using those accumulated derivatives.

For a scalar tanh recurrence $h_t=\tanh(w_xx_t+w_hh_{t-1}+b_h)$, the local derivative with respect to the previous state is

$$\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}=w_h(1-h_t^2).$$

A derivative from the final state to an earlier state multiplies these factors along the intervening chain. A shared input weight also receives a contribution at every timestep: multiply the derivative at that timestep's pre-activation by its input, then add the resulting terms. The recurrent-weight contribution uses the previous state as its incoming multiplier; the hidden-bias contribution uses 1.

[figure: sg-paths]

Products whose magnitudes are repeatedly below 1 can make distant sensitivities small. Repeated factors above 1 can make them large. The tanh derivative depends on the current states: saturation near ±1 can shrink a factor even when the recurrent weight is large. Neither the recurrent weight alone nor the bounded hidden-state range completely determines the backward behavior.

For an exact sensitivity example, set all inputs, the hidden bias, and the initial state to zero. Every tanh state remains zero, with derivative 1. With $w_h=2$, four recurrent factors multiply to $2^4=16$. The hidden states are bounded and equal to zero while their local sensitivity to the initial state grows. With $w_h=0.5$, the same derivative is $0.5^4=0.0625$. This separates forward state from backward sensitivity.

The browser experiment fits five parameters: input weight, recurrent weight, hidden bias, output weight, and output bias. It trains on all sixteen length-4 sequences over $\{-1,1\}$, with target 1 for a positive first input and 0 otherwise. Its final sigmoid probability is evaluated with binary cross-entropy. All five parameters update simultaneously from the averaged derivatives.

Inspect one sequence before training, including every timestep's contribution and their sums. Apply one update, then several groups of 200 updates. The separate length-6 measurement enumerates 64 longer sequences and does not supply gradients. This is a transparent memory experiment, not proof that one scalar state solves arbitrary long dependencies. Query edits do not fit the model; changing a manual parameter starts a new fitting history.

visuals.predict: Will the same recurrent weight receive one contribution or contributions from every timestep?
visuals.reflect: Inspect forward states, local multipliers and summed BPTT terms. Train the memory task and distinguish state values from sensitivity and held-out performance.

reading.takeaway: Multiply derivatives along recurrent paths and sum contributions for shared parameters.

sections.title: Attention changes dependency paths
sections.body:
A recurrent state at position $t$ depends on the previous state. Those states must therefore be calculated in sequence for the ordinary forward recurrence. Parallelism can still be used across examples and within operations, but the chain creates a dependency between consecutive positions.

Self-attention offers another route. An output position can directly combine values from its permitted input positions using query–key scores and normalized weights. During training on a known sequence, many positions' query/key/value operations can be computed together, subject to the mask. A relationship between distant tokens need not travel through every intermediate recurrent state.

[figure: sg-transformer]

That does not remove every sequence difficulty. Position information is needed to distinguish arrangements when the same shared operations otherwise see the same set of token vectors. Full pairwise attention has a cost that grows with the number of pairs. A causal generator still must obtain a newly chosen token before treating it as a later generated input. Parallel computation over a known training sequence and sequential generation are different situations.

A Transformer combines attention with further transformations, including feed-forward layers and positional information. In an encoder–decoder translation structure, the encoder represents the source sequence. The decoder uses source representations together with permitted target-prefix information. “How are you?” and “¿Cómo estás?” illustrate the roles of source and target; displaying them is not evidence that a running model produced a translation.

Recall the distinction between scores, weights, and values. Queries and keys determine scores; softmax normalizes over allowed positions; the weighted sum combines projected values. A causal mask excludes future targets rather than merely giving them a small coefficient. Training must preserve that information restriction if the model will later predict without those targets.

The advantage is an architectural change in how information can flow, rather than a guarantee that distant relationships will be learned correctly. Useful behavior still requires appropriate representations, data, objectives, optimization, and evaluation. This provides the bridge to self-supervision: a model with access to context needs a training task that teaches which relationships to use.

reading.takeaway: Attention changes dependencies; known-sequence training and causal generation have different parallelism.

warnings.message: Stacking self-attention does not automatically solve every sequence limitation. Position information and masks remain necessary, pairwise attention has a cost, and causal token generation still depends on earlier generated choices.

sections.title: Self-supervision constructs targets from observations
sections.body:
Supervised learning uses targets associated with examples. **Self-supervised learning constructs such targets from the observed data itself through a defined task.** The targets do not appear from nowhere: the procedure identifies which part of the observation should be predicted and which information is visible to the predictor.

For masked-token prediction, start with an uncorrupted sequence, choose a position, conceal or modify that token, and use its original identity as the target. For next-token prediction, use a prefix as input and its following token as the target. Both provide numerical losses without requiring a person to manually annotate the correct token for every training case.

[figure: sg-targets]

Consider “how are you doing today.” Hiding “you” gives “how are [MASK] doing today.” The original word remains available to the training procedure so it can evaluate the prediction, but it must be treated according to the task's input rules. In the simple masked experiment, the hidden position contains only [MASK]. Copying its original identity into another supposedly hidden input feature would defeat that experiment's purpose.

Self-supervision can support a pretraining stage: fit representations on a broad data-derived objective, then adapt the model to a task. For example, a separate classifier can use token or sequence representations to predict labels provided for a specific application. Pretraining and task adaptation may optimize different losses, and task adaptation can update the underlying encoder as well as a new output head.

The absence of per-example human token labels does not make the process free of design choices. Someone selects the data, preprocessing, corruption rules, permissible context, objective, architecture, and evaluation. Raw data can contain noise or systematic patterns that a predictor learns. A low pretraining loss measures success on the selected prediction task, not correctness on every later use.

The distinction from ordinary supervised examples is the **source of the targets**, not whether gradients, losses, or parameters are used. The tiny masked predictor below receives explicit class targets from its miniature corpus and fits an ordinary softmax cross-entropy objective. Its labels are self-supervised because the uncorrupted text supplies them.

**Construct a pair yourself:** choose one token in a short sentence. State the visible input, selected target, positions included in the loss, and one way the target could accidentally leak into the input.

reading.takeaway: Self-supervised labels come from a specified transformation of observations, with explicit input/target separation.

sections.title: BERT produces contextual representations
sections.body:
BERT stands for **Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers**. Its encoder constructs a representation for each input token using permitted context on both sides. A token embedding alone represents its identity; a contextual output can also respond to the other tokens and their arrangement.

Original BERT uses [CLS] as a special sequence-level position for heads such as classification and next-sentence prediction. [SEP] separates or ends segments. A sentence-pair input can have the form [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP], with token, position, and segment embeddings providing the input representation. The encoder returns a contextual vector at each input position; the sequence head and selected-token heads use different positions and output spaces. These markers are input symbols, not a claim that the model has already supplied a class label.

The input sequence is tokenized and represented as vectors, with position and segment information where applicable. Transformer encoder layers transform these vectors into contextual outputs. A task-specific head uses an appropriate output representation. A token prediction head produces a distribution over vocabulary items; a sequence classification head produces a distribution over the task's labels. A sample “yes/no” output format does not by itself provide a measured classification result.

Bidirectional context is useful when the whole input is already available. A missing word can be predicted using both preceding and following tokens, and a completed text can be classified using its full content. This differs from a causal next-token task, where the future token being predicted cannot also be available as input.

Original BERT pretraining combines masked language modeling with next-sentence prediction. The two heads ask different questions and produce different kinds of output. They share the encoder rather than turning a masked-word prediction into a sentence-pair label. The masked-token objective is developed first, then the pair objective separately.

A representation's dimension need not equal the number of vocabulary items or class labels. The output head maps a hidden representation to task scores, and a normalization supplies probabilities when the chosen task requires them. Fine-tuning can change the shared representations, the task head, or both according to its stated procedure.

BERT's ability to use both sides of a token does not mean it always resolves meaning correctly. It describes available information and the encoder's dependencies. Learned performance needs task-specific evidence. Likewise, the original encoder and pretraining objectives are not by themselves a standard left-to-right generation procedure. Producing new text requires a specified prediction and decoding process.

The numerical masked experiment uses a much smaller function: ordered one-hot context features and a single affine softmax layer. It makes target construction and learning visible without presenting its 792 parameters as BERT's architecture or its corpus fit as general language understanding.

reading.takeaway: BERT produces bidirectional contextual representations that a task head maps to predictions.

sections.title: Predict selected tokens and train a small model
sections.body:
A masked language objective evaluates predictions at selected positions. For one selected target token $v$, the loss is $-\ln p(v\mid\text{visible context})$. A lower target probability produces a larger loss. The original token identities at other positions are not automatically extra prediction targets for that case.

The familiar example “how are [MASK] doing today” can place probability on “you” and competing tokens. The target is the original observed token, not every linguistically plausible completion. The model predicts a distribution rather than merely printing a guessed word, and its training loss evaluates the target's probability.

The [original BERT paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) selects 15% of token positions: among selected positions, 80% become [MASK], 10% become a random token, and 10% remain unchanged. The original identity remains the selected target. This policy is a property of that model's training setup, not a requirement for every masked objective. The small experiment always masks one selected position so its information flow is easier to inspect.

Its corpus contains six five-word sentences, such as “the cat likes fresh fish” and “a bird eats small seeds.” Each position in each sentence creates one training example, for thirty cases. The twelve-word vocabulary is listed. The visible input has five separate position blocks, each containing a one-hot indicator for one of twelve words or [MASK]. A constant bias feature gives 66 input coordinates.

Twelve output classes each have 66 fitted coefficients, totaling 792. Scores are affine functions of the visible input, followed by softmax. The derivative at class score $j$ is $p_j-1$ for the true target and $p_j$ otherwise. Multiplying by each active input feature gives its coefficient derivative. One update averages all thirty cases before changing the parameters simultaneously.

Select a sentence and mask position. Verify that the target is retained separately and its original word is absent at the hidden position. Before fitting, all weights are zero and probabilities are uniform. After actual gradient updates, inspect the target probability, all competing scores, and the measured mean loss. Changing the displayed sentence or position does not train.

High accuracy here means fitting thirty tiny corpus-derived cases. There is no separate claim of broad language generalization. The model is deliberately small enough that its active features and target construction can be inspected. Explain its success in terms of the evidence it receives and the fitted function, rather than treating a correctly filled blank as a complete measure of understanding.

visuals.predict: Where is the original hidden token retained, and can the model still see it in its selected input position?
visuals.reflect: Follow corrupted features, the separate original target and all predicted probabilities. Explain actual fitting without claiming tiny-corpus accuracy proves language understanding.

reading.takeaway: Only selected token targets enter each masked objective; prediction remains a probability distribution.

sections.title: Sentence-pair prediction is a separate objective
sections.body:
Original BERT's next-sentence prediction task asks whether a second text segment is the actual continuation of the first or a sampled alternative. The input combines both segments with their segment/position information. The binary target is obtained from how the pair was constructed, rather than a person manually judging a label for each pair.

[figure: sg-bert]

For a declared miniature example, a document might contain “The cat is hungry.” followed by “It walks toward the food.” That adjacent pair supplies a continuation label under the specified sampling rule. Replacing the second segment with text sampled from elsewhere supplies the alternative label. The target records the construction, not a guarantee that every sampled alternative is semantically unrelated or every real adjacent pair is obvious from meaning alone.

A sequence-level prediction head uses the relevant encoder representation and outputs scores for the two classes. This differs from a vocabulary head at a selected masked token. **IsNext/NotNext is a sentence-pair prediction**, not a masked-word distribution. The encoder can be trained using both losses while the targets remain distinct.

The original setup uses actual continuations and sampled alternatives in equal proportions. This matters for interpreting accuracy and the training examples. A classifier can exploit cues in the sampling procedure as well as semantic relationships, so successful prediction should not be equated with comprehensive understanding of every discourse relationship.

The masked objective provides pressure to represent token context; the pair objective provides pressure from the chosen segment-pair task. Their combination does not constitute a proof that all language understanding problems have been solved. Nor is next-sentence prediction a mandatory component of every pretrained language model. Define each model by its actual objectives rather than carrying a historical task label into all later architectures.

**Try:** state the target and loss for masked-token prediction and next-sentence prediction. Why do they need different heads?

reading.takeaway: Sentence-pair prediction and masked-token prediction have different targets while sharing an encoder.

warnings.message: An IsNext/NotNext head is next-sentence prediction, not masked language modeling. The two original BERT objectives have different targets and prediction heads.

sections.title: Autoregressive models predict the next token
sections.body:
An autoregressive model defines a sequence probability through conditional next-token probabilities:

$$p(x_1,\ldots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}).$$

Each prediction is conditioned on the earlier prefix under the model's information rules. A decoder-style Transformer can implement this with causal attention. The target is the next token from the original sequence, rather than a selected missing middle token with future context available.

[figure: sg-causal]

During teacher-forced training, observed prefixes supply the inputs. For “the cat likes fresh fish,” a shifted setup uses input tokens $[\text{BOS},\text{the},\text{cat},\text{likes},\text{fresh},\text{fish}]$ and targets $[\text{the},\text{cat},\text{likes},\text{fresh},\text{fish},\text{EOS}]$. The alignment is shifted by one position. A causal mask can allow training many positions together without permitting the target at a later position to leak backward into its prediction.

During generation, the model produces a probability distribution over candidates, a decoding rule chooses one token, and that chosen token becomes part of the next prefix. Greedy decoding selects a largest probability; sampling draws according to the distribution. A mistaken or unusual choice can change later inputs. The sequence stops at an explicit end token or a declared length bound.

Temperature changes a decoding distribution by applying softmax to log probabilities divided by a positive temperature. Lower temperature concentrates the distribution; higher temperature spreads it. This operation does not refit the training data or make the underlying model more knowledgeable. Greedy selection remains a different rule from sampling.

The browser example fits an actual **bigram** model to the same miniature corpus. It counts 36 observed next-token pairs and estimates probabilities conditioned on the last token. Additive smoothing gives a defined probability even to unobserved transitions. Its deliberately one-token context makes the whole fitted table inspectable; it is not a miniature claim about GPT's long-context behavior.

Inspect a transition row, fit the counts, then append tokens greedily or with seeded sampling. Compare the inspected row with the actual context used by the most recent generated step. Clear the prefix and repeat a seed to reproduce a sampled sequence. Positive smoothing can generate transitions absent from the corpus, so a generated sentence is evidence of this probability-and-selection procedure rather than proof of language quality.

visuals.predict: Will a generated prefix use the observed next word or the token chosen by the decoding rule?
visuals.reflect: Inspect fitted transition counts, smoothing, temperature and seeded choices. Distinguish training input/targets from model-fed generation.

reading.takeaway: Observed prefixes train the next-token model; generated choices become later inference inputs.

sections.title: Pretraining, adaptation, and scale are distinct ideas
sections.body:
GPT names a family of generative pretrained Transformer models. GPT-1 combined a language-model pretraining stage with supervised task adaptation. Pretraining fits a general prediction objective on text; fine-tuning changes a model for a specified task using its training examples and loss. These stages have different data roles even when they share parameters.

The broad idea of pretraining followed by task fine-tuning predates GPT-1. Its [original paper](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf) discusses earlier related methods. The useful historical point is how a Transformer-based language model was used for transfer, rather than assigning the invention of the entire strategy to that model.

GPT-2 increased model and training-data scale relative to GPT-1, while GPT-3 increased scale further and explored task performance from examples placed in the context, as developed in [its few-shot learning paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165). **In-context examples and fine-tuning are different operations:** examples in a prompt can change the current prediction context without applying parameter updates; fine-tuning changes fitted parameters through a training procedure. A next-token objective remains distinct from how a downstream task is presented.

Model size counts fitted parameters. Data scale concerns training evidence and exposure. Capability needs a defined task and measurement. A schematic rising line labeled “capacity” is therefore not a numerical scaling law, a reproducible result, or evidence that every larger model improves every property.

Scaling can alter performance under a stated training/evaluation setup, but comparisons also depend on data quality, architecture, computation, optimization, and task conditions. Holding only the model name or parameter count fixed does not specify an experiment. Neither larger size nor fluent generation establishes that a particular statement is correct.

The miniature language experiments isolate mechanisms rather than imitate the historical models' capacities. The masked model fits explicit gradient-based context coefficients; the autoregressive model estimates counts and samples tokens. Both can expose what a target, fitted probability, and decoding decision are, while their tiny corpora and restricted functions limit what conclusions can be drawn.

**Identify the operation:** if examples are added to the input prefix while parameters stay unchanged, the computation is context-dependent prediction. If gradients update parameters on those examples, it is training. State which happened before attributing improved performance to a “learning” demonstration.

reading.takeaway: Separate training stages, context examples, parameter scale and measured task performance.

warnings.message: Pretraining followed by task fine-tuning predates GPT-1. GPT-1’s contribution was a particular Transformer-based transfer approach; its original paper discusses earlier related methods.

reference.title: GPT-1 paper: related pretraining and fine-tuning work

warnings.message: A schematic capacity-versus-size curve without defined metrics, numerical observations and experimental setup is not a quantitative performance scaling law or a universal guarantee of task improvement.

sections.title: A generative model describes possible observations
sections.body:
A generative model defines a way to represent or sample possible data under a fitted distribution. It can produce text, images, audio, or numerical vectors depending on its representation and task. The central question is what distribution and dependencies it learns, rather than whether every generated item looks novel.

A discriminative classifier can model a label probability given an observation, such as $p(y\mid x)$. A generative model may model the observation distribution $p(x)$ or a conditional observation distribution $p(x\mid c)$. The condition $c$ can specify a class, text, or another input. These are different statistical questions, even when a complete system uses both kinds of component.

[figure: sg-models]

Generative models are not necessarily neural networks. A fitted Gaussian or mixture of probability distributions can generate numerical samples. Neural GANs, VAEs, and diffusion models are important examples developed here, rather than the entirety of the category. Similarly, generating a new sample does not guarantee it avoids duplication or memorization of training content.

Assessing generation involves several dimensions. **Fidelity** asks whether individual outputs have the properties required by the task. **Coverage** asks whether the model represents the range of relevant possibilities. **Conditioning** asks whether outputs respond appropriately to the requested condition. One convincing sample can have good local appearance while the model omits most of the distribution.

Use a simple distribution with two groups near −1.2 and +1.2. A generator returning +1.2 for every latent input produces a plausible member of the positive group but never covers the negative group. A generator producing varied but implausible values has a different failure. Neither a single example nor variance alone fully evaluates a generated distribution.

The experiments use small datasets and models so every sample, loss and derivative can be computed and inspected.

reading.takeaway: Generative modeling concerns a distribution of possible observations, including fidelity and coverage.

warnings.message: Generative models are not all neural networks. Producing a sampled output also does not guarantee that it is novel rather than duplicated or memorized from training evidence.

sections.title: GAN training uses two coupled models
sections.body:
A Generative Adversarial Network contains a generator $G$ and a discriminator $D$. The generator maps a latent sample $z$ to a synthetic observation $G(z)$. The discriminator returns a real-versus-generated probability-shaped score for an observation. Training couples the models: the discriminator learns to distinguish the current generated samples, while the generator learns through the discriminator's differentiable response.

[figure: sg-gan]

For the discriminator, real observations have target 1 and generated observations target 0. A balanced binary cross-entropy objective averages these two groups. A discriminator update treats the generator's current outputs as fixed input values and changes only discriminator parameters. It does not update the generator merely because generated samples appear in the batch.

For the generator, the experiment uses the **non-saturating objective** $L_G=-\text{mean}\ln D(G(z))$. Its goal is to increase the discriminator's score on generated samples. This objective is distinct from the original minimax generator expression involving $\ln(1-D(G(z)))$; the chosen numerical convention is explicit. The [GAN paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2661) develops the coupled training framework and the stronger-gradient alternative.

During a generator update, discriminator parameters remain fixed, but derivatives still pass through its function to its input. If $s_D$ is the discriminator logit, the derivative of this generator loss with respect to the generated observation contains $(D(G(z))-1)\,\partial s_D/\partial x$. That derivative then multiplies the generator's parameter derivatives.

**Freezing a parameter is different from cutting a computation path.** Removing the discriminator input derivative would remove the signal needed to train the generator. Conversely, changing discriminator parameters during this generator step would mix the roles and implement a different update.

The actual browser GAN has a scalar latent input, two tanh generator units and a linear output: seven generator parameters. Its discriminator has three tanh units and a sigmoid output: ten parameters. Twelve real numerical observations form two narrow groups; sixteen seeded latent samples supply each update. Every displayed generated value comes from current generator parameters.

Apply one discriminator update and inspect which network changed. Then apply one generator update and verify that the discriminator's parameters remain unchanged while generator values move. Each reported before/after loss uses the same batch for that update. Alternating several updates demonstrates the coupled process; it does not imply that both losses must fall monotonically together.

visuals.predict: Can generator gradients pass through the discriminator while its parameters remain fixed?
visuals.reflect: Step each player separately and inspect actual parameter/score changes. Compare plausible outputs with coverage; the constant generator is a declared illustration.

reading.takeaway: The generator receives gradients through a fixed discriminator; a discriminator update instead holds generator outputs fixed.

sections.title: Realistic output and diverse output are different goals
sections.body:
GANs can produce high-quality visual examples under suitable data, architecture, and training conditions. The important mechanism is that a fitted discriminator supplies a signal sensitive to the current real/generated comparison. Good visual appearance is an evaluated outcome, not something guaranteed by naming the method.

GAN training can also be unstable. The discriminator and generator objectives change as the other model changes. Rates, update ratios, capacity, initialization, and data can affect the trajectory. A low generator loss against one current discriminator is not a complete certificate that the generated distribution matches the data.

**Mode collapse** means generated outputs cover too little of the target distribution. A model might produce convincing examples of one type while missing other types. In the two-group numerical example, a constant output near +1.2 lacks the negative group even though each positive value is plausible.

[figure: sg-coverage]

The live experiment offers a deliberately constant initial generator to make that distinction visible. It is labeled as a hand-set degenerate state. Its near-zero generated spread is not presented as a recorded collapse of the ordinary training run. The normal initial generator varies with its latent input; training updates and current samples are measured directly.

Observe the real points, generated probes, and discriminator curve together. If the generator shifts a group to a region the current discriminator scores highly, that is evidence about the current objective and function. Inspect whether both target regions are covered instead of relying on the largest discriminator score. Fixed evenly spaced latent probes make changes repeatable, but their spread is not a universal image-diversity metric.

A discriminator that struggles to distinguish two distributions can reflect a good generator, a weak discriminator, or limitations of the evaluation. Its probability is not an independent perceptual-quality score. The mathematical ideal involving a sufficiently capable optimal discriminator does not guarantee that a small trained pair reaches that ideal.

**Explain a failure without a slogan:** if every $z$ returns the same +1.2, what is missing from the output distribution? If outputs vary widely but lie between the real groups, what is wrong instead? Explain why both fidelity and coverage are needed.

reading.takeaway: One plausible output cannot establish coverage or stable fitting of the full distribution.

sections.title: A VAE separates encoding, sampling, and decoding
sections.body:
A Variational Autoencoder defines a latent-variable generative model with an approximate encoder posterior. The encoder takes an observed input $x$ and produces parameters of $q(z\mid x)$, such as a mean and variance. The decoder specifies a likelihood $p(x\mid z)$ or its parameters. A prior $p(z)$ supplies latent values when generating without an observed input.

[figure: sg-vae]

For a one-dimensional Gaussian encoder, let $q(z\mid x)=N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. The mean and standard deviation depend on the input and fitted encoder parameters. A posterior sample can be written

$$z=\mu+\sigma\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim N(0,1).$$

This is the reparameterization form: independent noise is transformed by fitted quantities. Keeping a sampled $\varepsilon$ fixed during a derivative calculation exposes how the sample depends on the mean and standard deviation. The random realization is not itself a trainable encoder parameter.

For reconstruction, an input passes through the encoder, a posterior latent sample, and the decoder. A decoder output need not be an exact copy of the input. It is governed by the latent representation, model family, likelihood, and training objective. If the decoder specifies a Gaussian likelihood, its mean and a sample from that likelihood are also different quantities.

For new generation, there is no input to encode. Sample $z$ from the chosen prior, then obtain a decoder output or likelihood sample. Drawing an encoder posterior for an absent input is not a defined generation procedure. Nor is one randomly sampled latent value enough to show that an entire posterior matches the prior.

The worked calculation below uses $\mu=1,\sigma=0.5$ and $\varepsilon=-2$. Its sample is zero, but its Gaussian posterior still differs from $N(0,1)$. This illustrates why a distributional regularizer must compare the distributions, rather than check whether one sample looks typical of the prior.

The diagram's latent bottleneck therefore carries a probabilistic interpretation. It is not just an ordinary deterministic code with decorative noise added afterward. The next section connects sampling with the actual reconstruction and KL terms that fit both encoder and decoder.

reading.takeaway: Posterior reconstruction and prior generation use different latent sources.

sections.title: Reconstruction and KL form the VAE objective
sections.body:
A usual VAE training objective minimizes an expected reconstruction negative log-likelihood plus a positive KL divergence from the approximate posterior to the prior:

$$J=\mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[-\ln p(x|z)]+\mathrm{KL}(q(z|x)\Vert p(z)).$$

The reconstruction term encourages the latent/decoder path to explain the observation. The KL term encourages compatibility with the prior used for generation. These terms express different pressures; an accurate reconstruction alone does not guarantee appropriate prior generation.

For one Gaussian latent coordinate and standard-normal prior,

$$\mathrm{KL}=\frac{1}{2}(\mu^2+\sigma^2-1-\ln\sigma^2).$$

It is zero at $\mu=0,\sigma=1$. Reducing standard deviation toward zero does not remove the penalty: the $-\ln\sigma^2$ term grows. A posterior mean of zero alone is also insufficient; the variance must match. The [VAE paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114) provides the variational training and reparameterized-sampling framework.

[figure: sg-gaussian]

The experiment trains a **linear Gaussian VAE** on six declared two-coordinate vectors. Its encoder predicts one mean and one log variance through affine maps. Log variance is exponentiated to obtain a positive variance; the standard deviation is its square root. The decoder mean has two coordinates, each affine in the sampled latent. There are ten fitted parameters total.

Its decoder likelihood has fixed independent standard deviation 0.2 per coordinate. For a linear decoder coordinate $cz+d$, the expected squared residual is $(c\mu+d-x)^2+c^2\sigma^2$. Dividing by $2(0.2^2)$ gives that coordinate's expected negative-log-likelihood up to a constant. The experiment can integrate this expectation exactly because the model is linear and Gaussian. It does not treat a single sampled latent as though sampling had no variance.

The default KL weight is 1. Other selectable weights are explicitly a weighted-objective extension. Inspect every term and gradient, apply one simultaneous update, then fit further. Changing a displayed input or noise draw does not train. Changing the objective weight starts a new measured objective history while retaining the parameters.

Compare Posterior reconstruction and Prior generation using the same noise realization. In Prior mode, the decoder output is independent of the selected input vector. Draw seeded independent latent and decoder noise to obtain an actual likelihood sample; the table also retains the decoder mean. The colored output point, latent distribution, expected objective, and KL answer different questions.

visuals.predict: If the posterior mean matches the prior mean, does that alone make Gaussian KL zero?
visuals.reflect: Inspect mean, log variance, standard deviation, samples, expected reconstruction and KL. Fit the actual model, then compare prior and posterior decoding and likelihood samples.

reading.takeaway: The VAE combines expected reconstruction likelihood with a positive posterior-to-prior KL term.

sections.title: Likelihood choices affect reconstructions and comparisons
sections.body:
A probabilistic latent representation can describe uncertainty within the specified model. Encoder variance says something about its approximate latent posterior for an input; it does not automatically certify calibrated uncertainty in every downstream prediction. Anomaly detection likewise needs a defined score and evaluation. Reconstruction errors or likelihood-related quantities can be useful evidence without guaranteeing that every unusual observation is detected correctly.

A VAE's objective has a direct expected likelihood term and a prior regularizer, rather than an adversarial opponent whose function changes during fitting. That difference can make some training setups easier to inspect. It does not establish a universal ranking of stability or quality across every architecture, objective, and dataset.

Why can an averaged reconstruction look less sharp? Under squared error, uncertain alternatives can favor their coordinatewise mean. Suppose a two-by-two binary pattern is equally likely to contain one diagonal or the opposite diagonal. Their mean has value 0.5 at all four positions. It minimizes expected coordinatewise squared error for those ambiguous alternatives but resembles neither individual binary pattern.

[figure: sg-mean]

This calculation explains a possible mechanism behind softened outputs. It is not a claim that every VAE must produce blurry images, that every GAN is sharp, or that a particular displayed comparison is a controlled benchmark. Decoder likelihood, latent capacity, optimization, data, and evaluation affect the result. A generated sample and a decoder mean must also be distinguished before judging appearance.

The tiny VAE uses one latent coordinate and a linear decoder. Its possible decoder means lie on a line in two-coordinate space, so it cannot express every complicated two-dimensional distribution. That is a declared model limitation, not a universal limitation of all VAEs. Its KL/reconstruction balance can be explored without inventing a high-resolution image result.

Generative modeling offers several ways to trade off representation and training behavior. GANs use an adversarial signal; VAEs use a latent likelihood/regularization objective. Diffusion provides a different strategy: fit a predictor across corruption levels, then use a specified iterative sampling process. These mechanisms should be compared through their actual objectives and sampling rules, rather than treating them as interchangeable image-style effects.

reading.takeaway: Likelihood choices, capacity and training conditions affect reconstruction and generation quality.

warnings.message: A qualitative VAE/GAN image pair without matching data, models, likelihoods and training settings cannot establish a universal quality or stability ranking. Averaging under some reconstruction objectives can soften output, but neither blur nor sharpness is guaranteed by the model family.

sections.title: Diffusion defines a forward corruption process
sections.body:
A diffusion model begins with a specified forward noising process and fits a reverse prediction/sampling procedure. For a Gaussian diffusion step, define $\beta_t$ as the noise variance added at that step and $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$. A Markov forward transition can be written

$$x_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\,\varepsilon_t,$$

with independent standard-normal noise. The previous signal is scaled as well as noise being added. Bare successive additions would define a different process with a different variance.

Let $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s$. The marginal noisy observation can be drawn directly from a clean input:

$$x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,$$

where this $\varepsilon$ is a standard-normal realization for the whole marginal construction. It need not equal the last incremental noise draw from a separately simulated Markov path.

[figure: sg-forward]

As cumulative retention becomes small, the clean signal contributes less and the noise term dominates. The chosen schedule determines how quickly this happens. A sufficiently noised terminal distribution can approximate the prior used for reverse generation, but a finite terminal retention is not literally zero signal.

The worked arithmetic uses cumulative retention 0.64, clean value 2, and noise −1. The noisy value is $0.8(2)+0.6(-1)=1$. A predicted noise of −0.5 yields clean estimate $(1-0.6(-0.5))/0.8=1.625$. Exact knowledge of the constructed noise would recover the clean value; a generated sample does not have such known clean/noise targets.

The term **estimated clean value** is important. That expression gives $\hat x_0$, not the next reverse state $x_{t-1}$. A complete reverse sampler needs its transition mean, variance policy, schedule, and stochastic terms. Treating estimated clean data as the next state at every step silently changes the algorithm.

A scalar noising example makes coefficients inspectable; the same forward form can apply coordinatewise to a vector or image with the specified noise distribution. The small trained experiment uses scalar conditional Gaussian data so the full prediction and reverse process remain visible, rather than claiming an untrained illustration generated a cat picture.

reading.takeaway: The marginal noisy input has explicit signal/noise coefficients; a clean estimate is not a reverse transition.

sections.title: Noise prediction supplies a known training target
sections.body:
For noise-prediction training, select a clean training observation $x_0$, choose a timestep $t$, and sample standard-normal $\varepsilon$. Construct the corresponding $x_t$ through the stated marginal formula. A predictor $\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ then estimates that known sampled noise. A simple objective is the mean squared difference between prediction and target.

The noisy input, timestep, and any declared condition enter the predictor. The clean example and sampled noise remain available to the training procedure to form input and loss. The true sampled noise must not be secretly available to the predictor as an extra feature; otherwise the exercise would no longer require learning the relationship.

This produces a supervised numerical objective from data and sampled corruption. A training example includes a known target even though a future generated chain will not. Learning to denoise does not require manually labeling a “correct generated image” for every noisy input. The target is produced by the chosen training construction.

A randomly selected timestep can be built directly using $\bar\alpha_t$. The training loop does not have to compute all preceding noisy states. The forward Markov definition establishes the family of corruption levels, while its marginal formula makes these training draws efficient. Distinguish that calculation from the later iterative reverse sampling.

In the experiment, each timestep has 48 fixed seeded observations. Their class-like condition is $c=-1$ or $+1$, and clean data follow $x_0=c+0.3\xi$ with independent standard-normal $\xi$. Independent sampled noise produces $x_t$, and its known realization is the target. Twelve timesteps give 576 training pairs.

The predictor has three coefficients per timestep: $\hat\varepsilon=a_tx_t+b_tc+d_t$, for 36 parameters. Full-batch updates differentiate the actual average noise MSE over all 576 pairs. A separately seeded held-out set measures predictions without entering gradients. This conditional Gaussian example admits a verified analytic reference predictor, which is shown as a separate selectable comparison rather than substituted for the fitted coefficients.

The learned predictor can reduce its target error while leaving some irreducible conditional uncertainty. The same noisy input can be compatible with different clean/noise combinations. A reference conditional mean predicts expected noise under the specified distribution; it is not the actual injected realization for each example. Inspect fitting and held-out losses rather than assuming that the only successful loss is zero.

reading.takeaway: Known sampled corruption provides a training target; generation has no corresponding known noise answer.

warnings.message: The noise target must match the forward construction. In the cumulative-retention marginal formula, it is the aggregate sampled standard-normal noise, not automatically the last incremental noise. Bare addition diagrams omit the signal/noise scaling needed for DDPM arithmetic.

sections.title: Reverse sampling needs coefficients and stochastic transitions
sections.body:
Generation starts from a sampled terminal state, commonly a standard-normal prior under a compatible forward schedule. It then applies reverse transitions from high noise to low noise. The model is conditioned on the current generated state and timestep, not on a known clean answer for that generated chain.

[figure: sg-reverse]

For the noise-prediction DDPM parameterization, a reverse mean is

$$\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right).$$

The next state is this mean plus a noise term with a specified variance. The experiment chooses

$$s_t^2=\beta_t\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t},$$

with $\bar\alpha_0=1$. It computes $x_{t-1}=\mu_\theta+s_t\zeta$ for $t>1$, with independent standard-normal $\zeta$, and no added noise at the final $t=1$ step. This is an explicit posterior-variance policy, not a complete menu of diffusion samplers. [The DDPM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239) supplies the noise-target training and reverse-sampling framework.

The browser uses twelve coarse steps with $\beta_t=0.05t$. Its terminal cumulative retention is approximately 0.00589, making the conditional data marginal close to, but not exactly, $N(0,1)$. Its short schedule and fixed variance policy can also change the final sample spread. Accurate noise prediction does not turn those chosen approximations into an exact distribution-recovery guarantee.

Train the coefficients, start a seeded reverse chain, and inspect one transition. The table lists old state, predicted noise, reverse mean, variance, sampled noise, and new state. Finish the remaining steps, or draw 32 complete seeded chains. Switching between Learned, Untrained, and Analytic reference makes the predictor source explicit.

Use the same seed and condition for controlled comparisons. Training or changing the predictor/condition resets the sampling trace so a single chain does not mix different model states. The forward-query table still has a constructed known clean/noise pair; the generated reverse table does not. Their different information roles explain why subtracting a known training noise is not an unconditional generation algorithm.

visuals.predict: Does a generated reverse chain know the true injected training noise for its current sample?
visuals.reflect: Train known noise targets, then follow coefficients and stochastic reverse transitions. Compare learned, untrained and analytic predictors without mixing them into one sampling trace.

reading.takeaway: Reverse sampling uses a defined mean, variance and schedule, with the predictor source kept explicit.

warnings.message: A subtraction-only denoising diagram is not a complete DDPM reverse transition. The schedule-dependent signal scaling, reverse mean and selected variance/noise policy must be specified; an estimated clean x₀ is not the next state xₜ₋₁.

sections.title: A condition accompanies training and generation
sections.body:
Conditional generation models possible observations given another input. A text-conditioned image model can receive a caption such as “a cat in the snow.” Training needs a stated relationship between images and their accompanying text so the model can learn how that condition should affect its predictions.

[figure: sg-conditioning]

For conditional noise prediction, the predictor becomes $\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c)$. A paired training image supplies the clean observation, its caption supplies the condition, and sampled corruption supplies the noise target. The target does not become the caption; it remains the known numerical noise under the selected objective.

During generation, the requested condition is supplied through the reverse process along with the current state and timestep. The condition can influence predicted noise and therefore each reverse mean. It does not specify every pixel of a unique correct output. Multiple generated observations may be compatible with the same condition, depending on the modeled distribution and sampling choices.

The small numerical diffusion model uses $c=-1$ and $+1$ to select Gaussian data means. It is a reduced conditioning mechanism rather than a text encoder or an image generator understanding a caption. Its two conditions change a known scalar data distribution. The learned condition coefficient and generated means can therefore be inspected without inventing semantic image-generation results.

Hold the sampling seed fixed and compare the two conditions after fitting. Then inspect the corresponding per-timestep condition coefficients. Changing the condition affects the reverse prediction problem; changing only a noise realization changes a sample within that problem. Fitting changes coefficients, while these sampling controls do not.

The quality of text-conditioned output requires more than the presence of a text input arrow. It depends on paired evidence, how text is represented, how the condition enters the model, training, and evaluation of both output fidelity and condition adherence. A plausible image can fail to follow its requested caption, just as a plausible numerical sample can belong to the wrong conditional group.

reading.takeaway: The condition changes the prediction problem while sampled noise remains the training target.

sections.title: Explain why training and generation differ
sections.body:
Two questions connect the diffusion mechanism. **Why define gradual corruption instead of only one final noisy observation?** A schedule supplies a family of prediction problems and reverse transitions between noise levels. It organizes an iterative generative procedure. That does not mean every training example must be simulated through every forward step: a selected noisy level can be constructed directly from its marginal formula.

**How can a model learn denoising if the data construction only adds noise?** The procedure knows the sampled noise used to create each noisy training input. It evaluates the model against that target and updates parameters. The forward construction generates training evidence; the learned reverse prediction is fitted using that evidence. At generation time, the model estimates from its current state without a corresponding known noise answer.

These distinctions recur in the other models. An RNN's hidden state is a computed value, while its shared weights are fitted parameters. A masked predictor's target comes from uncorrupted text, while its input obeys the chosen corruption policy. An autoregressive model trains on observed prefixes and later generates from model-chosen prefixes.

A GAN updates different parameter sets under different objectives; freezing discriminator parameters still permits an input gradient for the generator. A VAE reconstructs through an input-conditioned posterior but generates through a prior, and its decoder mean differs from a likelihood sample. A diffusion model fits noise-related targets but samples through a specified reverse transition and variance policy.

**Final mechanism exercise:** choose one actual training update from the experiments. Name the visible inputs, targets, objective, parameter set changed, and any state held fixed. Then describe generation for that model: where randomness enters, which fitted function is used, and what causes stopping. The explanation should remain correct when the numerical values change.

Comparisons between models need the same care. A confident output, low training loss, attractive sample, or complicated diagram provides only a particular kind of evidence. Inspect fidelity, coverage, conditional behavior, separate evaluation data, and the limits of the declared model before drawing a broader conclusion.

reading.takeaway: Forward construction, training updates and generated reverse transitions use different information.

warnings.message: Noise-prediction training need not add noise step by step for every example. A randomly selected noisy level can be drawn directly from its marginal formula; iterative reverse sampling is a separate procedure.

questions.prompt: When an RNN is unrolled, what is shared across time?
choices: Nothing.
The recurrent model parameters.
Only the input tokens.
questions.why: The diagram repeats the computation; it does not allocate separate weights for every time step.

questions.prompt: Which task is self-supervised?
choices: Predicting masked tokens from the surrounding text.
Using a human to label each image.
Manually writing all classification rules.
questions.why: The original text provides the target for the masked position.

questions.prompt: What is GAN mode collapse?
choices: The generator covers too few kinds of real samples.
The output has too many classes.
The model becomes bidirectional.
questions.why: A generator may produce convincing but insufficiently diverse outputs.

questions.prompt: A trained Gaussian VAE must generate a new image without an input image. Where should its latent sample come from?
choices: The encoder posterior for a missing input.
The chosen prior, such as N(0,I).
The reconstruction error.
questions.why: For reconstruction, the encoder supplies q(z|x). New generation samples the prior and passes that latent vector to the decoder.

questions.prompt: For one Gaussian latent coordinate and a standard-normal prior, which encoder distribution has zero KL penalty?
choices: Mean 0, standard deviation 0.
Mean 1, standard deviation 1.
Mean 0, standard deviation 1.
questions.why: KL = (μ² + σ² − 1 − log σ²)/2. It is zero when the posterior matches the prior; collapsing σ toward zero increases the penalty.

questions.prompt: In noise-prediction DDPM training, what provides the target for a randomly selected timestep?
choices: The Gaussian noise sampled to construct the noisy training input.
A human-drawn clean image recovered from the noisy input.
A discriminator real/fake label.
questions.why: The clean training example, noise level and injected noise are known. The predictor learns that noise target; generation has no corresponding known target.

questions.prompt: Which information distinguishes [0,1,2] from [2,1,0] for a motion predictor?
choices: The unordered collection of values.
The order and direction of changes.
Only the vocabulary size.
questions.why: Both sequences have the same unordered values. Their ordered changes are +1 versus −1.

questions.prompt: An unrolled architecture emits one output above every corresponding input step. Which length condition matches that aligned architecture?
choices: Tₓ=Tᵧ.
Every RNN must have Tₓ<Tᵧ.
Every RNN must have one input only.
questions.why: One output per input gives equal lengths. Unequal-length encoder–decoders and many-to-one models specify a different output schedule.

questions.prompt: Which output schedule fits a single label for an entire input sequence?
choices: One independent required label per input position.
Many inputs followed by one sequence-level output.
An unspecified number of outputs with no stopping rule.
questions.why: Many-to-one uses the sequence to produce one final prediction. It differs from aligned tagging.

questions.prompt: For a scalar tanh recurrence with all states zero and recurrent weight 2, what is ∂h₄/∂h₀?
questions.why: Each local tanh derivative is 1 at zero. Four recurrent factors multiply to 2⁴=16.

questions.prompt: A recurrent weight is used at four timesteps. How is its derivative assembled?
choices: Keep only its last use.
Add the chain-rule contributions from all four uses.
Fit four unrelated weights.
questions.why: The same parameter influences several nodes in the unrolled computation. Its derivative sums those uses.

questions.prompt: Can bounded tanh state values coexist with a growing local derivative through time?
choices: Yes; repeated recurrent multipliers can exceed one near unsaturated states.
No; a bounded value forces every derivative below one.
Only if weights differ at every step.
questions.why: The zero-state, recurrent-weight-2 example has bounded states and derivative 2ᵀ. State magnitude and sensitivity are different quantities.

questions.prompt: Why can causal attention training over known tokens be parallel while token-by-token generation still has a dependency?
choices: Generation must obtain a chosen new token before reusing it as a later prefix input.
The causal mask disappears during training.
Training uses no targets.
questions.why: A known shifted training sequence supplies all prefixes under its mask. In generation, later context includes tokens selected by the model.

questions.prompt: Where does a self-supervised masked-token target come from?
choices: A separately invented class unrelated to the observation.
The original token retained from the uncorrupted data.
Only the current model prediction.
questions.why: The corruption procedure hides a chosen input token while the original token supplies its target.

questions.prompt: Which would leak the target in the simple always-masked predictor?
choices: Keeping the original hidden token as an extra input feature at its selected position.
Showing the original target separately to the learner reading the experiment.
Evaluating cross-entropy on the selected target.
questions.why: The model must receive the corrupted input. The training procedure and visible teaching explanation can retain the original target separately.

questions.prompt: What describes BERT’s encoder context for a completed input?
choices: Only preceding tokens at every layer.
Permitted tokens on both sides of a position.
Only the token identity with no context.
questions.why: Bidirectional contextual representations use left and right input context, unlike the causal restriction for standard next-token generation.

questions.prompt: If original BERT randomly replaces a selected token, what remains its prediction target?
choices: The random replacement token.
The original token before replacement.
Every unselected token.
questions.why: The selected original identity remains the MLM target under mask, random-replacement and unchanged cases.

questions.prompt: Twelve softmax outputs each use 65 ordered token features plus one bias. How many coefficients does the tiny masked model fit?
questions.why: Twelve output classes ×66 features=792 coefficients. Its simple affine architecture is explicitly distinct from a Transformer.

questions.prompt: An IsNext/NotNext output is which original BERT head?
choices: The sentence-pair prediction head.
The vocabulary head at a hidden token.
A Gaussian latent decoder.
questions.why: Next-sentence prediction classifies a constructed segment pair; masked prediction classifies token identities.

questions.prompt: What does an original next-sentence prediction label directly record?
choices: A universal judgment of all possible sentence meaning.
Whether the pair used an actual continuation or a sampled alternative.
Which word had the largest attention weight.
questions.why: The label is determined by the training pair-construction process. Its success is not a complete semantic-understanding certificate.

questions.prompt: For the training input token “fish” at the end of a miniature sentence, what is its shifted next-token target?
choices: fish again.
<BOS>.
<EOS>.
questions.why: The terminal word predicts the end token. Input and target sequences are shifted by one position.

questions.prompt: Changing decoding temperature while retaining the fitted model does what?
choices: Changes the normalized selection distribution without updating fitted parameters.
Retrains the entire corpus.
Makes future observed target tokens visible.
questions.why: Temperature rescales log probabilities at decoding. It changes sampling concentration, not learned parameters or the causal information rules.

questions.prompt: Which statement about GPT-1 and pretraining followed by fine-tuning is correct?
choices: It invented the entire strategy.
It used a Transformer-based transfer approach; earlier related methods already existed.
It used only manually written rules.
questions.why: The original GPT-1 paper explicitly discusses earlier pretraining/fine-tuning methods, including earlier sequence-learning work.

questions.prompt: Does a schematic curve with axes “Size” and “Capability,” but no measured task/values/setup, establish a numerical scaling law?
choices: Yes, its shape is enough.
No; a quantitative claim needs a specified measurement and experiment.
Only if the curve rises steeply.
questions.why: Parameter count and a drawn curve do not define a capability metric or reproducible comparison.

questions.prompt: Which can be a generative model without being a neural network?
choices: A fitted Gaussian distribution used to sample observations.
Only a hard classifier label.
Only a fixed deterministic label with no observation sampling.
questions.why: Generative modeling is a broader probability-model category; GANs, VAEs and diffusion are neural examples, not the whole category.

questions.prompt: A generator always returns +1.2 while real data have groups near −1.2 and +1.2. What is missing?
choices: The negative group’s coverage, despite a plausible positive output.
Any possible plausible individual sample.
A larger token vocabulary only.
questions.why: Fidelity of one output and coverage of the distribution are different requirements.

questions.prompt: During a generator update, which statement is correct?
choices: Discriminator parameters stay fixed, but its input derivative contributes to the generator gradient.
The discriminator must be removed from the computation graph.
Only discriminator parameters update.
questions.why: The generator loss depends on D(G(z)). Freezing D parameters does not eliminate the derivative through D’s input.

questions.prompt: During a discriminator update in the experiment, what happens to generator parameters?
choices: They are changed with every real/fake label.
They stay fixed; generated values supply detached inputs to D.
They are replaced with real samples.
questions.why: The selected update changes the discriminator objective’s parameters only. Generator and discriminator updates have distinct roles.

questions.prompt: Which generator objective does the small GAN actually minimize?
choices: −mean log D(G(z)).
Mean image pixel count.
The VAE Gaussian KL alone.
questions.why: The declared non-saturating objective increases D’s score on generated samples. It is separate from the minimax log(1−D) expression.

questions.prompt: Must discriminator and generator losses both decrease monotonically during alternating GAN training?
choices: Yes; they are one fixed regression objective.
No; each model changes the other’s current training problem.
Only the generator is ever updated.
questions.why: The losses are coupled to changing opponents and batches. A same-batch improvement for one update is not a monotonic joint guarantee.

questions.prompt: For posterior μ=1, standard deviation σ=0.5 and ε=−2, what is sampled z?
questions.why: The reparameterized sample is μ+σε=1+0.5(−2)=0. Use standard deviation, not variance, to scale noise.

questions.prompt: That sample z=0 implies what about KL to N(0,1)?
choices: KL must be zero.
Nothing by itself; the posterior distribution still has μ=1 and σ=0.5.
The entire posterior is deterministic.
questions.why: KL compares distributions, not a single sample. The stated posterior has KL approximately 0.818147.

questions.prompt: For z with μ=0, variance 1, decoder mean z, and target x=1, what is E[(z−1)²]?
questions.why: Expected squared residual=(μ−1)²+variance=1+1=2. A single mean-latent reconstruction would miss the variance term.

questions.prompt: Two equally probable binary 2×2 patterns are [1,0;0,1] and [0,1;1,0]. What coordinatewise mean minimizes expected squared error?
choices: All four values 0.5.
One randomly chosen complete diagonal always minimizes it.
All four values 0.
questions.why: Each coordinate is equally likely 0 or 1, so its mean is 0.5. This is an explicit averaging example, not a universal VAE quality claim.

questions.prompt: In xₜ=√ᾱₜx₀+√(1−ᾱₜ)ε, what does ε represent?
choices: The standard-normal noise for the whole marginal construction.
Necessarily only the last incremental Markov noise draw.
A caption embedding.
questions.why: The marginal has an aggregate standard-normal realization. Its training target must match that construction; it is not automatically the last step’s incremental noise.

questions.prompt: Is (xₜ−√(1−ᾱₜ)ε̂)/√ᾱₜ the next DDPM reverse state?
choices: Always.
No; it estimates clean x₀, while xₜ₋₁ needs the stated reverse transition.
It is the discriminator score.
questions.why: The reverse step also uses αₜ, βₜ and a variance/noise policy. A clean estimate and one reverse transition are different quantities.

questions.prompt: Under the declared DDPM sampling policy, what additional Gaussian noise is used at the final t=1 transition?
choices: No added noise.
The original true training ε.
An independent noise draw with variance 1.
questions.why: The final variance is zero for the specified posterior-variance formula, and the sampling algorithm uses no added noise at t=1.

questions.prompt: Does noise-prediction training require simulating every earlier forward state for each selected timestep?
choices: Yes, the marginal formula cannot be used.
No; xₜ can be drawn directly from x₀ and the cumulative-retention formula.
Noisy inputs never have targets.
questions.why: A selected timestep’s marginal draw provides xₜ and its known noise target directly. Reverse generation is the separate iterative procedure.

questions.prompt: In conditional noise prediction, what supplies the numerical loss target?
choices: The paired caption itself.
The known sampled noise; the condition is an extra predictor input.
An unknown generated clean picture.
questions.why: Conditioning changes εθ(xₜ,t,c), while the sampled corruption still defines the noise target.

questions.prompt: With terminal ᾱ≈0.00589, is the conditional noised data marginal exactly N(0,1)?
choices: Yes; any small positive retention is identical to zero.
No; it is close under this fixture but retains a small signal contribution.
It has no stochastic part.
questions.why: Finite retention leaves a scaled conditional mean and modifies variance. Starting from N(0,1) is a stated approximation.

title: Computer Vision — Part 1
summary: Visual tasks, perception, camera geometry, learned shortcuts, continual learning and the observe–plan–act loop.

sections.title: What does a vision system infer?
sections.body:
**Computer vision turns visual observations into useful information about a scene.** Its input may be one photograph, a video, a depth map, or several synchronized sensor streams. Its output depends on the question: the kind of place, the locations of objects, the number of people, the identity of an enrolled person, a pixel-level boundary, or a representation that supports an action.

Consider a view of a university entrance. “This is an entrance” is a scene-level statement. “A tree occupies this region” is a spatial statement. “There are three people” is a count. “This person matches a particular enrolled identity” is a matching decision. These statements require different evidence, and one correct answer does not establish the others. A system could classify the scene correctly while missing a small person near the edge.

The analogy with human vision is useful at the level of a pipeline: an eye receives a signal, and a nervous system processes it; a camera receives a signal, and a computer processes its representation. **A camera is not an eye in every relevant respect, and an image-processing network is not a faithful model of the whole human visual system.** Sensors differ in their resolution, field of view, noise and sampling. Computation differs in its objectives, representations and experience.

[figure: vp-pipeline]

Images are useful because they contain spatial evidence about many objects at once. Video adds change, persistence and interaction. A moving person may become easier to separate from a stationary background; another person may become harder to track when they pass behind an obstacle. The extra information comes with new dependencies rather than an automatic solution.

**Start by writing the available information.** What is observed? What must be returned? Which uncertainties can remain? How will the output be checked? “Understand the image” is too broad to specify a dataset, a model or an evaluation. “Return a mask for each visible cup, keeping separate identities” is much more precise.

sections.title: How visual representations changed
sections.body:
Early computer vision emphasized measurements such as edges, shapes and geometric relationships. An edge can mark a strong change in intensity, but it is not automatically an object boundary. A shadow creates an edge without creating a new object. A faint boundary can separate two objects without creating a strong intensity change. Geometry adds constraints: how a scene projects into a camera, how views correspond, or how a shape might explain an observed contour.

A later common pipeline separated **feature design** from **decision learning**. A designer chose descriptors of image patches or objects; a classifier such as k-nearest neighbors or a support vector machine used those measurements. Matching local descriptors could help connect corresponding regions in two building photographs even when the images were taken from different viewpoints. The descriptor and matching rule still determined which variations were tolerated.

Deep learning made learned representations central to many visual tasks. A convolutional network can fit filters and later decision layers together under a training objective. AlexNet’s 2012 ImageNet result is a historical milestone in that development. It should be distinguished from the earlier LeNet-5 digit-recognition architecture. LeNet-5’s familiar chain begins with a 32×32 input and progresses through convolution, subsampling and later recognition layers; that particular architecture is not AlexNet. The [LeNet-5 paper](https://leon.bottou.org/papers/lecun-98h) and [AlexNet paper](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/hash/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Abstract.html) describe different systems.

[figure: vp-history]

These approaches coexist. A learned detector can provide image locations to a geometric reconstruction method. Designed features remain useful when data or computation are limited. Camera calibration is still relevant when a powerful network supplies correspondences. **A historical progression explains changing capabilities and resources; it does not make every earlier technique obsolete.**

When comparing two pipelines, identify what is fixed by the designer and what is fitted from data. Also identify the final objective. A representation good for distinguishing digit identities may discard information needed to estimate an exact stroke location. Representation quality is always relative to a purpose.

warnings.message: The digit-recognition diagram with a 32×32 input and the classic convolution/subsampling chain depicts LeNet-5, although it is placed beside the AlexNet milestone. These are different architectures from different historical developments.

sections.title: Patches, language and action interfaces
sections.body:
A Vision Transformer represents an image as a sequence of patches. Each patch is projected into a vector, with positional information indicating where it came from. A Transformer encoder then allows patch representations to depend on other permitted patches. A classification interface converts the resulting representation into a class prediction. **Treating patches as tokens does not make an image a sentence; it supplies a computational interface for contextual representation.**

[figure: vp-patches]

Several influential vision methods answer different learning questions. [ViT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929) demonstrates patch-based Transformer image classification. [CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) learns related representations from paired images and text. [SAM, or Segment Anything](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02643), provides promptable image masks. [DINO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14294) learns visual representations with a self-supervised teacher–student objective. These names do not designate interchangeable architectures, objectives or output formats. In particular, SAM and Segment Anything name the same project, and the presence of a Transformer does not imply that a method has an image–text objective.

Language can specify a target, such as “the cup beside the ball.” It can also specify a robot instruction. A vision–language–action system connects a visual/language representation with an action interface.
