A pretrained visual-language component may supply representations, while robot data supply targets for an action-producing component. The action may be a continuous command rather than a word or object label.

That connection raises a different evaluation question. A representation that correctly recognizes a cup does not by itself specify a stable grasp, the cup’s reachable position, or the consequences of moving it. Robot behavior depends on state estimation, the command convention, timing and new observations after execution. A learning diagram should state which data train each component and which information is available when it acts.

**Compare interfaces before comparing names.** A class score, text-aligned embedding, prompt-conditioned mask and robot action are different objects. Their errors have different meanings, even when all begin with a photograph.

warnings.message: SAM and Segment Anything are two names for the same project. ViT, CLIP, SAM and DINO have different objectives and interfaces; they should not be treated as one interchangeable category of multimodal models.

sections.title: Classification, detection and two kinds of segmentation
sections.body:
**Classification** returns a category or set of categories for an input. An image-level “cup present” answer does not locate the cup. **Detection** returns object hypotheses with locations, often bounding boxes and class scores. A box contains a rectangular region; it can include background and cannot by itself describe an exact contour.

**Semantic segmentation** assigns a class to image positions. Three cups can share the same cup label. **Instance segmentation** additionally keeps individual objects separate: cup 1, cup 2 and cup 3 can have different instance IDs while sharing one class. A foreground mask that merges touching cups may answer “which pixels belong to cups?” correctly while failing to count or separate them.

In the experiment, a declared scene contains three cup silhouettes and one red ball. The same annotations produce several representations. Classification lists the two foreground classes. Boxes enclose each visible object. Semantic labels merge the cups into a class. Instance labels preserve their IDs. A referring mask selects a target using a declared query. **The rendering computes these outputs from known annotations; it does not pretend to run a trained visual recognizer.**

The mask is a 24×18 array. A box uses exclusive right and bottom edges, so a region covering columns 3 through 7 has horizontal bounds [3,8), width 5. This convention prevents an off-by-one error when relating a box to pixel area. A class count of two is different from an instance count of four and from the number of labeled pixels.

**Try this sequence:** show semantic labels, then instance labels. Explain which information the first representation loses. Move the ball and inspect “cup nearest the red ball.” The rule uses image-center distances, which are explicit and inspectable. It does not infer physical depth. At an exact tie, the result marks both candidates rather than manufacturing certainty.

A full detector or segmenter would need to estimate the annotations from observations, then be compared with independent targets. Keeping the output contract separate from the inference method makes that missing step clear.

visuals.predict: Will three cup instances receive three different semantic class labels?
visuals.reflect: Compare boxes, semantic and instance masks. Move the ball to a tie and explain why a referring query can become ambiguous.

sections.title: Reading text requires more than finding a region
sections.body:
License-plate recognition illustrates a pipeline with several distinct outputs. First locate a plate. Then align or rectify the region so that the character sequence has a usable orientation. Then recognize characters or a sequence. Finally produce a string, possibly with uncertainty or a validity check. The same broad structure applies to many visual text-reading problems.

[figure: vp-recognition]

A plate detector might return an accurate box while the reader confuses two characters. Conversely, a reader can succeed on a manually cropped plate while the complete system fails to find it in a road image. **Evaluate the complete pipeline as well as its components.** A crop supplied by another process is part of the input contract, not evidence that localization succeeded.

Rectification uses a model of how the plate plane projects into the image. If four corners are available and the planar approximation is appropriate, a geometric transformation can reduce perspective distortion. That transformation cannot recreate unreadable characters hidden by glare, extreme blur or an obstruction. Enlarging the crop changes its sampled display size without adding the missing evidence.

A syntax constraint can rule out some strings, but it should not silently turn uncertainty into a confident incorrect reading. Suppose two candidates differ in one ambiguous position. If both satisfy the expected format, the format supplies no basis for choosing between them. If only one satisfies it, the choice depends on the assumption that the expected format is actually applicable.

**Work the error chain:** define success as the correct full string for each plate in a scene. List at least four possible failures: missed plate, wrong region, poor alignment, wrong character sequence. Which remain visible in a character-only accuracy measured on clean crops? A useful final output can include the recognized string, its location and a clear representation of unresolved positions.

sections.title: Faces, smiles and biometric matching
sections.body:
A face image can support several questions, but their labels should remain separate. Face detection asks where a face is. A visible-attribute classifier might ask whether its configuration fits a defined smile category. Verification compares an observation with one claimed enrolled identity. Identification searches among several enrolled identities and may need an “unknown” outcome.

[figure: vp-identity]

**A smile label is neither an identity label nor proof of an internal emotional state.** The training annotation describes a visible configuration under a specified convention. Someone can smile for many reasons, and an apparently similar expression can occur under different circumstances. The system’s observable target should be named precisely.

Biometric matching also includes iris and fingerprint patterns. A representation is compared with an enrolled reference, and a threshold converts a score into an acceptance or rejection. Lowering a threshold can admit more genuine matches while also admitting more incorrect matches. Raising it can reject more incorrect matches while also rejecting genuine observations. A matching score is not automatically a calibrated probability that two observations belong to the same person.

Pose, illumination, occlusion and acquisition quality affect the comparison. A set-to-set method can compare several observations with several enrolled examples rather than relying on a single frame. That changes the available evidence; it does not change verification into smile detection or establish unrestricted identification accuracy.

**Specify the negative cases.** In verification, negatives are different identities under the relevant acquisition conditions. In open-set identification, a person absent from enrollment should not be forced into the nearest known name. An identity system needs a rejection policy and evaluation of false matches and false rejections, rather than only a few convincing selected examples.

For a classroom model, use synthetic or clearly authorized examples and declared targets. The conceptual distinction is already visible without assigning real personal identities to photographs.

warnings.message: The smile-detection example is paired with a face-identification citation. Face identification and smile classification are different tasks; that citation does not establish performance on the smile target.

sections.title: Detection becomes useful through time and relationships
sections.body:
Checkout-free retail combines more than object boxes. A system may need to track a person, locate a hand and item, infer a pickup or return, associate the event with a particular person, and update an inventory state. Each step can depend on observations before and after the apparent event.

[figure: vp-events]

A hand overlapping an item in one image is compatible with reaching, carrying, putting it back, or passing it to someone else. **An event is a hypothesis about a temporal relationship.** Tracking preserves identity across frames so that the system can connect changes to the same actor and object. An identity switch can create an incorrect event association even when every individual box is well located.

Driving support similarly combines outputs: road or lane regions, nearby vehicles, pedestrians, relative locations and change over time. A perception representation can inform a later decision, but a labeled road image alone does not establish full autonomous driving. Missing an object, misestimating its movement, or using a stale observation can change what an action-producing component receives.

Surveillance and crowd analysis can involve detection, tracking, counting and event alerts. The intended event must be operationally defined. “An unusual situation” is too vague unless the system states what observable condition triggers its output. A box around a vehicle identifies a candidate; it does not establish that the vehicle’s behavior violates a rule or that an alert is justified.

**Reason through an occlusion:** two people pass behind a shelf and reappear. The detector supplies two correct boxes. What evidence connects each new box to its earlier identity? Appearance, predicted motion and scene constraints can help, but indistinguishable observations may remain ambiguous. Keeping multiple hypotheses or reporting uncertainty can be more faithful than inventing an association.

A useful evaluation separates localization errors, tracking association errors and event errors. Strong performance on one component cannot be substituted for evidence about the whole temporal task.

sections.title: Pose, gaming and mixed reality
sections.body:
Pose estimation represents a body or hand using landmarks or joints. The output can be a set of 2D image coordinates, 3D coordinates, or both, with confidence and a stated reference frame. A visible wrist landmark is not the same thing as a complete joint-angle state. Missing or occluded joints may require inference rather than direct measurement.

RGB/depth gaming systems illustrate how pose supports interaction. An RGB image supplies appearance; a depth observation supplies a different kind of spatial measurement. Estimated joints can define a gesture or control an avatar. A gesture recognizer also needs timing: one hand position may be part of several actions, while a sequence can distinguish them.

[figure: vp-spatial]

Mixed reality adds **registration**: place virtual content consistently relative to the estimated physical environment. The camera, display, user and room can all move. An object drawn at a fixed pixel coordinate will not remain attached to a real surface during that motion. Spatial tracking and the transformation between coordinate frames therefore matter as much as recognizing the surface once.

Remote avatars transfer selected aspects of a person’s movement into a different representation. The mapping can preserve joint motion while changing body shape, clothing or the surrounding virtual scene. Reconstructing a motion trajectory does not guarantee that the avatar is geometrically identical to the person, nor does it infer every intention behind a gesture.

**Trace a hand interaction:** image/depth observation → hand landmarks → gesture state over time → interface event → new displayed state. At each arrow, identify a possible ambiguity. Does an occluded finger make two gestures indistinguishable? Does delayed processing trigger an event after the hand has moved away? Does a coordinate-frame error move a virtual object in the wrong direction?

These applications share components, but success criteria differ. Accurate body pose for a broad game gesture may not supply the precision required to align a small virtual object with a fingertip.

sections.title: Camera projection, sports and stereo depth
sections.body:
A sports image records a projection of a three-dimensional scene. A court point, a ball in the air and a point on a vertical net can appear near one another in the image while occupying different world locations. **Image proximity is not automatically physical proximity.** Geometry supplies constraints that an image-only coordinate comparison lacks.

For an ideal pinhole camera, a point expressed in camera coordinates $(x_c,y_c,z_c)$ projects to $u=c_x+f_x x_c/z_c$ and $v=c_y-f_y y_c/z_c$ under an upward camera-y convention and downward image-v convention. The division by depth is essential. In homogeneous notation, $s[u,v,1]^T=P[X,Y,Z,1]^T$ includes a scale $s$; ordinary pixel coordinates require normalization.

The experiment projects a declared 6×12 court and a height-one net. Move the camera or selected world point, then inspect camera and pixel coordinates. Raising the point changes its relationship to the court plane. Moving the camera changes the projection of the whole scene. Increasing focal length changes the image scale while leaving world coordinates fixed. Off-screen coordinates remain numerical results even though the display clips them.

A ground-plane mapping is useful for a point known to lie on the court. Applying it to an airborne ball treats the point as if it had the wrong height. Likewise, a net occupies a different plane. **A planar assumption is information about the scene, not a property granted to every observed object.**

The separate stereo example uses parallel cameras with focal length $f$, baseline $B$ and disparity $d$. Under its declared geometry, $d=fB/Z$, so $Z=fB/d$. With $f=120$, $B=1$ and $Z=6$, disparity is 20 pixels. At larger depths disparity shrinks, making a fixed disparity error more consequential. Real reconstruction also depends on calibration and correct correspondence, which the ideal arithmetic explicitly supplies rather than estimates.

visuals.predict: If a world point rises above the ground plane, is a ground-plane mapping still the same geometric contract?
visuals.reflect: Inspect the actual camera/pixel values and the separate stereo disparity. Explain perspective division and sensitivity at larger depth.

warnings.message: The projected coordinate equation omits the homogeneous scale/normalization needed to obtain ordinary pixel coordinates. A camera matrix produces homogeneous coordinates; divide by their final component under the stated convention.

sections.title: Fingerprints and semantic search answer different questions
sections.body:
Visual content retrieval begins by deciding what counts as a relevant match. One goal is to find a particular recording or image despite permitted changes such as compression, scaling or a short extract. Another is to find content with a related subject or meaning. These goals can use compact representations and distance comparisons, but the desired equivalence is different.

[figure: vp-retrieval]

An identity-oriented fingerprint should retain evidence that distinguishes a specific content item while tolerating the transformations declared by the application. A semantic embedding may intentionally bring different recordings of similar scenes close together. **Two nearby representations can indicate relevance without proving shared content origin.** Conversely, a system optimized for exact content matching can retrieve little useful material for a broad conceptual query.

A database pipeline encodes the query, compares it with stored representations, ranks candidates and applies a retrieval or acceptance rule. The representation and distance define the search behavior together. A Hamming distance on binary hashes counts differing bits; a distance on learned real-valued embeddings measures something else. Neither has universal meaning independent of its construction.

Consider a query showing a football player on a field. “Find this broadcast segment” requires identity evidence. “Find other football scenes” requires semantic similarity. “Find every frame containing this particular person” combines identity with temporal localization. Reusing one ranking metric for all three can conceal a task mismatch.

Compact or semantic hashing is an idea about representation and retrieval, not proof that a particular visual identification pipeline has been validated. **Evaluate relevant transformations and confusing alternatives.** A useful negative example is one that shares colors and scene layout while coming from a different recording. A useful positive example is the same recording after a permitted change that makes its raw pixels differ substantially.

sections.title: Medical imagery and resource-constrained monitoring
sections.body:
Medical visual applications include recognition of image patterns, localization or segmentation of structures, alignment of observations and visual support for an intervention. Different modalities expose different signals. A radiograph, a CT slice and a visible-light camera image are not interchangeable arrays merely because they can all be displayed as grayscale pixels.

The output must be stated at the appropriate level. A segmentation mask identifies a proposed region under a labeling convention. A classification score assigns a model category. A tracking system estimates movement of a visible tool or structure. **None of these outputs becomes a verified clinical conclusion just because it is overlaid convincingly on an image.** Task definitions, appropriate targets and independent validation determine what the result supports.

Home monitoring can instead use body pose, interactions or activity-related events. Several people in one frame create an association problem: landmarks need to be grouped into the correct individuals. Occlusion and camera placement affect which movements are observable. A small model intended for limited hardware must still be evaluated on the actual acquisition conditions and task.

Resource constraints can motivate model compression or distillation. However, “small” should be measured: parameter storage, memory during inference, latency under a stated workload and numerical precision, or operation count. FLOPs denote a number of floating-point operations; FLOP/s denotes a rate. These differ from advertised integer operations at another precision. A hardware label without a benchmark contract cannot establish usable inference speed.

**Work a design choice:** a home camera reports a pose-based event, while a hospital image system reports a structure mask. List the input modality, target, coordinate convention and likely missing information for each. They share some computational ideas but require different data and error interpretation.

For this chapter, medical examples explain the range of vision tasks. The numerical exercises use synthetic images and make no diagnostic claims or invented measured medical results.

warnings.message: The device specification and “~2T FLOPs” claim lack a verified workload, rate, numerical precision and measurement procedure. FLOPs are an operation count, not an inference-speed rate. Those values cannot substantiate the monitoring system’s measured performance.

sections.title: Reconstruction and free-viewpoint generation
sections.body:
Several views can constrain a three-dimensional scene because the same physical point projects to different image locations. With calibrated cameras and correct correspondences, the back-projected rays constrain the point’s location. A reconstruction may represent a building as a point cloud, a surface mesh or another scene representation.

[figure: vp-views]

**Correspondence is a substantive inference step.** Two image patches with similar appearance may come from repeated windows or different parts of a texture. A geometric method can reject some incompatible matches, but incorrect correspondences can still produce incorrect structure. Textureless surfaces and occlusion reduce the usable evidence.

Free-viewpoint generation uses a recovered or learned scene representation to render from a different camera position. A camera array observing performers on a stage can supply several views of the action. An interpolated view between observed cameras and a view far outside their coverage can have very different evidence. The new viewpoint may reveal a surface hidden in every original observation.

A visually plausible result does not tell us whether every visible surface was measured. Geometry, learned priors and synthesis can fill gaps differently. If the purpose is to measure a structure, inventing a plausible hidden region is an error. If the purpose is visual content generation, a plausible completion may be useful, but it should be assessed as generation rather than as a measured reconstruction.

**Trace one point:** select a visible feature in two original views, identify the two camera rays, and ask where they agree. Then move the requested viewing camera behind an object. Which region lacks original evidence? The exercise distinguishes triangulation from the separate problem of generating a complete appearance.

Temporal consistency matters for moving performers. A reconstruction that assigns incompatible geometry across successive frames can flicker or change shape in the rendered video, even when individual frames look plausible.

sections.title: Dehazing and the limits of inversion
sections.body:
A hazy observation can lose contrast because light from the scene mixes with an atmospheric contribution. A simple model is $I=tJ+(1-t)A$, where $J$ is clean intensity, $I$ is observed intensity, $A$ is airlight and transmission $t$ determines how much scene signal remains. This is a model with assumptions, rather than a complete description of every real atmospheric image.

If $t$ and $A$ are known and $t>0$, algebra gives $J=(I-(1-t)A)/t$. That formula explains a useful distinction: **inverting known corruption parameters is easier than estimating those parameters from an unfamiliar photograph.** A real restoration method has to obtain or infer relevant information, and its assumptions can fail.

The exercise begins with four declared RGB colors. It computes hazy observations and then inverts them with a separately adjustable assumed transmission. At matched transmission and zero noise, recovery is exact. Add a channel noise term $n$ and the same matched inversion returns $J+n/t$. Thus, low transmission amplifies noise. At $t=0.1$, an observation error of 0.01 produces a recovered-channel error of 0.1 under the stated model.

Changing the assumed transmission creates a different error even without noise. Display clipping can conceal that error: two raw reconstructed values outside [0,1] may be shown as the same saturated color. The table therefore reports raw values, and reconstruction RMSE is calculated before display clipping.

**Try to explain the output before moving a control.** If the true transmission drops while the assumed transmission remains fixed, should contrast and accuracy remain unchanged? If both drop together, can correct parameters prevent noise amplification? Separating these interventions makes restoration limitations visible.

At zero transmission the model observation is independent of $J$. There is no unique clean intensity to recover from that observation alone. A plausible generated completion would use additional assumptions; it would not reverse missing information by algebra.

visuals.predict: With matched transmission, will correct parameters prevent observation noise from growing during inversion?
visuals.reflect: Inspect unclipped values and RMSE. Separate parameter mismatch, noise amplification and color clipping.

sections.title: Multimodal inputs and a distilled student
sections.body:
RGB, thermal, depth and medical imaging observe different physical signals. RGB primarily records visible-light appearance under its acquisition conditions. A thermal observation reflects thermal radiation under the sensor’s spectral and calibration assumptions. Depth supplies estimated or measured spatial information. CT and MRI have different acquisition physics again. **Sharing a pixel grid does not make these measurements equivalent.**

Combining modalities can supply complementary evidence. A region difficult to distinguish by visible color may be clearer in another sensor stream. Fusion also creates alignment requirements: are the observations from the same time, and do their coordinates refer to the same physical location? A moving person can be mismatched if one stream is delayed; nearby surfaces can appear at different pixel locations in different cameras.

[figure: vp-modalities]

Knowledge distillation trains a student using information from a teacher, such as its outputs or representations. A teacher may combine RGB and thermal data through several branches, while a student uses a simpler architecture. The training objective must specify what is matched and which inputs the student receives. **One computational stream does not, by itself, mean one particular sensor modality.**

Consider two possible contracts. Student A receives RGB and is trained toward outputs of an RGB/thermal teacher. Student B receives a pre-fused RGB/thermal input through one branch. Both can be described as simpler students, but only the first eliminates thermal input at deployment. Their missing-information problem is different. Do not infer the deployed sensor contract from a branch count alone.

Changing modality can create new task difficulties, but no universal ranking makes every non-RGB problem harder than every RGB problem. Difficulty depends on signal quality, targets, training coverage and ambiguity. A useful comparison states the exact acquisition/task conditions and evaluates actual outputs, rather than treating “different modality” as a measured disadvantage.

warnings.message: The distillation diagram does not clearly establish which sensor inputs the student receives at deployment. A single computational stream does not prove that thermal input is removed. That input contract remains unspecified.

sections.title: Questions and referring masks
sections.body:
Visual question answering combines an observation with a question and returns an answer. The question determines which information matters. For an image containing three differently colored cups and a red ball, “How many cups?” asks for a count; “What color is the ball?” asks for an attribute; “Which cup is nearest the ball?” asks for a relation. A correct count does not establish a correct relation or localization.

[figure: vp-language]

**Referring segmentation returns a spatial target identified by language.** The phrase can distinguish one instance from others of the same class. “The person holding an umbrella” combines an object category with a relation. “The person in a pink shirt riding a skateboard” combines an attribute with an activity. “The child holding the yellow puppy” requires connecting the child and animal, rather than selecting every child or every yellow region.

A video reference adds persistence. The target can change image position, be briefly occluded, or alter appearance while remaining the same referred entity. Selecting an appropriate mask in one frame is different from maintaining the target through the sequence. A similarly dressed person appearing later should not automatically inherit the reference.

The cup experiment implements exactly three declared queries over known object annotations. For “nearest,” it computes Euclidean distances between 2D centers. It returns ambiguity at equal distances. This restricted rule is useful for understanding the output contract, but it is not a language model, an image recognizer or a general spatial reasoner.

**Work an ambiguous reference:** two cups have the same color, and both are equally close to the ball. What output is justified? The phrase lacks enough information to select one uniquely. A system can request a more specific reference or return multiple candidates. A forced confident mask conceals an ambiguity in the input rather than resolving it.

Some relations require evidence outside a still image. “The person who just picked up the cup” requires temporal context, while “the person left of the cup” requires a stated spatial frame. Question design is part of the task definition.

sections.title: Facial reconstruction, style transfer and video synthesis
sections.body:
Visual generation produces a new image or sequence rather than only assigning labels to an existing observation. Several application names hide different goals. Restoration estimates a cleaner signal. Style transfer changes appearance while attempting to preserve selected content. Avatar retargeting maps observed movement into another geometry. Video generation creates a sequence conditioned on a description or other input.

[figure: vp-synthesis]

Facial reconstruction can estimate landmarks or visible facial motion and use them to animate an avatar. A low-light camera may make those estimates uncertain. The reconstruction target should be the observable geometry or motion. **Reproducing a facial expression is different from establishing a person’s internal emotional state.** The same visible movement can be compatible with different intentions and feelings.

Style transfer separates aspects of content and appearance only under a chosen model or objective. A transformed portrait might preserve pose while changing hair texture or rendering style. It may also alter small identity cues. Saying “content is preserved” requires naming which content properties are intended to remain and checking them. A convincing visual resemblance does not settle every property.

A generated video of a vehicle traveling through a forest introduces temporal requirements. The vehicle should maintain its identity and shape; motion should remain consistent with the scene; newly revealed surfaces should not contradict earlier frames. Frame-level plausibility and sequence-level consistency are different assessments. A video model can produce a convincing trajectory without simulating the underlying physical world accurately.

**Compare outputs:** a road mask describes an observed image; a synthesized road scene invents pixels. A tracked vehicle trajectory estimates observed motion; a generated trajectory constructs one. The outputs can look similar on screen while having different relationships to evidence.

When evaluating generation, inspect what changed, what should remain consistent, and which visible details are unsupported by the conditioning information. Do not turn visual fluency into a claim of measured physical accuracy or unrestricted scene understanding.

warnings.message: “Emotion reconstruction” overstates what the illustrated facial-landmark/avatar pipeline establishes. It reconstructs visible facial geometry or motion; those observations do not uniquely identify an internal emotional state.

sections.title: Human generalization draws on prior experience
sections.body:
People can sometimes recognize a new object category after seeing very few examples. A squirrel in one pose may help identify another squirrel in a different pose. However, **one newly shown example is not the observer’s complete training history.** Prior experience supplies knowledge of animals, bodies, viewpoint changes, language and typical environments.

[figure: vp-human]

The comparison becomes clearer when a query animal resembles several candidates: a squirrel, fox, rabbit, small primate or koala can share color, texture or silhouette. A useful representation must emphasize distinctions relevant to the category while tolerating variations within it. A fur-color match alone may favor an incorrect category; contextual knowledge can help but can also mislead.

A similarity score must have a defined origin. Numbers placed beside selected example images can illustrate a ranking, but without a model, measurement procedure or dataset they are not measured human probabilities or demonstrated machine recognition scores. A useful explanation can instead state the competing cues and why the category remains uncertain.

Human perception also interacts with memory, attention, language and expectations about action. This helps explain why an unfamiliar arrangement can become recognizable after a hint. It does not support a simple claim that every human sees every scene effortlessly, nor that a diagram of brain regions establishes a complete mechanism for recognition.

**Try a fair comparison:** give a person and a model one new labeled example, but also state their earlier experience. Does the model have pretrained visual representations? Does the person already know the category family? Are both asked to identify the same unfamiliar views? Comparing only the final example count hides the role of prior learning.

Few new examples can suffice when prior representations transfer. They may fail when the task needs distinctions those representations cannot resolve.

warnings.message: The one-example recognition illustration omits prior human experience, and its example similarity numbers have no stated measurement procedure. Treat them as illustrative, not measured probabilities or validated machine/human recognition scores.

sections.title: Contours and two-tone grouping
sections.body:
Recognition does not always require photographic texture. A sparse contour can preserve enough shape structure to suggest an animal, even after many local details disappear. The Attneave cat example motivates a question: which locations along a boundary carry useful information about the form?

[figure: vp-contour]

The new cat-like construction keeps a declared sequence of vertices, then simplifies it with a recursive rule. Find the point farthest from the segment joining a sequence’s endpoints. If its distance exceeds the tolerance, split the sequence there and simplify the two parts. Otherwise retain only the endpoints. The retained points concentrate where straight segments poorly approximate the original contour.

This is an explicit geometric compression example, not a learned recognition system or a proof that humans apply this exact algorithm. The output reports a measured distance error against the declared contour. **A small geometric error and successful category recognition are different quantities.** A subtle change near a diagnostic part could matter more for classification than a larger change along an uninformative boundary.

Two-tone face examples emphasize grouping. Dark and light regions can be difficult to interpret locally yet form a face-like structure when considered together. The schematic below constructs eyes, a nose, mouth and shadow as binary regions. It explains the grouping idea associated with Mooney faces without presenting a copied or thresholded original photograph.

[figure: vp-grouping]

**Ask what supplied the interpretation.** Was a single dark patch sufficient, or did the arrangement of several regions matter? Would rotation or a different arrangement change the interpretation even if the same amount of dark area remained? A bag of pixel intensities discards these spatial relationships.

Neither example establishes effortless recognition for every observer or every image. Instead, they show why a representation’s retained structure matters: less data can be enough when the relevant relationships survive, and many pixels can be insufficient when they remain ambiguous.

sections.title: Measured pixels and perceived appearance
sections.body:
A visual system can estimate a property of the world rather than report only the signal at the sensor. Surface appearance depends on illumination and context. Two patches with equal displayed gray values can appear different when one seems to be a light surface in shadow and the other a dark surface in stronger light.

In the checker-shadow experiment, target A and target B have exactly the same sRGB byte value. The construction makes B from a light tile with twice the intensity scale, multiplied by a shadow factor of one half. A is an unshadowed dark tile. The bridge and isolation controls let you compare the targets without changing their values. The [checker-shadow explanation](https://persci.mit.edu/gallery/checkershadow/) is the primary reference for the underlying perceptual example; the interactive diagram is independently rebuilt.

**Equal recorded values and equal perceived surface lightness are different claims.** The experiment verifies the first numerically. Your observation addresses the second for this construction, display and viewing condition. A weak or absent effect for one viewer does not change the equality of the numbers.

The surrounding-size experiment makes a related distinction. Two orange centers initially have the same radius. Large and small surrounding circles can affect apparent relative size. Hiding the context removes that particular cue. Changing the right radius then introduces an actual geometric difference, reported as diameter and area ratio. An appearance judgment should not be confused with the stored dimensions.

The static contrast pattern illustrates apparent movement with no moving coordinates. Some observers perceive motion while shifting their gaze around ordered contrast regions. Others perceive little or none. The pattern contains no animation. Reversing its contrast order creates another static stimulus; it does not rotate the old one. Published [peripheral-drift examples](https://www.psy.ritsumei.ac.jp/akitaoka/rotsnakee.html) motivate this independently generated pattern.

**Do not generalize from an illusion to every machine.** A program comparing gray bytes can return equality. A learned model asked to estimate surface lightness performs a different task. A human’s contextual perception and a computer’s raw measurement should be compared under matching questions before declaring one correct and the other fooled.

visuals.predict: Will isolating the equal checker patches change their stored gray values?
visuals.reflect: Compare measured equality, apparent lightness, actual radius and static coordinates. Distinguish observer responses from computed measurements.

sections.title: Variation, clutter and missing evidence
sections.body:
**Intra-class variation means different appearances within one category.** A car can remain a car across viewpoint, illumination, scale and partial occlusion. Shape itself can vary within a class: cars, people and animals are not identical templates. An octopus adds a particularly vivid example because changes in visible color and body configuration can interact with camouflage.

[figure: vp-variation]

Background clutter introduces competing patterns. A texture that resembles part of an object can create false evidence. Occlusion removes visible structure. Scale changes how many sensor samples cover a feature. At a sufficiently small resolution, a fine-grained distinction may no longer be represented in the observation. A model cannot recover a unique answer merely by becoming more confident.

**Desired invariance depends on the task.** Translating an object within an image should usually preserve its category but change its location. Rotating a vertical stroke into a horizontal one should change the orientation label. Changing illumination may preserve an object identity while changing the recorded color. Augmentation must preserve the intended target or update it appropriately.

The classifier exercise later uses an 8×8 stroke example. Moving a stroke among permitted positions preserves its orientation. Changing its border brightness preserves its declared orientation. Rotating it by a quarter turn would change its label. These statements are explicit because the data are constructed; real applications need equally careful target conventions.

**Separate difficulty from impossibility.** A partially hidden animal can remain recognizable from visible diagnostic features. If all relevant evidence is hidden and several categories fit equally well, the observation is underdetermined. Context may supply a prior preference, but it does not reveal the hidden pixels as a measurement.

When asking why recognition is hard, name the transformation or ambiguity. “Machines find vision difficult” is too broad to guide a method or evaluation. “This task must distinguish two categories despite changing pose, while the diagnostic region is often occluded” describes a concrete requirement.

sections.title: Similar species expose subtle distinctions
sections.body:
Fine-grained recognition distinguishes categories that share much of their overall appearance. Tennessee Warblers and Orange-crowned Warblers provide a visual example: both are small birds whose photographs can share a broadly similar shape and color range. Identifying a generic bird can be easier than identifying its species under an unfamiliar pose or acquisition condition.

[figure: vp-birds]

The two photographs are real examples with documented reusable licenses. They also differ in background, viewpoint and illumination. **A model should not learn that the branch, framing or camera color balance defines the species.** Those correlations could be strong in a small training set while failing on another photographer’s images.

A useful comparison asks which visible regions contain potentially discriminative evidence, whether those regions are well resolved, and how much variation occurs within each species. A feature visible in one selected individual need not be present with the same appearance in every age, season or pose. A two-photo comparison therefore illustrates the task, rather than validating a species classifier or giving a complete identification key.

Bounding boxes can focus attention on the bird while still including much background. A segmentation mask can reduce some background influence but may remove useful context or introduce its own errors. A part-oriented representation can emphasize the head or another region, yet depends on locating that part accurately. These are choices with costs, not automatic solutions.

**Design a split:** if all Tennessee examples come from one photographer and all Orange-crowned examples from another, what can image-level random splitting fail to detect? The model can learn acquisition cues that persist in both halves. Holding out acquisition sources and collecting overlapping conditions can test whether the intended distinction transfers.

Fine-grained recognition links representation and data design. The smaller the relevant visual differences, the more carefully the observation quality, labeling and nuisance correlations need to be assessed.

sections.title: Generalization and misleading visual shortcuts
sections.body:
Generalization asks how a fitted system behaves on observations beyond those that supplied its parameter updates. Distribution shift changes the conditions under which the system is used. A road model trained in sunny conditions may encounter snow, altered contrast, new scene layouts or different cameras. The class names can stay the same while the available evidence and correlations change.

[figure: vp-evaluation]

The numerical exercise makes one shift fully inspectable. Each 8×8 image contains a vertical or horizontal stroke. In domain A, border brightness correlates perfectly with orientation. Domain B reverses that correlation. A four-parameter logistic classifier receives two interior contrast features, a normalized border feature and a bias. It can use the border as a shortcut even though border brightness does not define the intended orientation label.

**Fit A, then inspect B.** At the default rate, 300 full-batch updates give perfect accuracy on A and zero accuracy on B in this constructed example. The coefficient table explains the result: the border term dominates the current logits. These are actual computed outcomes for the listed data and settings, not claimed performance of a real vision benchmark.

Selecting Both backgrounds resets the model and averages all sixteen A/B observations during fitting. Because border brightness no longer predicts the label consistently, stroke contrasts can determine the solution. Compare the resulting coefficients and both-domain errors. This intervention changes the evidence supplied during training; it does not insert a handwritten correct answer into the predictor.

Keep evaluation observations separate from gradient updates. Adjacent video frames often share nearly the same scene, so random frame splitting can put closely related observations on both sides. A recording-session split reduces that particular leakage. It does not guarantee coverage of every new place or condition.

**A vision model does make assumptions.** Its representation, architecture, preprocessing, objective and training distribution all restrict what it can learn. Reporting raw pixel equality is one simple computational task; learned recognition is not an assumption-free extension of that measurement.

visuals.predict: Can a perfectly predictive training border be the wrong rule for orientation under a new acquisition condition?
visuals.reflect: Train A and reverse the border. Inspect exact contributions and both-domain errors, then fit balanced backgrounds from reset.

warnings.message: “Computers don’t assume” is incorrect for learned vision. Representations, architectures, preprocessing, objectives and training data all introduce assumptions. Reading an intensity value and estimating a scene property are different tasks.

sections.title: Scene reasoning and the role of expectations
sections.body:
Recognizing objects does not settle every question about a scene. Interpreting an interaction, a surprising arrangement or a humorous situation can depend on relationships, prior knowledge and expectations. A list of detected people and objects may omit the very relation that makes the scene meaningful.

[figure: vp-context]

Consider an unusually tall figure approaching a standard-height doorway. The visible geometry supports a height mismatch. Knowledge of how doorways are normally used supports an expectation that a person can walk through while upright. An observer may interpret the mismatch as surprising or humorous, but the photograph alone does not establish the person’s intention, what happened before, or every observer’s reaction.

**Separate observation from interpretation.** “The figure is taller than the opening” can be tied to geometry under appropriate perspective information. “The person will crouch” is a prediction about action. “The person intended a joke” is a claim about intent requiring different evidence. Combining these into one confident label conceals which part is directly supported.

Language can help express a relation, but a fluent description is not proof that the relation was inferred from the image. A model may rely on a frequent textual association or on a scene cue unrelated to the requested judgment. An evaluation should include alternative scenes that break those correlations.

**Work a counterexample:** show the same object identities in a different arrangement that removes the doorway mismatch. A detector’s object list can remain unchanged while the interpretation changes. This reveals information that object presence alone does not contain. Similarly, the same facial configuration in two different contexts can support different interpretations without changing a smile classifier’s output.

Context is useful evidence, but it can also bias a conclusion. A careful system states what it observed, which assumptions connect that observation to an interpretation, and where competing explanations remain possible.

sections.title: Aggregate accuracy can conceal uneven errors
sections.body:
A vision system can have the same overall accuracy under two designs while distributing its errors differently. Acquisition conditions, visibility, object scale or representation quality can make some subsets perform worse. In applications involving people, data coverage and consequences can also vary among relevant population groups. **A pooled metric does not reveal these differences.**

The A/B classifier provides a deliberately simple numerical illustration. After correlated-A fitting, its balanced combined accuracy is 50%, yet that total combines 100% on A and 0% on B. The two subsets here are synthetic acquisition domains, not demographic groups. They demonstrate the arithmetic of concealed uneven performance without claiming a measured fairness result about people.

Inspect the confusion matrix rather than only its diagonal total. For a two-class task, false positives and false negatives have different meanings. A system detecting an event can miss true events or flag events that did not occur. The consequences depend on how those outputs are used. Equal accuracy can coexist with different error types, sample prevalence or uncertainty.

A meaningful assessment states the groups or conditions, the task, the denominator and the relevant error measures. Small subsets can give unstable estimates, and missing categories cannot be assessed by a metric on observed data. Reporting several values does not eliminate the need to understand who or what the data represent.

**Work the comparison:** one domain has four vertical and four horizontal examples. Suppose all vertical examples are correct and all horizontal examples wrong. Another domain has the reverse pattern. Both have 50% accuracy, but their class-specific errors differ. Would equal accuracy alone establish equivalent behavior for an application concerned primarily with missed horizontal patterns?

Fairness is not reducible to one universal instruction that every group and situation must have exactly the same accuracy. It requires a stated application and criteria, evidence about error patterns, and attention to the outcomes supported by the system.

warnings.message: Equal accuracy across groups or situations is not a complete or universal definition of fairness. Equal totals can conceal different error types, prevalence, coverage and consequences; the application and relevant criteria must be stated.

sections.title: Explain a computation and test a dependence
sections.body:
Interpretability asks what a representation or computation means. Explainability asks for information that helps account for a result or behavior. A large network’s parameter count can make direct inspection difficult, but a small explicit model offers a useful starting point for separating different explanation claims.

In the stroke classifier, the logit is $z=\sum_j w_jx_j$ and the horizontal-class probability is $p=1/(1+\exp(-z))$. The table lists every feature, fitted coefficient and product. Their sum is exactly the displayed logit. **This is an exact decomposition of this model’s score, not a post-hoc visualization claimed to expose a different model.**

A contribution is not the same thing as sensitivity. A feature with current value zero has zero current product even if its coefficient is large and a change would matter. A large current product can also be offset by another term. To assess a dependence, intervene on a declared input, recompute the features and inspect the changed prediction.

Change only border brightness while retaining the same stroke. If the prediction changes substantially, the model depends on that border intervention under the stated example. Change occlusion and observe that interior contrast features can change together. The latter intervention is not an independent edit of one feature, because all features are calculated from the same pixels.

**A transparent wrong rule remains wrong.** Seeing the border contribution explains why the correlated model fails on B; it does not make that dependence acceptable for an orientation task. Likewise, an attractive attention or heat map in a larger system does not by itself establish causal faithfulness, reliability or a complete explanation.

Use an explanation to form a testable hypothesis. “The model follows the border” leads to a controlled border reversal and independent domain evaluation. Then distinguish the measured finding from broader claims: the test demonstrates one dependence in this example, not every behavior on every possible image.

sections.title: Continual learning and forgetting
sections.body:
A deployed vision problem can change as new scenes, sensors or tasks arrive. Continual learning studies how a model can learn from new experience while retaining useful previous capabilities. A fixed offline model is one baseline; periodically retraining from a collected dataset is another. Continual updating introduces a particular challenge: new gradients can change parameters that earlier behavior depended on.

**Catastrophic forgetting is a loss of previous performance during learning of new experience.** It should be measured on old tasks or conditions after the updates, rather than inferred merely from the fact that parameters changed. Improvement on new data and retention on old data are separate evaluation curves.

The experiment reuses the same four-parameter stroke classifier and A/B observations. First fit A for 300 updates. Then fit B without replay. At the default settings, B reaches perfect accuracy while A falls to zero. This is actual measured forgetting in the declared example. The target labels remain compatible: the border correlation changes, while vertical/horizontal orientation retains its meaning.

Replay includes old observations in the new objective. With replay weight $r$, the B-phase objective is $J=(1-r)J_B+rJ_A$. At $r=0$, only B supplies gradients. At $r=0.5$, both domains have equal loss weight. Here the model has features capable of representing the shared orientation rule, so balanced replay can fit both conditions. The numerical curves show what actually happens after every update.

**Replay is a method with a resource and objective contract.** This example retains all old synthetic observations; its weight is a loss coefficient, not a measured memory size. Larger systems may retain only selected data or representations and may face incompatible tasks or insufficient capacity. A successful tiny example does not guarantee universal retention.

Compare the two runs from the same reset. Record old/new losses as well as accuracy. Explain why a model can remain correct while its margins or loss change before a later error appears. The history makes gradual parameter effects visible rather than reporting only the final category choices.

visuals.predict: Will an update optimized only for B necessarily retain A performance?
visuals.reflect: Compare actual old/new losses after sequential fitting and after explicit replay. Explain the weighted gradient and the fixture’s representational capacity.

sections.title: Observe, map, plan, act, observe again
sections.body:
Navigation uses vision or another sensor to support action in a changing world. A useful loop separates observation, mapping, planning and execution. The next observation arrives after movement, so it can reveal something different from the previous one. **A plan is conditional on the current state estimate and map, not a guarantee that the scene will remain unchanged.**

[figure: vp-loop]

The simulation uses a declared six-by-six world and a supplied toy occupancy sensor. The agent begins at (1,4) and seeks (4,1). Its map distinguishes unknown, observed-free and wall cells. The reader can see the ground-truth world separately, while planning uses only the agent’s map. This makes the information boundary inspectable without pretending to run image recognition.

Observe reveals the current cell and cardinal rays up to the selected range, stopping at walls. Plan uses breadth-first search with a fixed neighbor order to find a shortest route under the map policy. Act executes one step only if the next cell has been observed free, then the loop repeats. Unknown traversable can plan through unexplored cells; Known free only can fail to find a goal route while unexplored space remains.

Turn on the new-obstacle option. After the first movement, a wall appears at (3,4). The next observation must update the map before the agent relies on the old route. A stale representation can be incorrect even when it was accurate when first built. Replanning is therefore part of the task, not an admission that a single correct perception should have been sufficient forever.

**Trace one cycle manually.** Which cells are known? Which planned steps pass through unknown space? Which step is actually executed? What new information becomes visible from the next pose? The bounded run automates these same computations and records recent events.

This prototype uses deterministic sensing and classical search rather than learned perception or a learned control policy. It demonstrates the closed-loop structure relevant to embodied vision while keeping each computation and omitted component explicit.

visuals.predict: Can the agent plan a goal route while some cells remain unknown, and does that make the route guaranteed clear?
visuals.reflect: Advance Observe, Plan and Act separately. Insert a wall, inspect stale versus updated maps, and explain the actual executed route.

sections.title: Choose a system by the information it must preserve
sections.body:
The chapter’s tasks connect through a common design question: **what information must survive each transformation for the final output to be justified?** A scene category can discard precise boundaries. A segmentation mask cannot. A tracked event needs identity and time. A measured reconstruction needs geometric evidence. A generated scene can add appearance but cannot retroactively make hidden regions measured.

Start with an output contract. For a road/non-road map, specify pixel labels and a spatial evaluation. For a plate string, include the localization and reading pipeline. For a referred object, state how language resolves the instance and what happens when it is ambiguous. For navigation, connect uncertain observations with a map, action and updated observation.

Then name the required variation. Which viewpoints, illumination conditions, scales, occlusions and sensors are expected? Which should preserve the label, and which should change it? The answer determines sensible data collection, augmentation and evaluation. A representation cannot be judged without knowing what it is expected to keep or discard.

Evaluate more than selected demonstrations. Separate correlated recordings when appropriate, hold out relevant conditions and inspect errors by class or condition. A model that performs well in one domain may be following a shortcut. Explain its dependence with controlled interventions where possible, then evaluate the intended behavior on independent evidence.

Finally consider change and action. Will new data overwrite older behavior? Which previous cases remain available for replay or evaluation? Does a command change the next observation? Can the system distinguish a stale map from the present environment? These questions connect recognition with continual and embodied learning.

**Work a final design exercise:** propose a system that identifies a requested cup and guides an agent toward it. Describe the observed signals, referring-mask output, geometric assumptions, uncertainty policy, data split, shift test, explanation test, retained old-domain evaluation and observe–plan–act loop. Keep each claim tied to a component that actually supplies the needed information. That discipline turns a list of impressive applications into a coherent and testable vision system.

questions.prompt: Which statement requires a spatial output rather than only a scene class?
choices: This is a university entrance.
The tree occupies this image region.
The image belongs to the entrance category.
questions.why: A region requires localization or a mask; an image class does not retain that location.

questions.prompt: What should be fixed before choosing a vision architecture?
choices: The observation, required output and evaluation contract.
The newest product name.
A claim of general image understanding.
questions.why: A task contract determines the evidence and representation that need to be preserved.

questions.prompt: Why is a strong image edge not automatically an object boundary?
choices: All objects have the same intensity.
A shadow or texture change can create an edge inside one object.
Edges cannot be calculated.
questions.why: An intensity change is a measurement, while an object boundary is a scene interpretation.

questions.prompt: Which architecture is identified by the 32×32 digit input and classic convolution/subsampling chain?
choices: AlexNet 2012.
CLIP.
LeNet-5.
questions.why: This is the earlier LeNet-5 architecture, not the AlexNet ImageNet network.

questions.prompt: Which pair names one project rather than two independent methods?
choices: SAM and Segment Anything.
ViT and CLIP.
CLIP and DINO.
questions.why: SAM abbreviates Segment Anything; the other pairs have different objectives/interfaces.

questions.prompt: Why does recognizing a cup not by itself specify a robot action?
choices: Recognition prevents geometric reasoning.
An action also requires state, command conventions and consequences.
All cup labels encode stable grasps.
questions.why: Category identity does not supply the full reachable geometry or execution state.

questions.prompt: You need a road/non-road label for every pixel. Which task fits?
choices: Image classification
Semantic segmentation
Text retrieval
questions.why: The output is a spatial class map, not a single image label or bounding boxes.

questions.prompt: Three touching cups share one semantic class label. What additional information separates them?
choices: A brighter color palette.
A single image class.
Distinct instance identities and masks.
questions.why: Semantic labels name categories; instance segmentation preserves individual object identity.

questions.prompt: A plate reader is accurate on supplied clean crops. Which claim remains untested?
choices: Its ability to locate plates in full road images.
Its output character alphabet.
Its ability to read those supplied crops.
questions.why: Clean-crop evaluation supplies localization rather than testing it.

questions.prompt: A comparison with one claimed enrolled identity is which task?
choices: Verification.
Open-set identification among many enrolled identities.
Smile detection.
questions.why: Verification is a one-to-one matching question; identification and attributes use other output contracts.

questions.prompt: Does a visible smile label establish an internal emotional state?
choices: Yes, for every person.
Only if the face box is accurate.
No; it describes a visible configuration under a convention.
questions.why: Internal state is not uniquely determined by the visible expression.

questions.prompt: Correct boxes reappear after an occlusion. What can still be wrong?
choices: The boxes must have no pixels.
Their association with earlier tracked identities.
Every scene category must change.
questions.why: Framewise localization and temporal identity association are separate outputs.

questions.prompt: What does one hand–item overlap fail to distinguish?
choices: Pickup from return or passing an item.
The fact that two regions overlap in that image.
Their declared pixel coordinates.
questions.why: An event requires temporal and relational evidence beyond one overlap.

questions.prompt: Why does a virtual object at a fixed pixel coordinate fail to remain attached to a physical surface?
choices: The display has too many pixels.
The surface has no category.
Camera/user movement changes its projection.
questions.why: Registration needs spatial transformations updated as the viewpoint changes.

questions.prompt: For parallel stereo, f=120 pixels, B=1 and Z=6. What is disparity?
choices: 720 pixels.
20 pixels.
0.05 pixels.
questions.why: d=fB/Z=120×1/6=20 pixels under the declared parallel-camera model.

questions.prompt: Why must a homogeneous camera projection be normalized?
choices: Its scale is arbitrary; ordinary image coordinates require division by the final coordinate.
It is an image classification score.
Every world point has depth one.
questions.why: P times the world vector produces homogeneous coordinates, not already normalized pixel coordinates.

questions.prompt: Which result establishes relevance without necessarily establishing shared recording origin?
choices: A byte-identical file comparison.
An exact same-file identifier.
A nearby semantic embedding.
questions.why: Semantic similarity can intentionally group different recordings with related content.

questions.prompt: Which distinction is essential when interpreting hardware claims?
choices: FLOPs are an operation count; FLOP/s is a rate under a defined workload.
FLOPs always mean latency in seconds.
Precision never matters.
questions.why: Count, rate, numerical precision and benchmark conditions are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A requested viewpoint reveals a surface hidden in every source view. What is justified?
choices: The hidden surface was necessarily measured.
A plausible synthesized completion may be possible, but it is not measured evidence.
Two cameras always resolve every hidden surface.
questions.why: Unobserved appearance needs additional assumptions; plausible generation does not create measurement.

questions.prompt: With matched transmission t=0.1, how large is recovered error from additive observation noise 0.01?
questions.why: The matched inversion amplifies additive error by 1/t: 0.01/0.1=0.1.

questions.prompt: What happens at t=0 in I=tJ+(1−t)A?
choices: I is independent of J, so unique inversion is impossible from I alone.
J is recovered without any noise.
Every scene has J=A.
questions.why: The scene contribution vanishes; a prior completion is different from a unique inverse.

questions.prompt: A distilled student has one branch. What cannot be inferred from that alone?
choices: Its branch count.
Whether it still receives thermal input.
That it is a student in the declared setup.
questions.why: A single branch can receive a single modality or fused multimodal data; the input contract must be stated.

questions.prompt: Two cups are equally near the ball under the declared 2D distance rule. What should the referring result report?
choices: A randomly confident unique answer.
That the image has no cups.
Multiple tied candidates or ambiguity.
questions.why: The given reference and relation do not uniquely identify one instance.

questions.prompt: Which reference requires temporal evidence?
choices: The person who just picked up the cup.
The yellow cup.
The ball at a stated pixel position.
questions.why: “Just picked up” describes an event across time rather than a static attribute.

questions.prompt: Why is a plausible generated driving video not proof of accurate physics?
choices: Generated frames cannot have temporal structure.
Visual plausibility and measured physical consistency are different assessments.
A forest has no geometry.
questions.why: Generation can look convincing while violating motion, geometry or other physical constraints.

questions.prompt: What is missing from “the person learned it from one example”?
choices: The displayed example count.
The new task name.
The person’s extensive prior visual and conceptual experience.
questions.why: One new example can adapt prior representations rather than create them from scratch.

questions.prompt: What does a contour-simplification distance bound establish?
choices: A stated geometric approximation, rather than guaranteed category recognition.
That every observer recognizes the category.
That the original cat pixels were copied.
questions.why: Geometric error and recognition behavior are separate quantities.

questions.prompt: In the checker experiment, hiding context changes appearance but leaves which quantity equal?
choices: Every viewer’s lightness judgment.
The two target sRGB byte values.
All board tiles.
questions.why: Both target values remain exactly g even when their context changes.

questions.prompt: Apparent motion in the contrast experiment implies what about its SVG coordinates?
choices: They rotate automatically.
They must be animated.
Nothing changes: the pattern has no animation or frame updates.
questions.why: A perceptual impression of motion is distinct from changing the displayed geometry.

questions.prompt: What is intra-class variation?
choices: Different appearances of the same class.
The number of model layers.
The gap between training and validation set sizes.
questions.why: Lighting, pose, occlusion, and viewpoint can change appearance without changing the category.

questions.prompt: Which augmentation changes the intended label in the stroke fixture?
choices: Changing border brightness.
Rotating a vertical stroke by a quarter turn.
Moving a vertical stroke between permitted columns.
questions.why: Orientation is the target, so a quarter-turn changes vertical to horizontal.

questions.prompt: All examples of one species come from one photographer. What can a random image split conceal?
choices: The fact that there are species labels.
The need for any pixels.
A shortcut based on acquisition conditions rather than species.
questions.why: Photographer-specific backgrounds or color processing can persist across both halves.

questions.prompt: Why split video data by recording session?
choices: To guarantee perfect accuracy.
To make training slower.
To reduce leakage from nearly identical frames.
questions.why: Adjacent frames in both splits can overstate performance on genuinely new scenes.

questions.prompt: After default correlated-A fitting, A accuracy is 100% and B is 0%. What explains the failure?
choices: A learned border shortcut reverses its correlation in B.
B has different target category meanings.
The query secretly supplies gradients.
questions.why: The label stays orientation; the fitted border dependence is wrong under the new condition.

questions.prompt: An object list remains unchanged when a scene’s arrangement changes. What can still change?
choices: The object labels must disappear.
The contextual interpretation or relation.
The image must become byte-identical.
questions.why: Relations and expectations contain information beyond object presence.

questions.prompt: Two domains each have 50% accuracy. What remains possible?
choices: They have identical error types necessarily.
They contain no incorrect decisions.
Their class-specific errors are opposite.
questions.why: Equal aggregate accuracy can conceal different false-positive/false-negative patterns.

questions.prompt: A feature is zero and its fitted coefficient is large. What is its current logit contribution?
choices: Zero, though a feature change could matter.
Automatically the largest contribution.
Equal to the probability.
questions.why: The current term is w×x=0; sensitivity and current contribution differ.

questions.prompt: What does an exact score decomposition establish?
choices: Reliability on every future image.
The arithmetic of this model’s current score, which can still be wrong.
That all contributions are causal claims about the world.
questions.why: Transparent computation does not by itself validate the learned rule.

questions.prompt: At replay r=0.5, what is the B-phase objective?
choices: J_B only.
J_A only.
questions.why: Both old/new domains contribute equally to the explicitly weighted objective.

questions.prompt: How should forgetting be measured?
choices: Evaluate old performance after new updates, alongside new performance.
Assume every parameter change is forgetting.
Report only the new training loss.
questions.why: Parameter change alone does not establish performance loss on earlier conditions.

questions.prompt: Why does the navigation simulation observe again after moving?
choices: The old image is guaranteed complete forever.
New pose and world changes can alter available evidence and the map.
BFS can only run once.
questions.why: The next observation updates a partial or stale representation before replanning.

questions.prompt: Which design description best supports a reviewable vision claim?
choices: A list of impressive product names.
One selected output image.
Inputs, outputs, assumptions, independent error evidence and stated limits.
questions.why: A concrete information/evaluation contract identifies which component supports each claim.

title: Computer Vision — Part 2
summary: Pixel arithmetic, color and texture features, real SVM/CNN fitting, metrics, box refinement and original detection pipelines.

sections.title: An image is a spatial array
sections.body:
**An image is already numerical data.** A digital grayscale image stores an intensity at each sampled location. An RGB image stores three components per location. A model receives a particular tensor representation of those measurements; converting a visible picture into a usable input means decoding and arranging its stored samples, not discovering that the picture has numbers for the first time.

For an image with R rows and C columns, use $I[r,c]$ with $0\le r<R$ and $0\le c<C$. Geometric coordinates often use x horizontally and y vertically, while array access places the row first. Thus, the point (x=3, y=2) corresponds to array entry [2][3] under this convention. Mixing the two can select the wrong sample or transpose an image unintentionally.

An unsigned eight-bit channel has integer values from 0 to 255. Other representations use larger integer ranges, floating-point intensities, normalized values or signed feature responses. **The numeric type and value convention are part of the input contract.** A value of 1 can mean a dim byte intensity or the maximum of a normalized channel, depending on that contract.

[figure: vc-array]

The first experiment uses a declared four-by-four array. Select a row and column and edit its actual intensity. Mean, variance and histogram counts all update from the stored samples. Switch to RGB and inspect how three channel values combine into one displayed color. A channel statistic is not an unspecified statistic of the whole color image.

Transpose the current array. The arrangement changes, but the same samples remain. This intervention already shows a central distinction: an image’s values and their spatial relationships are separate information. Many later representations deliberately discard some of those relationships. Understanding what was discarded helps explain what a classifier can and cannot recover.

visuals.predict: Will transposing the current array change its intensity histogram?
visuals.reflect: Compare actual channel values, mean and variance before/after spatial rearrangement and edits.

sections.title: Mean, variance and standard deviation
sections.body:
The mean of a grayscale image is one number describing its average intensity. For N samples, $\mu=\sum_i I_i/N$. It does not specify where bright or dark regions occur. A uniformly medium image and a spatial mixture of dark and bright regions can have the same mean.

Population variance measures squared deviations from that image’s mean: $\sigma^2=\sum_i(I_i-\mu)^2/N$. Standard deviation is $\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}$. Variance has squared intensity units; standard deviation has the original intensity units. For the complete image array, division by N describes the population of its samples. The N−1 sample estimator answers a different statistical question and should not silently replace this formula.

[figure: vc-statistics]

Consider the declared intensities 0,0,8,8. Their mean is 4. Every squared deviation is 16, so variance is 16 and standard deviation is 4. The uniform array 4,4,4,4 has the same mean but zero variance. This distinguishes average brightness from intensity spread without needing a photograph or an opaque plotting tool.

**Statistics do not preserve shape.** Permuting the pixels leaves these quantities unchanged. If an object’s identity depends on the arrangement of its boundaries, neither mean nor variance alone provides enough information. A high variance can arise from an object edge, a patterned texture or unwanted noise; it does not label the cause.

For color images, state which channel is measured or which scalar conversion is used. Computing the mean of R, G and B independently preserves three summaries; averaging all channels together creates another statistic. The small experiment uses explicitly named channels so that these choices remain visible.

sections.title: A histogram counts values and loses location
sections.body:
An intensity histogram counts how many image samples have each value. For eight-bit grayscale, a full histogram has 256 possible bins. The count at bin i is $H(i)=|\{(r,c):I[r,c]=i\}|$. The sum of all counts is the number of pixels. A normalized histogram divides by that total so its entries sum to one.

[figure: vc-histogram]

A histogram reveals more about intensity distribution than a mean alone. It can show concentrations at dark or bright values, several peaks, or a broad spread. Mean and variance can be calculated from the histogram because they depend on values and counts rather than positions. The reverse is not possible: two summary numbers cannot uniquely reconstruct all bin counts.

**A histogram deliberately discards spatial arrangement.** Four dark pixels in a contiguous square and four scattered dark pixels can contribute the same counts. Transposing or shuffling complete pixels preserves each channel histogram. A classifier given only that representation cannot recover the original positions uniquely.

Bin width is a modeling choice. Grouping several intensities into a bin gives a shorter descriptor and tolerates some numeric changes, but loses distinctions within the bin. A narrow bin can preserve a subtle change while being sensitive to noise or acquisition differences. The representation’s intended invariances and task should guide the choice.

Work a limitation: two images have identical grayscale histograms, but one forms a vertical stripe and the other a horizontal stripe. Can a classifier that receives only the global histogram distinguish them reliably? The input features are identical. A more powerful decision rule cannot recreate information absent from its input. Spatial or local-pattern measurements are needed for that distinction.

sections.title: A filter samples a neighborhood
sections.body:
A linear image filter combines nearby samples with kernel coefficients. Let a centered three-by-three kernel have offsets u,v in {−1,0,1}. Under **strict convolution**, the output at (r,c) is $G[r,c]=\sum_u\sum_v h[u,v]I[r-u,c-v]$. The minus signs determine which input positions a displayed coefficient multiplies.

[figure: vc-orientation]

Cross-correlation uses $I[r+u,c+v]$ instead. Equivalently, strict convolution flips the displayed kernel in both axes before applying the usual local dot product. A symmetric kernel gives the same result under both conventions; an asymmetric shift or derivative kernel can produce a different direction or sign.
