Many neural-network libraries call their correlation operation “convolution.” The [OpenCV filtering documentation](https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d4/d86/group__imgproc__filter.html) explicitly distinguishes its unflipped filtering operation from strict convolution.

The filter experiment lists every kernel offset, actual input coordinate, sampled value, weight and product at a selected output center. Summing those products gives the displayed raw response. This makes the operation inspectable rather than relying on a blurred image as proof that the convention was correct.

Boundary behavior is another part of the definition. Valid filtering returns only centers whose complete neighborhoods fit. Zero padding supplies zero outside the image. Replication repeats the nearest border sample. These policies can produce different values near an edge while agreeing in the interior.

An odd-sized kernel has a natural central sample; for side length n its integer radius is (n−1)/2. Even-sized kernels are also possible with a stated anchor convention. A kernel’s size, anchor, direction, stride and boundary policy all matter. **Do not infer them from the word “filter” alone.**

warnings.message: Odd kernel sizes provide a convenient central sample, but they are not mandatory. For odd side length n, the integer radius is (n−1)/2, not n/2. Even-sized kernels require an explicit anchor convention.

sections.title: A one-entry kernel exposes direction
sections.body:
A shift kernel has one coefficient equal to one and all others zero. It selects one neighbor rather than averaging several. Put that one in the displayed top-left corner of a centered three-by-three kernel. Its offset is (−1,−1).

[figure: vc-shift]

Under strict convolution, $G[r,c]=I[r+1, c+1]$. The output at a location copies a sample one row down and one column right. Equivalently, a visible feature moves one row up and one column left in the output. Under correlation, $G[r,c]=I[r-1, c-1]$, so the feature moves in the opposite direction. Describing which source value is sampled and which way a feature appears to move avoids a common sign confusion.

The shift experiment is deliberately numerical. Switch the filter to Shift, retain the selected output center, and compare the two kernel conventions. The sampled coordinate changes even though the displayed kernel does not. Mean3 cannot expose this distinction because it is symmetric.

A shift also interacts with boundaries. A feature leaving the output frame is not necessarily deleted from the mathematical infinite-domain signal; it lies outside the chosen finite array. Zero padding can introduce a dark border, while replication can extend an edge value. Valid filtering reduces the returned domain instead.

**Work the coordinate check:** a bright sample lies at input [4][5]. Under this strict-convolution top-left shift, which output location receives it? Set r+1=4 and c+1=5, giving output [3][4], if that output lies within the selected domain. The coordinate calculation provides evidence independent of how the displayed image happens to look.

sections.title: Reproduce the averaging example exactly
sections.body:
A three-by-three mean filter places 1/9 at every kernel position. The output is the sum of nine sampled values divided by nine. A constant interior patch of value 9 therefore returns 9; it does not return 1 or 81. The kernel’s coefficients sum to one, which preserves constants wherever the boundary policy supplies a constant neighborhood.

The original numeric example is a ten-by-ten array. A four-row, five-column block contains 90s, with a zero at [4][4]; one additional 90 lies at [8][2]. All other entries are zero. Valid three-by-three filtering returns eight-by-eight outputs, corresponding to original centers [1…8][1…8]. The interactive implementation retains these exact values.

[figure: vc-mean]

At center [1][2], the neighborhood contains one 90 and eight zeros, so the result is 10. At a complete all-90 neighborhood it is 90. Near the central hole, one missing 90 can lower a nine-sample average from 90 to 80. These values follow from neighborhood membership, not a visual impression of a smooth region.

The isolated sample at [8][2] contributes to centers whose rows and columns differ from it by at most one. Within the valid domain, it produces 10 at [7][1], [7][2], [7][3], [8][1], [8][2] and [8][3]. It contributes nothing at [7][4] or [8][4]. The calculated matrix corrects those two inconsistent entries.

**Trace before editing:** identify every sample used at one output center, then change the isolated 90. Which outputs should change? A local filter has a limited dependency neighborhood. The full output recomputation and product table let you verify that prediction without assuming an animation is accurate.

visuals.predict: Which input location will a top-left shift coefficient sample under strict convolution?
visuals.reflect: Trace exact coordinates/products. Compare orientation and boundaries, inspect the corrected mean matrix and assess smoothing/detail loss.

warnings.message: The averaging matrix gives 10 at centers [7][4] and [8][4], but their neighborhoods contain only zeros. The isolated 90 is at [8][2], two columns away. Both entries should be 0 under the stated three-by-three mean filter.

sections.title: Smoothing trades noise reduction for detail
sections.body:
A mean filter spreads influence over a neighborhood. This can reduce some rapidly varying noise because nearby samples are averaged. It also averages genuine fine structures. A larger kernel uses more samples, so the relationship between smoothing and retained detail changes.

[figure: vc-smoothing]

Compare Mean3 and Mean21 on the added noisy structure. It is a fully specified 24×24 image containing narrow repeated regions and deterministic intensity fluctuations. The three-by-three result retains more local variation. The twenty-one-by-twenty-one result averages over much broader regions. Under Valid, that large kernel leaves only four-by-four output centers; under padding, the output can keep the original spatial dimensions but the boundary assumptions become influential.

**Reduced variance is not sufficient evidence of better task performance.** A blurred image can have a more concentrated histogram while losing a small object or boundary needed for recognition. Whether smoothing helps depends on the signal, noise and output contract. Preserving a global average is different from preserving the location of a thin line.

Boundary policy also affects constant preservation. Replication keeps a constant image constant under a unit-sum mean kernel. Zero padding lowers the average at border neighborhoods because some samples become zero. Valid avoids invented border samples by excluding those centers.

Work a small case: an image contains one bright pixel on a dark background. Averaging creates a wider, dimmer response. The bright pixel’s information is distributed, and local maxima decrease. If a later decision depends on detecting a tiny isolated object above a threshold, stronger smoothing can make it harder even while suppressing noise elsewhere.

The displayed synthetic comparison is calculated from its stated array; it is not a recreated benchmark claim about the original smoothing photographs.

sections.title: Sobel responses measure directional change
sections.body:
Sobel filters combine a difference along one direction with smoothing across the perpendicular direction. A common horizontal response kernel is [−1,0,1; −2,0,2; −1,0,1]. It emphasizes left-to-right changes while weighting the middle row more strongly. The corresponding vertical kernel is [−1,−2,−1; 0,0,0; 1,2,1].

[figure: vc-sobel]

These displayed kernels produce the named signs under correlation. Applying strict convolution flips them, reversing response signs. For an interior row ramp that increases toward the right, the horizontal correlation response is positive. A constant neighborhood gives zero because the coefficients sum to zero. Direction and sign conventions should be stated before interpreting an edge response.

A gradient magnitude can combine the two responses as $\sqrt{G_x^2+G_y^2}$. Flipping both signs leaves that magnitude unchanged, but changes a directional interpretation. Therefore, a plausible edge-magnitude image cannot verify that the signed conventions were implemented correctly.

**A derivative response is not a byte intensity.** It can be negative or exceed 255. The experiment keeps raw signed values and reports the display normalization separately. Mapping a current minimum to black and maximum to white helps inspect structure, but two separately normalized maps cannot be compared as if brightness were an identical response scale.

Sobel’s neighbor weighting can moderate some noise compared with a simple two-sample difference. It is not a universal denoiser, and a sharp unwanted fluctuation can still create a strong response. Likewise, a response can come from texture or shadow rather than an object boundary.

Try SobelX and SobelY on the same declared input, then change only the operation convention. Explain which signs change, which magnitudes remain, and what the selected response says about local samples rather than object identity.

warnings.message: The displayed Sobel kernels have the named derivative signs under correlation. Applying the earlier strict-convolution formula reverses those signs. Kernel orientation must be specified before interpreting a signed response.

sections.title: RGB channels are separate measurements
sections.body:
An RGB image stores a red, green and blue component at each spatial location. Each channel is a two-dimensional array, and combining corresponding samples yields the displayed color. A single pixel can be represented by a triple such as (220,40,30), while an input tensor also needs an explicit channel order and spatial arrangement.

[figure: vc-rgb]

Channel-first storage might have shape 3×H×W; channel-last storage might have H×W×3. Both can represent the same image, but a model or operation expecting one layout cannot safely consume the other without rearrangement. Channel order also matters: RGB and BGR place different components at the same numeric tensor index.

A grayscale conversion discards color distinctions according to a stated rule. For the later texture example, grayscale is the arithmetic mean (R+G+B)/3, an explicit teaching choice. Other conversions use different weights. Two RGB colors can map to the same scalar even when their hue differs substantially. A texture descriptor operating on that scalar no longer sees the full color triple.

A learned RGB convolution can combine all input channels. One three-by-three filter over three channels has 27 coefficients before its bias, rather than nine. The same weights are reused spatially, while different output filters produce different feature channels. The learned operation can emphasize one combination of colors and local positions rather than simply filtering each channel independently.

**State the preprocessing choices:** decoded sample type, range, channel order, layout and any normalization or grayscale conversion. A mismatch can change every later feature and prediction without changing the nominal architecture. The first experiment exposes raw RGB editing so this issue remains concrete.

sections.title: Define an image-classification problem
sections.body:
Image classification assigns a category or set of categories to an input image. “Dog” is an image-level output; it does not provide the dog’s location. A single-label task chooses one mutually exclusive category, while a multilabel task permits several simultaneously. A hierarchy can organize labels into broader and narrower categories, but that structure must be specified rather than inferred from a flat score vector.

[figure: vc-classification]

Consider three scene categories: Beach, Forest and Urban City. Broad visual tendencies can motivate features: blue water and sky or warm sand, green foliage and brown trunks, gray structures and repeated hard edges. These are possible cues rather than definitions that hold in every image. A beach under unusual illumination and a city full of trees can break a shortcut based only on dominant color.

Classification supplies a building block for applications such as photo organization or recognizing a visible traffic-sign category. Some medical or driving systems also contain classification components, but an image label alone does not establish a complete clinical conclusion or driving decision. The output’s meaning stays tied to its task and evidence.

**Specify category boundaries and ambiguous cases.** Does a coastal city photograph belong to Beach or Urban City, or can it have both labels? A single-label dataset imposes a convention that may simplify an ambiguous world. The model is trained toward that convention; a disagreement should not automatically be interpreted as failure to perceive every object.

The following two implementations compare representation design with end-to-end learning. A histogram pipeline fixes how pixels become a feature vector, then learns decision heads. A small CNN learns local filters and its decision head together. Their declared examples, labels and measured outcomes are kept separate from claims about real-world scene or animal recognition.

sections.title: Hue histograms need a color convention
sections.body:
HSV represents color using hue, saturation and value. Hue describes position around a color circle; saturation distinguishes more chromatic colors from achromatic ones; value is related to the maximum component in a standard RGB-to-HSV conversion. A hue histogram and a value histogram answer different questions.

[figure: vc-hue]

The scene feature pipeline uses sixteen hue bins. A chromatic sample with normalized hue h in [0,1) contributes to bin floor(16h). Hue wraps around: values near the two ends of that interval represent nearby colors on the circle, although a simple linear bin index does not automatically preserve that circular relationship.

**Hue is undefined for an exactly achromatic RGB sample.** Assigning gray pixels the implementation’s default numeric hue can make gray appear to be a saturated red cue. The declared exercise omits hue counting when saturation is below 0.05 and normalizes by the total pixel count. Its hue-vector sum can therefore be less than one; the missing mass records how much was omitted. This is a specified policy, not an unspoken default.

RGB-to-HSV formulas, channel ranges and low-saturation handling must agree between fitting and prediction. A library might represent hue with degrees or another integer scale. Sixteen bins over [0,1) are not interchangeable with sixteen bins over a differently interpreted range.

Work a limitation: two pictures can have the same sixteen-bin hue distribution while arranging colors into different objects. A global color histogram preserves distribution and omits exact locations. Texture features can add some local structure, but their global histogram also discards neighborhood positions. The concatenated representation remains a deliberate summary, not a reversible image encoding.

warnings.message: The color feature is described as hue, but its accompanying histogram is labeled HSV V. Value and hue are different components; that chart cannot substantiate the stated hue distribution.

sections.title: Local binary patterns encode comparisons
sections.body:
A local binary pattern compares each neighbor with a center intensity. For eight neighbors, assign a bit equal to one when the neighbor is at least the center, and zero otherwise. Multiply each bit by a declared power-of-two weight, then sum the products to form a code.

The numeric example uses [7,1,12; 2,5,0; 3,5,15]. The center is 5. Starting at the top-left and moving clockwise, the weights are 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128. The active neighbors contribute 1,4,16 and 32, giving code **53**. The neighbor equal to 5 contributes because the comparison convention includes equality.

[figure: vc-lbp]

Eight bits permit 256 raw codes. A histogram counts code occurrences across eligible neighborhoods. It can describe the distribution of local ordering patterns while losing where each pattern occurred. Different LBP variants or code mappings produce different histogram dimensions; the number of neighbors does not directly specify that dimension.

The experiment applies a positive gain and an offset to every patch value without clipping the numeric calculation. Those changes preserve ordering, so the code stays the same. Changing a single neighbor can change a bit. Noise that changes comparisons can change the code even when a positive global brightness transformation would not.

**Inspect the convention:** neighbor order, bit weights, equality rule, eligible centers and any code mapping. A rotation can change a raw code because it changes which direction owns each bit. Rotation-invariant variants add another mapping; that invariance does not arise merely from using LBP.

The small patch makes every comparison visible. It is an exact reconstruction of the arithmetic example rather than a copied facial photograph or an unexplained texture chart.

visuals.predict: Does the neighbor equal to the center produce a one or a zero under the declared comparison?
visuals.reflect: Verify code 53, edit comparisons and apply a positive affine change. Separate eight bits from an explicitly mapped eight-bin histogram.

sections.title: Build a fixed feature vector before fitting
sections.body:
The conventional scene pipeline combines sixteen color entries and eight texture entries into a 24-dimensional vector. To reproduce such a pipeline, every step must be defined: RGB conversion, hue bin ranges, achromatic handling, grayscale conversion, neighborhood comparison, code-to-bin mapping and normalization.

[figure: vc-features]

The stated eight-dimensional texture description lacks a unique code mapping. The executable example therefore declares an added coarse mapping: bin=floor(raw LBP code/32). Codes 0…31 enter bin 0, and codes 224…255 enter bin 7. This creates exactly eight bins while grouping patterns that can be structurally different. It is a transparent teaching choice, not a claim that ordinary eight-neighbor LBP automatically uses eight bins.

Color counts are divided by all 144 pixels in a 12×12 query. Texture counts use the 100 interior centers, where a complete three-by-three neighborhood fits, and are normalized by that count. The resulting vector has sixteen hue values and eight texture values. Each classifier head adds a bias coordinate separately; that does not change the image representation’s stated 24 dimensions.

**Features and the decision rule play different roles.** The histogram calculation is fixed by design. SVM coefficients are fitted from labeled examples. If two images have identical feature vectors, every deterministic classifier using only those vectors must give them the same result. No optimization can restore the discarded arrangement uniquely.

The experiment shows the complete vector, bin counts and fitted coefficients. Its images are newly generated scene-like color/texture patterns with declared labels and variants. Success on those examples demonstrates that the actual implementation can fit its stated problem; it does not establish broad Beach/Forest/City recognition on photographs.

warnings.message: The eight-dimensional LBP histogram does not specify a code mapping or variant. Eight neighbors give 256 possible raw codes, not automatically eight bins. The executable example declares its own coarse mapping rather than claiming to recover the unspecified one.

sections.title: Margins, hinge loss and three SVM heads
sections.body:
A binary linear SVM computes a score $f(x)=w^Tx+b$. With targets y in {−1,+1}, the functional margin is yf(x). Correct sign alone does not ensure a unit margin. The hinge loss is $\max(0,1-yf(x))$. A positive example with score 0.4 is correctly classified by sign but still has hinge loss 0.6.

[figure: vc-margin]

Geometric distance divides the signed score by $\Vert w\Vert$. Multiplying w and b by the same positive number preserves the separating boundary and signed geometric distances. It changes functional margins and the positions of the canonical f=−1 and f=+1 lines. This distinguishes a geometric property from the objective’s parameter scale.

For three classes, the experiment fits three one-versus-rest heads: each class is positive for its own head and negative for the others. Prediction selects the largest raw score, with a declared first-class rule at an exact tie. These three independent scores are not softmax probabilities and need not sum to one.

The objective combines weight regularization with mean hinge loss over twelve images and three heads. Biases are unregularized. Each full-batch update uses the old coefficients to calculate all subgradients, then updates every coefficient simultaneously. At a hinge margin exactly one, the chosen subgradient contribution is zero. All 75 fitted parameters are inspectable.

**Run the fitting rather than assuming the picture proves it.** Compare loss, class decisions and held-out example variants as coefficients change. The color/texture representation supplies the input; the learned heads supply boundaries. A dataset’s small size alone does not guarantee SVM superiority over neural methods. Feature suitability, regularization, prior representations, tuning and the evaluation task also matter.

visuals.predict: Can a learned classifier restore image positions already discarded by a global histogram?
visuals.reflect: Compute all 24 features, fit the three real heads and inspect margins on separately generated variants; distinguish raw scores from probabilities.

warnings.message: The small-data advantage claim does not specify a benchmark or comparable preprocessing, prior representations and tuning. Dataset size alone does not establish whether an SVM or neural model will perform better.

sections.title: Learn convolutional features and the classifier together
sections.body:
A CNN can learn local filters as well as the later decision rule. The output of one filter is a spatial feature map. A nonlinearity such as ReLU changes those responses, and pooling can reduce their spatial dimensions. A later head combines the retained features into class scores. **End-to-end training means the final objective supplies gradients to both feature extraction and classification parameters.**

[figure: vc-cnn]

The browser network is fully specified and small enough to inspect. An 8×8 grayscale input passes through two learned 3×3 correlation filters with biases, giving two 6×6 maps. ReLU follows. Two-by-two max pooling with stride two gives two 3×3 maps. Flattening produces eighteen values, and three affine heads produce logits for Vertical, Horizontal and Cross. Softmax turns those logits into a normalized three-class distribution.

There are twenty filter parameters: two times nine coefficients plus one bias. The head has 3×18 weights and three biases, adding 57. The total is **77 trainable parameters**. Parameter count and spatial activation count are different: the same filter coefficients are reused at several input positions.

Training uses twelve declared pattern images and mean cross-entropy. Evaluation uses the same positions with different brightness and fixed added noise; it never supplies gradients. Query edits also supply no gradients. The loss history, probabilities, filter maps and all 77 gradients are computed from the actual model state.

**Compare before and after fitting.** A map’s appearance can change because its filter changed, because its input changed, or because the display rescales a matrix. The exercise labels display normalization and retains raw numeric responses. It does not portray its tiny pattern model as a pretrained animal, car or scene recognizer.

The network is a concrete example of representation learning. Its success supports a claim about the specified patterns and evaluation conditions, rather than proving that every CNN learns the same hierarchy or handles every visual variation.

visuals.predict: Which parameter sets should change when cross-entropy trains the network end-to-end?
visuals.reflect: Inspect all intermediate tensors, fitted filters/head and measured losses. Explain the stated pooling/activation backward rules and query-only changes.

sections.title: A feature map is not a photograph of a concept
sections.body:
Convolution creates responses from local weighted input combinations. Different learned filters can respond to different combinations of positions and intensities. Repeated layers permit later responses to depend on broader and more transformed input structure. Descriptions such as “edges, shapes, objects” provide an intuition for that progression, but they are not mandatory meanings assigned to every channel.

[figure: vc-hierarchy]

A map can have strong responses in many places, including background textures. A channel that sometimes responds near an eye is not necessarily an exclusive eye detector. Its meaning can depend on the rest of the network, the task and the training data. A collection of selected activations is illustrative evidence, rather than a complete interpretation of the learned model.

**Separate response magnitude from visualization brightness.** The small CNN rescales each displayed matrix for visibility while listing its actual values. A dark-looking map can have large values under a different display range. Conversely, a bright patch can be the largest of several very small values. Comparison requires the reported scales or the numbers themselves.

In an RGB network, “depth” often means the number of feature channels, while height and width are spatial dimensions. It does not mean geometric distance from the camera. A 32×32×3 input example therefore describes two spatial dimensions and three color channels. The number of output channels depends on how many filters are applied.

Work an intervention: select one channel, change the query pattern or line position, and inspect its convolution, ReLU and pooling maps. Then train and repeat the same query. Which changes come from input pixels, and which come from fitted parameters? This distinction keeps a visual explanation tied to the actual computation rather than a label pasted onto a channel.

sections.title: Nonlinearity and pooling change different information
sections.body:
ReLU applies $\max(0, z)$ to each response. It sets negative values to zero while retaining positive ones. Pooling aggregates a spatial neighborhood. They are different operations, and their order is part of the network definition.

The original max-pooling example uses [1,1,2,4; 5,6,7,8; 3,2,1,0; 1,2,3,4]. Two-by-two windows with stride two give [6,8; 3,4]. The top-left window contains 1,1,5,6, so its output is 6. The bottom-left contains 3,2,1,2, so it gives 3. The exact reconstruction below preserves those values.

[figure: vc-pool]

**Reduced spatial size does not imply unrestricted spatial invariance.** Moving a response within one pooling window can leave the maximum unchanged, but crossing a window boundary can change the pooled map. Pooling also discards the precise location and many nonmaximum values. A later classifier cannot uniquely reconstruct that information from the maxima alone.

Backward propagation through max pooling routes the output sensitivity to the selected maximum under a stated tie rule. The browser CNN uses the first maximum in row-major order. ReLU’s backward derivative is zero for negative values, one for positive values, and a declared zero convention at exactly zero. These rules determine actual training paths.

Flattening retains the remaining pooled values in a declared order for the affine head. Softmax then normalizes logits using exponentials, preferably after subtracting the largest logit for numerical stability. The resulting values sum to one. **Normalization does not establish probability calibration or correctness** on a new image.

Inspect the CNN’s selected pool coordinates and class probabilities. The forward tensors and backward routing are connected: a changed maximum can change which earlier response receives a gradient, even when a similar-looking pooled value remains.

warnings.message: Max pooling does not guarantee unrestricted spatial invariance. A movement within a window may preserve its maximum, while a movement across window boundaries can change the pooled map.

sections.title: Derive metrics from labels and decisions
sections.body:
A confusion matrix compares predicted and actual classes. True positives are actual positives predicted positive. False negatives are actual positives predicted negative. False positives are actual negatives predicted positive. True negatives are actual negatives predicted negative. State which class is positive and which axis is actual before interpreting a table.

[figure: vc-confusion]

Precision is TP/(TP+FP): among positive predictions, how many are true? Recall, or sensitivity, is TP/(TP+FN): among actual positives, how many were found? Specificity is TN/(TN+FP), and negative predictive value is TN/(TN+FN). Accuracy divides all correct predictions by the total. F1 combines precision and recall through 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN).

The worked score table contains ten positives and ten negatives. At threshold 0.5, six positives and two negatives are predicted positive. Thus TP=6, FN=4, FP=2 and TN=8. Precision is 6/8=0.75; recall is 6/10=0.6; specificity is 8/10=0.8; accuracy is 14/20=0.7. The denominator determines what each number means.

**Threshold changes decisions, not the supplied observations.** The experiment uses score≥threshold, including exact ties. It recomputes every row and confusion count. Its precision–recall trace enumerates distinct score thresholds; undefined precision when no positives are predicted is explicitly omitted from the curve and remains undefined in the metric table.

The imbalance example has ten positives and ninety negatives. Predicting everything negative gives 90% accuracy and zero recall. A favorable total can hide failure on the class of interest. Selecting a row shows which confusion cell its actual decision enters.

These are image-classification metrics for a declared labeled score table. Detection also requires spatial matching and a duplicate policy. Background true negatives are not naturally enumerated as a finite list of all possible boxes, so classification accuracy should not be transferred unchanged into a detection claim.

visuals.predict: What denominator does precision use when six true and two false positives are predicted?
visuals.reflect: Enumerate actual score decisions and confusion cells, inspect undefined denominators, then compare threshold changes with class imbalance.

sections.title: Diagnose an error with evidence
sections.body:
A cat image classified as Dog can result from several causes: an unrepresentative dataset, a misleading feature correlation, insufficient representation or model capacity, noise, a preprocessing mismatch, an ambiguous labeling convention, or an optimization problem. The observed wrong class does not uniquely identify the cause.

[figure: vc-diagnosis]

**Turn each explanation into a test.** To investigate preprocessing, compare decoded channels, range and tensor layout with the training contract. To investigate representation loss, ask whether different labeled images produce identical features. To investigate data coverage, evaluate unfamiliar acquisition conditions separately. To investigate fitting, inspect losses and gradients rather than assuming that a training button ran the intended update.

A high softmax value can accompany a wrong label. It describes the fitted model’s normalized score under its current representation, not certainty that the real category is correct. Similarly, an SVM’s large raw margin can be based on an irrelevant training correlation. Confidence and correctness are separate observations.

A useful experiment changes one relevant factor while preserving the intended target. Brightness can be varied in the pattern CNN; the orientation label remains fixed until visibility or the actual shape changes. Rotating Vertical into Horizontal would change the target, so treating that intervention as a required invariance would be inappropriate.

Work the original reasoning question: why feed numeric tensors into a model? Its operations compute with a defined numerical representation. A digital image already stores samples, but decoding, channel ordering, scaling and layout determine the tensor actually presented. The question is about an input convention rather than a mysterious extra step that creates numbers from nothing.

Diagnosis connects computation with evaluation. A plausible story becomes stronger when a controlled measurement supports it and weaker when the predicted intervention does not produce the expected result.

sections.title: Detection adds locations, count and scale
sections.body:
Object detection returns hypotheses about both category and location, often as boxes with class scores. A scene containing two people and two horses requires separate object hypotheses even when the image-level category list contains only Person and Horse. The output therefore has a variable number of spatial entries rather than one fixed scene label.

[figure: vc-localization]

**Localization precision matters independently of recognition.** Several boxes can overlap the same horse while differing in how tightly they enclose it. A correct category attached to a poor box can fail a spatial evaluation. Pose changes alter the region an object occupies, so localization needs more than recognizing that some characteristic texture is present.

Occlusion introduces a labeling convention. Is the target the visible extent or an estimated full-object extent? An obscured person can have a small visible region while a full-object box extends behind another object. Neither target should be substituted for the other silently. Multiple hypotheses can also refer to one object, inflating a count if duplicates are not handled.

Small objects occupy few samples. A small pedestrian in the distance may lose useful detail after resizing or downsampling. A slight box displacement can represent a larger fraction of a small object than of a large one. This helps explain why object scale affects localization as well as category recognition.

**Separate instances from candidates.** Three overlapping boxes can be three hypotheses for one person, or boxes for several nearby people. Overlap alone does not establish which. NMS applies an explicit heuristic to reduce redundant hypotheses; it can suppress a real nearby instance if the configuration and threshold are unfavorable.

The original horse, crowd and distant-person cases motivate these issues. Their relationships are rebuilt as spatial diagrams and a declared person/ball scene, without copying unlicensed photographs or claiming newly drawn boxes came from a trained detector.

sections.title: R-CNN separates proposals and recognition
sections.body:
Original R-CNN combines bottom-up region proposals with CNN features, class-specific linear classifiers and box refinement. A proposal supplies a candidate region; it does not already identify a correct object. The system processes candidate regions and later removes some redundant detections.

[figure: vc-rcnn]

The original approach uses about two thousand proposals per image. Candidate regions are warped to the CNN’s required input dimensions, and the CNN supplies feature vectors. Class-specific SVMs score those vectors. Separate regressors refine box geometry, and NMS reduces overlapping alternatives. The [original R-CNN paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2524) specifies the method; later Fast/Faster R-CNN systems should not be treated as identical implementations of this per-proposal pipeline.

**A region proposal is a hypothesis with a spatial extent.** Missing a relevant object at this stage limits what the downstream classifier can recover from the supplied regions. Generating many proposals can improve coverage while increasing repeated processing and duplicate hypotheses. Proposal count, coverage and computational cost are related but different quantities.

Warping a nonsquare region to a fixed-size square changes its sampled shape. The classifier must tolerate that preprocessing, or another region representation must be chosen. Supplying a clean correctly centered crop is easier than finding and interpreting suitable candidates in a full scene; crop-level accuracy does not establish complete detector performance.

The postprocessing experiment receives declared proposals, scores and regression deltas. It computes box decoding, score filtering and exact NMS. Its person/ball scene also has known annotations for a separately marked evaluation. **It does not pretend to implement selective search or a pretrained proposal CNN.** The earlier trainable CNN teaches feature fitting on its own explicit miniature task.

Tracing the component contract makes the pipeline reviewable: which information is supplied, which is inferred, which parameter set is fitted, and which stage can create the observed error?

sections.title: Proposals are not a fixed partition
sections.body:
Selective search begins from image-region structure and combines regions to produce candidate extents. The resulting boxes can overlap and exist at different scales. This differs from dividing the input once into disjoint equal grid cells.

[figure: vc-proposals]

A fixed partition can cut an object across several cells. A proposal mechanism instead aims to offer regions that could enclose useful objects, while retaining alternatives. Intermediate segmentation regions can motivate candidate boxes without becoming the final semantic segmentation output. The task remains detection when the final interface returns classed object boxes.

**Candidate coverage and classification quality are separate.** If no proposal encloses a small distant object adequately, a strong classifier on other regions does not solve that missed object. If several proposals enclose the same object, a later duplicate policy becomes important. Increasing the number of proposals alone does not establish the best tradeoff.

Each proposed region also needs a representation compatible with its classifier. Original per-region warping and feature extraction can repeat considerable computation over overlapping image areas. A later architecture that shares whole-image feature computation addresses a different organization of work, rather than merely renaming original R-CNN’s stages.

Work a hypothetical failure: the proposal stage produces tight regions around a person’s head and torso separately but no adequate full-person candidate. A classifier can correctly identify visible parts while still failing the requested full-person box convention. The error belongs partly to the region contract and target convention, not only to a category score.

When comparing two detectors, identify whether candidate regions are supplied externally, learned, generated densely or represented by another mechanism. That choice determines where coverage and computational costs enter the pipeline.

sections.title: Refine a box with explicit coordinate units
sections.body:
A common refinement parameterization represents a proposal by center (x,y), width w and height h. Four deltas describe center displacement in proposal-size units and logarithmic size changes. Decoding gives $x'=x+wt_x$, $y'=y+ht_y$, $w'=w\exp(t_w)$ and $h'=h\exp(t_h)$.

[figure: vc-boxes]

The inverse target encoding is $t_x=(x^*-x)/w$, $t_y=(y^*-y)/h$, $t_w=\log(w^*/w)$ and $t_h=\log(h^*/h)$. Widths and heights must be positive for these formulas. Center coordinates and top-left coordinates are different conventions; using the same equation with an unstated switch changes the decoded box.

**A delta is relative, not a direct pixel offset.** For proposal width 60, $t_x=0.1$ moves the center by 6 coordinate units. With height 120, $t_y=0.1$ moves it by 12. Zero deltas reproduce the proposal exactly. Log-size delta $t_w=\log 2$ doubles width, while $t_w=0$ preserves it.

The interactive candidates use explicitly supplied deltas, and all decoded values are calculated. Change one candidate’s center or log-size delta, then inspect its dimensions and overlaps. A box can extend beyond the displayed scene; clipping a drawn rectangle is different from changing its numerical area. The overlap computation uses the reported uncut rectangles.

A trained regressor would learn these deltas from examples and a target convention. The executable decoder demonstrates their meaning without inventing a trained regression head. Likewise, a refinement that reduces localization error does not guarantee the correct category or remove duplicates. Those are separate outputs and later decisions.

sections.title: IoU measures overlap; NMS makes decisions
sections.body:
For two boxes A and B, intersection-over-union is $\text{IoU}=|A\cap B|/|A\cup B|$. The union is the sum of their areas minus the intersection. Two area-four boxes with intersection two have union six, giving IoU=1/3. Disjoint positive-area boxes have IoU zero; identical positive-area boxes have IoU one.

[figure: vc-iou]

**IoU is a comparison, not a confidence score or a decision rule by itself.** Comparison with known truth can measure localization during training or evaluation. Comparison between two predictions can support duplicate suppression when truth is unavailable. These uses involve different second boxes and different meanings.

Greedy NMS ranks candidates by score, keeps the highest remaining candidate, then suppresses comparable lower-scoring candidates whose pairwise IoU exceeds a threshold. It repeats on the survivors. The experiment uses score≥score-threshold and IoU>overlap-threshold, with ascending candidate ID at a score tie. Equality at the overlap threshold therefore does not suppress.

[figure: vc-nms]

Class-aware NMS compares boxes of the same supplied class. Class-agnostic NMS can suppress overlapping hypotheses with different classes. Both are explicit policies. Neither proves that every retained detection is correct: a wrong-class box can survive class-aware suppression because it is not compared with an overlapping different-class candidate.

The stepper displays every selected ID, suppressed ID, pairwise IoU and remaining ranked list. Known annotations are used only in a separate one-to-one evaluation after prediction processing. The algorithm does not consult ground truth to decide which candidate is relevant.

**Try a threshold tradeoff:** a low overlap threshold can remove duplicates aggressively and also remove nearby distinct instances. A high threshold can preserve crowded instances while retaining duplicate hypotheses. Category errors, missed objects and poor proposals are not fixed merely by adjusting NMS.

visuals.predict: Can a wrong-class box survive class-aware suppression even when it overlaps a correct different-class box?
visuals.reflect: Decode exact geometry and step greedy NMS. Keep prediction-only decisions separate from the marked truth-based evaluation.

sections.title: One network predicts a grid of outputs
sections.body:
Original YOLO frames detection as a joint prediction problem from the whole image. A single network produces spatially organized box and class outputs rather than running original R-CNN’s external proposals through a separate CNN for each candidate. Introduced by Joseph Redmon, Santosh Divvala, Ross Girshick and Ali Farhadi, the name means You Only Look Once, referring to this unified organization rather than a claim that no postprocessing remains.

[figure: vc-yolo-architecture]

The original 2015 design uses a 448×448 detection input, 24 convolutional layers and two fully connected layers. Its first convolution is seven-by-seven with stride two; later one-by-one reductions and three-by-three convolutions form part of the architecture. It uses leaky ReLU in hidden layers and a linear final output. The [original YOLO paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02640) supplies these historical conventions; later variants differ.

**A version-specific architecture should not mix later techniques into an earlier diagram.** Ordinary ReLU, batch normalization and a first one-by-one layer are not an accurate combined description of that original network. Dropout and other regularization choices also reduce particular risks under conditions rather than guaranteeing the absence of overfitting.

A unified prediction can use whole-image context and reduce repeated per-proposal work. Its output and training constraints can also limit localization or crowded-scene behavior. Speed, localization accuracy and generalization must be assessed under a stated workload and dataset rather than inferred from the model’s name.

The experiment encodes grid targets and decodes supplied box predictions. It does not train or run the original YOLO network on images.

warnings.message: The architecture description mixes conventions: original YOLO starts with a 7×7 convolution, uses hidden leaky ReLU rather than ordinary ReLU, and is not accurately described by importing later batch-normalization conventions. Regularization also does not guarantee prevention of overfitting.

sections.title: Grid responsibility follows the object center
sections.body:
Divide the image into S×S cells. In original YOLOv1, a cell is responsible for an object when the object’s center falls inside it. **The set of cells crossed by the object’s rectangle is not its set of responsible cells.** A large rectangle can span several cells while having one center.

[figure: vc-grid]

Grid assignment is also different from a residual block. A residual block combines a transformed representation with a skip path, such as x+F(x), subject to compatible shapes. Partitioning an image into cells changes how outputs are indexed; it does not perform that skip-connection computation.

The grid exercise computes row=floor(S·cy) and column=floor(S·cx) for normalized target center coordinates, then encodes within-cell offsets. Moving the center across a cell boundary changes responsibility. Width and height can remain fixed, and the rectangle may continue crossing cells on both sides. The highlighted cell therefore tracks the center rather than every covered pixel.

For S=7, cx=0.55 and cy=0.4, column is 3 and row is 2. The within-cell x offset is 7×0.55−3=0.85, and y offset is 7×0.4−2=0.8. These values have a different scale from whole-image normalized coordinates.

**Test the information boundary:** the example supplies an annotated target and numerical predictions. It can encode responsibility and decode candidates exactly. It does not infer an object center from raw pixels. A trained detector must estimate its outputs from observations, and those estimates can be wrong or outside an ideal target range.

Adding a second differently classified target in the same cell demonstrates a constraint of the original shared per-cell class representation. Multiple geometric slots do not automatically give each slot an independent class distribution.

visuals.predict: Does a large object make every overlapped cell responsible for it in original YOLOv1?
visuals.reflect: Move its center, inspect original coordinate units and shared class outputs, decode supplied slots and distinguish predicted confidence from measured truth overlap.

warnings.message: The heading “Residual blocks” is incorrect for the grid-partition step. Dividing an image into grid cells is different from the skip-connection computation of a residual block.

Highlighting every grid cell crossed by an object is not original YOLOv1 responsibility. Its responsible cell contains the object center; box confidence also includes estimated localization quality rather than only object presence.

sections.title: Box coordinates, confidence and class outputs
sections.body:
Original YOLOv1 encodes box centers relative to their cell, while width and height are normalized by the whole image. These conventions must be kept distinct. An illustrative height of 1.5 cell heights in a seven-row grid corresponds to whole-image height 1.5/7, not a normalized image height of 1.5.

[figure: vc-yolo-units]

Each cell predicts B groups of five values: box geometry and confidence. It also predicts one shared C-dimensional conditional class vector. The full output shape is S×S×(5B+C). For S=7, B=2 and C=20, it is 7×7×30, containing 1,470 values. A seven-entry single-box/two-class vector is a useful simplification but not the complete original output format.

**The confidence convention includes localization quality.** It is intended to combine object presence with overlap quality, rather than being only a pure object-presence probability. At prediction time, the network supplies an estimate; it cannot calculate its true overlap with an annotation that is unavailable. The grid experiment reports supplied confidence separately from measured IoU to its known target.

Class-specific box scores multiply that box’s confidence by the shared conditional class probability. A supplied confidence 0.8 and Person probability 0.75 give Person score 0.6. Both slots share the class vector but have their own confidence and geometry. The product is a ranking signal under this convention, not proof of perfect probability calibration.

The two-class example shows both slots, decoded centers and whole-image dimensions. Target bounds are explicit; raw candidate rectangles can extend beyond the displayed region. A score vector, geometric encoding and decoded box are different representations of information. Confusing their units or interpreting a supplied number as measured correctness produces an error even before a learned network is considered.

warnings.message: The illustrated widths and heights are measured in cell units, while original YOLOv1 normalizes them by the whole image. The seven-entry single-box/two-class vector is also a simplification of its B-box/shared-class output. Keep those formats and units distinct.

sections.title: Separate assignment, prediction and evaluation
sections.body:
Training can use annotated objects to establish targets, responsibility and localization losses. Evaluation can compare predictions with those annotations. Deployment prediction normally receives the observation without its true boxes. **A step that requires true boxes cannot be described as an ordinary prediction-time filter.**

[figure: vc-truth]

Original YOLO uses overlap with known targets during training to help assign a responsible box predictor and assess localization. NMS instead compares predicted boxes with one another. A statement such as “discard predictions with low IoU” must identify the comparison box: truth during evaluation, or another prediction during suppression. Those are not interchangeable operations.

A class score can be high for an incorrect location. A box can fit an object tightly while carrying the wrong class. Two individually accurate hypotheses can describe the same object and cause duplicate counting. A useful detection evaluation therefore defines class compatibility, overlap threshold and one-to-one matching.

The postprocessing example makes these distinctions visible. It includes an intentionally wrong Ball-class hypothesis over a Person region. Class-aware NMS can retain it because overlap with a Person-class box is not considered comparable. The separate truth-based evaluation then marks the class error. This is not a failure of the NMS arithmetic; it exposes what the suppression policy was designed to do.

**Never use unknown truth secretly to improve the displayed prediction.** Supplying candidates or annotations for a teaching example is legitimate when declared. Calling annotation-derived boxes model inference is a different claim. The chapter’s trained models have their own stated tasks, while detection geometry and postprocessing receive explicit numerical inputs.

warnings.message: Ordinary prediction cannot reject boxes using their true IoU to unavailable ground-truth annotations. Truth-based IoU belongs to training/evaluation; NMS uses overlap between predicted boxes and their scores.

sections.title: Choose a detector under a measured contract
sections.body:
A mobile detector must satisfy a workload, rather than merely carry a familiar model name. Relevant quantities include input resolution, latency, memory, operation count, numerical precision, required object sizes, acquisition conditions and error tolerance. Latency for the model alone can differ from latency for decoding, preprocessing, model execution and postprocessing together.

[figure: vc-efficiency]

Original R-CNN’s repeated candidate processing motivates more shared or unified computation. A compact one-stage model can be an appropriate starting point for a limited-device comparison, but it must be evaluated on the actual task and runtime. Later two-stage designs also share work differently from original R-CNN. **The historical comparison is not a rule that every network with one label is faster or more accurate than every network with another.**

A latency/accuracy chart requires comparable measurements: dataset and split, overlap/averaging convention, resolution, device, precision, implementation and timing scope. FLOPs count operations under a convention; they do not determine latency independently of memory behavior and hardware. Version numbers and plotted lines do not provide missing benchmark conditions.

Application examples include localizing regions in medical images and finding fruit among leaves. They share the box-output interface but have different sensor properties, occlusions, object scales and error consequences. A result image illustrates the task; it does not certify performance on all relevant cases or establish a medical conclusion.

Work the original mobile-choice question: define a latency budget and smallest relevant object, compare candidate implementations under the same inputs and device, then inspect errors and memory. If faster processing comes from reducing resolution, did the small-object detection requirement survive? A responsible choice connects the resource gain with the task cost.

warnings.message: The detector latency/accuracy comparison lacks the full measurement contract here: exact input resolution, device, precision, timing scope and evaluation setup. Do not treat plotted rankings or version numbers as portable performance guarantees.

sections.title: Follow the full information path
sections.body:
The chapter connects sampled numbers to visual decisions. Pixels supply spatial/color evidence. Statistics summarize values. Filters combine local neighborhoods. Histograms deliberately discard some locations. A fixed feature representation can support a learned SVM; a CNN can learn the feature extraction and decision head together. Both require independent evaluation under a stated task.

**Detection adds geometry and multiple hypotheses.** A proposal, a class score, a refinement delta, an IoU comparison and a retained detection are different objects. Original R-CNN and original YOLO organize those computations differently. Their historical interfaces should remain distinct from later architectures and from the reduced numerical demonstrations.

For every result, ask which information was supplied and which was calculated. The small SVM and CNN fit actual parameters. The averaging and LBP exercises reproduce exact original arithmetic. The detection and grid experiments decode supplied candidates and execute postprocessing without pretending to run a missing pretrained recognizer. This contract makes explanations and warnings useful rather than decorative.

Work a complete design exercise: you need to recognize a small fruit category and return one box per visible fruit on a limited device. Specify RGB preprocessing, target box convention, representation or learned model, training/evaluation split, score rule, duplicate policy, spatial matching and runtime measurement. Include occlusion and tiny-object cases. State which changes preserve the target and which destroy the necessary evidence.

Finally propose an improvement based on a measured failure. If objects are absent from proposals, improve coverage. If color shortcuts fail under new light, improve data or representation. If crowded objects disappear after NMS, test the suppression policy. If runtime exceeds the budget, profile the actual stages. A more complex architecture is useful only when its changes address the task’s demonstrated limitation.

questions.prompt: Geometric point (x=3,y=2) selects which array entry under the stated row-first convention?
questions.why: Rows correspond to y and columns to x, so row-first access is [2][3].

questions.prompt: Which numeric claim is valid for general image tensors?
choices: Every image value must be an unsigned byte.
A value of 1 has the same meaning in every range.
Type, layout and range are part of the input contract.
questions.why: Images/features can be unsigned, floating-point, normalized or signed; consumers must agree on the convention.

questions.prompt: What are mean and population variance of 0,0,8,8?
choices: 4 and 16.
4 and 4.
8 and 16.
questions.why: The mean is 4; each squared deviation is 16, so their mean is 16.

questions.prompt: A pixel permutation leaves which quantities unchanged?
choices: Every object position.
Mean, population variance and intensity histogram.
The orientation of every stripe.
questions.why: Those quantities depend on sample values/counts rather than their arrangement.

questions.prompt: Two differently oriented stripes have identical global histograms. Can a deterministic classifier receiving only those histograms distinguish them uniquely?
choices: Always, with more layers.
Only if its scores are called probabilities.
No; its input features are identical.
questions.why: The discarded spatial arrangement cannot be uniquely recovered by a more complex decision rule.

questions.prompt: Which sample multiplies centered kernel offset (u=−1,v=−1) under strict convolution?
choices: I[r,c].
questions.why: The strict formula uses I[r−u,c−v].

questions.prompt: Which kernel condition is required mathematically?
choices: Every kernel must be odd-sized.
The size and anchor convention must be stated; even sizes are possible.
Every coefficient must be positive.
questions.why: Odd sizes have a convenient center; even kernels and signed coefficients are also valid with an explicit convention.

questions.prompt: A bright input at [4][5] passes through a strict-convolution top-left shift kernel. Where does it appear?
questions.why: G[r,c]=I[r+1,c+1], so r=3,c=4 copy that sample.

questions.prompt: The mean-filter output for a 3×3 patch filled with 9 is…
questions.why: Each value is weighted by 1/9, so a constant patch retains its value.

questions.prompt: Which valid centers receive the isolated 90 at [8][2]?
choices: Rows 7…8, columns 1…3.
Rows 7…8, columns 1…4.
questions.why: The kernel radius is one; column 4 is two columns away and must not receive it.

questions.prompt: Why can a lower-variance smoothed image be worse for detecting a tiny object?
choices: Variance uniquely determines category.
Averaging can remove task-relevant fine structure as well as noise.
A mean filter never changes maxima.
questions.why: Noise and genuine small-scale evidence can both be weakened.

questions.prompt: A 21×21 kernel filters a 24×24 input under Valid. What shape results?
questions.why: Stride one valid output side is 24−21+1=4.

questions.prompt: Horizontal correlation Sobel applied to [0,1,2;0,1,2;0,1,2] gives what center response?
questions.why: Each row contributes weighted right-minus-left differences: 2+4+2=8.

questions.prompt: Switching both Sobel responses from correlation to strict convolution changes what?
choices: It leaves each sign unchanged.
Signs reverse, while squared-gradient magnitude stays unchanged.
It forces every response to be positive.
questions.why: Both kernels are antisymmetric; squaring the reversed signs leaves magnitude unchanged.

questions.prompt: One 3×3 RGB filter has how many coefficients before its bias?
questions.why: There are nine spatial coefficients for each of three input channels.

questions.prompt: Which preprocessing mismatch can alter every prediction?
choices: Changing RGB to BGR without adapting the expected channel order.
Using the same stated layout.
Keeping the same decoded values.
questions.why: The model can consume different color components at the same indices.

questions.prompt: What does an image-level Dog label fail to supply?
choices: Its declared category.
The dog’s spatial location and exact extent.
The fact that the model returned a label.
questions.why: Classification and localization are different output contracts.

questions.prompt: What should be remembered when histogramming gray RGB samples?
choices: Their hue is always meaningful saturated red.
Their value must equal zero.
Hue is undefined when saturation is zero.
questions.why: Achromatic handling must be specified rather than interpreting an implementation default as chromatic evidence.

questions.prompt: With the original patch and declared weights/equality rule, what is its LBP code?
questions.why: Active contributions are 1+4+16+32=53.

questions.prompt: Why does a positive affine patch change preserve this code?
choices: It removes the center.
It preserves comparison order without numeric clipping.
It makes all neighbors equal.
questions.why: A positive scale plus common offset preserves neighbor≥center comparisons.

questions.prompt: Eight LBP neighbors automatically imply which histogram dimension?
choices: Eight bins.
Sixteen bins.
No unique mapped dimension; raw codes allow 256 bins.
questions.why: The code-to-bin mapping or LBP variant determines the histogram dimension.

questions.prompt: What is explicitly added to make the demonstration’s texture vector eight-dimensional?
choices: floor(raw code/32) coarse mapping.
Replacing it with HOG.
Treating raw code 53 as eight independent histograms.
questions.why: The coarse mapping is declared as a teaching choice because the source does not specify one.

questions.prompt: A positive-class point has score f = 0.4. What is its hinge loss max(0, 1 − y f)?
choices: 0: it is correctly classified
questions.why: With y = +1, the functional margin is 0.4, so hinge loss is 0.6. Correct classification alone does not satisfy the unit margin.

questions.prompt: Multiply both w and b by 3 without changing their direction. What stays unchanged?
choices: The functional score y f
The width between f = −1 and +1
The signed geometric distance y f / ‖w‖
questions.why: Both the numerator and denominator of the geometric distance triple. Functional scores change, and the canonical band narrows.

questions.prompt: How many fitted parameters does the declared small CNN have?
questions.why: There are 20 filter parameters and 57 affine-head parameters.

questions.prompt: Which data supply gradients to the small CNN?
choices: The displayed query after every edit.
The separately listed evaluation images.
Only the twelve training images under the stated objective.
questions.why: Queries/evaluation recompute outputs without participating in parameter fitting.

questions.prompt: Two feature maps use separate display normalization. Which comparison needs raw scales?
choices: Comparing their absolute response magnitudes.
Reading their labels.
Counting the stated channels.
questions.why: Brightness is not a common physical response scale when each matrix is rescaled separately.

questions.prompt: What is the top-left result for 2×2 max pooling of [1,1,2,4;5,6,7,8;3,2,1,0;1,2,3,4]?
questions.why: The top-left window is 1,1,5,6, whose maximum is 6.

questions.prompt: Does max pooling guarantee invariance to every translation?
choices: Yes, regardless of window boundaries.
Only for images with three classes.
No; moving a response across windows can change the pooled output.
questions.why: Limited aggregation is different from unrestricted spatial invariance.

questions.prompt: A classifier finds 6 of 10 actual positives and makes 2 false positive predictions. What are its precision and recall?
choices: Precision 0.6, recall 0.75
Precision 0.75, recall 0.6
Precision 0.8, recall 0.6
questions.why: TP = 6, FN = 4 and FP = 2. Precision divides by the 8 positive predictions: 6/8 = 0.75. Recall divides by the 10 actual positives: 6/10 = 0.6.

questions.prompt: Ten positives and ninety negatives are all predicted negative. What are accuracy and recall?
choices: 1 and 1.
questions.why: Ninety negatives are correct, while none of the ten positives is found.

questions.prompt: One cat is wrongly labeled Dog. What does that alone identify?
choices: The unique cause must be small capacity.
An error, with several possible causes still needing tests.
Proof that the histogram implementation is wrong.
questions.why: A result can arise from data, representation, preprocessing, noise or fitting; controlled evidence separates them.

questions.prompt: Three overlapping same-class boxes establish what count of real objects?
choices: Exactly three.
Exactly one.
The count is unresolved without association/target evidence.
questions.why: They may be duplicate hypotheses for one object or nearby distinct instances.

questions.prompt: What is supplied by a region proposal?
choices: A candidate spatial region, not a guaranteed correct object label.
A verified class probability.
A complete ground-truth annotation.
questions.why: Coverage and downstream classification remain separate inference problems.

questions.prompt: Why is selective-search proposal generation different from a fixed disjoint grid?
choices: It can produce overlapping candidates at several scales.
It requires every object to occupy one fixed cell.
It already supplies final semantic labels.
questions.why: A region-hypothesis set is not a single partition of the image.

questions.prompt: Proposal width is 60 and tx=0.1. How far does the decoded center move?
choices: 0.1 unit.
6 units.
60 units.
questions.why: Center displacement is proposal width times tx: 60×0.1=6.

questions.prompt: Two area-4 boxes overlap in area 2. What is IoU?
questions.why: The union is 4+4−2 = 6, so IoU = 2/6.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of NMS?
choices: Remove redundant overlapping detections.
Increase image brightness.
Train the region proposal network.
questions.why: It keeps high-scoring boxes while suppressing overlapping lower-scoring alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the original historical YOLO architecture coherently?
choices: Every later YOLO has exactly the same architecture.
Grid assignment is a residual block.
448×448 input, 24 convolutions, two fully connected layers and hidden leaky ReLU.
questions.why: These are original-version conventions; later variants and ordinary-ReLU claims must be separated.

questions.prompt: Under original YOLOv1, which cell is responsible for an object?
choices: The cell containing its center.
Every cell crossed by its box.
Only the highest-intensity cell.
questions.why: Center responsibility differs from rectangle coverage.

questions.prompt: For S=7, cx=0.55, cy=0.4, which (row,column) is responsible?
What is the original 20-class, two-box, seven-grid output size?
questions.why: The class vector is shared per cell; each box contributes five geometry/confidence values.

questions.prompt: A supplied confidence 0.8 and conditional Person probability 0.75 give which Person score?
questions.why: The class-specific score multiplies them: 0.8×0.75=0.6.

questions.prompt: Which ordinary prediction-time comparison can NMS compute without annotations?
choices: Overlap between two predicted boxes.
True IoU to an unknown target annotation.
Guaranteed target correctness.
questions.why: NMS uses prediction-to-prediction overlap; truth belongs to training or evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which evidence supports a mobile-detector choice?
choices: A larger version number alone.
Task errors and latency/memory measured on the target device under comparable inputs.
FLOPs alone guarantee latency.
questions.why: The workload, precision, timing scope and task requirements determine the comparison.

questions.prompt: Which improvement most directly addresses a measured missing-proposal failure?
choices: Only rename the output score.
Assume NMS can invent the missing candidate.
Improve candidate coverage or the mechanism supplying spatial hypotheses.
questions.why: A later classifier/suppression rule cannot reliably recover an absent adequate proposal from this pipeline contract.

title: Computer Vision — Part 3
summary: Pixel labels, fully convolutional prediction, learned upsampling, skip features, and actual miniature image-GAN training.

sections.title: A box does not describe an irregular object
sections.body:
**Segmentation assigns information to image locations, rather than returning only a category or rectangular extent.** A chair can have thin legs and gaps that its bounding box includes as background. A bin occupies a different shape. Knowing that Chair and Bin are present, locating their boxes, and identifying their actual visible regions are three different output requirements.

A cat, dog and duck in one scene make the same distinction. Image classification can list categories. Detection can provide one box per hypothesis. A mask can follow an irregular contour and separate object pixels from surrounding regions. None of these output formats automatically proves that the estimated category or boundary is correct.

[figure: ss-tasks]

**Semantic segmentation** assigns a class to each eligible location: both people can have the same Person ID. **Instance segmentation** additionally distinguishes individual objects within a category. A class ID is not an instance ID, and a larger number for Person does not create an identity distinction. Labels for background or broader regions can also be part of the task.

The first experiment contains two declared chair instances and one bin. Rectangle fill provides a deliberately coarse semantic prediction. It includes gaps between chair legs, even though it identifies the correct broad class. Compare that prediction with the known reference and edit individual labels. The overlap counts make the cost of the rectangular approximation measurable.

Switch the reference among image, class IDs and instance IDs. The reference is supplied teaching data; the editable prediction is a semantic map. Copying the target provides an exact comparison, not evidence that a model inferred the mask. This keeps the output contract separate from the algorithm that would need to estimate it from unfamiliar observations.

visuals.predict: Where will filling an enclosing rectangle assign the wrong category?
visuals.reflect: Compare semantic IDs, instance IDs, foreground IoU and whole-map accuracy. Explain why background gaps matter.

warnings.message: A segmentation definition that promises accurate boundaries for all objects is too strong. Accuracy is measured, not guaranteed; a semantic map covers its declared classes and annotation policy, and does not automatically identify every instance or hidden object.

sections.title: Class IDs identify categories, not intensity or identity
sections.body:
A semantic label map is an H×W array of discrete category IDs. A convention might use Person=1, Purse=2, Plants/Grass=3, Sidewalk=4 and Building/Structures=5. The numbers identify categories. They are not measured brightnesses and do not imply that Building is numerically five times Person.

[figure: ss-labels]

Changing the color used to display an ID changes the visualization without changing the annotation. A mask’s apparent brightness therefore cannot be interpreted like the grayscale intensity of its input photograph. Likewise, renumbering categories consistently can preserve a task, while changing the labels inconsistently between training and evaluation breaks the contract.

**Instance information requires another representation.** Two people can both have semantic ID 1 and still be different objects. Separate masks or identity assignments are needed if the goal includes counting instances or following one particular person. Pixels at occlusions also require a stated convention: visible extent and estimated full-object extent are different targets.

In the chair example, semantic Chair=1 appears for both chairs, while reference instance IDs 1 and 2 identify the two objects. The bin has semantic ID 2 but instance ID 3. Reusing a numeric value in two different conventions does not make those meanings equivalent.

Work an interpretation: a model returns an H×W array with three integer values. Is that enough to conclude it performed semantic segmentation? You need the ID meaning, the annotation convention and the relationship to the input. The same three values could be arbitrary clusters, depth bins or palette indices. Shape alone does not establish semantics.

sections.title: Measure the mask you actually need
sections.body:
For a selected class, count target-and-predicted pixels as TP, predicted-only pixels as FP and target-only pixels as FN. Class IoU is TP/(TP+FP+FN). Dice is 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN). Both emphasize overlap for that class rather than rewarding every unrelated background pixel.

[figure: ss-overlap]

**Whole-map accuracy and foreground overlap answer different questions.** When background dominates, predicting background everywhere can produce a high total accuracy while finding none of a foreground class. Conversely, a prediction that captures a small object but adds a broad false region can have reasonable recall and poor IoU. The denominator determines what the value measures.

The rectangle-filled chair prediction includes nonobject gaps. Those pixels become false positives for Chair. Editing one to Background reduces that count without changing the class name or object count. Removing a genuine chair-leg pixel instead creates a false negative. The experiment enumerates these changes from the actual arrays.

If a class is absent from both maps, its IoU denominator is zero. This chapter reports Undefined rather than silently setting it to zero or one. A larger evaluation can choose a documented absent-class policy, but it must not conceal which convention it used. Averaging several class scores also differs from pooling all pixels into one count.

Boundary accuracy can matter beyond an aggregate overlap. A missed thin structure may have a small pixel count yet be important for a downstream task. State whether the goal is region coverage, boundary placement, instance separation or another output. A single favorable mask metric cannot certify every property.

sections.title: Pixel clustering can create regions without naming objects
sections.body:
K-means can group pixels using intensities or color features. Choose a number of clusters, initialize centers, assign each observation to its closest center, and update each center to the mean of its assigned observations. Repeating these phases reduces the stated squared-distance objective under the selected conventions.

[figure: ss-clustering]

A grayscale example with k=2, k=3 or k=6 changes the number of intensity groups. More groups can preserve more tonal distinctions, but they do not automatically correspond to more object categories. Different parts of one object can fall into separate groups because illumination or texture differs. Two objects can share a group because their observed values are similar.

**A cluster ID has no semantic name by itself.** Cluster 1 is not necessarily Person, Chair or Background. An additional mapping or supervised task is needed to attach those meanings. K-means also does not automatically separate instances that share appearance. Counting nonempty clusters is therefore different from counting objects.

The experiment runs actual Lloyd assignment and centroid phases on the declared scene. It supports mean-RGB grayscale or RGB features, with an optional weighted spatial coordinate. Position changes the distance problem: nearby pixels can become more likely to group even when their colors are less similar. It does not provide object identity as a hidden feature.

The table lists every center, membership count and before/after update cost. Exact ties choose the first cluster. Empty groups retain their old centers. Initialization and k can affect the outcome, so a fixed iteration count is a bounded computation rather than a promise of a global optimum. Compare results under one objective before judging improvement; costs from different feature scales are not directly comparable measures of semantic quality.

visuals.predict: Will changing grayscale to RGB necessarily preserve pixel cluster assignments?
visuals.reflect: Execute assignment and mean updates, inspect the declared feature vectors/SSE, and explain why cluster IDs have no built-in semantic names.

sections.title: A spatial score tensor precedes the label map
sections.body:
A learned multiclass segmentation system can return a score for each class at each output location. Its tensor can have shape C×H×W, with C class channels. A per-location softmax normalizes across those C scores. Argmax then selects a class ID to create an H×W label map.

[figure: ss-scores]

The class axis is different from the spatial axes. An image’s red, green and blue channels are input measurements; class channels such as Person, Purse or Sidewalk are prediction scores. A deeper feature channel is another representation again. Calling all three “channels” does not make their interpretations interchangeable.

**A score map contains information that a hard mask discards.** A location with two almost tied classes and a location with one strongly preferred class can have the same argmax label. The selected ID loses the relative scores. Normalized values also do not automatically establish calibration or correctness on an unfamiliar scene.

Spatial dimensions must match the intended target or be related through a specified alignment. If the network produces a coarse map, a rule is needed to connect it with the original image locations. Interpolation, learned upsampling and cropping make different assumptions. A map with the desired dimensions can still have incorrect boundaries or categories.

Work the tensor check: for five categories and a 12×16 output grid, there are 960 class scores and 192 hard labels. A single 12×16 numeric image does not preserve all five distributions. When measuring a loss or visualizing a class response, identify which representation you are using.

sections.title: Predict the center of a local patch
sections.body:
A straightforward pixel classifier extracts a patch around one image location, runs a classifier on that patch and assigns the result to its center. Repeat for each eligible pixel. A patch showing part of a cow and surrounding grass can supply context for the center’s class rather than simply thresholding one intensity.

[figure: ss-sliding]

The patch extent determines the visible context. A small neighborhood can preserve precise local structure but omit information needed to distinguish similar appearances. A broader patch can include useful object context while requiring more computation or complicating boundary interpretation.
