The prediction target remains the selected center, not a class assigned indiscriminately to every pixel in the patch.

**Adjacent patches overlap substantially.** Running a complete network independently on every patch can repeat many early computations. If the network’s operations and interfaces permit it, whole-image computation can reuse local feature work and return spatial responses together.

Boundary handling must also be defined. A patch near the image edge may require padding, cropping or omission. The chosen rule affects which original locations have predictions and what evidence they receive. A valid response grid can therefore be smaller than the input even without pooling.

The experiment applies the same affine-head weights to a flattened region and as a spatial filter. Their equivalence requires matching input regions and preprocessing.

sections.title: Convolutionize a classifier without inventing new weights
sections.body:
An affine layer over a fixed-size feature tensor computes weighted sums and biases. The same coefficient arrangement can be viewed as filters covering that tensor’s entire spatial extent. Applied to a larger compatible feature map, those filters produce a spatial grid of responses instead of one score vector.

[figure: ss-convolutionize]

The original example uses a three-channel 2×2 tensor and two output neurons. Each neuron has twelve input coefficients. Together they have **24 weights**, whether drawn as dense connections or two 3-channel 2×2 filters. If each neuron has a bias, retain two biases in both descriptions; the parameter total then becomes 26.

Equivalence requires matching the flatten order, channels, spatial extent, coefficients, bias and operation convention. A coefficient belonging to red/top-left cannot be silently reassigned to another channel or location. The browser experiment uses channel–row–column order and neural-library correlation convention, then lists every product.

At the original input size, each filter has one valid spatial response, exactly equal to its affine score. Increasing the input to side n gives two maps of side n−1 for this 2×2 head. Parameter count remains fixed because weights are reused at each valid region.

**Converting the interface changes where scores are produced, not what the model learned.** A classifier trained to recognize an image category can produce local responses after a compatible conversion. Those responses do not by themselves supply fine-grained pixel supervision, exact original-resolution masks or verified object boundaries. A segmentation objective and appropriate spatial architecture are still needed.

warnings.message: Replacing a dense classifier head with convolutional filters creates shared spatial responses. It does not by itself guarantee one prediction per original pixel or train the model for segmentation. Output stride, resolution handling, alignment and spatial supervision still matter.

sections.title: Check the products, not just the diagram
sections.body:
The equivalence experiment specifies a three-channel tensor and two affine heads. The input value at channel k and location (r,c) is 0.2(k+1)+0.03r−0.01c. Coefficients and biases are declared arithmetic values that can be edited; they are not presented as a pretrained semantic classifier.

[figure: ss-equivalence]

For a selected two-by-two region, flatten its twelve values in the stated order. Multiply each by its head coefficient, sum the products and add the bias. The corresponding filter response uses those same values and parameters. The side-by-side results therefore agree by construction, and the term table permits independent verification.

**Weight sharing changes dependencies.** Editing one coefficient changes every map location where that coefficient multiplies an input value. It does not add a new parameter for every output location. Changing input size can add responses while retaining the same parameter set.

A mismatch is informative. If the two calculations disagree, inspect ordering, offset, padding, bias and kernel convention before blaming numerical learning. The experiment has no parameter fitting step, so an arithmetic disagreement cannot be explained by a different training outcome.

Work a dimension case: input side four, head extent two, stride one and no padding. There are three valid rows and three valid columns, giving nine responses per head. This is a spatial score grid, not sixteen original pixel labels. The difference explains why the phrase “all pixels at once” needs a spatial-domain convention.

visuals.predict: What should happen to the parameter count when the input becomes larger?
visuals.reflect: Compare each affine patch result with its corresponding shared-filter response. Trace a coefficient edit across multiple locations.

sections.title: A local class response is not yet a precise segmentation
sections.body:
A convolutionized image classifier can produce heatmaps showing where its current features support a class response. Larger inputs provide more regions to evaluate. The map can help localize relevant evidence, but its values and spatial resolution depend on the original network’s receptive fields and strides.

[figure: ss-heatmaps]

A class response can be strong over background context associated with an object, or over several objects sharing an appearance. A weak response can occur at an object boundary even when an image-level category is correct. Turning a heatmap into a mask requires an explicit prediction rule and evaluation against the intended spatial target.

**Classification supervision and segmentation supervision differ.** An image label can reward a model for finding enough evidence somewhere in the image. A pixel target requires the category assignment at each eligible location. Converting a fully connected layer to filters preserves its computation; it does not create missing location-specific labels or guarantee that the learned evidence aligns with object boundaries.

The arithmetic maps in the browser use declared weights and raw values. Each is rescaled only for display. Their brightness is not a calibrated probability, and a different display range can make the same response look stronger or weaker. Compare the listed scores when testing exact equality or magnitude.

This distinction motivates a fully convolutional segmentation model trained with a spatial loss and a way to relate coarse responses to image pixels. The [original FCN work](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4038) connects classifier conversion with those additional steps rather than equating an unmodified category heatmap with a complete pixel classifier.

sections.title: Pooling changes the spatial information available
sections.body:
Pooling or strided operations reduce a feature map’s spatial sampling. That can expand context and reduce later computational work, but it can also discard detail relevant to boundaries and thin structures. A coarse class map may identify the broad region of an object while missing its precise shape.

[figure: ss-coarse]

Suppose a two-by-two average contains values 0.1,0.9,0.9,0.1. Its result is 0.5. The opposite arrangement also gives 0.5. The pooled value contains no indication of which of those arrangements supplied it. Returning to a larger grid cannot uniquely choose between them from that number alone.

**Spatial size and information content are separate properties.** Repeating a coarse value into several output cells creates more samples without restoring their original distinctions. A learned decoder can use correlations, priors or other feature paths to estimate plausible detail. That estimate should not be described as recovery of uniquely measured information when the coarse representation is ambiguous.

A deeper feature map can contain useful semantic context while having lower spatial resolution. Its learned representation may retain some detail across channels, but there is no blanket guarantee that every local distinction remains. The design problem is to combine the needed context with sufficient evidence about location.

The following experiments expose both sides. Transposed convolution shows exactly how a larger output is calculated. Kernel training shows what one decoder can fit. Fine-feature fusion supplies observed information that a coarse-only path omitted. Keeping those mechanisms distinct explains why an upsampling layer and a skip connection solve different parts of the problem.

sections.title: Transposed convolution scatters contributions
sections.body:
A forward correlation gathers an input neighborhood into one weighted output. The corresponding transposed operator sends each input value into several output locations using kernel-scaled contributions. Contributions from different input sites are added where they overlap.

[figure: ss-scatter]

For input location (r,c), kernel offset (u,v), stride s and padding p, add input[r,c]×kernel[u,v] to output[rs−p+u,cs−p+v] when that location belongs to the selected output domain. A value at one input site therefore scales a whole kernel placement. The output is an accumulation of these placements, not a set of independently assigned copied pixels.

For dilation one, the forward output side is floor((n+2p−k)/s)+1. A 4×4 input with kernel three and padding one therefore returns 4×4 at stride one and 2×2 at stride two. The transpose demonstration begins with a declared 2×2 numeric input and a 3×3 kernel. Advance one site at a time to see its actual products and current overlap sums.

**Overlaps must be summed.** Replacing an earlier contribution with a later one implements a different operation. The trace identifies out-of-domain contributions, which are discarded under the chosen shape rather than clamped onto the border.

Raw responses can be negative or exceed an image intensity range. The experiment preserves their numbers and reports separate display normalization. It is an exact arithmetic operator demonstration, not an image generated by a trained segmentation network.

visuals.predict: Which input sites contribute to an overlapping output position?
visuals.reflect: Scatter one site at a time; inspect discarded border contributions and explain the difference between output domain and zero-appending.

sections.title: The output-size choice resolves stride ambiguity
sections.body:
With dilation one, transposed-convolution output side length is $(n-1)s-2p+k+o$, where n is input side, s stride, p padding, k kernel side and o the output-size choice often called output padding. For n=2, s=2, p=1 and k=3, the result is 3+o.

[figure: ss-output-size]

The four-by-four illustration therefore needs o=1, or an equivalent explicit output-size convention. At o=0, the output is three-by-three. The missing choice matters numerically because it determines which scattered border contributions belong to the domain.

**Output padding does not mean appending zero-valued output pixels.** A newly selected border location can receive nonzero kernel products. The experiment calculates those values. With an all-one kernel and nonzero input, compare choice zero and one, then inspect the extra row and column rather than assuming they are zero.

Stride creates this ambiguity because several input sizes can map to the same forward output size after the floor operation. For kernel three, stride two and padding one, both a three-by-three and four-by-four input can produce a two-by-two forward output. The transpose needs a selected domain to distinguish those cases.

The browser interface uses choices from zero to stride−1 with fixed dilation one. Changing stride updates those bounds and resets the scatter trace. The [ConvTranspose2d documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.modules.conv.ConvTranspose2d.html) distinguishes output-shape resolution from adding zeros to the calculation. All kernel, padding and shape parameters remain explicit.

warnings.message: The illustrated 2×2→4×4 transposed operation omits an output-size choice. With kernel3, stride2, padding1 and dilation1, the default size is3; size4 requires output padding1 or an equivalent explicitly selected output domain.

reference.title: PyTorch: ConvTranspose2d shape and transpose semantics

sections.title: A transpose is not a general inverse
sections.body:
For a fixed kernel and domain, a forward convolutional operation can be represented by a matrix A acting on flattened samples. The transposed operation uses $A^T$. Its defining relation is an inner-product identity: $(Ax)^Ty=x^T(A^Ty)$. This is different from an inverse identity such as $A^{-1}Ax=x$.

[figure: ss-adjoint]

A four-by-four input contains sixteen scalar values, while the stride-two example returns four. Its linear matrix has four rows and sixteen columns. It cannot uniquely retain every possible input vector. Different inputs can have the same output, so no general decoder can recover all originals from those four values alone.

**A backward input gradient uses the transpose of the forward local linear operator.** That relationship helps explain why transposed convolution appears in gradient computations and learned decoders. It does not turn the transpose into a reconstruction guarantee. Nonlinearities and pooling add their own information loss and backward conventions.

A contracting VGG-style path can reduce a 224-wide image representation through a 7-wide grid to a 1-wide representation. An expanding path can reverse that sequence of sizes through learned upsampling and unpooling. Unpooling may place values using recorded pooling locations when those are available; it cannot invent all discarded nonmaximal values. Matching the contracting path’s sizes is therefore a structural correspondence, not a guarantee of reproducing its original image.

The term “deconvolution” is often used informally for transposed convolution in network diagrams. Actual deconvolution as inverse estimation is a different problem with assumptions about the forward process and noise. Calling an expanding network “upside down” describes its organization, not proof that it inverts the contracting network.

Work a counterexample: two opposite two-by-two arrangements average to 0.5. Any deterministic reconstruction receiving only that pooled value must return the same output for both. The limitation comes from missing information, regardless of how many layers the decoder contains.

warnings.message: An expanding network or a layer called “deconvolution” is not a general inverse of the contracting network. Transposed convolution uses the transpose operator; lost information prevents unique recovery without additional assumptions or evidence.

reference.title: PyTorch: ConvTranspose2d shape and transpose semantics

sections.title: Fit a decoder rather than assume it restores detail
sections.body:
A learnable upsampling kernel changes how coarse values contribute to a larger output. Its coefficients can be fitted to targets using a reconstruction or segmentation objective. Learning supplies a data-dependent rule; it does not remove ambiguity in the input contract.

[figure: ss-learned-upsample]

The experiment trains nine actual coefficients in a three-by-three transposed kernel. Input is four-by-four, stride two, padding one and output-size choice one, giving an eight-by-eight output. Mean squared error is averaged over the 64 raw responses, and every coefficient gradient sums its scattered contributions to output residuals.

Target A and Target B are opposite 0.1/0.9 checker arrangements. Both average to the same four-by-four input of 0.5. Train against A and observe its measured error decrease. The fitted output can become worse for B because the same input supplies no evidence about which target was intended.

**This is actual fitting on an explicitly reduced reconstruction task.** It is not a trained semantic decoder for cats or road boundaries. Raw outputs are used in loss and gradients; grayscale clipping affects only display. The coefficient table lets you inspect whether an apparent improvement came from an actual update.

Changing the selected target retains parameters and starts a new objective history at the current update. Reset provides a comparable initialization. This distinction is useful when comparing a new fitting objective with a separate evaluation target rather than conflating all changes into one loss curve.

visuals.predict: Can a deterministic decoder distinguish two targets with the same reduced input?
visuals.reflect: Fit one target and then both. Inspect actual coefficients and both MSEs, and derive the 0.16 two-target lower bound.

sections.title: Identical coarse inputs cannot select two different truths
sections.body:
The two reconstruction targets have an exact information conflict. At each output position, one target is 0.1 and the other 0.9. Their shared pooled input is 0.5 everywhere. A deterministic decoder receiving that same input cannot emit a different answer merely because a different target exists outside its observation.

[figure: ss-ambiguity]

For a predicted scalar v, the average of its squared errors to 0.1 and 0.9 equals $(v-0.5)^2+0.16$. Averaging over all positions preserves that identity. Thus the smallest possible mean two-target MSE is 0.16, achieved by the constant 0.5 output. A larger deterministic network with the same input cannot lower this information-theoretic bound.

**A convincing fitted pattern is not proof of uniquely recovered detail.** Training only on A can learn its regular arrangement. If the world can also supply B under the same observation, that learned preference is a prior or dataset convention. New evidence is needed to distinguish the two cases reliably.

A stochastic generator could choose different plausible completions, but a sampled completion still would not identify which hidden original produced the observation. Producing alternatives and recovering a known target are different output contracts.

Skip paths can supply details lost at the bottleneck. Their benefit depends on the information they carry and how the output head uses it.

sections.title: Combine coarse context with observed fine detail
sections.body:
A segmentation decoder can combine deeper, coarser representations with shallower, finer ones. The goal is to use broader context without relying only on a spatially sparse bottleneck for precise boundaries. The two paths must be aligned and their combination specified.

[figure: ss-skip]

In the FCN-style example, predictions from different feature depths are brought to compatible spatial grids and combined as class scores. In original U-Net, cropped encoder features are concatenated with decoder features along the channel axis, then transformed by later convolutions. **Adding aligned class scores and concatenating feature channels are different operations.**

The original FCN-32s design predicts from a stride-32 representation and upsamples to the target grid. FCN-16s also incorporates stride-16 pool4 predictions: upsample the coarse prediction by two, align it with the finer class-score map, add, then upsample toward the image grid. FCN-8s additionally incorporates stride-8 pool3 predictions. The suffix describes the finest prediction stride before the final upsampling, not the number of classes or learned layers. Cropping/alignment and matching class channels make these sums meaningful.

The small fitted pixel head receives a pooled observation and, optionally, its corresponding fine observation. With only coarse means, within-block detail is missing. Adding observed fine values supplies information about those locations; three logistic coefficients learn the class mapping from separately provided targets.

The example includes irregular foreground shapes, a hole and thin extensions, with fixed observation noise. Its fine input is an observed grayscale value, not a secretly supplied target label. Training and evaluation variants are separately listed. Compare query masks, overlap and measured losses after fitting both feature modes from reset.

**This reduced model does not pretend to be a complete FCN or U-Net.** It makes the contribution of retained evidence and an actual learned head inspectable. A full model would learn richer representations and their fusion under a spatial objective. More fine detail alone does not guarantee correct semantics; the mapping and context still matter.

visuals.predict: Can a learned coarse-only pixel head represent the gaps removed by pooling?
visuals.reflect: Fit both feature modes from comparable starts. Compare actual query maps and IoU; separately check original U-Net crops and output size.

sections.title: Original U-Net crops and concatenates
sections.body:
Original U-Net has a contracting path for context and an expanding path for spatial prediction. Its encoder applies two unpadded three-by-three convolutions per block, followed by two-by-two pooling. Its decoder upsamples, crops a corresponding encoder feature map, concatenates channels and applies further convolutions.

[figure: ss-unet]

The original architecture takes an input side of 572 and returns an output side of 388. Each unpadded three-by-three convolution shrinks a spatial side by two. These reductions accumulate through the network. The mismatch is part of that architecture; it is not evidence that an output mask should be stretched silently to the entire input tile.

At the first decoder level, a 28-wide bottleneck upsamples to 56, while the corresponding encoder map is 64 wide. Cropping four cells from each side aligns the skip map. Later pairings require larger crops. At the final level, 568-wide encoder features are cropped to the 392-wide upsampled decoder grid before two convolutions produce 388.

**Channel concatenation preserves both feature sets as separate channels.** It requires matching spatial grids, not equal channel counts. Subsequent convolutions learn combinations of the joined features. A residual addition would require compatible channel structure and would form sums instead.

The independent geometry inspector computes every encoder size, crop and decoder output. At 572 it reproduces the original 388 result. This inspector is separate from the tiny fitted pixel head. The [original U-Net paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04597) supplies the architecture; its clinical/example performance is not inferred from the reduced exercise.

sections.title: A dense map supports several application contracts
sections.body:
Road-scene segmentation can distinguish regions such as road, vehicles, people, vegetation and structures. That spatial representation can inform a larger perception/action pipeline. A correct-looking overlay is not evidence that every object was recognized, that uncertainty is resolved or that a complete driving system is reliable.

[figure: ss-applications]

Medical image segmentation can propose tissue regions, cells or vessel structures under a specified acquisition and labeling convention. Instance-level cell separation and semantic tissue labeling are different tasks even when both produce colored maps. A mask alone does not constitute a verified clinical conclusion.

Scene understanding can assign categories to surfaces or objects in an indoor environment. A three-dimensional scene representation may carry labels on points or surfaces rather than only on a two-dimensional pixel grid. The observation, coordinate frame, visibility and annotation convention must still be stated.

**Choose an evaluation that matches the output.** Region overlap, boundary accuracy, individual-object separation and downstream action requirements emphasize different properties. Thin vessels, narrow road regions and gaps between furniture can carry important information despite occupying a small number of pixels.

The application diagrams here are reconstructed task relationships, not fabricated measured results on original driving, tissue, retina or indoor-scene photographs. The computational exercises use declared arrays and actual reduced models to expose the mechanisms without borrowing the appearance of a validated deployed system.

sections.title: From describing an image to constructing one
sections.body:
Segmentation receives an observed image and predicts a structured description of it. Visual generation instead constructs image values. These tasks share neural-network components, but their interfaces and learning questions differ. A semantic mask is not a photograph; an image generator does not automatically supply object identities, boundaries or a semantic explanation of its pixels.

[figure: ss-generation]

A generative adversarial network, or GAN, couples a generator with a discriminator. The generator constructs candidate samples. The discriminator learns to distinguish samples drawn from a declared data distribution from samples produced by the generator. Their objectives create a feedback loop: the discriminator learns evidence that separates the two sources, and the generator receives gradients that change its outputs in response.

The GAN framework was introduced in 2014 by Ian Goodfellow and collaborators. Its central idea is an adversarial training procedure rather than a particular image size, convolutional architecture or photographic style. A small dense network can instantiate that procedure. Realistic large images require a much more substantial model and data setup than the numerical experiment in this lecture.

**Generating a plausible sample and identifying the content of an existing image are different capabilities.** A generator can create an image that resembles a training population without recognizing every object in it. A discriminator's source score can reward learned visual evidence without being a general object classifier. Neither role removes the need to define the data population and evaluation criteria.

The following sections connect the image representation, objectives and gradient paths. The final experiment generates actual four-by-four grayscale patterns from a two-dimensional latent input. It is deliberately small enough to inspect every parameter and every generated pixel. Its outputs are calculated by the trained model; they are not preselected pictures standing in for learning.

sections.title: An image vector is a representation, not a category
sections.body:
An n-by-n grayscale image contains $n^2$ scalar samples. Flattening it produces a vector of length N=$n^2$ under a chosen row/column order. An RGB image has three samples per location and therefore $3n^2$ scalar components. Flattening changes the indexing interface; it does not change what the image depicts or make its category known.

[figure: ss-vectors]

For example, the browser generator produces sixteen sigmoid outputs. Reshaping them row-major gives four rows and four columns. The same output index always refers to the same image location. A vertical bright stripe and a horizontal bright stripe use different component patterns even though they contain the same number of bright pixels.

Describing a vector as a “dog image” requires semantic evidence about the sample. A dimension count alone only says how many scalar values are stored. Random sixteen-dimensional values form a valid numeric image array, but not necessarily a recognizable object or a draw from the intended data distribution.

The final generator uses sigmoid output units, so each component lies strictly between zero and one for finite logits. The declared target intensities are 0.1 and 0.9. Those ranges make a direct grayscale display possible and avoid treating an unconstrained output logit as an intensity. No RGB interpretation or photographic realism is silently attached to this grayscale array.

Spatial structure also matters. A dense output layer can assign a separate learned mapping to every pixel; a convolutional generator shares local mappings across locations. Both can produce image arrays, but they impose different parameter-sharing assumptions. This lecture's small dense model makes the adversarial update transparent. The earlier transposed-convolution experiment explains a spatial building block without claiming that either small model reproduces a large image-generation system.

sections.title: Latent randomness and the generated distribution
sections.body:
A generator maps a latent vector z to an image, written $G(z;\theta_g)$. The parameters $\theta_g$ specify the current mapping. A prior distribution specifies how latent vectors are sampled. Together, the prior and the mapping induce a distribution over generated images, $P_G$.

[figure: ss-prior]

In the experiment, z has two independent coordinates, each uniform on [−1,1]. A seeded pseudorandom procedure draws sixteen training vectors for each update. The generator transforms those vectors through four tanh hidden units and sixteen sigmoid output units. Sampling more z values supplies more input draws; it does not change the fitted parameters.

**Random input does not guarantee varied output.** A generator may ignore one or both latent coordinates. If every z maps to the same image, its output distribution is concentrated on that image despite the broad latent prior. The constructed constant-pattern preset makes this possibility explicit: the latent-path coefficients are zero and the output biases produce the vertical pattern.

Changing the prior changes which parts of the generator's input space are visited. Changing the generator changes the image returned at a fixed z. These are different interventions. A controlled training comparison keeps a fixed set of probe latents so that image changes can be attributed to parameter updates rather than to drawing a different batch.

There is no one-to-one requirement between latent vectors and target examples. The desired population in the tiny experiment has two equally weighted patterns; the generator need not be told which pattern corresponds to each z. Adversarial feedback acts on distributions of samples. Whether both patterns are actually represented must be examined separately from whether an individual generated image looks close to one of them.

sections.title: What each player observes and changes
sections.body:
Let $P_D$ denote the declared data distribution and $P_G$ the distribution induced by the current generator. A discriminator receives an image x and returns a score $D(x;\theta_d)$ between zero and one. During training, a data sample receives source label one and a generator sample receives source label zero.

[figure: ss-players]

These labels describe the sample's origin in the training procedure. They do not establish whether an image is true, useful, ethically acceptable or physically possible. A high source score means the fitted discriminator currently treats the sample as more similar to its data-source examples under its learned decision function.

For a discriminator update, data images and generated images are both inputs to a binary learning problem. Increasing the real-example score and decreasing the fake-example score improves the declared discriminator objective. The generator's parameters stay fixed during that update; its current images supply the fake examples.

For a generator update, the current discriminator provides a differentiable signal on generated images. The generator changes its parameters to improve its selected objective against that fixed discriminator. It does not receive a pixel-by-pixel target paired with each latent vector. This differs from the earlier reconstruction model, which minimized squared error to an explicitly specified target array.

The tiny experiment's data distribution is exactly two four-by-four patterns with equal weight: one vertical stripe and one horizontal stripe. Calling them “real” means they are samples from this declared target population. The discriminator is a fitted dense network, not an oracle. Its scores must be interpreted alongside the generated pixel arrays and distribution diagnostics.

Keep three things separate when tracing an update: the input samples, the parameters allowed to change, and the scalar objective being optimized. Losing any one of these distinctions can make a formally correct derivative implement the wrong training operation.

sections.title: Keep objective signs and optimization direction together
sections.body:
For a discriminator, the original value uses a real-sample log term and a fake-sample log-rejection term:

$$V_D=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_D}[\log D(x)]+\mathbb{E}_{z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))].$$

The discriminator maximizes this value. Equivalently, it minimizes the negative value $L_D=-V_D$. The two descriptions give matching parameter updates if their scaling is the same: gradient ascent on the value equals gradient descent on its negative.

[figure: ss-signs]

With one real score 0.8 and one fake score 0.2, the value is $\log(0.8)+\log(0.8)$, approximately −0.4463. Its negative loss is approximately 0.4463. Increasing real acceptance and decreasing fake acceptance moves the value toward zero from below and reduces the negative loss. Minimizing the unnegated value would reverse the discriminator's intended learning direction.

The original generator minimax term is different:

$$L_G^{\text{minimax}}=\mathbb{E}_{z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))].$$

The generator minimizes this term while the discriminator is fixed. Increasing a fake score from 0.1 to 0.8 changes the term from approximately −0.1054 to −1.6094. The term falls, so that change improves the original minimized generator objective. A negative scalar is not evidence of a faulty loss; its optimization direction and meaning determine how to interpret it.

A training implementation must state whether it stores a maximized value or a minimized loss. Writing “log loss” without its sign can hide a consequential choice. The experiment shows both discriminator forms and labels the chosen generator objective explicitly. For batches, the discriminator uses the mean real term plus the mean fake term, matching the sum of two expectations rather than silently averaging both groups together into a different scale.

warnings.message: The displayed discriminator log expression is a value to maximize. Calling it a loss without stating the sign is ambiguous: the binary negative-log loss is its negative and is minimized. The displayed formula and ascent direction are consistent; reversing that direction without negating the formula would be incorrect.

reference.title: Goodfellow et al.: Generative Adversarial Nets

sections.title: The original and non-saturating generator terms differ
sections.body:
Let a be the discriminator logit for a generated image and $p=\sigma(a)$ its sigmoid score. The original generator term is $\log(1-p)$. Its derivative with respect to a is −p. When the discriminator strongly rejects a fake image, p is near zero, so this scalar derivative is small.

[figure: ss-saturation]

The commonly used non-saturating alternative minimizes $-\log p$. Its logit derivative is p−1, which is near −1 when p is near zero. Both derivatives encourage an increase in the fake logit under scalar gradient descent, but they can have very different magnitudes. They are distinct objectives; substituting one for the other must be an explicit choice.

At p=0.01, the original derivative is −0.01 and the alternative derivative is −0.99. This comparison concerns the derivative with respect to the discriminator's fake logit. The actual generator parameter gradient also includes the discriminator's input derivative and the generator's parameter derivative. A large logit derivative does not guarantee a large or useful update through every other part of the chain.

The objective explorer adjusts real and fake logits and calculates all four quantities: discriminator value, discriminator negative loss, original generator term and alternative generator term. Its optional one-step operation changes an independent scalar fake logit to illustrate the sign. It is not presented as actual generator training. The image experiment later performs the complete parameter update.

Stable implementations compute these log terms from logits rather than subtracting a sigmoid score from one and then taking a potentially underflowed logarithm. The browser uses stable softplus forms. Extreme confidence therefore retains a finite objective and the appropriate derivative. This numerical safeguard preserves the chosen mathematics; it does not resolve adversarial instability or missing sample diversity.

visuals.predict: When fake acceptance is near zero, which generator logit derivative is smaller?
visuals.reflect: Keep signs and descent/ascent directions explicit. Separate a scalar-logit illustration from full parameter training.

warnings.message: The original minimized generator expression log(1−D(fake)) must not be confused with the positive real-target cross-entropy −log D(fake). They are different objectives. Both are shown explicitly here; the original expression is retained and its negative values are expected.

reference.title: Goodfellow et al.: Generative Adversarial Nets

sections.title: Alternate updates without mixing their targets
sections.body:
A GAN training cycle usually includes a discriminator update followed by a generator update. In the first step, the generator produces fake samples with its current fixed parameters. The discriminator fits source labels: data examples one, generated examples zero. Only $\theta_d$ changes.

[figure: ss-alternation]

In the second step, the discriminator's parameters are fixed. Generated samples pass through it, and the generator receives gradients of its selected objective. Only $\theta_g$ changes. With a non-saturating generator loss, the generated samples are encouraged toward discriminator score one; this does not mean they were relabeled as data examples for a discriminator update.

The same network can therefore participate in two different computational roles. During discriminator fitting, it is the model being optimized. During generator fitting, it is a fixed differentiable function through which an input gradient is calculated. Freezing its parameters must not erase the path from the objective back to generated pixels.

**A heading or arrow is less reliable than the actual update path.** Identify which parameter vector changes, which is held fixed, and where the gradient terminates. If the generator goes from version one to version two while the discriminator stays fixed, the operation is a generator update even if a label calls it discriminator learning.

The image experiment exposes separate D and G buttons plus a paired-cycle button. Its counters are independent, so you can deliberately perform several updates of one player. A fixed opposite network lets the before/after comparison for a single update refer to one objective on the same latent batch. Across alternating updates, however, the opponent changes. There is no guarantee that both diagnostic curves fall together or that one curve summarizes overall sample quality.

warnings.message: The heading calls this discriminator learning, but the depicted update changes G from one version to another while D stays fixed. That is a generator update. Gradients pass through the fixed discriminator to update G.

sections.title: A fixed discriminator still supplies an input gradient
sections.body:
For one latent input, the generator creates x=$G(z;\theta_g)$ and the discriminator evaluates its logit a=$a_D(x;\theta_d)$. A generator gradient follows the chain from the selected scalar loss to a, from a to every generated pixel, and from those pixels to the generator's parameters.

[figure: ss-gradient]

Symbolically, the parameter gradient has the form:

$$\frac{\partial L_G}{\partial\theta_g}=\frac{\partial L_G}{\partial a}\frac{\partial a}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta_g}.$$

Holding $\theta_d$ fixed means that those weights are not updated in this step. It does not set $\partial a/\partial x$ to zero. The discriminator's current weights determine how a pixel perturbation affects its logit, so they remain necessary for backpropagation into the generator.

The image experiment displays a four-by-four map of these input derivatives for the current generated query. A positive derivative means increasing that pixel alone would locally increase the discriminator logit; a negative derivative means it would locally decrease it. The map is a local differential description, not a semantic segmentation or a promise about large image changes.

The selected generator logit derivative multiplies this map. Backpropagation then passes through the generator's output sigmoids, its output weights, hidden tanh derivatives and latent inputs. All ninety-two generator parameter gradients are calculated analytically. A single update uses the complete gradient evaluated at the old parameter state, avoiding accidental mixing of old and newly changed coefficients within one step.

To test the distinction, perform a G-only update and inspect both parameter tables. G changes while D remains identical. The generated image and D's score can nevertheless change because D receives a different input. Fixed parameters do not imply fixed output when the input is allowed to move.

sections.title: Train a complete miniature image GAN
sections.body:
The live GAN has ninety-two generator parameters and seventy-three discriminator parameters, for 165 total. G maps two latent coordinates through four tanh units to sixteen sigmoid pixels. D maps sixteen pixels through four tanh units to a sigmoid source score. Every weight and bias is inspectable.

[figure: ss-image-gan]

For each D update, the two real patterns contribute equally to the real term. Sixteen generated images from seeded uniform latent vectors contribute to the fake term. For each G update, sixteen latent vectors provide the chosen generator objective, with D held fixed. The update is ordinary gradient descent on the selected minimized objective; no pretrained coefficients or hidden sample substitution are used.

Start with a D-only step and confirm that only its counter and parameters change. Reset, take a G-only step, and inspect the reverse. Then run one hundred paired cycles. The query image, sixteen fixed-probe images, objective histories and nearest-pattern diagnostics all come from the current fitted model. Their displayed values are recomputed after the actual updates.

The default varying initialization uses seeded small random coefficients. The constant vertical preset is constructed explicitly by removing latent dependence and setting output biases to that pattern. It is a diagnostic starting condition, not evidence that a previous run learned a collapse. Keeping this distinction visible prevents an educational preset from being mistaken for a measured training trajectory.

This model's scale makes complete browser computation practical. It also limits what the experiment establishes. Four-by-four stripes are not anime faces, medical images or real-world photographs. Useful progress here means understanding gradients, optimization direction, generated variation and coverage of the declared two-pattern population. It does not establish quality or stability for a large GAN.

visuals.predict: Can low nearest-target error coexist with a missing target mode?
visuals.reflect: Use separate D/G steps and actual paired training. Inspect frozen parameter vectors, gradient paths, fixed-probe images, errors, counts and variance together.

sections.title: One convincing sample can hide a missing mode
sections.body:
Suppose a generator returns the vertical target pattern for every latent vector. Its nearest-target squared error is zero. Every image is individually plausible under the two-pattern population, yet the horizontal pattern is absent. Good sample fidelity alone therefore does not demonstrate a matching generated distribution.

[figure: ss-coverage]

The experiment reports three complementary diagnostics on sixteen fixed latent probes. Nearest-pattern MSE measures the average squared distance to the closer of the two targets. Nearest-assignment counts show how many samples are closer to each pattern, using the vertical pattern at an exact tie. Mean pixel variance measures how much generated pixel values vary across probes.

Read these together. An almost constant generator can have low nearest MSE and low variance with all probes assigned to one mode. A blurry compromise may have small variation and arbitrary nearest assignments while remaining far from both patterns. Counts split across both targets are not convincing coverage if all corresponding images are poor matches.

Sixteen probes are a small diagnostic sample, not an exact calculation of output probabilities. Nearest assignment partitions image space even for implausible arrays. Pixel variance can increase because of unwanted noise instead of useful structural diversity. No single number is a complete quality measure.

A varying run may concentrate on one pattern even while its samples become sharper. This is an observation to investigate rather than conceal with a handpicked gallery. Compare the actual arrays, counts and variance. Change a seed, objective or update balance and inspect what happens, while keeping each comparison's conditions explicit. In adversarial learning, visual plausibility, distribution coverage and optimization diagnostics answer different questions.

sections.title: Compare actual checkpoints under fixed conditions
sections.body:
Training iteration counts describe how many updates have been performed. They do not by themselves specify model size, data, objective, batch construction, random seed or evaluation conditions. A gallery arranged from early to late samples can illustrate a run, but it cannot establish a universal rule that more iterations always produce better images.

[figure: ss-progress]

The browser records its own initial samples and checkpoints at paired multiples of one hundred cycles. Each checkpoint uses the same fixed probe latents. The gallery therefore shows changes in a specific model's mapping under a specific live run. Checkpoints remain in memory for that run and disappear on reset or leaving the lecture.

Diagnostic losses use the fixed probe batch as well. The D loss and selected G loss belong to current opposing models. When D changes, the function facing G changes; when G changes, D's fake population changes. A rising curve may reflect an opponent's improvement, a poor update or several interacting effects. It is not interchangeable with a supervised validation-loss curve against fixed labels and a fixed data population.

The last-update message provides a narrower comparison: before and after the chosen step, on the same latent batch with the opposite network fixed. This isolates the immediate objective effect more clearly. Even an improved local objective does not prove improved coverage or image quality.

Use checkpoints to make a concrete claim: under this initialization and these update settings, these probe outputs changed in these ways. If the gallery loses one target mode, say so. If errors fall while variance collapses, connect both observations. Reproducible conditions and multiple diagnostics make the visual story more informative than attaching an impressive iteration number to an unexplained image montage.

warnings.message: The image progression does not specify enough model, data, seed or evaluation conditions to reproduce a measured quality trend. Iteration counts alone cannot verify that trend. The live checkpoints here belong to the explicitly declared small model and should be assessed with its actual outputs and diagnostics.

sections.title: Prediction, reconstruction and generation use different evidence
sections.body:
Three operations now connect the lecture. Segmentation maps an observed image to class or instance information at spatial locations. Reconstruction maps a reduced representation back to a larger array under a learned rule. Adversarial generation maps a sampled latent input to an image while a discriminator supplies distribution-level training feedback.

[figure: ss-synthesis]

For segmentation, ask whether outputs represent classes, individual objects, scores or final labels. Identify which spatial detail reaches the prediction head, how different resolutions align and how overlap is evaluated. A class label cannot substitute for an instance ID, and a coarse class response cannot automatically substitute for a full-resolution mask.

For reconstruction, ask which information the input retains. Transposed convolution scatters weighted contributions and adds overlaps; it is not a general inverse. If two fine targets share one reduced input, a deterministic decoder cannot uniquely reconstruct both from that input alone. Skip features help only when they carry additional observed evidence.

For adversarial generation, ask which prior is sampled, which parameter vector changes, which objective is optimized and what the generated population actually contains. A frozen discriminator still supplies an input gradient. A convincing sample may coexist with missing modes, and a loss curve alone does not settle image quality.

The experiments make these questions inspectable: edit a mask, execute pixel clustering, reuse dense weights spatially, trace transposed scatter, fit a decoder, fit coarse/fine pixel heads, compare objective derivatives and train an actual image GAN. The small models isolate mechanisms; their measured outputs belong to their declared arrays and architectures.

The common habit is to track **representation, information, parameters and evaluation** together. A diagram becomes useful when each arrow names a defined transformation and each displayed result has a clear origin. That habit turns an expanding tensor or changing image into an explanation you can test rather than a picture you have to trust.

questions.prompt: Why does an FCN combine shallow and deep features?
choices: To recover spatial detail while retaining semantic information.
To avoid using any labels.
To turn segmentation into one image label.
questions.why: Shallow features have finer resolution; deep features encode broader semantic context.

questions.prompt: Is transposed convolution an exact inverse of every convolution?
choices: Yes.
No.
Only when the image is RGB.
questions.why: It uses the transpose operator and does not generally recover information lost through downsampling.

questions.prompt: During a generator update, can gradients pass through a frozen discriminator?
choices: No, freezing always removes the graph.
Yes, to update the generator while keeping discriminator weights fixed.
Only if the data has labels.
questions.why: The gradient path through the discriminator is needed to tell the generator how to improve.

questions.prompt: Two overlapping people receive the same person label in a pixel map. What additional output is needed for instance segmentation?
choices: A larger number for the person class.
Separate identities or masks assigning pixels to each person.
Only the total number of person pixels.
questions.why: Semantic labels identify the category. Instance segmentation must distinguish individual objects within that category.

questions.prompt: With dilation 1, input size 2, kernel 3, stride 2 and padding 1, what output-padding value gives a transposed-convolution output size of 4?
questions.why: The size is (2−1)×2−2×1+3+o = 3+o, so o=1. Output padding selects the output shape; it does not append zero-valued output pixels.

questions.prompt: A fake image’s discriminator score rises from 0.1 to 0.8. What happens to the original minimax generator term log(1−D(fake))?
choices: It falls from about −0.105 to −1.609, which improves the minimized objective.
It rises, so the generator must reverse its gradient.
It stays fixed because discriminator weights are frozen.
questions.why: A higher fake score makes 1−D smaller and its log more negative. Frozen discriminator weights still allow its output to change as the generator changes the input.

questions.prompt: A box around an irregular chair includes the gap between its legs. Which output can describe that gap as background?
choices: Only an image-level category.
A pixel mask with foreground and background labels.
A higher chair confidence score.
questions.why: A mask describes the labeled set of pixels; a rectangle only specifies an enclosing region.

questions.prompt: Two chairs have semantic ID 1 and instance IDs 1 and 2. What does their shared semantic ID express?
choices: They belong to the same category.
They are one physical object.
Their masks must overlap.
questions.why: Semantic IDs identify categories; separate instance identities distinguish individual objects.

questions.prompt: Does adding many correctly labeled background pixels directly improve foreground IoU?
choices: Yes, they increase its denominator.
No, true negatives do not enter TP/(TP+FP+FN).
Only when Dice is also reported.
questions.why: Foreground overlap depends on intersection and foreground union, unlike whole-map accuracy.

questions.prompt: If TP=6, FP=2 and FN=4, what is foreground Dice?
A Lloyd centroid update uses which vectors?
choices: Only annotated class labels.
The mean of the full observed feature vectors assigned to that cluster.
The brightest pixel in the image.
questions.why: The mean minimizes within-cluster squared distance for fixed assignments.

questions.prompt: Why can adding heavily weighted spatial coordinates change pixel clustering?
choices: It changes the distance objective by adding position terms.
It automatically supplies semantic classes.
It restores the omitted RGB channels.
questions.why: Clustering is defined in the full declared feature space; changed coordinate scale changes nearest-center decisions.

questions.prompt: For C×H×W class scores, over which dimension is per-pixel softmax taken?
choices: H only.
W only.
The C class scores at each location.
questions.why: Each spatial location gets one probability distribution over declared categories.

questions.prompt: After class argmax, what is the shape of the class-ID map?
choices: H×W.
C×H×W unchanged.
One scalar for the entire image.
questions.why: Argmax replaces the class-score vector at each pixel with one integer category ID.

questions.prompt: Why can independent overlapping patch classification repeat computation?
choices: Neighboring patches share many pixels and intermediate neighborhoods.
Every patch must have different weights.
Pixel categories are always independent.
questions.why: Dense convolutional computation can reuse intermediate responses instead of recomputing overlapping local work.

questions.prompt: How many weights and biases belong to two affine heads over a 3×2×2 tensor?
choices: 24 weights and 2 biases.
12 weights and no biases.
26 weights plus 24 biases.
questions.why: Each head uses twelve input coefficients plus one bias: 2×12 weights and two biases.

questions.prompt: What is required for exact dense-to-convolution equivalence?
choices: Matching extent, flatten order, coefficients, bias and operation convention.
Any two filters with the same shape.
Removing the channel dimension.
questions.why: The same sample/coefficient products must be paired; equal parameter counts alone do not prove equality.

questions.prompt: A valid 2×2 head runs on a 6×6 spatial input with stride one. What is each output map size?
questions.why: A valid patch starts at five positions along each axis: 6−2+1=5.

questions.prompt: Does converting a fitted image classifier to shared spatial filters automatically train it for segmentation?
choices: Yes, every response is a pixel category.
No, it preserves the original mapping and still needs suitable spatial supervision and resolution handling.
Only if its bias is zero.
questions.why: Conversion supplies spatial reuse, not new task labels or a guarantee of input-resolution masks.

questions.prompt: A total stride of 32 reduces a 224×224 grid to which illustrative response size?
questions.why: 224/32=7; a coarse grid cannot directly resolve every original pixel boundary.

questions.prompt: Two transposed-convolution contributions reach the same output site. What happens?
choices: The last contribution replaces the first.
Their products are added.
The larger absolute value is selected.
questions.why: Transposed convolution scatters weighted products and sums overlaps; it is not max unpooling.

questions.prompt: Does output padding simply append zero-valued output pixels?
choices: No, it selects the output domain and may expose nonzero border contributions.
Yes, that is its only role.
It changes all kernel coefficients.
questions.why: The selected output extent determines which scatter positions are retained; the additional border need not be zero.

questions.prompt: What identity defines the transpose of a linear operator A?
choices: AᵀAx=x for every x.
⟨Ax,y⟩=⟨x,Aᵀy⟩.
Aᵀ always has the same number of rows as A.
questions.why: The adjoint identity relates inner products; inversion is a separate property.

questions.prompt: Which parameters does the small learned upsampling experiment fit?
choices: Nine coefficients of its 3×3 transposed kernel.
All original U-Net weights.
A hidden pretrained segmentation network.
questions.why: Its explicit four-to-eight spatial decoder contains a nine-parameter scalar kernel.

questions.prompt: Two opposite checker targets share one pooled input. Can a deterministic decoder given only that input return the correct one for both?
choices: Yes, with sufficiently many iterations.
No, the distinguishing evidence is absent.
Yes, if its displayed output is larger.
questions.why: One identical input yields one deterministic output; training cannot identify which lost fine pattern was present.

questions.prompt: For target pairs 0.1 and 0.9, what is the minimum mean two-target MSE per pixel?
choices: 0.16, attained at output 0.5.
0.8, attained at either endpoint.
questions.why: The average squared error is (y−0.5)²+0.16, which has minimum 0.16.

questions.prompt: How do original FCN skip fusion and original U-Net skip fusion differ?
choices: Both only append zeros.
FCN can add aligned class-score maps; U-Net concatenates cropped encoder features with decoder features.
U-Net replaces every fine feature with a class ID.
questions.why: Addition and channel concatenation are different operations with different shape requirements.

questions.prompt: What is the original valid-convolution U-Net output for a 572×572 input?
questions.why: Repeated unpadded convolutions and the decoder geometry yield 388; later same-padding variants have different shape rules.

questions.prompt: An encoder skip has side 64 and the corresponding decoder has side 56. What centered crop is needed?
choices: Four samples per side.
Eight samples per side.
No crop because channels match.
questions.why: The spatial difference is eight, so a centered crop removes four from each side before concatenation.

questions.prompt: How does semantic labeling of a 3D scene differ from a 2D pixel map?
choices: It can attach categories to points or surface elements in 3D coordinates.
It must be one class for the entire room.
It needs no coordinate convention.
questions.why: The spatial domain changes; labels and geometry still need a defined interface.

questions.prompt: Which interface describes adversarial image generation?
choices: Observed image to pixel category IDs only.
Sampled latent vector to a constructed image, trained using discriminator feedback.
A box list converted directly to photographs.
questions.why: The generator constructs image values rather than labeling each pixel of an observed image.

questions.prompt: A 4×4 grayscale vector has sixteen components. Does that count establish that it depicts a dog?
choices: Yes, all sixteen-dimensional images have that category.
No, dimension specifies numeric storage rather than semantics.
Only when flattened row-major.
questions.why: Semantic category requires evidence about the component pattern and context; representation shape alone does not supply it.

questions.prompt: What induces the generated image distribution P_G?
choices: The prior over z together with the current mapping G.
Only the number of output pixels.
Only the discriminator source labels.
questions.why: Sampling the prior and applying the fitted generator determines which outputs occur.

questions.prompt: Can random latent inputs produce identical images for every z?
choices: No, randomness guarantees output diversity.
Yes, the generator may ignore its latent coordinates.
Only when the discriminator is frozen.
questions.why: A constant generator maps a broad prior to one image, so input diversity need not survive the mapping.

questions.prompt: What does source label one mean for the tiny discriminator?
choices: The sample came from the declared data distribution.
Its depicted content is universally true.
It is an instance-segmentation ID.
questions.why: Source supervision distinguishes data-origin and generator-origin samples within the declared procedure.

questions.prompt: If a discriminator maximizes V_D, which minimized objective gives the same direction under the same scale?
choices: V_D unchanged.
−V_D.
The generator term alone.
questions.why: Negating the scalar and switching ascent to descent preserves the parameter update.

questions.prompt: At D(fake)=0.01, which fake-logit derivative belongs to the original minimax generator term?
questions.why: For log(1−sigmoid(a)), the derivative with respect to a is −sigmoid(a).

questions.prompt: Is the non-saturating term −log D(fake) numerically the same loss as log(1−D(fake))?
choices: Yes, they differ only by a name.
No, they are distinct selected objectives with different derivatives.
Only their parameter counts differ.
questions.why: Both encourage greater fake acceptance locally, but their values and gradient magnitudes differ.

questions.prompt: During a D-only update, which fitted parameter vector should change?
choices: Only θ_d.
Only θ_g.
Both without distinction.
questions.why: Current G supplies fake samples while its parameters remain fixed for discriminator fitting.

questions.prompt: Why can D output change after a G-only update although D weights stay fixed?
choices: D receives a changed generated image.
Frozen weights randomly change each evaluation.
Its source label was overwritten.
questions.why: A fixed function can return different outputs for different inputs.

questions.prompt: What is the parameter count of the miniature image GAN?
choices: 92 generator + 73 discriminator = 165.
16 total because there are sixteen pixels.
The full original U-Net count.
questions.why: G uses 2×4+4 plus 4×16+16; D uses 16×4+4 plus 4×1+1.

questions.prompt: Changing a query latent coordinate without pressing a training button does what?
choices: Samples the current mapping without changing fitted weights.
Performs a gradient update.
Changes the real-data population.
questions.why: Query inference evaluates G at a new input; fitting requires an objective gradient and parameter update.

questions.prompt: A generator always produces the exact vertical target and never the horizontal target. What can still fail despite zero nearest-target MSE?
choices: Coverage of the two-pattern population.
Validity of array dimensions.
The existence of a sigmoid output.
questions.why: Every individual sample can match one target while an entire target mode is missing.

questions.prompt: Do sixteen nearest-assignment counts alone prove exact distribution coverage?
choices: Yes, any split is conclusive.
No, samples may be poor matches and sixteen probes are only a small diagnostic set.
Only if the counts sum to sixteen.
questions.why: Nearest assignment classifies even implausible images; quality and sampling uncertainty must also be inspected.

questions.prompt: Why keep the same latent probes across checkpoints?
choices: To isolate changes in the generator mapping from changes in sampled input.
To secretly train on them.
To guarantee both losses always fall.
questions.why: A fixed input comparison makes parameter effects more interpretable; these probes remain outside training.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly helps a decoder distinguish fine targets that share a coarse representation?
choices: Additional observed fine features through an aligned skip path.
A larger displayed tensor alone.
An impressive iteration label.
questions.why: Distinguishing information must reach the decoder; output size and iteration count alone do not supply it.

title: Natural Language Processing
summary: Tokenization, learned word vectors, contextual encoding, BERT objectives, labeled classification, and actual conditional sequence training.

sections.title: Language connects symbols, structure and purpose
sections.body:
**Natural language processing turns human language into inputs and outputs that a computational system can work with.** A message can contain words, characters, punctuation and other symbols. Grammar helps organize them, while a speaker's purpose and the surrounding situation affect what the message communicates. Recognizing the characters is only the beginning of interpreting the text.

[figure: np-language]

Language can express thoughts, share information and communicate feelings. Written, spoken and signed language use different physical signals, but all require conventions that connect forms with communicative roles. A text-based model receives a representation of one of those forms. It does not automatically observe a speaker's gesture, tone or physical surroundings.

Scientific information search, business message processing and extraction from health documents are among the possible application settings. You encounter NLP when searching a document, sorting messages, translating a sentence, extracting a name, asking a question or reading a generated summary. These examples require different output interfaces. A spam classifier returns a category, an entity recognizer marks spans, and a translator returns a new sequence. Calling all three “understanding” must not conceal which observable task each system actually performs.

Computers can process large amounts of text quickly, but a numeric text representation does not arrive with every relevant meaning already attached. A model needs a defined learning problem or an explicit rule system. Its success must be evaluated on the intended inputs and outputs rather than assumed from the existence of fluent text.

The chapter follows the information through a pipeline: text becomes tokens; tokens become numeric representations; models use those representations for contextual prediction, classification or generation. At each step, ask what is retained, what is discarded, and what evidence is needed to interpret the result.

sections.title: The same word can express different meanings
sections.body:
“The children sat on the bank and watched the boats” suggests the edge of a river. “I need to go to the bank to deposit some money” suggests a financial institution. The character sequence bank is identical, but surrounding words support different interpretations.

[figure: np-bank]

**A token's identity and its contextual meaning are different properties.** A vocabulary can assign bank one integer ID. That ID identifies the spelling under a tokenizer's convention; it does not settle which meaning is active. A static vector lookup likewise supplies the same vector whenever that ID appears, even when the surrounding sentence changes.

Contextual representations address this limitation by calculating a token's output from the sequence in which it occurs. The representation can therefore change between the river and money examples. A changed vector is still a model state, not a proof that every relevant interpretation is correct. The task and training evidence determine what distinctions the model learns to make.

Ambiguity is not limited to individual words. An attachment, pronoun reference or implied relationship can leave several readings available. More text can resolve some cases, but a passage may genuinely support multiple possibilities. A model that always produces one confident answer can hide this uncertainty rather than remove it.

Test ambiguity by holding a word fixed and changing its context. Compare a static embedding with a contextual representation, then check whether the difference improves the downstream decision.

sections.title: Literal wording does not specify every intended action
sections.body:
“It is cold in here” can report a temperature or indirectly request that someone close a window. The same sentence can play both roles in different situations. Tone, politeness, shared expectations and the speaker's circumstances affect how a listener interprets it.

[figure: np-pragmatics]

A text-only system may receive none of those extra observations. An apparent failure can therefore result from missing evidence rather than a failure to recognize the sentence's words. If the conversation includes “Could you close the window?”, an action request is more explicit. If it includes a sensor reading, a factual interpretation becomes more likely.

World knowledge also helps connect events. “The glass fell and broke” is unsurprising because glass can be fragile and falling can cause impact. The sentence does not enumerate every physical assumption needed for that interpretation. Language routinely relies on a reader to supply background relationships.

An idiom introduces another distinction. “Break a leg!” conventionally wishes someone good luck in appropriate settings. A word-by-word physical interpretation misses its communicative role. Jokes, cultural references and memes can depend on similarly unstated conventions, which may vary between communities.

**Separate observable text from inferred intent.** A model can estimate an interpretation from learned patterns, but unobserved context can remain unresolved. Useful questions identify what additional information would discriminate interpretations. An application that must act on a message should not treat a plausible inferred request as if every intention were explicitly stated.

sections.title: Choose an output before choosing a model
sections.body:
Text classification maps a passage to a label, such as Positive/Negative or Spam/Not Spam. Named entity recognition marks spans associated with categories such as person or place. Question answering produces an answer to a question, while information extraction returns specified facts or structured fields.

[figure: np-tasks]

Generation tasks return sequences. Machine translation expresses source content in another language. Summarization produces a shorter account while deciding which information to preserve. Dialogue produces responses in a conversational context. Story or code generation creates new text under a requested purpose and constraints.

These interfaces imply different evaluation questions. For a classifier, did the assigned category match the intended label definition? For an entity extractor, were the right spans and categories returned? For a summary, were the relevant facts retained without unsupported additions? For translation, was the meaning expressed accurately in a suitable target-language form?

A fluent answer does not establish correct extraction or faithful translation. Conversely, a correct class label does not explain every token in the passage. Measuring a convenient property of the output can miss the task's actual requirement.

An NLP pipeline normally includes input acquisition, preprocessing, representation, modeling and output interpretation. The stages are linked: punctuation removal can erase an entity boundary; a vocabulary mismatch can corrupt a model input; a classifier's numeric score needs a defined label convention. **The output contract should guide those choices**, rather than being attached after an arbitrary representation has already discarded useful information.

sections.title: Rules, counts and neural representations solve different problems
sections.body:
A rule-based approach uses explicit linguistic patterns and processing steps. A statistical approach estimates patterns from observed text, such as word and phrase frequencies. Neural approaches fit numeric representations and transformations through training objectives. Large pretrained language models extend the scale and reuse of learned language representations.

[figure: np-history]

These are broad families rather than a rule that one method instantly replaces every earlier method. A tokenizer can use explicit rules inside a neural application. A count representation can still support a useful classifier. A large model can be combined with deterministic extraction or validation constraints.

Rules make an intended condition inspectable: if a specified pattern occurs, return a defined result. Their coverage can be limited when language varies beyond those patterns. Counts make observed regularities measurable, but sparse data can leave unseen combinations without reliable estimates. Learned vectors can share information across observations, while their behavior depends on training data, objective and model capacity.

The progression from one-hot vectors to counts, n-grams, embeddings and contextual states is a progression in representation. It does not guarantee that each more elaborate representation is best for every application. More parameters can add capability and also require more data, computation and careful evaluation.

Use the chapter's small models to inspect the mechanisms. Their inputs, parameters and objectives are completely stated. A measured improvement on the declared examples demonstrates that computation under those conditions; it does not establish a benchmark for unrestricted human language.

sections.title: Tokenization decides which units the model receives
sections.body:
A token is a basic unit supplied to a text-processing system. It can be a word, subword or character. Examples include student and campus as words, parts such as un- and happy as subword components, or 我 and 你 as characters. The choice depends on the language, tokenizer and task.

[figure: np-tokenization]

For “I love natural language processing!”, a simple word split can return I, love, natural, language and processing. Removing the exclamation mark is a preprocessing choice. A tokenizer that preserves punctuation may return an additional token, and a subword tokenizer can split unfamiliar words into several pieces.

Chinese text commonly does not place spaces at every word boundary, making segmentation a substantive choice. For “我喜欢自然语言处理。”, one possible word segmentation is 我 / 喜欢 / 自然语言处理, with a separate punctuation decision. Character tokenization produces smaller units. A declared teaching lexicon can reproduce this particular word segmentation, but it is not evidence that a general Chinese segmentation problem has been solved.

**Normalization changes the evidence available downstream.** Lowercasing can merge distinctions between names and common words. Discarding punctuation can remove emphasis, boundaries or code syntax. Such changes can simplify a representation, but their usefulness must be justified for the task and the model's expected preprocessing.

The experiment compares a simple English split, a fixed Chinese teaching lexicon, characters and genuine BERT uncased WordPiece tokenization. It lists the resulting tokens and IDs. The teaching modes use local IDs, while WordPiece uses a specific fixed vocabulary. Comparing them reveals why a familiar-looking word sequence is not necessarily the actual input sequence of a pretrained model.

visuals.predict: Will the same words always give the same token boundaries and IDs?
visuals.reflect: Compare the original sentences across conventions, inspect the actual WordPiece search and distinguish exact tokenization from model inference.

sections.title: Subwords reuse a vocabulary without making every word atomic
sections.body:
WordPiece first receives basic text units, then searches a fixed vocabulary for a sequence of known pieces. A greedy search tries the longest available prefix. After accepting it, the search continues from the remaining suffix, using a continuation marker such as ## for pieces inside the same basic word.

[figure: np-wordpiece]

In the BERT base uncased vocabulary used here, NLP becomes nl / ##p after lowercasing. A vocabulary entry may cover an entire familiar word, so WordPiece does not require every word to be split. A different vocabulary can produce different pieces for the same text.

The search must account for failure. If a basic word cannot be covered completely, this implementation emits [UNK] for that whole basic word. Successfully matched early pieces are not retained as if an unresolved suffix had disappeared. A maximum basic-word length also bounds the search.

The [original BERT tokenizer](https://github.com/google-research/bert/blob/master/tokenization.py) supplies the verified conventions for the local implementation. The complete licensed vocabulary is included locally, allowing exact splits and IDs without downloading model weights. The experiment's search trace exposes accepted and rejected candidates rather than using a schematic label that resembles a tokenizer.

**Tokenization is an input computation, not language-model inference.** Exact WordPiece IDs do not imply that a contextual encoder or classifier has run. An English checkpoint's vocabulary can also map many Chinese characters to [UNK], even though a different Chinese or multilingual vocabulary could represent them. Select the tokenizer and model together; switching one side silently changes the contract.

sections.title: IDs are coordinates in a particular vocabulary
sections.body:
A vocabulary maps token strings to integer IDs. These IDs are lookup indices, not magnitudes of meaning. If cat has ID 5 and dog has ID 3, cat is not semantically larger than dog. Renumbering the vocabulary consistently changes coordinates while preserving token identities.

[figure: np-vocabulary]

A compact example assigns the→1, and→2, dog→3, period→4 and OOV→5. The sequence “the cat and the dog play .” becomes 1,5,2,1,3,5,4 because cat and play are not entries in that particular vocabulary. The unknown bucket records a limitation; it does not preserve which unknown word occurred.

Pretrained models require the exact vocabulary associated with their learned embedding rows. The IDs 101 for [CLS] and 102 for [SEP] apply to the BERT base uncased vocabulary demonstrated here. They are not universal special-token numbers for every language model.

A vocabulary fitted on two documents can be kept fixed while new text is processed. New words then become unknown occurrences under an explicit rule. Growing the vocabulary changes the representation dimension and may require new parameters; it should not happen invisibly in the middle of a comparison.

Vocabulary construction is also part of evaluation discipline. Fit a learned preprocessing rule from the intended training material and apply that rule to separate inputs. Letting an evaluation document silently change the coordinate system can make the model input inconsistent or allow information from outside the intended fitting stage.

sections.title: One-hot encoding identifies a token without measuring similarity
sections.body:
For a vocabulary of size V, a one-hot vector has V coordinates. Exactly one is one and the rest are zero for a known token. An embedding lookup can be understood as selecting the corresponding row of an embedding matrix with this indicator.

[figure: np-one-hot]
