The gradients pass through both cosine normalization and both softmax directions. One update changes all twenty-four weights simultaneously from the current full-batch gradient.

Inspect the matrices before training, perform one update, then train several hundred steps. The plotted losses are evaluated from the actual current weights. Change the inspected pair without changing the fit. Finally swap the first two caption assignments and observe how the objective and gradients change. Numerical features make this a transparent contrastive-learning calculation rather than a hidden image-recognition service.

[figure: tf-contrastive]

visuals.predict: Before any updates, will every associated pair already score highest? Predict which matrices training must change.
visuals.reflect: Compare loss, diagonal probabilities and both encoder gradients. Explain what a pairing swap changes and what selecting another inspected pair leaves fixed.

sections.title: Build a classifier by changing candidate descriptions
sections.body:
After image/text alignment, a classification interface can be constructed from descriptions. Encode each offered class description, normalize it, and compare it with the normalized image vector. A softmax over temperature-scaled similarities can provide a distribution over the offered candidates. Selecting the largest value produces a candidate choice.

**Zero-shot refers to the downstream task's training condition.** The model has already learned from image/text data. The claim is that a new task can be specified without fitting on that task's labeled training examples. It does not mean that the model learned nothing about relevant objects before this use, or that it is guaranteed to recognize every new concept.

Candidate wording affects the text vector. A broad phrase may emphasize different features from a specific phrase. The offered set also matters. If the correct category is absent, an argmax still returns the best offered alternative. Duplicating a candidate divides probability mass between duplicate entries even though their identical similarities carry no new visual evidence.

In the frozen tiny-model experiment, reference weights come from six hundred locally computed updates on the same four synthetic shape pairs. They stay fixed while descriptions change. The parser recognizes only red, blue, square and circle, with simple filler words ignored. Unsupported words are reported. An all-zero text vector has undefined cosine and is excluded from the probability normalization.

Remove the red descriptions while viewing a red image. Observe that a winner can still exist among blue alternatives. Then duplicate red square and compare its individual probability with the combined probability of both duplicate entries. These interventions separate encoder evidence from the mechanics of candidate selection.

[figure: tf-zero-shot]

visuals.predict: Predict the result if a red image is compared only with blue descriptions. What would a duplicate description do to the probability denominator?
visuals.reflect: Separate the highest offered score, recognized words and candidate probability. Explain why unsupported all-zero text cannot supply a valid cosine.

warnings.message: A winning CLIP-style candidate is the highest-scoring offered description, not proof that the correct class was offered or that its probability is calibrated correctness. Example predictions alone do not establish unrestricted recognition ability.

sections.title: Scaling laws describe fitted trends under stated conditions
sections.body:
Parameters, data and compute are related resources. A model with more capacity may capture patterns that a smaller model cannot, but it also needs data and optimization. A larger dataset may improve coverage, but processing it requires compute. More computation may permit additional training or a different model/data allocation. Changing one resource without considering the others can leave a bottleneck unchanged.

Empirical scaling laws fit relationships between resources and a measured quantity such as held-out language-model loss. A simple power-law form is:

$$L(r)=A r^{-\alpha}.$$

Here r denotes a resource quantity, A is a fitted scale and α is a fitted exponent. Increasing r by a factor k changes this idealized loss by the ratio k^(−α). The relationship is smooth and has diminishing improvements in this loss scale. A tenfold increase does not mean a tenfold improvement in loss or a tenfold increase in a downstream skill.

The historical trends use small exponents for compute, data and parameters. The rebuilt graph keeps those exponents while normalizing each curve to a common baseline. It calculates the ratio directly instead of inventing experimental points. The [scaling-law study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361) concerns particular training conditions. Later [compute-allocation research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) also emphasizes balancing model size and training data within a compute budget.

A useful reading of such a graph asks which axis is logarithmic, what loss was measured, what was held fixed, which model family supplied the points, and how far the fit was observed to hold. Extrapolating beyond those conditions introduces uncertainty. The trend motivates resource planning; it is not a guarantee that every larger system improves every task or that size can compensate for unsuitable data.

[figure: tf-scaling]

sections.title: Distinguish sudden task scores from sudden internal changes
sections.body:
A model may appear to acquire an ability abruptly when a task score rises from near chance to a useful level across a sequence of increasingly large models. This observation is interesting, but its interpretation depends on how success is measured. Each point can describe a different trained model rather than a continuous observation of one model changing internally.

Task comparisons can involve modular arithmetic, IPA transliteration, word unscrambling, figures of speech, truthful question answering, grounded mappings, multitask language understanding and word meaning in context. Their metrics and chance baselines differ, so they do not define one universal ability scale.

Consider a task that requires four parts to be correct. In a declared illustration, suppose each part succeeds independently with probability p. The expected fraction of correct parts is p, while the probability of a completely correct answer is p⁴. Both change smoothly, but exact success rises much more slowly at low p and accelerates toward the high end. Reporting only whether a system exceeds a fixed threshold can create an abrupt pass/fail boundary from smooth values.

This does not prove that every reported emergence is a metric artifact. It shows why a sharp plot alone does not prove a discontinuous internal mechanism or a predictable threshold for acquiring a skill. Better evidence compares appropriate metrics, uncertainty, task conditions and related model outputs.

The [metric-choice study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004) demonstrates this concern in analyses of reported emergent abilities. For study purposes, separate three questions: Did performance improve? Does a particular score appear sharply different? What evidence supports a claim about the underlying mechanism?

The table below is an exact calculation under a stated independence assumption. It is not a recreated benchmark dataset. Changing an evaluation metric can change the picture without changing any model prediction. That distinction is as important as increasing the model's resource budget.

[figure: tf-emergence]

warnings.message: An abrupt benchmark score does not alone prove a discontinuous internal ability or a universal scale threshold. Nonlinear metrics, reporting thresholds and uncertainty can change the apparent transition. Examine the task and metric before interpreting the mechanism.

sections.title: Trace the complete encoder–decoder contract
sections.body:
An encoder–decoder Transformer maps a source sequence to an output sequence. In translation, the source and target languages differ. The encoder builds contextual states for the source tokens. The decoder uses those states together with an already available target prefix to predict the next target token. For example, How are you? can become ¿Cómo estás?, with different source and target wording.

The encoder input is a matrix with one row per source token. Token embeddings and position information initialize those rows. An encoder layer performs self-attention, residual addition and normalization, then a position-wise feed-forward transformation followed by another residual addition and normalization. Repeating layers yields final source memory, still with one row per source position.

The decoder begins with target-side embeddings and position information. Each decoder layer has three sublayers: masked target self-attention, encoder–decoder cross-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network. Each has a residual connection and normalization. The final decoder states feed a vocabulary projection and softmax.

**The source and target lengths need not match.** Translation can express one phrase with more or fewer target tokens, and generation length is determined incrementally. Encoder memory supplies source-length keys and values; target-side queries determine how many decoder output rows are produced.

The original base architecture used six encoder layers and six decoder layers. Our numerical example uses one complete layer on each side so that every intermediate value can be inspected. Its smaller dimensions preserve the architecture's information flow while making no claim of reproducing the original model's performance. The later full trace includes all attention projections, both feed-forward networks, five residual/normalization stages and the vocabulary head.

[figure: tf-architecture]

warnings.message: The translation description incorrectly names English as both input and output language. Its example is English input and Spanish output. Encoder–decoder translation here maps a source-language sequence to a target-language sequence.

sections.title: Embeddings initialize token rows once
sections.body:
A token ID identifies a row in an embedding table. If the source vocabulary has V_s entries and the model width is d_model, its table has V_s×d_model parameters. Looking up n tokens returns an n×d_model matrix. The ID is an index, rather than a scalar whose numerical distance defines semantic similarity.

A repeated token selects the same embedding row. Its position and context can later distinguish occurrences. The embedding table supplies the initial token representation; successive encoder layers consume hidden states rather than repeatedly translating the original IDs into new lookup vectors. Target tokens use a corresponding target-side lookup at the bottom of the decoder.

In a trained model, learning can shape the table so that useful distinctions are represented numerically. An initialized table does not already possess those meanings. This distinction matters when inspecting a small architecture example: naming a row red does not make its random vector a learned visual or linguistic representation of redness.

Our example has five source tokens and six target tokens, with four coordinates per row. The tables are separate and explicitly initialized. Target names such as como and estas are ASCII labels in a synthetic token-mapping task; they are not a complete Spanish tokenizer or grammar model. Embeddings are scaled by √d_model=2 before position vectors are added. This multiplication changes the input amplitude; it does not change which row the token selects. The original architecture's scaling convention is verified in [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7#S3.SS4).

All table entries are available in the complete-trace inspector. Unknown free-form words are not silently assigned plausible vectors: the teaching interface offers a bounded vocabulary. This keeps every lookup, dimension and subsequent matrix multiplication reproducible.

[figure: tf-embedding]

sections.title: Add a position signal without changing token identity
sections.body:
Self-attention can compare all token rows, but those rows need a way to represent order. Without position information, moving a token and moving its associated row together does not automatically tell a content-only computation which original slot it occupied. The token identities alone do not distinguish a reordered sentence.

The sinusoidal scheme adds one vector per position. For zero-based position p and pair of coordinates 2i and 2i+1:

$$PE(p,2i)=\sin\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right),$$

$$PE(p,2i+1)=\cos\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right).$$

Different coordinate pairs use different frequencies. At width four, the first pair uses p and the second uses p/100. At position zero, the vector is [0,1,0,1]. These values follow sine and cosine; they are not a binary encoding of the position. Other positions usually contain fractional or negative coordinates.

The position-aware row is the scaled embedding plus the position vector. Both must have the same width because addition is coordinate-wise. A repeated how token at positions zero and one uses the same embedding row but receives different position additions. Contextual transformations then operate on those different initialized rows.

In the experiment, hold the token fixed and move p. Inspect every coordinate rather than only the final vector. Turn off positions to recover the scaled token embedding. This intervention changes an input signal while keeping the lookup parameters fixed. The full Transformer also permits disabling position information, allowing you to distinguish position effects from learned attention projections and other transformations.

[figure: tf-position]

sections.title: Image patches also need a spatial interpretation
sections.body:
A vision Transformer can treat image patches as a sequence of inputs. A patch projection converts the content of each patch into a feature vector, and a position signal indicates where that patch belongs. Content and location are different pieces of information: two identical patches can occupy different spatial slots.

Flattening a two-by-two patch grid yields a sequence such as top-left, top-right, bottom-left and bottom-right. A consistent flattening convention connects sequence positions to image locations. If the computation has no spatial signal, a content-only set of patch vectors does not by itself identify which patch belonged at the top-left. Other architectures or biases can supply location information, so the precise claim concerns what the chosen computation includes.

**Removing positional embeddings does not physically rearrange image pixels.** A shuffled montage is an analogy for lost location information. The actual change is in which signals the model receives. Reconstruction, classification and spatial localization are different outputs; demonstrating a sequence calculation is not demonstrating a reconstructed photograph.

The numerical patch example uses four intensities, A = 0.1, B = 0.9, C = 0.3 and D = 0.7. A declared four-coordinate patch projection feeds the same small attention matrices. Reverse the sequence and track the output associated with content A. Without positions, self-attention permutes the rows and preserves A's content-linked result, up to numerical roundoff. With position vectors, A moves to a different slot and receives a different added signal.

This example isolates permutation behavior using explicit data. It avoids treating an unexplained photograph shuffle as a measured output of a vision model.

[figure: tf-patches]

visuals.predict: Hold a token identity fixed and move its position. Then reverse four numeric patches with positions disabled.
visuals.reflect: Account for every added coordinate. Track patch A across reversal and distinguish permutation-equivariant content computation from added slot information.

warnings.message: Missing position information does not literally shuffle image pixels. The rearranged-patch analogy represents lost spatial information, rather than a measured vision-model reconstruction. The numeric patch computation below isolates that distinction.

sections.title: Multi-head attention is several parallel views
sections.body:
A single attention head produces one set of weights and one value mixture for each query. Multi-head attention provides several such computations in parallel. Each head uses its own query, key and value projections, so different heads can represent different comparison coordinates and value features.

The heads start from the same relevant hidden-state matrices. They do not represent successive encoder layers. Head two does not take head one's output as its input. Instead, their results are concatenated across feature coordinates for each query row, and a final output projection maps that concatenation back to model width.

For h heads, each returning n×d_v, feature concatenation returns n×(h d_v). The row count n is preserved. An output matrix of shape (h d_v)×d_model then returns n×d_model. This width is essential for adding the result back to the original residual input.

Calling a head syntactic or positional requires evidence about its learned behavior. The architecture permits different projections; it does not assign a guaranteed linguistic role to every head. In the initialized teaching example, heads have different matrices but no learned semantic specialization. We can inspect the numerical differences without inventing those roles.

We first calculate one head's scores and value mixture, then return to concatenation and projection. In the two-head example, model width is four and each head uses two query/key coordinates and two value coordinates. Switching to one head keeps the four-coordinate projection parameters but changes how their columns are grouped into attention computations and how the scale factor is chosen.

[figure: tf-head-preview]

sections.title: Project queries and keys, then calculate scaled scores
sections.body:
Given a hidden-state matrix X, self-attention forms Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K and V=XW_V. The three projection matrices are separate trainable parameters. They begin from the same rows while serving different roles: queries ask what to compare, keys supply comparison features, and values supply the information that will be mixed.

For one head, Q has n_q×d_k entries and K has n_k×d_k entries. Multiplying Q by K transposed gives n_q×n_k scores. Entry i,j is the dot product of query i and key j. Transposing keys is what aligns the shared coordinate dimension while leaving query positions as rows and key positions as columns.

The scaled score is:

$$s_{ij}=\frac{q_i\cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}.$$

The divisor is based on the query/key width per head, not the number of tokens or the value width. Dot products can grow in magnitude as more coordinate products are summed. Scaling helps keep the logits in a range where softmax is less likely to saturate. It does not force every score to fall between zero and one; scores can remain negative or large.

In the original independent unit-variance motivation, the sum's variance grows with d_k. This explains the √d_k factor rather than establishing that every learned vector always follows that distribution. The probability interpretation arrives only after softmax.

The inspector lets you change the selected query, head, source length and attention stage. It shows every key, dot-product-derived score, weight and weighted value contribution. Disable scaling to inspect how the same projections yield sharper or flatter weights. No trainable parameter changes during this comparison.

[figure: tf-scores]

visuals.predict: Predict the score matrix shape for three target queries and two source keys. Which target weights must be zero under a causal mask?
visuals.reflect: Sum the displayed weighted value contributions. Trace parallel heads through concatenation and projection; compare scaling, source changes and deliberate mask removal.

warnings.message: The claim that attention preserves only high-score words is misleading. Softmax attention forms a weighted sum of all permitted value vectors; it does not perform hard selection. A mask, rather than a small weight, excludes a position.

sections.title: A separate distribution belongs to every query row
sections.body:
For each query, softmax converts its permitted key scores into nonnegative weights summing to one. A query with three permitted keys therefore receives three weights, while another query computes its own distribution from its own score row. Normalizing the entire score matrix at once would answer a different question.

For score row s, the weight for key j is exp(s_j) divided by the sum of exponentials across that row. Subtracting the row maximum before exponentiation leaves every weight unchanged because the common factor cancels. This stable calculation avoids unnecessary overflow when finite logits are large.

A mask determines which keys are allowed. Setting a disallowed score to negative infinity makes its exponential zero. The remaining permitted entries are normalized so they still sum to one. Setting a disallowed score merely to zero would not exclude it: exp(0)=1 and the key could still receive substantial weight.

If scores are [0, ln2], their exponentials are [1,2] and the weights are [1/3,2/3]. Adding five to both scores preserves those weights. If the second key is masked, the first receives weight one and the second exactly zero.

A row with no permitted keys cannot define an ordinary attention distribution. Implementations need a deliberate policy for such a case rather than allowing an unexplained division by zero. The teaching inputs retain at least one allowed key, including a decoder's current shifted-input position.

Keep distinct a score, a weight and a mask. A negative score is not a negative contribution weight, a small positive weight is not a hard exclusion, and attention weights are distributions over keys rather than output vocabulary classes.

[figure: tf-softmax]

sections.title: Weighted values carry the result
sections.body:
After the attention weights are calculated, each query row forms a weighted sum of the permitted value vectors. If A is the n_q×n_k weight matrix and V is n_k×d_v, the result AV has n_q×d_v entries. The shared n_k dimension connects one weight for each key to the corresponding value row.

The key and value rows must refer to the same available positions. Scores use keys, while contributions use values. A high score gives its associated value more weight; it does not copy the key vector into the output. Values can contain negative coordinates even though weights are nonnegative, so a weighted output coordinate can also be negative.

For weights [1/3,2/3] and scalar values [3,9], the contributions are one and six and the result is seven. Neither permitted value is discarded. Before any output projection, a normalized weighted sum lies within the convex combinations of the available value vectors. The later projection and residual stages change that geometry.

**Attention is a soft mixture rather than a word-selection operation.** A large weight can emphasize information from one position, but the returned object is a vector. It is not a shorter sentence containing only high-scoring words. Explicit masks can remove positions from the mixture; the softmax weighting alone does not implement that removal.

In the inspector, add each weighted value contribution and compare it with the displayed output. Then view a second head: its value projections and weights can differ. This calculation makes clear why comparing only attention heatmaps does not fully describe what information a head contributes. The projected values and the output projection also matter.

[figure: tf-values]

sections.title: Concatenate heads and project back to model width
sections.body:
Multi-head attention combines the independent head results after their value mixtures have been computed:

$$M=\operatorname{Concat}(H_1,\ldots,H_h)W_O.$$

Concatenation joins columns for the same query row. If there are three queries and two heads of width two, the concatenated matrix is 3×4. A 4×4 output projection returns another 3×4 matrix. The number of query rows remains three throughout.

The output projection allows a coordinate to combine information from several heads. It is a trainable linear transformation, not an averaging rule that requires equal contributions from each head. Different heads may already mix different source positions; W_O then combines their feature coordinates. This is why a head's attention weights alone do not determine the final residual contribution.

The original base dimensions were model width 512, eight heads and query/key/value width 64 per head. Their eight mixtures concatenate to width 512. Our width 4, two-head, width 2 example follows the same shape relationship. These are two explicit architectures rather than competing claims about the dimensions of one model.

In the numerical inspector, expand the concatenation and output-projection tables. Select a query row, concatenate its two displayed mixtures in head order, and calculate one projected coordinate as a sum of four products. Compare it to the corresponding projected output entry.

Switching the example to one head groups all four projected coordinates into a single attention computation. The parameter count stays unchanged, but scores, normalization and mixtures can change. More heads do not merely duplicate an identical probability row, and changing head grouping is an architectural intervention even when the underlying projection arrays remain fixed.

[figure: tf-heads]

sections.title: Residual addition and layer normalization have distinct jobs
sections.body:
An attention sublayer returns a model-width update for each token. A residual connection adds that update to the input row. If x is the input and F(x) is the sublayer result, the residual sum is r=x+F(x). Equal widths are required for this coordinate-wise addition. The connection provides a direct computational path alongside the learned transformation.

The original post-norm ordering then applies layer normalization to the sum. For a row of d coordinates, calculate its mean μ and population variance σ² across those coordinates. Normalize each coordinate and apply a learned feature-wise scale γ_j and offset β_j:

$$z_j=\frac{r_j-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\varepsilon}},\qquad y_j=\gamma_j z_j+\beta_j.$$

Layer normalization here operates **within each token's feature row**. It does not normalize together all tokens in a batch. Another token can have different mean and variance while using the same learned affine parameters. The denominator uses population variance, dividing the sum of squared deviations by d, and includes ε inside the square root.

With γ=1 and β=0, the centered normalized row has mean zero. Its variance is σ²/(σ²+ε), so it is close to one for substantial nonzero variance rather than exactly one in every case. A constant row has zero variance and returns z=0; its final affine output is β.

The experiment separately displays input, sublayer output, residual sum, centered value and affine-normalized result. Change one coordinate, then inspect constant-row mode. The complete Transformer uses this pattern after both encoder sublayers and all three decoder sublayers. Other normalization orderings exist, but this chapter's numerical contract stays explicitly post-norm.

[figure: tf-normalization]

visuals.predict: Predict the normalized result of a constant residual row before and after a nonzero affine offset.
visuals.reflect: Identify the feature axis, mean, population variance and epsilon. Keep residual addition separate from centering/scaling and the learned affine transformation.

sections.title: Transform features independently at each position
sections.body:
The position-wise feed-forward network has two affine transformations with a ReLU between them:

$$F(x)=\max(0, xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2.$$

If x has d_model coordinates and the hidden width is d_ff, W_1 has shape d_model×d_ff and W_2 has shape d_ff×d_model. The first map changes feature width; the second returns model width so the result can enter a residual addition. Biases belong to the corresponding output coordinates.

The same parameters are used for every token row within that layer. Different layers can have different parameters. Position-wise means that one row's feed-forward calculation does not read another row. Attention mixes evidence between positions; this sublayer transforms the features available in each already contextualized row.

ReLU replaces negative preactivations with zero and leaves positive ones unchanged. This nonlinear step prevents the pair of affine maps from simply collapsing into one affine map. A hidden unit can contribute nothing for one token and a nonzero value for another under the same weights, depending on their input coordinates.

The original base design used width 512 and hidden width 2048. The teaching example uses width 4 and hidden width 6, including six first-map biases and four second-map biases. One such network has 24+6+24+4=58 parameters.

Choose a token and a hidden unit in the inspector. Add its four input×weight products and bias, apply ReLU, then follow its contribution through W_2. Expand the tables to verify that every row uses the same matrices. Finally distinguish the feed-forward result from the subsequent residual sum and normalized output: they are three different intermediate objects.

[figure: tf-feedforward]

visuals.predict: Select one hidden unit and predict whether its preactivation survives ReLU.
visuals.reflect: Add all products and biases, then follow six hidden contributions into one output coordinate. Explain why changing a token row does not make this sublayer read another row.

sections.title: The encoder retains contextual memory at every source position
sections.body:
An encoder layer combines cross-position attention with per-position feature transformation. Attention first allows each source row to compare itself with all permitted source keys and mix their values. Residual addition and normalization integrate that update. The feed-forward network then transforms each row independently, followed by another residual addition and normalization.

The layer preserves both source length and model width. Its output is an n×d_model matrix of contextual states. The model does not need to collapse the entire source into a single vector for decoder use. Cross-attention can access the separate source rows directly.

Contextualization is a numerical transformation, not a guarantee of semantic understanding. In a trained model, objectives can shape useful representations; in the initialized example, the same architectural operations are still calculable while their language behavior is untrained. Similar-looking diagrams do not remove that distinction.

Stacking several encoder layers repeats the architecture using the previous layer's hidden states as input. Layers share a structural design while ordinarily having distinct parameter values. The word identical in a stack description refers to that design, not a requirement to copy the same learned matrix into every layer.

RNNs and LSTMs can also produce context-dependent sequence states. The Transformer difference is how information is combined: self-attention directly compares permitted rows without a recurrent hidden-state chain. This permits source-row computations within a layer to be parallel, while retaining a cost for the pairwise score matrix.

For n source rows, each head's dense score matrix has n² entries. Doubling n therefore quadruples this matrix's entry count, even if model width is unchanged. The architecture's broad information access is useful, but it does not imply that arbitrarily long sequences are computationally free.

[figure: tf-encoder]

warnings.message: Earlier sequence models do not generally process tokens independently: RNNs and LSTMs produce context-dependent states. The Transformer distinction is direct attention between permitted positions rather than recurrent state propagation.

sections.title: The decoder combines a target prefix with source memory
sections.body:
A decoder predicts target tokens using two kinds of information. Target self-attention reads the already available target-side sequence. Cross-attention reads encoded source information. A feed-forward sublayer transforms the resulting target rows. All three sublayers return model-width updates and have their own residual addition and normalization.

The target self-attention mask is crucial. A prediction must not depend on future target tokens that would be unknown when generating the sequence. Training can process several teacher-forced rows in one matrix computation while masking the disallowed key positions. Parallel computation is compatible with causal information restrictions.

Cross-attention has a different role. It lets target-side queries retrieve relevant information from the source sequence. A translation decoder is usually allowed to read the entire already supplied source, including source words located later in source order. **Target causality does not imply a triangular target-to-source mask.**

The decoder remains target-length. If source length is two and target input length is three, self-attention scores are3×3 and cross-attention scores are3×2 for each head. Both sublayers produce three target output rows. Source and target tokens need not align one-to-one.

The final decoder states are representations, not yet token identities. The vocabulary projection converts them to class logits. A decision policy selects a next token from the resulting distribution, and that selected token can enter the next generated prefix.

The following sections make the causal contract precise by separating shifted input, gold targets, cross-attention roles and actual generation. They also show why feeding an entire target sentence without a mask would leak information that generation cannot access.

[figure: tf-decoder]

sections.title: Shift target inputs so the answer stays outside the visible prefix
sections.body:
For teaching target como, estas, EOS, the decoder input is BOS, como, estas. Row zero predicts como from BOS. Row one predicts estas from BOS and como. Row two predicts EOS from BOS, como and estas. The gold next token is retained separately for evaluating loss.

A causal mask allows input row i to attend to rows j≤i. The diagonal is allowed because the input token at row i is already the previous output in the shifted construction. Allowing that token is different from giving the row its gold next token. Shift and mask work together to define what the model knows.

Teacher forcing supplies the earlier gold tokens during training. The model predicts a distribution for each next target, and cross-entropy penalizes low probability on that target. Processing these rows in parallel does not grant future access because masked scores contribute exactly zero weight.

At generation time, gold target tokens are unavailable. Begin with BOS, predict a token, append the actually selected token, and run the next step with that prefix. If the first selected token is wrong, the second step's input differs from the teacher-forced input. A later correct teacher-forced prediction does not prove the same prediction will occur after that wrong prefix.

The full trace offers an edit of target input row two from estas to azul. With the causal mask active, row zero and row one outputs stay unchanged. Removing the mask deliberately permits leakage, so the future edit can influence earlier rows. This is a direct numerical test of the information restriction, through every downstream sublayer and the vocabulary probabilities, rather than just a picture of a triangular mask.

[figure: tf-shift]

sections.title: Cross-attention queries come from the decoder
sections.body:
Let D be decoder states after masked self-attention and its residual/normalization stage, and let E be final encoder memory. Cross-attention forms Q=DW_Q, K=EW_K and V=EW_V. Queries therefore describe target-side information needs, while keys and values describe available source-side memory.

For m target rows and n source rows, Q has m×d_k, K has n×d_k, and V has n×d_v. QK transposed has m×n entries. Row-wise softmax gives each target query a distribution over the n source keys. Multiplication by V returns m×d_v, one retrieved source mixture for each target row.

This shape argument also diagnoses an incorrect assignment. If queries and keys both came from source memory while values came from a target sequence of different length, the score matrix would be source×source and generally could not multiply target-length values. It would not preserve the required target-side query rows.

All final encoder rows are available in ordinary encoder–decoder translation. The target causal mask belongs to target self-attention; source access is governed by a source validity mask when needed, such as excluding source padding. The bounded example has no padding tokens, so its source positions are all valid.

The corrected query/key/value origins are also explicit in [the original Transformer description](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.03762v7#S3.SS2.SSS3). In the inspector, choose decoder cross-attention and a two-token source. Confirm the 3×2 scores, three result rows and source-derived values. Then change the source while holding the target prefix fixed. The source memory, source keys/values and resulting target-side mixture can change; the query role remains decoder-side.

[figure: tf-cross]

warnings.message: The cross-attention explanation and diagram reverse the roles. Correct encoder–decoder attention uses decoder states for queries and encoder memory for both keys and values. The incorrect assignment fails the target/source shape contract when lengths differ.

sections.title: Convert a decoder state into a vocabulary distribution
sections.body:
A final decoder row contains d_model features. A linear vocabulary map multiplies it by a d_model×V matrix and adds V biases, producing one logit for each target-vocabulary token. A softmax across those V logits gives the next-token distribution. This is a different softmax axis from attention over key positions.

The vocabulary entries may be words, subwords or other token units. V counts the chosen token vocabulary, not necessarily a set of whole words. A model with a thousand vocabulary entries produces a thousand logits per prediction row. Batch and sequence dimensions remain separate from that vocabulary dimension.

The distribution sums to one even when the model is untrained or its preferred token is incorrect. Probability normalization is a mathematical property, not a certificate of meaningful language. Similarly, a large maximum probability does not alone establish that the selected answer is correct.

Greedy decoding chooses the largest probability at each step. Sampling draws a token from the distribution. They can produce different sequences from identical model parameters. Greedy next-token selection also need not maximize the probability of an entire sequence: an early locally preferred choice can lead to less probable continuations.

In the six-token example, every logit and probability is displayed. BOS is included as a vocabulary class, so an initialized head can even emit it. No hidden rule repairs this behavior into a plausible translation. EOS is the explicit stopping token; an eight-token generation bound also stops a sequence that never selects EOS.

The output-head training exercise will fit thirty parameters while keeping the other 392 parameters fixed. Inspect which probability changes follow those actual updates, and distinguish them from a change in decoding policy.

[figure: tf-output]

warnings.message: Selecting the largest next-token probability is greedy decoding, one policy rather than a mandatory architectural step. Sampling can choose another token from the same distribution; a locally best next token need not maximize whole-sequence probability.

sections.title: Follow every stage of one complete tiny Transformer
sections.body:
The complete numerical example has one encoder layer, one decoder layer, model width four, two attention heads of width two, and feed-forward hidden width six. It uses five source entries and six target entries. All parameters are explicit initialized teaching values; there are no pretrained weights or hidden language-model calls.

Its parameter accounting is inspectable: 20 source-embedding values,24 target-embedding values,192 values across three attention modules,116 values across two feed-forward networks,40 affine normalization values, and 30 vocabulary-head values. The total is 422. Each attention module has four 4×4 projection matrices. Each feed-forward network has 24+6+24+4 values. Five layer norms each have four scales and four offsets.

Select a stage in the inspector to view its complete matrix. The stage/shape trace follows source input through encoder attention, residual normalization, feed-forward and final memory; then follows target input through masked attention, residual normalization, cross-attention, residual normalization, feed-forward, final normalization and vocabulary projection/softmax.

All fixed matrices and the exact initialization rule are available in an expandable table. The forward pass has no dropout or padding and uses untied embedding/output tables. It retains the sinusoidal input signal, √d_model embedding scale and post-norm ordering while deliberately reducing depth and width. These declared simplifications make the computation readable rather than suggesting numerical equivalence to a trained original-size model.

Test three independent interventions. Change source length and check that cross-attention shapes follow both lengths. Change the future target token and verify earlier outputs are preserved under the mask. Change the number of heads and observe regrouped projections, scaling and mixtures. These tests concern architecture and evidence access. They do not establish translation ability, which would require an appropriate fit and task evaluation.

[figure: tf-full-trace]

visuals.predict: Change target input row2 while the causal mask is active. Which earlier vocabulary probabilities must remain unchanged?
visuals.reflect: Follow all fourteen matrices, five residual/normalization stages and the422 parameters. Compare source/target lengths and the effect of changing head grouping.

sections.title: Train a small head, then inspect what generation actually does
sections.body:
The final experiment freezes the complete tiny Transformer backbone and trains only its vocabulary projection and bias. Four declared source/target pairs provide ten next-token training positions. Each position supplies a teacher-forced prefix, a fixed contextual decoder state and a separate gold next token. Full-batch cross-entropy gradients update the thirty head parameters.

One update calculates the current distributions, subtracts the one-hot gold target from each probability vector, accumulates feature-weighted gradients and applies the selected learning rate. The loss plot evaluates the actual updated head. All parameters and current gradients remain inspectable, and the backbone's 392 values stay fixed.

**A smaller teacher-forced loss need not produce a correct generated sequence.** In this finite fitting experiment, the learned head improves its objective while still making wrong early choices. This is a measured behavior to inspect, not a claim that every possible optimization of these features must fail. The frozen randomly initialized representation and limited head fit are a deliberately narrow learning contract.

Choose a pair, inspect its teacher-forced positions, then generate from BOS. Every trace row records the actual input prefix, emitted token, selection policy and probability. The next prediction uses that emitted prefix. Switching to generated-prefix inspection never substitutes gold tokens. A forced token is labeled as an intervention and affects later predictions; it is not recorded as a model-chosen answer.

Greedy and seeded sampling use the same fitted head. EOS ends generation, and the eight-token bound prevents an endless loop. A source or policy change restarts the sequence while retaining fitted weights. Training also restarts generation because the probabilities have changed. Reset restores the initialized head for another comparison.

The progression is now complete: broad learning motivates reuse; contrastive alignment creates a flexible matching interface; the Transformer defines a precise contextual computation; and actual prediction behavior depends on trained parameters, available evidence and decoding policy. Use the numerical traces to explain those dependencies, including where the small demonstrations fail.

[figure: tf-decoding]

visuals.predict: Will reducing teacher-forced loss by fitting only a vocabulary head necessarily produce the gold sequence from BOS?
visuals.reflect: Compare actual measured loss with emitted-prefix generation. Explain the first wrong choice, the effect of a forced intervention, and which30 parameters trained while392 remained fixed.

questions.prompt: A shared image backbone supports a detector and a segmenter. What still differs?
choices: Their output interfaces and task supervision.
Every image must have the same output.
Pretraining removes location information by definition.
questions.why: A detector returns boxes/classes; a segmenter returns masks. Shared starting parameters do not make those targets identical.

questions.prompt: Which observation would justify a reuse benefit on a particular task?
choices: A model is described as large.
The reused model reaches the desired held-out performance with fewer task labels under a comparable evaluation.
The model has a modern name.
questions.why: Reuse is an empirical claim about the task/data/evaluation, rather than a consequence of the name or size.

questions.prompt: Where does the gold label come from in a masked-token objective?
choices: The original observed token retained separately from the masked input.
The model first invents a label and assumes it is correct.
The hidden token is passed directly as the answer input.
questions.why: Self-supervision constructs a target from data; preventing answer leakage still matters.

questions.prompt: Two occurrences of bank select the same embedding row. Can their final encoder states differ?
choices: No, their token IDs must first change.
Yes, their surrounding evidence can change contextual transformations.
Only if one occurrence is removed.
questions.why: Static lookup identity and context-dependent hidden states are separate quantities.

questions.prompt: What changes in frozen-backbone head fitting?
choices: Only the task-head parameters.
Every backbone parameter.
Only the task label names, with no optimization.
questions.why: The representation is fixed while gradients optimize the task interface.

questions.prompt: A prompt changes at inference while the parameter arrays stay fixed. What operation occurred?
choices: Full fine-tuning.
A change to the model input.
A gradient update to all embeddings.
questions.why: Input changes can alter predictions without changing learned parameters.

questions.prompt: Which best characterizes a foundation model?
choices: Any network with attention, regardless of training.
Broad pretraining that supports adaptation to several downstream uses.
A system guaranteed to solve every possible task.
questions.why: Foundation refers to a broadly trained adaptable starting point, not a guarantee implied by architecture.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish total and active parameters in a mixture-of-experts comparison?
choices: They are different counts and describe different aspects of computation.
Active and total are always equal.
Neither needs an exact model variant.
questions.why: Only comparing compatible, verified quantities for specified variants makes a size comparison meaningful.

questions.prompt: A model accepts an image and returns similarity scores. Does this establish caption generation?
choices: Yes, any image input implies caption generation.
No, scoring candidate descriptions and emitting a token sequence are different output contracts.
Yes, provided the vector is long.
questions.why: The output operation determines whether the system ranks descriptions or generates text.

questions.prompt: How can the same scene support different visual questions?
choices: The question selects the relation or property to extract from visual evidence.
The image must first change for every new question.
Every scene has one fixed language answer.
questions.why: Color, count and spatial relations concern different distinctions in the same scene.

questions.prompt: What is the core CLIP-style learning interface?
choices: Generate a caption and compare every output word.
Jointly train image and text encoders to distinguish associated pairs from batch alternatives.
Use only a fixed image class head.
questions.why: The paired contrastive objective aligns representations from both modalities.

questions.prompt: A batch has four associated image/text pairs. How many off-diagonal alternatives are compared?
questions.why: There are16 total image/text combinations and4 designated diagonal positives, leaving12 off-diagonal alternatives.

questions.prompt: Can an off-diagonal description still be semantically compatible with an image?
choices: Yes; overlapping content can make a batch negative imperfect.
No; batch indexing proves semantic incompatibility.
Only if softmax returns a negative probability.
questions.why: Pair indexing supplies a training target, not a proof that every alternative description is false.

questions.prompt: How do the two contrastive probability matrices normalize?
choices: Image→text across each row; text→image down each column.
Both across all entries at once.
Both across parameter coordinates.
questions.why: The first direction chooses a caption for an image; the second chooses an image for a caption.

questions.prompt: Multiply a nonzero raw image vector by3, then L2-normalize. What happens to its cosine similarities?
choices: They triple.
They remain unchanged.
They all become zero.
questions.why: Positive rescaling preserves the normalized direction.

questions.prompt: The correct label is missing from the candidate set. What does argmax establish?
choices: The image belongs to the chosen offered class with certainty.
Only which offered candidate received the highest score.
That the encoder retrained itself.
questions.why: Candidate ranking cannot establish that the correct description was available.

questions.prompt: Duplicate an identical description while keeping encoders and temperature fixed. What changes?
choices: Its text vector acquires new visual evidence.
The softmax denominator and individual probabilities can change.
All similarity logits must change.
questions.why: Duplicate vectors have equal logits but add another term to the candidate normalization.

questions.prompt: For L(r)=A r^(−α), what is L(10r)/L(r)?
choices: α
questions.why: The fitted scale and r cancel, leaving the resource-multiplier ratio.

questions.prompt: Why can model size alone be an inadequate scaling decision?
choices: Data and compute can remain bottlenecks.
All models have the same capacity.
Scaling laws guarantee every task improves.
questions.why: Useful resource allocation considers how parameter capacity, training data and compute interact.

questions.prompt: In the declared four-independent-part example, each part succeeds with p=0.8. What is exact all-part success?
questions.why: Independence makes the all-correct probability0.8⁴=0.4096.

questions.prompt: A sharply rising exact-match plot alone proves what?
choices: A discontinuous internal ability appeared at a known universal scale.
The chosen score changed sharply; the mechanism needs further evidence.
All larger models always reason correctly.
questions.why: Metric choice, model family, task conditions and uncertainty matter when interpreting an apparent transition.

questions.prompt: Source length2 and target length3 imply which cross-attention score shape per head?
questions.why: Three target queries compare against two source keys.

questions.prompt: A vocabulary table has five entries of width4. How many source-embedding parameters does it contain?
questions.why: Five rows times four coordinates gives20 parameters.

questions.prompt: At position p = 0, what is the original sinusoidal position vector for width d = 4?
questions.why: The even channels use sin(0) = 0 and the odd channels cos(0) = 1. Positional encoding is not binary encoding even when these particular entries happen to be zeros and ones.

questions.prompt: Repeated how tokens appear at positions0 and1. With sinusoidal additions, what stays identical?
choices: Their final contextual states necessarily.
The selected token-embedding row.
Their positional vectors.
questions.why: Token identity selects one shared row; position vectors differ and later context can differ.

questions.prompt: In the content-only numeric patch experiment, reversing all input rows does what to the output associated with content A?
choices: Preserves it up to roundoff while permuting row order.
Physically reconstructs a shuffled photograph.
Forces all output values to zero.
questions.why: Content-only self-attention is permutation-equivariant when rows, keys and values are permuted consistently.

questions.prompt: Four attention heads each return an n × 8 matrix. What shape results from concatenating their features?
questions.why: Concatenation joins feature columns, preserving the n token rows. An output projection may then map width 32 back to the model width.

questions.prompt: Are attention heads within a multi-head module sequential encoder layers?
choices: Yes, each consumes the preceding head output.
No, they compute parallel projected views before concatenation.
Only when there are two heads.
questions.why: Heads share relevant input matrices but have distinct projections and parallel mixtures.

questions.prompt: For a head with dₖ=4, what is the score divisor?
choices: The number of source words.
questions.why: Scaled dot-product attention divides by√dₖ=2.

questions.prompt: What does QK transposed produce when Q is3×2 and K is5×2?
choices: 3×5 query-to-key scores.
2×2 token probabilities.
5×3 output vocabulary classes.
questions.why: The shared coordinate dimension2 contracts, leaving query rows3 and key columns5.

questions.prompt: Along which axis is attention softmax normalized?
choices: Across keys separately for each query.
Across every entry in Q.
Across model layers.
questions.why: Each query obtains its own distribution of weights over permitted keys.

questions.prompt: Why does replacing a forbidden attention score with0 fail to mask it?
choices: exp(0)=1 can still contribute to the softmax.
Softmax cannot accept zero.
Zero logits create negative weights.
questions.why: A forbidden entry needs an exact exclusion policy, represented here as negative infinity before softmax.

questions.prompt: Scores [0, ln 2] and values [3, 9] produce what scalar attention output?
questions.why: Exponentials are 1 and 2, so softmax weights are 1/3 and 2/3. The output is (1/3)×3 + (2/3)×9 = 7.

questions.prompt: An attention weight is positive and its associated value coordinate is negative. Can the contribution be negative?
choices: Yes, multiplying the positive weight by a negative value gives a negative contribution.
No, all attention outputs must be positive.
Only if softmax fails.
questions.why: Nonnegative mixing weights do not require nonnegative value coordinates.

questions.prompt: Which operation combines coordinate information from several concatenated heads?
choices: The learned output projection Wᴼ.
Changing the token IDs.
Appending extra token rows.
questions.why: Wᴼ maps the concatenated feature width to model width without changing the query row count.

questions.prompt: Across which axis is layer normalization computed in this chapter?
choices: The feature coordinates of each token row.
All token positions in all examples jointly.
The output vocabulary entries before every attention stage.
questions.why: Each token has its own feature-row mean/variance while sharing learned affine parameters.

questions.prompt: A constant residual row is normalized with ε>0. What is its normalized z before the affine map?
choices: A zero vector.
An undefined division by zero.
The unchanged constant row.
questions.why: Centered entries are zero; ε stabilizes the denominator, so z=0 and the affine output isβ.

questions.prompt: Which stage mixes different token positions directly?
choices: Position-wise W₁–ReLU–W₂.
Attention over key/value rows.
The per-row layer-normalization mean.
questions.why: The feed-forward and normalization calculations operate within a row; attention retrieves across permitted positions.

questions.prompt: How many parameters are in a4→6→4 feed-forward network with both biases?
Which describes the encoder output for n source tokens?
choices: One contextual model-width row per source token.
Only the next generated token.
Necessarily one collapsed scalar.
questions.why: Encoder memory retains the source-position rows for later decoder cross-attention.

questions.prompt: Must target causal order also forbid reading later source positions?
choices: Yes, use the same triangular mask for cross-attention.
No, the supplied source can be fully available while future targets remain forbidden.
Source and target lengths must first be equal.
questions.why: Target self-attention and source cross-attention have different validity conditions.

questions.prompt: Why is the causal diagonal allowed in shifted target self-attention?
choices: The row input is the already known previous output, while its next-token gold target is separate.
The row input is secretly the next-token answer.
Allowing the diagonal removes all future access restrictions.
questions.why: Shifting and masking together preserve the next-token prediction contract.

questions.prompt: In encoder–decoder cross-attention, where do queries come from?
choices: The decoder states.
The test labels.
Always the raw source token IDs.
questions.why: Keys and values come from encoder outputs; decoder states supply queries.

questions.prompt: Where do cross-attention keys and values come from?
choices: Final encoder memory.
Future target gold labels.
The output vocabulary softmax.
questions.why: Decoder states query source-derived keys and retrieve source-derived values.

questions.prompt: Does a vocabulary probability vector summing to1 establish a correct translation?
choices: Yes, normalization is semantic verification.
No, an untrained or wrong prediction can still be normalized.
Only if the vocabulary has six entries.
questions.why: Normalization is mathematical; task correctness requires appropriate learned behavior and evidence.

questions.prompt: Which complete architecture stage would be missing from an attention-only demo?
choices: Residual/normalization, feed-forward stages and vocabulary projection, among others.
All query-to-key comparisons.
The softmax weighting operation.
questions.why: A full Transformer includes more than its attention formula.

questions.prompt: With the causal mask active, editing target input row2 must preserve what?
choices: Earlier rows0/1 probabilities through the complete decoder.
Every later output under every possible input change.
The source and target sequence lengths must become equal.
questions.why: Forbidden future target information cannot influence earlier predictions through any allowed path.

questions.prompt: A frozen-backbone head fit lowers teacher-forced loss but generates a wrong first token. What follows?
choices: The displayed fitting objective improved, but correct free-running sequence behavior is not established.
The site should replace the result with the gold sequence.
Every backbone parameter must have trained.
questions.why: Actual generation uses its selected prefix; teacher-forced loss and free-running success are different evidence.

title: The Large Model Era — Part 2
summary: Pretraining and SFT, actual low-rank and preference learning, reranking, reference KL and an inspectable finite PPO actor.

sections.title: Three training stages change different parts of behavior
sections.body:
A broadly pretrained language model and an instruction-following assistant can share an architecture while behaving differently. The difference lies in the data, objectives and parameter updates that produced their distributions. A model can be good at continuing text without reliably answering a question, respecting a format or asking for missing evidence.

A foundation model provides a broadly trained starting point for several tasks. Transformer self-attention combines permitted token states through parallel matrix operations, with position signals and feed-forward transformations shaping their representations. That architecture does not by itself specify which learning objective shaped its parameters.

A useful training map has three stages. **Pretraining** learns reusable patterns from large amounts of observed data. **Supervised fine-tuning**, or SFT, learns from demonstrations of desired responses. **Preference-based policy improvement** uses judgments about generated responses to change which behaviors the model tends to produce. These stages are connected, but they do not use interchangeable learning signals.

For pretraining, a target can be a hidden or following token already present in the data. For SFT, a target is an example response to a prompt. For preference learning, a label says that one candidate is preferred to another. A reward model predicts these comparisons, and a policy update uses that learned scoring function. Producing a reward score and changing the policy are separate operations.

The self-study, mentor and practice analogy captures this progression but should not be treated as a literal account of a model's mind. Each stage is an optimization process. Inspect which inputs are visible, how a target is constructed, which parameters change and which evidence evaluates the resulting behavior.

This chapter extends the foundation-model and Transformer ideas through actual small calculations. The demonstrations use bounded token sequences, matrices and finite response sets. They make the learning mechanisms inspectable without presenting a miniature model as a pretrained conversational system.

[figure: al-stages]

sections.title: Pretraining predicts observed data under an objective
sections.body:
Self-supervised pretraining constructs learning targets from the observed material. Masked language modeling predicts selected hidden tokens from permitted context. Next-sentence prediction in original BERT classifies a constructed sentence-pair relationship. Autoregressive language modeling predicts the next token from an earlier prefix. These objectives expose different information and ask different prediction questions.

For next-token learning, retain the original token as the gold target while keeping it outside the visible prefix. A sequence such as china / highest / mountain / is / mount / everest provides several training examples. One prefix predicts the following token; a longer prefix predicts the next one. EOS supplies an explicit sequence-ending target. The model receives neither a secret completed answer nor a manually selected reward for each prefix.

The loss is the negative log probability of the observed target. Training adjusts parameters to reduce that loss over many examples. A high likelihood for a common continuation need not mean that the continuation satisfies a user's request. **Observed text and desired assistant behavior are different distributions.**

The browser model has twelve token entries and four hidden features. It learns both embedding rows and an affine output head, totaling 108 parameters. It averages the visible prefix embeddings, applies tanh and predicts a twelve-class distribution. This is a deliberately simple order-insensitive prefix model, rather than a Transformer. Every training row and parameter is shown.

Large-scale corpora can include books, websites, discussions, code and scientific writing, depending on the particular dataset. Their content and quality matter. A vague list of websites does not verify the exact training composition of a named product, and a token count cannot automatically be read as a word count.

[figure: al-pretraining]

visuals.predict: Predict which token supplies the next-token target and which tokens remain visible.
visuals.reflect: Compare actual NLL/probabilities after updates, inspect all108 parameters and explain the model’s order-insensitive mean-prefix limitation.

warnings.message: The pretraining size comparison labels dataset quantities as words while mixing model variants and quantities that may be reported in tokens. Those counts are not verified comparable measures. The listed websites also do not establish an exact named-product training dataset.

sections.title: Continuing a prompt is different from fulfilling its instruction
sections.body:
A next-token model learns what text tends to follow other text. A prompt that looks like the beginning of a list may be continued with another list item. A prompt that resembles a question may be continued with another question, an answer, a quotation or a discussion of questions, depending on the learned distribution and formatting.

Consider Explain the moon landing to a six-year-old in a few sentences. A continuation could be Explain the theory of gravity to a six-year-old rather than the requested explanation. The text can resemble a plausible document continuation while failing the instruction. The issue is the mismatch between the statistical continuation objective and the desired interaction contract.

Instruction-following systems still produce next-token distributions. SFT does not replace softmax with a fundamentally different text-generation operation. It changes the parameters and input/target examples so that the distribution after an instruction is more likely to begin and continue an appropriate response.

The small experiments preserve this distinction. Pretraining uses corpus-prefix targets. SFT later uses instruction prefixes followed by demonstrated answer tokens. The output vocabulary and parameter layout stay the same, while the target distribution and loss mask change. A probability vector alone does not tell you which objective produced it.

An initially pretrained model can sometimes answer a question through its learned continuation patterns. That does not make the two objectives identical, nor does it guarantee reliable instruction following. Examine actual outputs rather than assuming all base models only complete sentences or all fine-tuned models always answer correctly.

[figure: al-continuation]

sections.title: Limited demonstrations can support a shortcut
sections.body:
Suppose the only demonstrated question is What is the highest mountain in China?, with the response Mount Everest. A model that attends mainly to highest could reproduce the training response while ignoring the requested region. Applying that shortcut to Africa would give the same answer, although the intended regional distinction changes.

This example shows an **underdetermined learning problem**. The small dataset may not force the model to distinguish a region-sensitive rule from a region-insensitive rule. Both can fit the observed example. It does not prove that every model trained from scratch will necessarily learn exactly that shortcut, or that supervised data is impossible to collect.

Another question, Where is the deepest point in the ocean?, requires a different distinction and an answer about the Mariana Trench location. A highest-keyword template cannot justify that response.

Pretraining can supply useful distinctions before the task demonstration arrives, but it can also supply missing or misleading associations. Its benefit depends on data coverage, representation and the later objective. An initial representation is evidence of previous fitting, not proof that every required fact or distinction is encoded reliably.

The toy corpus distinguishes china and africa and includes different mountain-name continuations. The model remains small and imperfect: its mean-prefix representation loses order, and its finite pretraining fit does not predict every corpus position correctly. SFT on China alone can produce the demonstrated China response while still failing the Africa question. Training with both region demonstrations changes the available supervision.

Compare warm and random starting parameters under the same SFT examples and update budget. Then inspect the untrained-on question separately. A lower training loss on one question is a local result; it is not evidence that all unseen questions, countries or languages will generalize.

[figure: al-coverage]

warnings.message: Labeled data can be costly, but saying it is impossible to collect much supervised data is too strong. The highest-keyword shortcut is one possible fit to limited examples, not a guaranteed behavior of every model trained without pretraining.

sections.title: SFT learns from prompt–response demonstrations
sections.body:
Supervised fine-tuning begins with a set of instructions and demonstrated responses. A prompt may request translation, grammatical editing, a summary, a shopping list or a factual answer. The demonstration shows the desired output for that particular request and available input.

For a response y, training predicts each response token from the prompt and earlier response tokens. Gold earlier tokens are supplied during teacher forcing. The next gold token stays separate as the target. A response-only loss can exclude prompt-token prediction positions while still using the prompt as conditioning information.

This distinction is subtle: **masking a prompt's direct loss does not necessarily freeze its embedding**. Its visible tokens influence the hidden state used to predict response tokens, so gradients from those response losses can flow through the prompt representation. A loss mask controls which targets contribute, rather than which inputs can affect predictions.

A shopping-list demonstration can map a recipe into a list of its ingredients. It should extract the given recipe's items, not invent unrelated ingredients. For the recipe example, zucchini, beef, onion, mushrooms, peppers, cheese, ketchup, salt and pepper belong to the supplied ingredient evidence. The instruction and input determine what an appropriate response means.

SFT optimizes demonstrated behavior. It does not directly receive a comparison of every possible answer, and it does not guarantee factual correctness outside the demonstrations. Demonstration quality, task coverage, formatting and evaluation all matter. The same next-token machinery can become more useful by changing the examples on which its parameters are fitted.

[figure: al-sft]

sections.title: Initialization transfers parameters but does not constrain them
sections.body:
Using pretrained parameters as the SFT starting point lets the new objective begin from an already fitted representation. Starting from random weights requires the narrow demonstration set to support more of the representation learning itself. With limited task data, this can make the starting point consequential.

Initialization is not a distance constraint. Ordinary gradient descent can move far from the initial parameters if the objective, learning rate and update count encourage it. A statement that fine-tuning will not deviate too much needs an actual mechanism or measured result, rather than following automatically from warm starting.

The SFT experiment compares the same 108-parameter model from two starting arrays. The warm array is computed locally through 800 pretraining updates on the declared corpus. The random array comes from the same documented initial seed used by the pretraining experiment. SFT then updates all 108 values on response targets; it is not only training a new head.

An optional explicit L2-to-start penalty adds a separate term:

$$L=L_{response}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_j(\theta_j-\theta_{start,j})^2.$$

Its gradient adds λ times the displacement to the response-loss gradient. The displayed parameter distance measures the actual resulting movement. This penalty is a teaching intervention, not a claim that every SFT recipe includes it. Parameter distance also differs from a KL divergence between prediction distributions.

After fitting, generate from an instruction using the model's selected tokens. Compare that trace with teacher-forced probabilities, then inspect the other region. The demonstration intentionally shows both successful small-task fitting and limited transfer. It never repairs a wrong generated token by substituting the gold answer.

[figure: al-warmstart]

visuals.predict: Compare warm and random starts on the same China-only demonstrations. Will perfect China fitting guarantee the Africa answer?
visuals.reflect: Trace response-only targets, parameter drift, actual emitted-prefix generation and the effect of adding region coverage or an explicit penalty.

warnings.message: Starting from pretrained parameters does not ensure fine-tuning stays close to them. Parameter drift depends on the objective and updates; a distance penalty, frozen subset or other explicit mechanism must be specified if limited movement is intended.

sections.title: Low-rank adaptation changes a matrix through factors
sections.body:
Full fine-tuning updates many or all existing parameters. A parameter-efficient method instead restricts which quantities are trainable. LoRA uses a low-rank update to a frozen weight matrix, allowing an adapted computation without storing an independently updated full matrix for every task.

Using a column-vector convention, let W₀ have shape d_out×d_in. Define A with shape r×d_in and B with shape d_out×r. Their product BA has the same shape as W₀, so the adapted transformation is:

$$y=\left(W_0+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\right)x.$$

The rank of BA is at most r. The trainable factors have r(d_in+d_out) entries, compared with d_in d_out for an unrestricted full matrix update. A sufficiently small r can reduce trainable storage. The base matrix still exists and participates in the computation; fewer trainable values do not mean the full model has disappeared.

LoRA is a low-rank weight-update method. A bottleneck adapter that inserts an additional network is another parameter-efficient construction. Calling them identical obscures their computations. The [original LoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) verifies the frozen-base factorization mechanism and initialization convention.

Initializing B to zero makes the initial update zero even when A is nonzero. The adapted model therefore initially matches the base transformation. B can receive a nonzero gradient, while A's first gradient through the product is zero. Setting both factors to zero instead prevents either from starting to learn through that product.

A low-rank restriction also limits what updates can be represented. It is useful when the needed change can be captured sufficiently well within that restriction; it is not a universal guarantee of matching unrestricted fine-tuning.

[figure: al-lora]

warnings.message: LoRA’s low-rank update should not be confused with an inserted bottleneck adapter network. Both can be parameter-efficient, but their computations differ:LoRA freezes W₀ and trains factors for an additive matrix update.

sections.title: Inspect actual low-rank learning on four basis inputs
sections.body:
The matrix experiment freezes a 4×4 base and trains low-rank factors against a declared desired update. Its four training inputs are the basis vectors e₀ through e₃. Each input exposes one column of the effective matrix, so the four examples collectively reveal every output entry.

The rank-one target is an outer-product update. A rank-one factorization can represent it exactly. The other target is a diagonal matrix with four nonzero diagonal entries, which has rank four. Rank-one or rank-two factors cannot represent that full-rank change exactly. A residual error is therefore different from a hidden implementation failure when the hypothesis class excludes the target.

The objective is the mean squared error across sixteen output coordinates. Both factor gradients are derived through the product BA and the α/r scale. Updates are simultaneous: calculate gradients using the current A and B, then change both arrays. The base W₀ remains byte-for-byte unchanged.

Inspect the initial gradients, perform one update, then fit the rank-one target. Switch to the full-rank target and compare the error. Changing rank resets the factor layout because its dimensions change. Changing the desired target changes the fitting objective; it does not silently alter the base weights.

In this tiny matrix, rank one has eight trainable entries and rank two has sixteen. Rank two therefore gives no count saving over sixteen unrestricted update entries. This numerical example illustrates the formula rather than claiming that every rank choice is efficient. Its initialized factors, targets, scale, gradients and loss history are all visible.

[figure: al-matrices]

visuals.predict: With B=0 and A nonzero, which factor has the first nonzero gradient?
visuals.reflect: Compute BA and all products, compare rank-one/full-rank targets and explain why setting both factors to zero stalls learning.

sections.title: Shared multilingual representations can support transfer
sections.body:
A multilingual pretrained representation can expose related patterns across several languages. Fine-tuning on a task in one language may therefore support some performance on another language without task-labeled examples in that target language. This is cross-lingual task transfer, rather than a guarantee that the model automatically learns every language's version of the task.

The multilingual BERT example begins from a model pretrained across 104 languages and applies reading-comprehension supervision. A reading-comprehension system must connect a question to information in a passage and select or produce an answer. Training language, passage language and evaluation language are separate parts of that setup.

Transfer may depend on vocabulary coverage, shared structure, the pretraining distribution, task framing and differences between evaluation data. Similar token strings alone are not enough. Conversely, different writing systems do not make transfer logically impossible when learned representations connect useful distinctions.

An appropriate comparison separates target-language supervised learning from cross-lingual transfer. Fine-tuning on Chinese QA and evaluating Chinese QA is a different condition from fine-tuning only on English QA and evaluating Chinese QA. Adding Chinese task supervision changes the experiment and cannot still be counted as zero-shot task-label transfer into Chinese.

The historical results below provide a concrete bounded comparison. They show useful transfer and a gap between training conditions.
