They do not establish that English supervision automatically reaches the same performance as target-language supervision, or that one benchmark establishes understanding of every language and task.

[figure: al-multilingual]

warnings.message: Fine-tuning one task in one language does not guarantee automatic equivalent performance in other languages. Cross-lingual transfer depends on pretraining, representation, task and data; the measured English-to-Chinese QA condition remains below Chinese-supervised conditions.

sections.title: Exact match and F1 ask different questions
sections.body:
Exact match checks whether the complete predicted answer agrees with a gold answer under the chosen normalization. Token-overlap F1 gives partial credit for shared answer units, balancing precision and recall. A prediction containing only Everest can overlap Mount Everest without being an exact match.

In the declared English-word example, prediction Everest has one unit and the gold answer has two. The overlap is one, precision is one and recall is one-half. F1 is two-thirds while exact match is zero. Repeating mount twice does not create two matching units when the gold contains only one mount: overlap uses multiplicities bounded by the gold counts.

The primary Chinese QA comparison uses DRCD evaluation, with English SQuAD task supervision in the transfer condition. Rounded values are:

| Model / pretraining | QA fine-tuning language | Chinese EM | Chinese F1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| QANet / no language-model pretraining | Chinese | 66.1 | 78.1 |
| Chinese BERT | Chinese | 82.0 | 89.1 |
| Multilingual BERT | Chinese | 81.2 | 88.7 |
| Multilingual BERT | English | 63.3 | 78.8 |
| Multilingual BERT | English + Chinese | 82.6 | 90.1 |

These rows match the [authors' primary research poster](https://liangtaiwan.github.io/assets/emnlp2019_poster.pdf). Their dataset context matters: they are historical Chinese reading-comprehension results, not universal model accuracies or probability forecasts for a new question.

The metric experiment computes exact match and multiset overlap under a separately declared normalization rule. Chinese-character mode makes partial-span behavior visible without claiming to implement the full DRCD evaluator. It teaches why EM and F1 differ, while keeping evaluation arithmetic separate from the unimplemented multilingual encoder.

[figure: al-evaluation]

visuals.predict: Predict EM/F1 for Everest versus Mount Everest under word units.
visuals.reflect: Count multiset overlap, then compare Chinese-character partial spans and repeated predictions under the explicit normalization rule.

warnings.message: The model rows can be verified as historical DRCD Chinese-QA results, but the stated human F1 of93.30 lacks a verified evaluation protocol in the identified primary poster. Do not treat it as a universal human baseline or a probability of correctness on a new question.

sections.title: Specialized task models retain explicit task interfaces
sections.body:
One adaptation path produces several task specialists from a shared pretrained starting point. A translation specialist uses translation demonstrations, an editing specialist uses editing demonstrations, and a summarization specialist uses examples of source text paired with summaries. They can share an initial architecture and representation while ending with different fitted parameters.

For translation, the prompt and training distribution determine the source/target language direction. Good morning can map to 早安 when English-to-Chinese translation is specified. For editing, who care requires cares in the intended singular construction Who cares? The task output is an edit or corrected text rather than a translation of the phrase.

Specialization can simplify task routing and focus supervision, but maintaining several adapted models has storage and deployment costs. Parameter-efficient updates may reduce those costs by sharing a frozen base, while still requiring a clear choice of task-specific update or interface.

A benchmark suite can compare such systems on several language-understanding tasks. GLUE includes grammatical acceptability, sentiment, paraphrase, textual similarity, entailment and related inference tasks. Individual tasks have their own metrics; an aggregate score is a constructed summary, not a direct universal measure of intelligence.

| Task | Main distinction | Metric |
|---|---|---|
| CoLA | Grammatical acceptability | Matthews correlation |
| SST-2 | Sentiment | Accuracy |
| MRPC | Paraphrase | Accuracy / F1 |
| STS-B | Sentence similarity | Pearson / Spearman correlation |
| QQP | Paraphrase | Accuracy / F1 |
| MNLI | Natural-language inference | Matched / mismatched accuracy |
| QNLI | Question–sentence inference | Accuracy |
| RTE | Textual entailment | Accuracy |
| WNLI | Coreference / inference | Accuracy |

The human baseline in a normalized comparison is also task- and protocol-specific. A ratio above one says that a reported score exceeds that baseline under the comparison's normalization. It does not establish that the model exceeds humans at all language activities. The [GLUE benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.07461) and [human-baseline study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10425) clarify why the evaluation setting matters.

[figure: al-specialists]

warnings.message: A score above a normalized human baseline does not establish generally superhuman language ability. The historical chart mixes task metrics and an aggregate; its exact plotted data/provenance are not recovered here. The rebuilt ratio calculation is explicitly illustrative, rather than fabricated benchmark measurements.

sections.title: A generalist uses instructions to distinguish tasks
sections.body:
Another adaptation path combines demonstrations from several task families into one instruction-conditioned model. The instruction identifies whether to translate, summarize, edit, classify or answer a question. This reduces the need to choose a separate complete model for every task, while increasing the importance of diverse and well-specified demonstrations.

A translation request needs an identifiable target language. An editing request needs the text to edit. A summarization request needs the source to summarize. Examples whose target language is missing or whose answer simply repeats already-English input are ambiguous evidence for learning a translation behavior.

FLAN illustrates instruction tuning on diverse task families. These include natural-language inference, commonsense reasoning, sentiment, paraphrase, closed-book QA, reading comprehension, reading comprehension with commonsense, translation, structured-data-to-text, coreference, summarization and other tasks. **Task diversity and instruction formatting are part of the learning setup**, rather than a property implied by the word generalist.

The [original FLAN study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01652) verifies this broad instruction-tuning approach. It should be distinguished from saying that one model is universally competent. A model may learn a useful instruction interface while retaining uneven performance, coverage gaps and failures on new requests.

Concrete demonstrations can include Translate “Good morning” into Chinese → 早安, Correct “who care” → Who cares?, and Summarize the following supplied article → an evidence-based short summary. The output changes with the operation requested. A generalist's strength is a shared instruction-conditioned interface, whose success still needs task-specific evaluation.

[figure: al-instructions]

warnings.message: The translation examples omit a target language or repeat already-English input as English output. That does not clearly demonstrate a translation transformation. Use an explicit source/target direction, such as English Good morning to Chinese 早安.

sections.title: Combining instructions adds another evaluation condition
sections.body:
A user can ask for a summary and then a translation of that summary. The model must identify both operations, apply them in the correct relationship and preserve the source information. Demonstrations of summarization and translation separately do not by themselves prove reliable performance on their combination.

The input contract matters. If an article is supplied, the summary should reflect its content. If the requested output is English, the translated summary should satisfy that language requirement while retaining the summarized meaning. A response such as No problem followed by unrelated fluent text does not meet the task merely because it acknowledges the instruction.

One way to study a combined request is to separate observable requirements: preserve relevant claims, omit unsupported additions, meet the requested length and use the target language. Then examine whether errors arise in extraction, transformation, language choice or final formatting. This is more informative than one unqualified judgment that the generalist succeeded.

The same principle applies to a shopping list from a recipe. The model needs to select ingredients from the provided evidence, remove preparation details if they are irrelevant and use the requested list format. It should not infer that every recipe contains an ingredient absent from this one.

Task composition is therefore a new evaluation condition. Shared parameters and diverse training can support it, but measured behavior is the evidence. The chapter's bounded token model demonstrates how an objective changes distributions; it does not claim to perform unrestricted summarization, translation or multistep composition.

[figure: al-composition]

sections.title: Demonstrations and preferences provide different supervision
sections.body:
A demonstration says what response to produce for a prompt. A preference says which of two or more available responses is better under a judgment criterion. Comparing candidates can be easier than writing an ideal answer from scratch, particularly when many acceptable outputs exist, but the workload depends on the task.

For the highest-mountain question, a demonstrator can write Mount Everest. A comparison label can instead say that Mount Everest is preferable to Who knows? or Mount Tai. These labels convey different information. A comparison does not provide a unique ideal answer in every possible situation, and a demonstration does not explicitly rank every alternative.

Creative tasks make this distinction clear. A request for a three-line poem about AI can have several acceptable responses. A rater may compare their relevance, clarity, structure and style without being able to write a uniquely best poem. Different raters can nevertheless disagree about style or priorities.

**Preference supervision is still supervision.** The candidates, instructions, comparison criteria and raters determine the learning signal. Ranking an output does not turn the label into an objective measure of truth. It also does not automatically make feedback cheap: careful factual checking or evaluating a long response can be substantial work.

Writing demonstrations, ranking responses, fitting a reward model and updating a policy are separate steps. Each can introduce different errors or biases.

[figure: al-feedback]

warnings.message: The workload labels in the visual contradict the accompanying account of demonstration versus comparison effort. Neither method is always easier:writing can be demanding, but ranking may also require substantial checking. The relevant distinction is the supervision supplied.

sections.title: Evaluate the requested constraint as well as style
sections.body:
A response can be fluent and relevant while failing a precise instruction. If a prompt requests three lines, a six-line poem violates the stated format even when both of its three-line stanzas sound appropriate. The response should be evaluated against the whole request rather than only whether it mentions AI.

For a poem, useful criteria include the actual line count, topic relevance, readability and any specified style. For a factual answer, relevant criteria include whether it answers the particular question and whether the asserted fact is supported. For a summary, the source evidence and omission of invented claims are central.

These criteria can compete. A longer answer may be more detailed but fail a concise format. A confident answer may sound polished while being wrong. An honest request for missing source material may be preferable to a fluent invented summary. Raters and reward models need a clear account of which properties matter for the task.

A reconstructed three-line example is:

```text
Words become vectors and patterns take shape.
Questions guide learning through choices we make.
Evidence matters when answers take form.
```

This is an authored format example, not a model-generated performance claim. Its visible line count can be checked directly. A reward model can learn from judgments about such responses, but that learned score is still a prediction of the comparison labels supplied to it.

The later deliberate confident-style preset isolates one failure: a scoring function can favor assertive wording while neglecting the support for its factual claim. Optimizing that function then amplifies the wrong property.

[figure: al-criteria]

warnings.message: A three-line poem was requested, but the shown response contains two three-line stanzas, six lines in total. Fluency and relevance do not make that response satisfy the stated format.

sections.title: A reward model scores a prompt and response
sections.body:
A reward model maps the prompt and candidate response to a scalar score. Its purpose in this pipeline is to predict which responses raters would prefer. It is separate from the policy that generates the candidate text, although a practical system can reuse a related pretrained architecture to initialize it.

For one prompt, compare Mount Everest and Mount Tai. A label that prefers the first can train the scoring function to assign a higher value to that prompt/response combination. The score is not a required literal value such as one or ten. Relative differences determine a pairwise preference probability under the chosen formulation.

Including the prompt is essential in general. The same response can be appropriate for one question and inappropriate for another. The finite demonstration uses one fixed prompt so that candidate features and score arithmetic stay fully visible. It is not a prompt-independent replacement for a general reward model.

Our four candidate responses include the correct mountain answer, a wrong mountain answer, honest uncertainty and a long confident repetition of the wrong answer. Four supplied feature values describe each candidate. A linear scoring model learns four coefficients from declared pairwise labels. The feature annotations are explicit teaching inputs, rather than evidence that a browser model can independently verify arbitrary facts.

After training, inspect the coefficients as well as the ranking. A supported-answer label set and a confident-style label set can produce different score functions on exactly the same candidates. The learning mechanism follows its objective; it does not independently decide that one label set expresses the user's true purpose.

[figure: al-reward]

sections.title: Learn score differences from pairwise comparisons
sections.body:
For preferred response a and other response b, define the score difference d=r(a)−r(b). A logistic comparison model assigns probability σ(d) to the labeled preference. The negative log probability is the pair loss:

$$L_{pair}=-\log\sigma\left(r(a)-r(b)\right).$$

For a linear score r(x)=w·x, the relevant feature vector is the difference x_a−x_b. The gradient is (σ(d)−1)(x_a−x_b). This changes the coefficients in a direction that increases the preferred score difference. A full-batch update averages gradients over all listed pairs.

The experiment also applies a small explicit L2 penalty to keep coefficients bounded. It displays the unregularized pair loss separately from the regularized fitting objective. The update changes four weights; it never changes the candidate strings, their supplied features or the reference generation probabilities.

At equal scores, the labeled comparison probability is one-half and its loss is ln2. Adding the same constant to both scores preserves their difference and therefore preserves every preference probability. Pairwise data does not identify a unique common score offset. Absolute score magnitudes should not be interpreted as calibrated probabilities of factual correctness.

Conflicting labels expose another limitation. If the data equally prefers A over B and B over A, driving their score gap in either direction hurts one of the labels. The balanced optimum for that pair is a zero gap and probability one-half. This is disagreement in the supervision, rather than an optimizer that secretly knows which rater was right.

The learned reward table is then held fixed in the policy demonstrations, making its influence on selection and optimization observable.

[figure: al-pair-loss]

visuals.predict: What pair probability begins at equal scores? Would a common score offset change it?
visuals.reflect: Inspect all feature differences/weights/gradients, actual fitting, contradictory labels and how a biased label preset changes ranking.

sections.title: Best-of-N selection changes returned answers without training
sections.body:
A generator can produce several candidates, a reward model can score them, and an interface can return the highest-scoring candidate. With illustrative scores one, five and ten, the third candidate wins. This procedure is **reranking at inference**. It does not by itself update the generator's parameters.

Increasing the number of sampled candidates can change the distribution of returned answers. If the scorer reliably prefers useful outputs, sampling more alternatives can make a useful candidate more likely to be available. If the scorer favors a bad property, a larger pool can instead make a highly scored wrong response more likely to be selected.

The finite experiment keeps generator probabilities at[0.55,0.15,0.25,0.05] for candidates A through D. It samples a bounded pool and shows every uniform draw, candidate, reward and selected result. The frozen scoring coefficients come from actual local pairwise training on the chosen label preset.

Because all four candidates are enumerated, the experiment also calculates exact returned probabilities. For a candidate with a unique score r_j, its probability of being the highest score among N independent draws is P(score≤r_j)^N−P(score<r_j)^N. The calculation includes repeated draws. Ties use a stated policy rather than a hidden semantic judgment.

At N=1, the returned distribution equals the generator distribution. At larger N, the distribution can change while the generator remains fixed. Comparing the current generator to the returned answers prevents us from mistaking inference-time selection for policy learning. Both mechanisms can use a reward model, but only a parameter update changes the policy itself.

[figure: al-reranking]

visuals.predict: Can returned-answer probabilities change without changing generator parameters?
visuals.reflect: Compare sampled pools with exact best-of-N probabilities, including tied scores and the wrong scorer’s amplification at larger N.

warnings.message: Scoring several candidates and displaying the highest-scoring one is reranking, not by itself reinforcement learning or a generator parameter update. A separate optimization step is needed to change the policy.

sections.title: A chosen response is not automatically a true response
sections.body:
Preference labels reflect a judgment process. They can encode useful criteria, incomplete checks, style preferences, disagreements or systematic bias. Replacing absolute ratings with relative comparisons may make some annotation decisions easier, but it does not remove these sources of error.

A chosen/rejected data field identifies the label used for training. It is not an independent proof of the chosen response's facts. An unsupported comparison of political groups' intelligence remains unsupported even if it appears inside a preference-training example. Asking for evidence can be a useful response without establishing the premise as true.

Our neutral finite candidates make the same point without reproducing an irrelevant partisan exchange. The correct factual answer and the assertive wrong answer have different scores depending on the rater-label preset. Changing those labels can make the wrong response preferred under the fitted reward model.

The supplied task-utility values[1,0,0.2,0] deliberately distinguish a supported answer, wrong assertions and partial credit for honest uncertainty. They are declared teaching judgments, rather than a universal human-utility scale. The probability of candidate A supplies an additional directly inspectable supported-answer measure.

When policy optimization increases expected learned reward, check whether that measure and the task-specific evidence improve too. A reward score is a proxy target. If it neglects the actual requirement, optimizing it can worsen the result even while the reported optimization objective improves.

Disagreement and dataset bias therefore matter at the learning-signal stage. Evaluation must not simply ask the same imperfect score function whether its own optimization was successful.

[figure: al-limits]

warnings.message: The chosen/rejected example contains unsupported political-group intelligence comparisons. Preference labels are judgments, not evidence that those claims are true. Relative ranking can still encode bias or reward an unsupported premise.

sections.title: RLHF connects comparisons to policy optimization
sections.body:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback uses human judgments to shape a learning signal for policy improvement. In the common language-model pipeline, demonstrations first support SFT. Candidate responses are then compared, a reward model learns those comparisons, and a policy is optimized against the learned reward.

The policy generates outputs; the reward model scores prompt/output pairs. The human comparisons train the reward model rather than requiring a human to score every later optimization sample in real time. This reduces one particular feedback bottleneck while introducing dependence on how well the learned score generalizes.

The [historical InstructGPT research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155) verifies the SFT → comparison-trained reward → PPO policy-improvement mechanism. This is a defined research pipeline, not a complete current specification of every ChatGPT version or every foundation model. Other training systems can use different components or recipes.

A small response bandit isolates part of this mechanism. One action chooses one of four complete candidate responses and receives a scalar learned reward. An actual language policy normally chooses many tokens and accumulates sequence-level behavior. Our finite calculations do not implement a full language-model environment, critic network or multi-token PPO training run.

This simplification is useful because every possible action, probability, score and gradient can be exposed. It lets us distinguish the consequences of reward choice, reference regularization, sampling and clipping. These are algorithmic questions that a three-stage diagram alone cannot answer.

[figure: al-rlhf]

warnings.message: A historical pretraining/SFT/RLHF mechanism is not a complete current specification of every ChatGPT version. The specific GPT-3.5 pretraining/data attribution is not established here. Teach the verified research pipeline without inferring hidden product details.

sections.title: Policy, reward, old policy and reference have different roles
sections.body:
Several parameter sets can appear in one policy-improvement diagram. Confusing them makes both the update and its constraints hard to understand. The current policy is the distribution whose trainable logits or language parameters are being updated. The reward model supplies scores and is held fixed during the demonstrated policy update.

A reference policy supplies the distribution used for a divergence penalty. It is not necessarily the original pretraining checkpoint. In a common post-SFT recipe, the reference is the frozen SFT policy from which policy improvement starts. Its purpose is to discourage excessive movement away from that selected distribution.

PPO also uses an old policy: the policy that collected the current rollout. Ratios compare current probabilities with those old collection probabilities. The old snapshot remains fixed while the collected batch is optimized. Collecting another batch refreshes that old snapshot; the reference can remain unchanged across many such batches.

Thus π, π_old and π₀ answer three different questions: What does the model do now? How were these samples collected? Which fixed distribution defines the reference penalty? They can start equal while later becoming different. Equality at initialization does not make their roles interchangeable.

The four-action policy is a separate teaching calculation initialized to supplied reference probabilities [0.55,0.15,0.25,0.05]. These values define its finite starting distribution; they are independent of the earlier token-model fit.

The browser PPO calculation records all three distributions. Native updates change current logits, collection refreshes the old snapshot, and the reference stays at its original four probabilities. The reward coefficients also stay fixed. Expanding the tables reveals the actual arrays rather than treating all arrows as an unspecified model getting better.

[figure: al-components]

sections.title: KL divergence compares probability distributions
sections.body:
A forward KL penalty from current policy π to reference π₀ is:

$$D_{KL}(\pi\mid\mid\pi_0)=\sum_j\pi_j\log\frac{\pi_j}{\pi_{0, j}}.$$

It is zero when the distributions agree and nonnegative for valid distributions with the required support. The current policy weights the log ratios. Reversing the arguments produces a different quantity; KL is not generally symmetric.

The reference must assign positive probability to every action that the current policy might select if a finite forward KL is required. In the finite demo, all reference entries are positive and softmax current probabilities are positive. A zero-probability reference action would require special attention instead of silently dividing by zero.

Individual log-ratio terms can be negative. Moving probability away from an action gives a negative log ratio for that action, while other terms compensate so the weighted total KL remains nonnegative. Calling every term a positive distance would misrepresent the calculation.

A coefficient β weights this divergence against reward. A larger β puts more cost on distributional movement under the stated objective. It is a **soft tradeoff**, rather than a hard rule that guarantees the policy remains inside a particular radius. Changes in raw parameter distance and changes in output distributions are also different measures.

The penalty compares distributions, not the wording of two response strings. A sampled language-model implementation may estimate log-ratio rewards along generated tokens, but that estimate must be distinguished from exact enumeration. Our four-action calculation enumerates the forward KL exactly and displays its contribution separately from expected learned reward.

[figure: al-kl]

sections.title: Optimize an exact finite reward–KL objective
sections.body:
The first policy experiment uses all four possible actions rather than sampled rollouts. Its objective is expected learned reward minus the forward KL penalty:

$$J=\sum_j\pi_j r_j-\beta D_{KL}(\pi\mid\mid\pi_0).$$

Four logits define π through softmax. The reward values and reference distribution are fixed. The analytic gradient adjusts each logit according to its reward relative to current expected reward and its log ratio relative to current KL. A native update uses gradient ascent because larger J is the goal.

When β is positive, the exact optimal distribution for this finite problem is proportional to π₀,j exp(r_j/β). This relation follows from the normalization-constrained objective. Subtracting a common maximum before exponentiation makes its calculation stable. Adding a common constant to all rewards changes the objective value but preserves the optimal distribution.

At β=0, the limiting optimal distribution places mass on maximum-reward actions. This is an optimum of the declared reward objective, not a guarantee of correctness. A finite sequence of logit updates generally approaches concentration rather than producing a literal one-hot distribution instantly.

Compare the supported-answer and confident-style reward presets. The optimizer can raise expected learned reward under either. In the second case, it can shift probability strongly toward the unsupported wrong answer. The supported-answer probability visibly falls even though the optimized objective rises.

This calculation is an exact enumerated policy gradient, not PPO. Keeping it separate from the sampled clipped experiment helps identify which effects come from the objective itself and which come from estimating and optimizing a surrogate on a collected batch.

[figure: al-policy]

visuals.predict: Will maximizing confident-style reward necessarily increase supported-answer probability?
visuals.reflect: Separate learned reward, exact forward KL, objective and independent task evidence. Compare actual gradients with the analytic finite optimum.

sections.title: Collect actions under an old policy and freeze their advantages
sections.body:
A policy-gradient method can learn from sampled actions instead of enumerating every possible output. A rollout records what was selected, the policy probability at collection and the resulting reward. A batch then supports an estimate of a policy-improvement objective.

In the one-step response bandit, each episode ends after choosing a complete candidate. Its return is the frozen reward-model score. An advantage subtracts a baseline from that return. Our baseline is the exact expected reward under the collection policy, so an action above that expectation has positive advantage and one below it has negative advantage.

Using this known baseline is a deliberate simplification. A full implementation can estimate returns and advantages through a value function and temporal credit assignment. Those components are not present in the browser's one-step experiment, and the displayed advantages are not a claim of executing a language-model critic or generalized advantage estimator.

The collection snapshot π_old and the sampled advantages stay fixed during repeated actor updates. The current policy changes. If an action was collected with probability 0.1 and now has probability 0.14, its ratio is 1.4. The ratio accounts for the relationship between the new distribution and the one that supplied the batch.

The reference π₀ has another role: its divergence penalty remains separate from the old/current ratio. Recollecting refreshes π_old and sampled action counts while preserving π₀. Changing the requested count or seed configures the next collection; it does not retroactively rewrite a batch already collected.

Inspect action counts as well as probabilities. A finite sample can omit an action even when its probability is positive, and its estimated improvement can differ from exact expected reward. This is why the sampled surrogate and exact reward are different reported quantities.

[figure: al-rollouts]

sections.title: PPO-Clip limits the incentive in a sampled surrogate
sections.body:
The PPO-Clip actor objective compares an unclipped and a clipped probability-ratio term for each sampled action. Let ρ=π(a)/π_old(a), and let A be its fixed advantage. The selected term is:

$$\min\left(\rho A,\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A\right).$$

The batch objective averages these terms over the collected samples. The browser adds a separate exactly enumerated reference KL penalty. This is a reduced one-step categorical actor calculation with explicit advantages, rather than a full implementation of sequence RLHF.

The [original PPO research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347) verifies the clipped-surrogate construction. Clipping removes some incentive to continue changing a sampled action's ratio in an already favorable direction. It does not overwrite the current policy probabilities with the clipped values.

The advantage sign determines which side becomes a plateau. A positive-advantage action whose ratio exceeds 1+ε uses the upper clipped term. A negative-advantage action whose ratio falls below 1−ε uses the lower clipped term. On the opposite sides, the raw term remains active because reducing good-action probability or increasing bad-action probability should still be penalized by the surrogate.

The inspector displays raw term, clipped term, selected minimum, sample count, gradient and current/old/reference probabilities. A manual logit edit makes a clipping case visible without pretending the edit was learned. One actor update or ten updates then use the actual analytic surrogate gradient with fixed rollout data.

The numeric results are measured from the resulting logits. The display never labels a generic probability nudge PPO: ratios, advantages, clipping branches, batch weights and reference penalty all appear in the calculation.

[figure: al-ppo]

visuals.predict: For positive advantage and ratio above1+epsilon, which minimum term remains?
visuals.reflect: Inspect old/current/reference distributions, sampled counts/advantages, exact clipping branches and actual actor updates. Explain why a plateau is not a hard probability clamp.

sections.title: Clipping is not a hard probability bound
sections.body:
For ε=0.2 and advantage A=2, ratio 1.4 gives raw term 2.8 and clipped term 2.4. The selected minimum is 2.4. The action's own favorable-direction surrogate contribution is on a plateau. Its actual ratio can still be 1.4; clipping the term did not change that ratio to 1.2.

For advantage A=−2 and ratio 0.6, raw term is−1.2 and clipped term is−1.6. The minimum is−1.6. The lower-side plateau prevents an increasingly small probability from continuing to improve this action's contribution beyond the clipping threshold.

Now reverse the directions. Positive A with ratio 0.6 selects the raw term 1.2, while negative A with ratio 1.4 selects the raw term−2.8. The surrogate still responds to those unfavorable changes. Blindly clipping every gradient whenever a ratio leaves the interval would implement a different calculation.

A zero gradient from one clipped contribution is not necessarily a zero gradient for the whole policy. Softmax probabilities share a denominator. Other action contributions and the KL penalty can still change the selected action's probability. An unobserved action also participates in normalization even if its sampled reward term has zero count.

The old policy stays frozen within an optimization batch. A new rollout makes a new old snapshot; the reference distribution can stay fixed. These distinctions prevent the clipping interval from being mistaken for a universal bound on distance from the initial pretraining model.

Use the manual selected-action logit control to reproduce both plateau cases, then inspect the complete gradient table. The pedagogical goal is to identify which term becomes inactive and which terms remain active, rather than to assume that clipping guarantees all future behavior changes are small.

[figure: al-clipping]

warnings.message: The reference checkpoint is underspecified. A common historical recipe uses a frozen SFT policy, not necessarily the original pretraining model. KL penalizes distributional movement, and PPO clipping changes a surrogate incentive; neither is an unconditional hard bound on policy drift.

sections.title: Missing source material requires a different response
sections.body:
A request to summarize an article or video needs the relevant source. Without a link, transcript or supplied text, the system cannot ground a specific summary in that material. It can ask for the missing input or explain what evidence is needed, rather than inventing content to satisfy the surface form of the instruction.

An explanation of what a video-summary tool does is also different from summarizing a particular video. It may be irrelevant to the request, but it does not establish that the system has actually produced a factual summary of an unseen source. Evaluate the visible response and available evidence separately.

This example highlights an instruction/data boundary. A useful answer must recognize what the prompt supplies and what it omits. Fluent text alone is insufficient. For an article summary, generated claims should trace to article content; for factual QA, the requested regional distinction and factual support matter; for a poem, the specified line count matters.

One poor output does not by itself identify overfitting as its cause. Overfitting is a relationship between fitting data and generalization behavior, which requires appropriate evidence. Missing-input failures can arise from several mechanisms. Label the observed failure precisely before making a causal diagnosis.

SFT demonstrations can teach appropriate clarification responses. Preference data can favor asking for missing evidence over fluent fabrication. A reward model can nevertheless misjudge either behavior, and policy optimization can amplify that mistake. All three stages therefore need evaluation against the task's actual evidence requirements.

[figure: al-grounding]

warnings.message: The visible response describes a video-summary tool; it is not a summary of a supplied video. Without source content, a specific grounded summary cannot be verified. This single example also does not establish overfitting as the cause of the failure.

sections.title: Trace data, parameters and evidence through the whole pipeline
sections.body:
For any training claim, begin by identifying the data and target. Corpus next-token targets, demonstrated responses and pairwise preferences are different objects. A learned reward score is another prediction, while a policy update changes the distribution of possible outputs. This chain makes the learning mechanism assessable.

Next identify the parameter relationships. SFT can start from pretrained values and update all or a subset of them. LoRA freezes a base matrix and trains restricted factors. Reward-model fitting changes scoring parameters. Policy optimization holds those scores and a reference fixed while updating policy parameters; PPO additionally holds collection snapshots and advantages fixed within a batch.

Then inspect what is measured. Training loss concerns the fitting objective. Teacher-forced response loss uses gold earlier response tokens, while generation uses emitted earlier tokens. Candidate reranking changes which sampled output is returned while preserving the generator. Expected learned reward can increase without increasing supported-answer probability.

The browser experiments make each distinction concrete. They show actual 108-parameter pretraining/SFT updates, actual low-rank factor learning, exact answer-overlap metrics, actual four-coefficient reward learning, exact/sampled reranking, four-logit reward–KL optimization and a sampled clipped actor update. Their models and inputs are small and explicitly declared; they do not report pretrained conversational-model capabilities.

A reliable interpretation asks whether the result meets the task, whether the required information was available and whether evaluation is independent of the proxy that was optimized. The three-stage map explains a development path. The calculations reveal where that path can help, where it can fail and which evidence supports a particular conclusion.

[figure: al-synthesis]

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the three-stage map most directly?
choices: A different font for each model.
Every stage uses the same gold response.
Different data, targets and parameter-update objectives.
questions.why: Observed token targets, demonstrations and preferences supply different learning signals.

questions.prompt: Which step must occur separately from assigning a reward score?
choices: Displaying a candidate.
A policy parameter update if the generator is to learn.
Changing the response string into a score label.
questions.why: Scoring alone does not change the generator; optimization requires an actual update.

questions.prompt: Where is the next-token gold target during a causal training example?
choices: Separate from the visible earlier prefix.
Hidden inside the prefix as the answer input.
Always absent from the loss.
questions.why: The prefix contains earlier tokens, while the observed next token supplies the loss target.

questions.prompt: What limitation does mean-prefix pooling explicitly have in this toy model?
choices: It executes a complete Transformer.
It contains verified knowledge of every country.
It loses token order.
questions.why: Averaging token embeddings is order-insensitive; its limited scope is disclosed.

questions.prompt: Does SFT remove next-token prediction from language generation?
choices: Yes, output tokens no longer need a model.
No, it changes the fitted conditional distribution through demonstrations.
Yes, it replaces all vocabulary probabilities with a reward score.
questions.why: Instruction-following models still predict tokens; their fitting data/objective shapes what follows the instruction.

questions.prompt: One China question is fit perfectly. Does that identify a region-sensitive rule?
choices: No, several different rules may fit that one example.
Yes, all unseen country questions are thereby solved.
Yes, a training match proves universal reasoning.
questions.why: Training agreement alone does not distinguish the intended rule from a shortcut.

questions.prompt: What does adding an Africa demonstration change?
choices: The truth of the China answer.
Only the browser color scheme.
The supervision available to distinguish the regional responses.
questions.why: Additional task coverage can constrain a distinction missing from the earlier demonstration set.

questions.prompt: What does SFT typically use?
choices: Only a table of reward scores with no responses.
Instruction–response demonstrations and pretrained starting weights.
Random weights with no training data.
questions.why: SFT adapts broad pretrained representations using demonstrations of desired task behavior.

questions.prompt: Prompt positions have no direct target loss in response-only SFT. Can their embeddings still receive gradients?
choices: Only if gold targets are leaked into the prompt.
Yes, through their effect on response predictions.
No, a loss mask freezes every prompt parameter.
questions.why: Inputs can affect response hidden states even when their own token-prediction losses are excluded.

questions.prompt: Does pretrained initialization impose a hard bound on parameter drift?
choices: No, such a bound needs an explicit mechanism.
Yes, initialization itself prevents all large updates.
Yes, the optimizer cannot change old arrays.
questions.why: Warm starting chooses an initial point; it does not constrain subsequent optimization by itself.

questions.prompt: For an L2-to-start term λ/2 times squared displacement, what gradient is added?
choices: θ_start alone.
A constant unrelated to the parameters.
λ(θ−θ_start).
questions.why: Differentiating the quadratic adds a displacement-proportional restoring gradient.

questions.prompt: For W₀ of shape4×4 and rank1, what shapes produce BA with the same shape?
choices: Two4×4 identity matrices only.
B4×1 and A1×4.
B1×4 and A4×1.
questions.why: The inner rank dimension contracts, leaving output4 by input4.

questions.prompt: If B=0 and A is nonzero, which factor can receive a nonzero first gradient?
choices: B; the first A gradient through BA is zero.
A only.
Neither under any target.
questions.why: The B derivative uses A, while the A derivative is multiplied by B.

questions.prompt: Why can rank1 fail to fit a diagonal update with four nonzero entries exactly?
choices: The base matrix disappears.
A basis input cannot expose a matrix column.
The target has rank4 while BA has rank at most1.
questions.why: The factorized hypothesis class cannot represent that full-rank target exactly.

questions.prompt: Does rank2 save trainable entries for a4×4 update?
choices: Yes, the full model has only two parameters.
No,2(4+4)=16 equals the full matrix count.
Yes, it always uses fewer than16.
questions.why: Low-rank savings depend on dimensions and rank; this small case has no count reduction at rank2.

questions.prompt: Which condition is task-label transfer into Chinese?
choices: English-only QA fine-tuning followed by Chinese QA evaluation.
Chinese QA fine-tuning followed by Chinese QA evaluation.
Showing an English model name beside a Chinese prompt.
questions.why: Transfer is measured without task-labeled Chinese training examples in that condition.

questions.prompt: Prediction Everest versus gold Mount Everest has which English-word EM/F1?
questions.why: One shared unit gives precision1 and recall1/2, so F1=2/3 while the full sequences differ.

questions.prompt: Prediction mount mount versus gold mount everest has how much multiset overlap?
choices: Zero tokens.
One token.
Two tokens.
questions.why: The gold contains only one mount, so repeated predicted mounts cannot create a second match.

questions.prompt: A normalized benchmark ratio exceeds1. What does that support?
choices: A score above the selected task-specific baseline under that protocol.
Proof of greater ability than all humans on every language task.
A guarantee of factual answering.
questions.why: Benchmark metrics/baselines concern defined tasks and evaluation conditions.

questions.prompt: What makes a translation demonstration well specified?
choices: An absent target language and an unchanged source as the only answer.
A claim that every task is the same.
An identifiable source/input and target-language direction.
questions.why: The task instruction must distinguish the transformation the demonstration teaches.

questions.prompt: What does FLAN exemplify here?
choices: PPO clipping with no demonstrations.
Instruction tuning across diverse task families.
A guarantee that one model solves every task perfectly.
questions.why: Its role is a broad instruction-conditioned adaptation approach with measured limitations.

questions.prompt: Separate translation and summarization demonstrations establish what about a combined request?
choices: They can help, but reliable composition still needs evaluation.
They prove every composition will work.
They remove the need for source text.
questions.why: A combined operation introduces linked requirements not established by the individual tasks alone.

questions.prompt: How does a preference label differ from a demonstration?
choices: It removes all supervision.
It is automatically unbiased factual proof.
It compares available responses instead of necessarily supplying one ideal response.
questions.why: Pairwise or ranked judgments and written target outputs are different label types.

questions.prompt: Is ranking always less work than writing?
choices: Yes, labels are generated with no human judgment.
No, annotation effort depends on the task and required checks.
Yes, no comparison ever needs factual verification.
questions.why: Comparison can help on some tasks, but careful checking can still be expensive.

questions.prompt: A request for three lines receives two three-line stanzas. Does it satisfy the format?
choices: No, the visible response has six lines.
Yes, each stanza has three.
Yes, mentioning AI is sufficient.
questions.why: The constraint applies to the requested response, not to each stanza independently.

questions.prompt: What should a general reward model condition on?
choices: Only a model name.
Only a universal response-length score.
Both the prompt and the candidate response.
questions.why: Response appropriateness depends on the question/request and supplied context.

questions.prompt: Does fitting preference scores change the candidate generator automatically?
choices: Yes, displaying scores trains embeddings.
No, reward fitting and policy optimization change separate parameters.
Yes, every scoring operation updates the generator.
questions.why: A subsequent policy-learning step is required to change generator parameters.

questions.prompt: Two equal scores imply what logistic labeled preference probability and loss?
choices: Probability1/2 and loss ln2.
Probability1 and loss0.
Probability0 and loss0.
questions.why: A zero score gap gives sigmoid(0)=1/2 and negative log probability ln2.

questions.prompt: Add5 to every reward score. What happens to pair probabilities?
choices: Every probability increases by5.
They become negative.
They are unchanged because score differences are unchanged.
questions.why: A common offset cancels from every score gap.

questions.prompt: Sampling and returning the highest-scored candidate updates which generator parameters by itself?
choices: Only the embedding table.
None.
All of them.
questions.why: Best-of-N is inference-time selection rather than a parameter update.

questions.prompt: What must the best-of-1 returned distribution equal?
choices: The fixed generator distribution.
A one-hot argmax reward distribution.
A new trained policy unrelated to the generator.
questions.why: A single sampled candidate is returned regardless of its score.

questions.prompt: Does a high reward-model score guarantee a factual answer?
choices: Yes.
Only for long responses.
No; the reward model is an imperfect proxy.
questions.why: The optimized score can differ from truth or the real user objective.

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes the historical preference-based pipeline?
choices: Reward display→automatic universal knowledge.
PPO→a mandatory current specification of every product version.
Demonstrations→SFT; comparisons→reward fit; generated actions/reward→policy improvement.
questions.why: The pipeline is a defined learning mechanism with distinct data and fitting steps.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between π_old and the reference π₀?
choices: Both are gold response strings.
π_old collected the current batch; π₀ defines the selected fixed divergence reference.
They must remain identical forever.
questions.why: Collection refreshes the old snapshot while the reference can remain fixed.

questions.prompt: Why use a KL penalty during RLHF?
choices: To discourage excessive divergence from a reference policy.
To erase the reward model.
To force all responses to be identical.
questions.why: It balances improving reward against moving too far from the reference distribution.

questions.prompt: Can an individual π_j log(π_j/π₀,j) term be negative?
choices: Yes, even though the total KL is nonnegative.
No, every term is a positive distance.
Only if probabilities do not sum to1.
questions.why: An action with π_j<π₀,j has a negative log ratio; the weighted sum remains a valid nonnegative divergence.

questions.prompt: If learned reward favors confident wrong answers, what can objective optimization do?
choices: Guarantee factual correction without new evidence.
Change the frozen labels into truth.
Increase learned reward while lowering supported-answer probability.
questions.why: The optimized proxy and the task requirement can diverge.

questions.prompt: Is the enumerated four-action reward–KL gradient necessarily PPO?
choices: Yes, KL alone defines clipping.
No, it is an exact finite objective calculation; PPO uses a separately defined sampled surrogate here.
Yes, any probability change is PPO.
questions.why: The two experiments expose different objectives and update contracts.

questions.prompt: What stays fixed while optimizing one collected PPO batch?
choices: The old collection policy and supplied advantages.
The current trainable policy logits.
All future batches and samples.
questions.why: The surrogate uses a fixed batch/snapshot while current parameters change.

questions.prompt: For A=2,ρ=1.4 and ε=0.2, what selected surrogate term results?
questions.why: The minimum of2.8 and2.4 chooses the upper-clipped plateau.

questions.prompt: For A=−2,ρ=0.6 and ε=0.2, what selected term results?
questions.why: The minimum of−1.2 and−1.6 chooses the lower-side plateau for negative advantage.

questions.prompt: Does clipping a surrogate term force the actual probability ratio into the clipping interval?
choices: No, it changes the objective term rather than clamping the policy.
Yes, the ratio is overwritten.
Yes, all probabilities become equal.
questions.why: Other terms and KL can still produce updates through shared softmax probabilities.

questions.prompt: A request to summarize a video provides no link or transcript. What evidence-grounded response is appropriate?
choices: Invent a specific summary.
Treat a description of a tool as a verified video summary.
Ask for the missing source material.
questions.why: The relevant content is unavailable, so it cannot support a specific summary.

questions.prompt: Which final check goes beyond asking the optimized reward model to grade itself?
choices: Only the name of the training recipe.
Independent task evidence and actual held-out/generated behavior.
Only the current learned score.
questions.why: A proxy can be optimized successfully while failing the user’s underlying task.

questions.prompt: Equally frequent opposite labels A>B and B>A favor which balanced pair probability?
choices: One-half.
Always one.
Always zero.
questions.why: A nonzero gap helps one label and hurts the other; a zero gap balances their logistic losses.

questions.prompt: Add a common constant to every fixed reward in the finite KL objective. What happens to its optimal policy?
choices: Every action probability increases by that constant.
Only the reference distribution changes.
It remains unchanged.
questions.why: The common exponential factor cancels during normalization; the objective value shifts but the preference tradeoff does not.

title: Autonomous Vehicles: Safety Evaluation and Enhancement
summary: Rare-event estimation, sparse adversarial traffic, statistical realism and critical-state learning.

sections.title: Driving is a closed loop
sections.body:
An autonomous driving system must repeatedly turn observations into actions while the world changes around it. A camera image is one input to that process. The outcome is physical: steering, acceleration and braking change the vehicle's position, which changes what its sensors will see next. Other road users react too. **The system being evaluated is a closed loop, not an isolated image classifier.**

Connected, automated and electrified transportation describe different changes. Connectivity exchanges information; automation performs driving tasks; electrification changes the powertrain. A connected electric vehicle can still be human driven. Conversely, an automated driving feature can operate with limited external communication. Keeping these ideas separate prevents an impressive technology demonstration from answering the wrong safety question.

A useful functional decomposition is perception, localization, prediction, decision making and control. Perception identifies relevant road users, road structure and signals. Localization estimates the vehicle's pose relative to its surroundings and map. Prediction anticipates plausible motion of other agents. Planning selects a feasible response. Control turns that response into actuator commands. These components interact: uncertain localization can make an otherwise sensible planned path miss its intended lane.

Cameras provide appearance and image geometry; lidar measures ranges through emitted light; radar supplies useful range and motion information. Their errors and failure conditions differ. Combining sensors requires synchronization, calibration and a policy for uncertainty. A high-definition map is prior information, not a live guarantee that the road is unchanged.

The history from remote-controlled demonstrations to navigation research, challenge competitions and modern automated fleets illustrates increasing capability. Remote control alone does not establish autonomy. For this lecture, the essential question is how to obtain meaningful evidence about the **whole driving loop** under interacting traffic.

[figure: av-loop]

reading.takeaway: Evaluate the sensing–decision–action loop under the environment in which it operates.

warnings.message: The statement that highway expansion made railways obsolete is an overgeneralization. Changing transport patterns do not establish the disappearance of rail transport.

sections.title: Automation levels describe responsibilities
sections.body:
The levels of driving automation distinguish which actor performs the driving task and handles its fallback. They do not assign a numerical safety score. The relevant unit is an **engaged driving feature under its stated conditions**, rather than a manufacturer's name or an entire car treated as one unchanging category.

At level 0, a person drives; warnings and momentary intervention can still exist. Level 1 assists either longitudinal motion or steering. Level 2 assists both, while the driver continuously supervises the driving environment and remains responsible for intervention. Hands-free operation in some circumstances does not by itself change those responsibilities.

At level 3, the system performs the driving task within defined conditions, while a fallback-ready user must be able to respond when required. At level 4, the system handles the driving task and fallback within its operational design domain without relying on that user to mitigate risk. Level 5 extends operation to all on-road conditions in which a human driver can operate. These distinctions concern roles and scope; they do not imply that every feature at a higher level is safer than every lower-level feature.

The **operational design domain**, or ODD, specifies conditions such as road type, geographic area, speed range, weather and lighting. A feature designed for a mapped urban area cannot be evaluated as if its evidence covered every rural road. Object and event detection and response, often abbreviated OEDR, concerns recognizing and responding to relevant conditions within that driving task.

A sensible test therefore states the feature, its domain, the driver or system responsibilities, and the event being measured before any comparison begins. SAE's [driving-automation taxonomy](https://saemobilus.sae.org/topics/electrical-electronics-and-avionics/automation/driving-automation/level-3-conditional-driving-automation) supports these role distinctions.

[figure: av-levels]

reading.takeaway: A level names responsibilities and domain; a safety claim needs separate evidence.

warnings.message: Automation level is not a safety ranking. A feature’s assigned level describes intended task and fallback responsibilities, and its operational domain still matters.

sections.title: Choose a comparable safety measure
sections.body:
Development forecasts and dramatic demonstrations can motivate research, but they are not measurements of safety. A safety comparison must define its endpoint and exposure. Crashes, injuries, fatalities, near conflicts and disengagements answer different questions.

A **disengagement** is an interruption of automated operation, such as a safety driver taking over. Some occur before a potential crash; others reflect discomfort, testing procedures or system limitations. A **crash** is a physical event. Treating every disengagement as a crash, or assuming every avoided crash causes a reported disengagement, introduces an unsupported conversion between measures.

Likewise, a rate per mile differs from a probability per simulation episode. If every episode covers the same distance, counts can be related to that declared exposure. When episode lengths vary or tests stop after a failure, dividing by the number of episodes alone does not yield a per-mile rate. Reweighting exposure is also necessary when estimating a natural rate from a changed testing distribution.

A thought experiment makes the issue clear. Suppose system A records one takeover per 100,000 miles, while a human-driving dataset records one crash per 1,000,000 miles. The numerical ratio is ten, but its numerator and denominator describe different events. It is not evidence of ten times the crash risk. Road mix, weather, traffic density and reporting practices may also differ.

Before interpreting a graph, write an evidence statement: “This system version, in this defined traffic environment, produced this specified event over this exposure, estimated using this procedure.” That statement makes the comparison auditable. A headline about rapid progress or disappointing deployment does not substitute for it.

[figure: av-endpoints]

reading.takeaway: Match the event, exposure, domain and system before comparing rates.

warnings.message: The crash-versus-disengagement comparison uses different endpoints and does not establish a numerical safety gap. Matching exposure, domain and reporting definitions is also necessary.

sections.title: Rarity and dimensionality are different obstacles
sections.body:
Most driving experience involves ordinary motion. The situations most informative about severe failures can be uncommon combinations: an unusual road user, an occluded conflict, an emergency vehicle, or a difficult maneuver under poor visibility. The “long tail” describes many infrequent cases, not one single exceptional image that a model must memorize.

The **curse of dimensionality** concerns how rapidly the possible joint configurations grow. Weather, road geometry, speed limits, positions, velocities and actions across many road users produce a large state and trajectory space. Even if each variable has only ten categories, ten such variables already give ten billion combinations. A dataset can be large in absolute size while sparse relative to that space.

The **curse of rarity** concerns the scarcity of the event or learning signal of interest under the natural distribution. If a relevant failure occurs with probability one in a million, a million independent tests produce only one expected failure. Most observations may teach routine behavior while providing little direct information about that endpoint.

These problems interact. A rare event can occur through several different high-dimensional mechanisms. Collecting more common cruising trajectories does not necessarily expose those mechanisms. Conversely, encountering one dramatic failure does not establish how much natural probability each mechanism has.

The distinction also affects learning. A gradient can be difficult to estimate when informative contributions are concentrated in a tiny region, even if the neural network can represent the required function. Model capacity, coverage, learning-signal variance and validation are separate issues. Rare events do not make all deep learning mathematically incapable; they make ordinary data collection and learning objectives an unreliable default for some safety questions.

[figure: av-rarity-space]

reading.takeaway: A large scenario space and a scarce event signal require separate remedies.

warnings.message: The claim that current deep learning cannot handle these cases is too broad. The concrete issue is sparse coverage and high-variance learning or evaluation signals, not a general proof of representational impossibility.

sections.title: Failure discovery and risk estimation
sections.body:
There are two related reasons to create difficult scenarios. **Failure discovery** finds concrete weaknesses and gives engineers informative cases for improvement. **Risk estimation** estimates the frequency of a defined event under a target population of driving conditions. A testing program can do both, but its evidence must distinguish them.

A worst-case search can demonstrate that a failure is possible under its constraints. It cannot turn a found scenario into a natural event frequency without exposure probabilities and a valid estimation procedure. The search may intentionally prefer situations that almost never occur naturally. That preference can be useful for diagnosis while making raw crash counts inappropriate for population risk.

Formal verification asks another question: whether a property holds under a mathematical model and assumptions. Its conclusions depend on those assumptions, the property, and the modeled system. Black-box behavior and complex interacting environments make some approaches difficult, but do not imply that every formal technique is useless or that statistical testing replaces all verification.

Testing typically combines software simulation, controlled physical facilities and public-road evidence. Simulation offers repeatability and scale. A test track exposes hardware, sensing, communication and control timing. Road observations reveal conditions and interactions that a model may omit. Each mode can challenge the others' assumptions.

Think of an agent interacting with an environment: the environment supplies observations, the driving agent acts, and the state evolves. An intelligent testing environment chooses background-agent behavior to make this interaction informative. The word “intelligent” does not automatically guarantee unbiased evaluation; the probabilities and correction still have to be specified.

The goal is to estimate natural risk with fewer tests. A high test crash count alone does not achieve that.

[figure: av-testing-goals]

reading.takeaway: A found failure is a mechanism; an estimated risk also needs a target distribution.

warnings.message: Descriptions such as “falsification cannot evaluate safety” or “testing cannot handle complex environments” are scope-dependent. Failure search, formal analysis and statistical evaluation support different claims and can be combined.

sections.title: What a naturalistic environment represents
sections.body:
A naturalistic driving environment, or NDE, models the distribution of traffic encountered in a specified real-world setting. It is a stochastic model of interacting behavior, not merely a road that looks familiar.

Represent a scenario trajectory by X: the initial conditions and the states or actions of the background road users through time. If there are N vehicles and T decision times, each entry Xᵢ,ₖ may contain position, speed and other variables. The natural distribution p(X) assigns probability or density to this joint object.

Matching each individual driver's average speed is insufficient to match p(X). Vehicles respond to nearby gaps, lane changes, yielding and conflicts. Correlations determine whether two individually plausible motions produce an implausible joint collision. Long rollouts can amplify a small error because the next prediction is conditioned on the simulator's own generated states.

The target domain matters. A highway-following model is not automatically a roundabout model. Even within one road type, traffic composition, conditions and driver populations can change the relevant distribution. Naturalistic driving data, or NDD, supplies observed behavior used to estimate these distributions. It is the evidence used to construct an NDE; the two terms are not interchangeable.

A scenario description should identify maneuvers such as following, cut-in, free driving, overtaking and lane change, then specify the variables that affect them. For a cut-in, the initial gap, relative speed, merge timing and neighboring traffic all matter. Exhaustively enumerating every detailed trajectory is generally impractical.

The question to carry forward is precise: **which distribution is the evaluation targeting, and how faithfully does the environment represent it?** Importance sampling can correct a deliberate change from a known p to q. It cannot correct an incorrect natural model p.

[figure: av-joint]

reading.takeaway: Naturalistic means distributionally representative of a stated domain.

sections.title: Why ordinary mileage grows so quickly
sections.body:
Let A be a defined event and p its probability in one independent, equal-exposure test. With n tests and m observed events, the crude Monte Carlo estimate is m/n. Its expectation is p and its variance is p(1−p)/n. For small p, reducing relative uncertainty requires many tests because the expected event count np is small.

An approximate 95% relative half-width is 1.96√[p(1−p)/n]/p. To target a relative half-width β, rearrange this expression to obtain n ≈ 1.96²(1−p)/(β²p). For rare events, the expected event count is approximately (1.96/β)². At β=0.20 this is 96.04 expected events, requiring about 96 million tests when p=10⁻⁶.

This is a planning approximation, not a rule that observing the ninety-sixth event proves safety. Confidence procedures, comparison hypotheses, dependence and stopping rules affect the conclusion. Injury and fatality endpoints can be rarer than all crashes, so their exposure requirements can be much larger.

Zero observed events also leave uncertainty. Under independent Bernoulli trials, the probability of no events is (1−p)ⁿ. Solving (1−p)ⁿ=0.05 gives the one-sided 95% upper bound 1−0.05¹⁄ⁿ after zero events. For large n this is approximately 3/n. Zero crashes in a million tests therefore does not establish a zero natural crash probability.

The experiment uses deliberately stated test probabilities and independent trials. Changing its trial count is not a vehicle simulation or a claim about modern fleets. Use it to connect rarity, expected events and precision rather than memorizing one spectacular mileage total.

$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat p)=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}$$

[figure: av-counts]

visuals.predict: With one expected event, will a zero-event batch still be plausible?
visuals.reflect: Explain the difference between an expected count, an observed count and a confidence bound.

reading.takeaway: Relative precision depends on informative event counts and statistical assumptions.

warnings.message: The notation mixes a 95% confidence level with α in z₁₋α/₂. Use 1−α=0.95 and α=0.05 to obtain 1.96. The resulting 96-event calculation is an approximate precision requirement, not a general safety proof.

sections.title: Build a trajectory probability step by step
sections.body:
A practical environment model uses structure to avoid estimating an unrestricted probability table over every trajectory. A Markov assumption makes the next background action depend on the current state. Locality restricts the relevant state to nearby road users rather than every vehicle on the map.

Under a further conditional factorization across agents, a natural trajectory likelihood consists of an initial-state term multiplied by the selected action probabilities across vehicles and times. Schematically, p(X)=p(s₀)∏ₖ∏ᵢp(uᵢ,ₖ | sₙᵢ,ₖ). The neighborhood state contains the information the local behavior model uses.

This factorization does not claim that road users are unconditionally independent. Two drivers can be dependent because they respond to the same state. But multiplying per-agent action probabilities at a given state does assume the residual joint action distribution factorizes in that representation. Unmodeled communication or hidden common intentions can violate it.

If state transitions are deterministic and identical under the natural and testing models, they cancel from a trajectory likelihood ratio. So do unchanged agent-action factors. If transitions include noise, or the initial-state distribution is altered, their probability ratios also belong in the weight. Leaving them out changes the estimator's meaning.

The traffic experiment later makes this contract explicit: it uses a fixed initial configuration and deterministic kinematics, changes only declared background-action probabilities, and evaluates the same tested controller under both modes. Its natural model is an invented finite policy. It does not claim to reproduce the real population of drivers.

For each trajectory step, record the state, sampled action, natural probability, test probability and likelihood-ratio factor.

[figure: av-factorization]

reading.takeaway: A likelihood ratio must cover every stochastic factor that the test changes.

sections.title: Importance sampling changes the test, not the target
sections.body:
Importance sampling makes informative scenarios occur more often while correcting for the change in sampling probabilities. Let p(x) describe the target natural scenario distribution and q(x) the testing proposal. For a deterministic event indicator I_A(x), the natural risk is μ=Σp(x)I_A(x).

Draw x from q and record Y=I_A(x)p(x)/q(x). Its expectation is Σq(x)I_A(x)p(x)/q(x)=μ, provided q is positive wherever the event has positive natural mass. Averaging n independent contributions gives the ordinary importance estimator. The denominator is **the probability used to draw that scenario**, not its natural probability.

A numerical example is useful. A dangerous category has natural mass 0.01 but test mass 0.20. Each occurrence contributes 0.05 when it is an event. It is sampled twenty times more often, so its contribution is twenty times smaller. The expected weighted contribution remains 0.01.

The six-category experiment has an exact natural event probability of 0.005. Useful oversampling raises the raw test event probability to 0.65, but the weighted estimator still targets 0.005. You can inspect actual finite draws, including different crash-producing categories, rather than merely moving a decorative probability slider.

Support is essential. If a naturally possible crash category has q=0, it is never observed under that proposal. No finite weight applied to other samples recovers its missing contribution. The experiment explicitly reports the covered expectation and calls out this failure.

For stochastic outcomes given x, an observed event indicator remains valid when the conditional outcome law is unchanged. If the conditional event probability is known exactly, using that conditional expectation is another estimator with its own second moment. These should not be silently interchanged.

$$\hat\mu=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}I_A(X_j)\frac{p(X_j)}{q(X_j)}$$

[figure: av-importance]

visuals.predict: Which proposal can have the most raw events but worse weighted precision?
visuals.reflect: Compare the true target, covered expectation, sampled estimate and both standard-error calculations.

reading.takeaway: Oversample informative cases, preserve support, and average their corrected contributions.

sections.title: Efficiency is about the second moment
sections.body:
Unbiasedness and efficiency are separate properties. Two proposals can have the same expected corrected estimate but very different variability. A proposal that concentrates almost all tests on one dangerous category may neglect another category with a large importance weight.

For deterministic event indicators, the second moment of one weighted contribution is Σ_A p(x)²/q(x). Its variance is that second moment minus μ². The variance of the mean of n independent contributions is divided by n. Therefore the goal is not simply to increase the raw event fraction; it is to make the **weighted contributions** stable.

In the finite experiment, natural sampling has one-test variance 0.004975. Useful oversampling reduces it to approximately 0.0000137308. Extreme oversampling generates events on 99.7% of tests yet has variance approximately 0.00163106, much worse than the useful proposal. Its allocation across event types is poor.

The ideal deterministic-event proposal samples only events in proportion to their natural masses: q*(x)=p(x)I_A(x)/μ. Every observed contribution then equals μ, giving zero variance. This is usually impractical because the event region and μ are the quantities being investigated. A defensive natural component is useful when a surrogate misses part of that region.

A finite batch can still give a misleadingly small empirical error. If no weighted event contributions occur, their sample variance is zero even though the true variance is positive. The experiment also reports an oracle standard error computed from its fully enumerated distribution. That oracle is available here because the toy problem is known exactly; it is not normally available for a black-box driving system.

For Bernoulli outcomes whose conditional probabilities are between zero and one, the observed-indicator second moment uses P(A|x), whereas averaging exact conditional probabilities uses its square. State which random quantity you are estimating before optimizing a proposal.

[figure: av-variance]

reading.takeaway: A high crash count is useful only when the weighted estimate also has good precision.

warnings.message: A squared conditional crash probability describes an estimator that averages known conditional probabilities. For actual sampled Bernoulli crash indicators, I_A²=I_A, so the second moment uses P(A|X), not its square. The objective must match the estimator.

sections.title: Why unnecessary adjustments multiply variance
sections.body:
Changing many background decisions can introduce noise into the trajectory weight even when only a few influence the event. This is the statistical reason to investigate sparse adjustments.

Consider one irrelevant binary variable. Under nature it is a fair bit. Under the test, it is one with probability b and zero with probability 1−b. Its likelihood ratio has mean one, but its squared-weight expectation is 0.25/b+0.25/(1−b). At b=0.5 the factor is one. At b=0.8 it is 1.5625.

Now add k independent irrelevant bits to the finite scenario experiment. The event still depends only on the original scenario category. If the test also biases all these bits, their squared-weight factors multiply. The mean remains the same, but the event second moment grows by 1.5625ᵏ. If the irrelevant bits retain their natural distribution, all their weight factors are one and the original scenario variance is preserved.

This construction is an exact counterexample to the idea that more adversarial changes always help. It also shows why dimension **alone** is not sufficient to conclude exponential variance growth: when b=0.5 there is no mismatch in those dimensions.

For a deterministic event, the ideal event-conditioned q* gives Var(Y)=μ²χ²(q* || q). Jensen's inequality yields the lower bound μ²[exp(KL(q* || q))−1]. A large divergence from the ideal proposal can make the problem difficult. Inferring linear growth of that divergence with dimension requires additional mismatch assumptions; it is not automatic from the number of variables.

The exact experiment isolates this mechanism without pretending to model a highway. In real traffic, choosing critical variables is harder because dynamics and interactions determine what matters, and apparently irrelevant choices can become relevant later.

[figure: av-dimensions]

visuals.predict: Will adding ten biased but irrelevant variables improve the event estimate?
visuals.reflect: Compare natural extra variables with biased ones, then explain the second-moment multiplication.
