reading.takeaway: Adjusting irrelevant variables preserves the mean but can inflate weight variability.

warnings.message: Exponential variance growth is not a universal consequence of dimension. The divergence bound requires valid likelihoods and support; linear divergence accumulation requires persistent mismatch assumptions. Matched extra variables add no weight variance.

sections.title: Naturalistic and adversarial driving environments
sections.body:
A naturalistic and adversarial driving environment, or NADE, combines two aims: preserve the connection to natural traffic and increase the frequency of informative interactions. Its key idea is **sparse adversarial adjustment**. Most background decisions remain natural; selected critical decisions use a different sampling distribution.

Suppose a scenario has critical variables X_c and remaining variables X_−c. In an idealized independent decomposition, sample X_c from q_c while leaving X_−c under its own natural distribution p_−c. The trajectory weight then depends only on the adjusted part. Whether the adjusted variables actually capture the rare-event mechanisms determines the remaining variance.

Independence is a simplifying assumption for that theorem, not a license to ignore traffic correlations. If the variables are dependent, one can instead preserve the appropriate natural conditional distribution of the unadjusted variables given the sampled critical values, when that distribution is available. The target joint law and the proposal joint law must both be defined.

For dynamic driving, “critical” is identified from the current state and the possible maneuvers of nearby background vehicles. The testing environment asks when to adjust a vehicle and which action to favor. A change is adversarial because it challenges the tested system, not because the vehicle is assigned an unrealistically malicious personality at all times.

Sparse adjustment reduces unnecessary probability changes, but its percentage is not a guarantee of realism. A small changed fraction can still dominate rare-event statistics. The point is to retain valid support and likelihood correction while improving the estimation variance, not to claim the test distribution equals nature.

The following sections calculate exposure, challenge, criticality, principal selection and the defensive sampling proposal.

[figure: av-sparse]

reading.takeaway: Sparse adjustment means changing selected informative decisions while accounting for the changed distribution.

warnings.message: The unadjusted-variable expression has an inconsistent subscript. Under the stated independence assumption use X_−c ~ p(X_−c), not p(X_c). With dependence, preserve the appropriate joint or conditional law rather than assuming independence.

sections.title: Criticality combines challenge and exposure
sections.body:
The most threatening maneuver is not always the most informative naturally occurring maneuver. A move can be dangerous in a surrogate while having negligible natural exposure. NADE's maneuver criticality combines both quantities.

For background vehicle i in state s and maneuver u, let h_i(s,u)=P(S_i | s,u) denote a surrogate challenge: the probability of an event involving that vehicle in a simplified model. Let p_i(u|s) denote its natural maneuver probability. Define V_i(s,u)=h_i(s,u)p_i(u|s). This product measures the surrogate's naturally weighted event contribution for that action.

For example, a very challenging maneuver with h=0.9 and exposure 0.001 has criticality 0.0009. Another with h=0.2 and exposure 0.10 has criticality 0.020. The second contributes more surrogate-weighted natural risk despite being less threatening conditional on being executed.

Sum V over a vehicle's maneuvers to obtain vehicle criticality C_i(s). Choose a principal other vehicle, or POV, with the largest C_i above a stated threshold. If no candidate exceeds the threshold, no principal adjustment is made at that moment. In the described highway mechanism, at most one POV is selected per moment.

The surrogate is useful because the tested controller may be inaccessible or expensive to evaluate. It can supply approximate domain knowledge about which interactions deserve extra testing. It is not identical to the tested system. A defensive mixture helps preserve support when the surrogate is wrong, but cannot ensure an efficient proposal.

This distinction appears in the traffic experiment: surrogate and tested AV reaction delays are separate controls. A deterministic surrogate lookahead provides a transparent binary challenge. That is an explicitly reduced proxy, not a measured human exposure table or a calibrated research risk model.

[figure: av-criticality]

reading.takeaway: Use challenge times exposure, then select a principal vehicle from summed maneuver criticalities.

sections.title: Learn a probability of eventual collision
sections.body:
Maneuver challenge can concern a future event, not only collision in the next instant. A state-action value Q(s,u)=P(S | s,u) can predict eventual collision under a specified continuation model. The target is a probability, so its boundary conditions matter.

The small learning experiment uses eight nonterminal gap bins. One bin represents three metres. Actions open, hold or close the gap by one bin. Gap zero is collision and gap nine is safe termination. After any nonterminal move, there is a 0.1 probability of exiting safely. Otherwise the fixed continuation policy chooses open with probability 0.15, hold with 0.70 and close with 0.15.

For a move directly into collision, the Bellman target is one. For safe termination, it is zero. Otherwise the target is 0.9 times the policy-weighted value of the next state's actions. A TD update moves each of the 24 tabular coefficients toward this target. All targets in a sweep use the previous coefficient table, so update order cannot accidentally change the calculation.

This is **actual fitting**: the values start at zero and repeated updates propagate collision information from the near boundary into more distant states. A separate exact absorbing-chain solution supplies a reference probability. You can inspect the current coefficient, its target, the reference and the maximum error after each sweep.

There is no max over future actions. That would answer a different question about an optimizing controller rather than risk under the stated continuation policy. The model also omits vehicle inertia and lateral interaction; the mechanistic experiment later handles declared kinematics separately.

A terminal-free recurrence can never create collision probability from an all-zero table. Explicitly setting the collision boundary to one is essential. Treat a missing terminal condition as a modeling error rather than an interesting training failure.

[figure: av-challenge]

visuals.predict: Which gap-action coefficients should receive nonzero information first?
visuals.reflect: Follow the collision boundary signal through actual TD sweeps and compare with the exact solution.

reading.takeaway: A probability-valued Bellman update needs a specified continuation policy and terminal events.

warnings.message: A future-challenge recurrence needs collision and safe-terminal boundary conditions. Without the collision value of one, an all-zero table can remain zero and fail to represent the event probability.

sections.title: A defensive mixture preserves natural support
sections.body:
Once a principal vehicle is chosen, its test maneuver probabilities favor naturally weighted surrogate challenge. Normalize V_i(s,u) by C_i(s) to obtain an event-focused action distribution. Then mix it with the natural action distribution.

The defensive proposal is q_i(u|s)=εp_i(u|s)+(1−ε)V_i(s,u)/C_i(s), with 0<ε≤1 and positive C_i. The other vehicles keep their natural action distributions. When no vehicle is principal, every background action remains natural.

The two terms have separate purposes. The normalized criticality term concentrates tests on the surrogate's informative maneuvers. The natural term preserves positive proposal probability for every naturally possible action, including one assigned zero challenge by the surrogate. At ε=1, the proposal is exactly natural. As ε decreases, the proposal becomes more concentrated and can become brittle when the surrogate is inaccurate.

For a simple three-action example, let natural probabilities be 0.80, 0.15 and 0.05, and surrogate challenges 0, 0.20 and 1. Criticalities are 0, 0.03 and 0.05, totaling 0.08. With ε=0.30, the proposal becomes 0.24, 0.3075 and 0.4525. It sums to one. The first action retains test probability even though its surrogate challenge is zero.

If C_i=0, V_i/C_i is undefined; the mechanism must fall back to natural sampling rather than divide by zero. Likewise ε=0 removes the defensive guarantee. The traffic experiment bounds ε away from zero and makes principal selection explicit.

Changing ε does not change the tested AV's physical controller. It changes how background actions are sampled. Every actual selected action then contributes the appropriate p_i/q_i factor to the episode weight.

[figure: av-mixture]

reading.takeaway: The natural mixture protects support; it does not guarantee an accurate surrogate or low variance.

sections.title: Step through a weighted driving episode
sections.body:
The traffic experiment executes a complete small interaction. One tested AV begins in lane zero; a slower lead vehicle starts ahead; another background vehicle begins in the adjacent lane. At each half-second step the environment evaluates candidate criticalities, chooses a principal vehicle if appropriate, samples background maneuvers, advances kinematics and checks collision.

The model states its units and assumptions. Vehicles have a declared length of 4.5 metres. Longitudinal position and speed follow piecewise constant acceleration, with a correct stopping-time calculation if braking reaches zero speed. A merge transfers the background vehicle into lane zero at the beginning of a step. This instantaneous lane change is a deliberate simplification rather than realistic lateral vehicle dynamics.

The AV has a stated delayed gap-based braking controller. The surrogate has its own reaction delay and a deterministic three-second lookahead. Changing these separately lets you see how a proxy can overestimate or underestimate the tested controller's difficulty. The selected action probabilities and their actual weight factors remain inspectable.

Collision checks use swept longitudinal overlap within each common-lane time interval. Checking only the final positions can miss a vehicle that passes through another between timestamps. A detected collision ends the episode; otherwise the horizon is eight seconds. The event follows from the computed motion.

The cumulative episode weight is the product of the sampled natural-to-test action ratios. Unchanged actions contribute one. Initial conditions and dynamics are identical under both policies, so their factors cancel in this particular experiment. A different experiment that changes initialization must include its ratio.

One weighted episode illustrates the estimator's contribution, not a meaningful estimate of population road safety. The finite scenario experiment provides repeatable estimation batches; this mechanistic one explains how a sequential proposal and a trace fit together.

[figure: av-episode]

visuals.predict: Will the selected principal vehicle be the closest vehicle, or the one with the largest exposure-weighted challenge?
visuals.reflect: Inspect the chosen actions, collision calculation and product of actual p/q factors; then change surrogate versus tested reaction delays.

reading.takeaway: The trajectory, event and likelihood ratio must come from the same executed episode.

sections.title: From recorded trajectories to maneuver probabilities
sections.body:
Natural action probabilities need evidence. The highway case uses recorded driving behavior to estimate exposure and calibrate background models. This is a transportation-data problem as much as a machine-learning problem.

Two research data collections illustrate different scales. The Safety Pilot Model Deployment involved over 2,800 vehicles and about 35 million miles or 1.2 million driving hours, with a subset equipped for detailed acquisition. The Integrated Vehicle-Based Safety System collection used sixteen instrumented vehicles and 108 adult drivers, combining radars, video, GPS and other signals. These are descriptions of particular research collections, not current universal traffic statistics.

Processing converts raw observations into usable behavior records. Detect vehicles and lane structure, link observations into trajectories, identify maneuver start and completion times, and categorize the surrounding configuration. Free driving, car following, cut-in and lane changes with zero, one or two adjacent vehicles require different conditioning variables.

For following, speed and bumper gap may be relevant. For a lane change, adjacent leading and following vehicles contribute additional gaps and relative speeds. A histogram without that context can mix substantially different decisions. Missing observations, measurement errors and selection bias affect the estimated exposure distribution.

The highway simulation uses a three-lane environment and equal 400 m test distances. Its tested AV and surrogate are distinct. The surrogate combines an Intelligent Driver Model for following with a stochastic adaptation of MOBIL for lane changing, calibrated to recorded behavior. The educational simulator here uses its own explicit finite action probabilities instead; it does not reuse these fitted data or models.

The diagram describes the research data pipeline; the live experiment uses separately specified example data.

[figure: av-data]

reading.takeaway: Exposure models need measured behavior, conditioning variables and a clear data-processing chain.

sections.title: Interpret the NADE highway evaluation
sections.body:
The highway case provides three kinds of evidence: changed encounter distributions, more informative interactions, and corrected event-rate estimates. They should be read separately.

Sparse adjustments increase exposure to small gaps, short time-to-collision values and difficult maneuvers. Time to collision, or TTC, is commonly defined under a constant-velocity closing assumption as gap divided by positive closing speed. If vehicles are not closing, that simple TTC is not a finite predicted crash time. It is a surrogate measure, not a substitute for simulating future braking and lane changes.

The reported case adjusted about 1.5% of background maneuvers. That describes sparsity in that experiment. It does not prove that the full trajectory distribution equals the NDE. Indeed, the test deliberately encounters more cut-ins, hard braking and lane conflicts. The importance weights are what connect its estimates back to the natural model.

For the AV-II case, the reported precision threshold was a relative half-width of 0.30. The compared test counts were 1.41×10⁸ under NDE and 2.32×10⁴ under NADE. Their ratio is approximately 6,078, supporting the rounded description “about 6,000” fewer tests at that criterion. Equal 400 m tests correspond to roughly 35 million miles of eliminated exposure in the reported comparison. These are research results, not measured output from the browser experiments.

The relevant claim is about estimation efficiency for the particular vehicle models, traffic model, proposal and precision rule. A count ratio does not necessarily equal a wall-clock ratio: proposal computation, simulation cost, hardware and parallelism matter. Nor does it establish the same improvement for a different road domain.

The [NADE research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-21007-8) documents the evaluation. The comparison uses the reported test totals, a declared precision threshold and a specific evaluation scope.

[figure: av-case]

reading.takeaway: Compare corrected estimates at a declared precision criterion, and keep test counts distinct from runtime.

warnings.message: Similar ordinary-driving marginals and a small adjustment percentage do not establish identical joint traffic distributions. Increased rare-event exposure is intentional; its raw frequencies must not be interpreted as natural rates.

sections.title: Preserve crash mechanisms as well as the total
sections.body:
An aggregate crash probability can conceal changes in mechanism. A test might find many rear-end events while missing lane-change conflicts. Estimation should therefore consider category-specific contributions as well as their sum.

The highway evaluation distinguishes five types involving the AV and background vehicles: the AV rear-ends a background vehicle; a background vehicle rear-ends the AV; the AV changes lanes into a sideswipe; a background vehicle changes lanes into a sideswipe; or both change lanes and sideswipe. The category concerns the collision geometry and maneuver, not simply which car looks more aggressive.

For a type k, replace I_A with the type indicator I_k in the importance estimator. If the categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive for the defined event, summing their weighted estimates gives the total estimate. If categories overlap or omit mechanisms, that identity no longer holds without an explicit counting rule.

The reported AV-II chart shows unweighted NADE frequencies dominated by types 1 and 4, with labels approximately 0.032 and 0.014 per test. Those are proposal frequencies. The weighted comparison instead reports values on the order of 10⁻⁷ per test for the major types, close to NDE estimates within the stated precision. A raw frequency and a weighted estimate can differ by several orders of magnitude without contradiction.

A displayed zero is another interpretive limit: it can mean no observed occurrences at the available resolution, rather than a proof that a mechanism is impossible. Very rare categories need their own support and precision assessment.

Read the small weighted probabilities alongside the collision geometry. Raw test frequencies and natural estimates have different meanings. Finding diverse adversarial examples helps diagnose mechanisms, while a population estimate still requires valid weighting and sufficient precision.

[figure: av-types]

reading.takeaway: Weight each defined mechanism, then check how its categories relate to the total.

sections.title: Connect simulated traffic to a physical AV
sections.body:
Augmented-reality testing combines a physical test vehicle and road infrastructure with simulated background traffic. It aims to expose a real driving stack to controlled interactions without requiring every challenging background vehicle to be physically present.

The architecture separates traffic generation, simulation, data management and the tested vehicle. The generator selects background maneuvers. A traffic simulator advances those virtual vehicles using a map. Data management coordinates simulated background information and the physical vehicle's reported state. A roadside or onboard communication path delivers the relevant information to the tested system, whose actions feed back into the next simulation step.

Timing is fundamental. A virtual vehicle placed correctly in a static image can still be inconsistent with the real vehicle's timestamp, camera pose or control loop. Latency, localization error and coordinate transforms can change the apparent gap and response time. These are part of the testing apparatus, not details that can be ignored after drawing a vehicle overlay.

There are different insertion points. Injecting tracked virtual objects into a perception output can test planning and control against those objects while bypassing part of the sensor and perception chain. Compositing virtual traffic into sensor observations exercises a different path, with additional requirements on occlusion, appearance and measurement physics. State explicitly what is injected and what components see it.

The implementation examples connect instrumented vehicle hardware with an automated-driving software stack, traffic simulation and messaging. Their value is the physical–virtual loop, not the logos of the software components. A view of the road, an onboard simulation view and an augmented view can help diagnose whether the loop is aligned.

Named data paths clarify which components the test exercises. Automotive engineering, AI and transportation behavior must be evaluated together because a statistically useful scenario can still be misaligned with a real sensor or controller.

[figure: av-ar]

reading.takeaway: Physical–virtual testing evidence depends on the injection point, synchronization and tested components.

sections.title: First model nature, then learn a better tester
sections.body:
An intelligent testing environment has two distinct learning tasks. First build p(X), a representative natural environment. Then learn q_θ(X), a testing proposal that allocates more effort to informative cases while retaining a valid correction to p. Confusing these tasks can make a tester efficient at answering the wrong population question.

Replay, heuristic simulation and learned behavior models have different strengths. Logged replay preserves recorded motion but is not inherently reactive to a new tested vehicle. Heuristic rules can offer stability and interpretability while oversimplifying complex interactions. Learned models can represent richer behavior but may produce accumulated distribution shift or implausible rare conflicts.

A low trajectory prediction error is useful but insufficient. Predicting one agent's short future in a recorded scene differs from rolling out many agents who respond to one another's generated states. Individual accuracy and environment-level accuracy are distinct targets.

The testing proposal has an estimation objective rather than only an imitation objective. In the deterministic-event case it can aim to minimize Σ_A p(X)²/q_θ(X), subject to retaining positive probability wherever the event has positive target mass. Sparse adjustments make that high-dimensional optimization more structured.

Neither stage excuses errors in the other. Perfect likelihood correction from q to a flawed natural model p gives an unbiased estimate **for that model**, not automatic accuracy for real roads. A statistically faithful p with a poor q can require an impractical number of tests. An efficient q without support can be biased.

The analogy to testing an intelligent agent with another intelligent process motivates adaptive testing. It does not replace the estimator, its assumptions or the validation of the environment. The next sections explain statistical realism and why deliberately preserving some conflicts can be necessary when modeling ordinary traffic.

[figure: av-two-models]

reading.takeaway: Natural environment modeling targets realism; proposal learning targets estimation efficiency.

sections.title: NeuralNDE models joint behavior and conflicts
sections.body:
NeuralNDE is a learned naturalistic environment framework. Its aim is statistical realism of traffic, including ordinary motion and safety-critical interactions. It is not simply a renderer, and it is not the same object as an adversarial importance-sampling proposal.

A behavior-modeling network uses the historical states of multiple road users to predict action distributions. Actions are sampled, so the resulting environment can be stochastic. A conflict critic checks potentially conflicting motion. A safety-mapping network can rectify dangerous actions before the state transition.

Crucially, the system does not remove every conflict. A trajectory-dependent acceptance mechanism allows some dangerous behavior to pass through, while other predicted conflicts are rectified. Calibration seeks agreement with real-world event frequencies and patterns. A simulator with zero crashes could be convenient for a demonstration while being a poor model of natural driving risk.

Training includes imitation signals from observed trajectories and adversarial signals that distinguish generated rollouts from real trajectories. A learned discriminator is a training component, not the safety evaluator's final evidence. A model can improve a discriminator objective while still missing a relevant rare-event statistic, so separate validation remains necessary.

The architecture connects these roles: joint historical state → predicted action distributions → sampled actions → conflict decision → optional rectification → new joint state → repeated rollout. The imitation and adversarial learning signals return to their relevant training components. Keep each component’s input, output and learning signal distinct.

High-resolution trajectory collection provides positions and interactions needed for that modeling. Accurate observation is necessary, but the resulting dataset can still be sparse in rare failures. The [NeuralNDE study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-37677-5) provides the verified distinction between behavior generation, conflict acceptance and safety mapping.

[figure: av-neural]

reading.takeaway: A natural simulator should reproduce relevant conflicts at realistic frequencies, rather than suppress all of them.

sections.title: Train a small conflict-acceptance model
sections.body:
The calibration experiment isolates one statistical mechanism from the larger architecture. It contains three mutually exclusive invented conflict groups: rear-end, sideswipe and angle. Their generated masses are 0.12, 0.08 and 0.04. The synthetic target masses are 0.008, 0.003 and 0.001. None of these values is a reported NeuralNDE measurement.

Let a_k be the acceptance probability for type k. The corrected mass is g_k a_k, where g_k is its generated mass. To match the target t_k by accepting or rectifying each group, the required acceptance is t_k/g_k. Rejected conflicts are mapped into the no-event category in this declared finite model.

Three sigmoid logits parameterize these acceptances. Starting at zero makes every acceptance 0.5. The browser performs real gradient updates on a mean Bernoulli cross-entropy with fractional target acceptances. For each logit, the derivative is [sigmoid(logit)−t_k/g_k]/3. The visible loss, error, coefficients and corrected rates come from the current parameters.

After sufficient fitting, the groups approach their distinct target rates. A single common acceptance would generally fail to preserve their relative proportions. The experiment displays all three groups, so matching the total alone cannot hide a mechanism error.

Acceptance can only reduce existing generated mass. If a target exceeds g_k, the required acceptance is greater than one. If g_k=0 with positive target mass, no acceptance coefficient can create that missing event. Both cases stop fitting and display a WARNING. Rectification can have downstream interactions in real traffic; this finite exercise explicitly assumes none.

This is useful small-model training, but it is not a reproduction of NeuralNDE's joint networks, learned safety mapper or calibration procedure. It lets you test the necessity of support, feasible acceptance and type-specific rate checks with transparent arithmetic.

[figure: av-calibration]

visuals.predict: Will accepting every predicted conflict or rectifying every one match the synthetic target?
visuals.reflect: Train the three coefficients, inspect per-type rates, then remove support or request an infeasible target.

reading.takeaway: Calibration is constrained by the event mass the generator can actually supply.

sections.title: Validate distributions at more than one scale
sections.body:
Statistical realism requires a collection of checks with different meanings. Ordinary behavior measures include instantaneous speed, inter-vehicle distance, yielding distance and yielding speed. Rare-event measures include crash probability, crash type and severity, and near-conflict statistics.

A matching speed distribution does not determine crash probability. A matching crash total does not determine crash-type composition. Short-horizon trajectory accuracy does not determine the stability of an hour-long interactive rollout. Each check can reveal a different failure in the generated environment.

The evaluation comparisons use distribution distances as well as visual overlap. For the speed distribution, printed Hellinger and KL values are 0.041 and 0.008 for NeuralNDE, versus 0.189 and 0.126 for the compared SUMO baseline. For vehicle distance, the corresponding printed values are 0.031 and 0.004 versus 0.172 and 0.088. These values belong to that particular evaluation and its distribution construction; they are not universal rankings of simulation packages.

Near conflicts are important even when no crash occurs. Post-encroachment time, or PET, measures the interval between one road user's departure from a shared conflict area and another's arrival. It differs from a constant-velocity TTC estimate. A small PET can signal a close temporal interaction without an actual impact.

These scalar distances summarize particular empirical distributions. They do not specify sampling uncertainty or establish every rare mechanism. Crash-type and severity comparisons ask different distributional questions and need their own sample support and precision.

A video that looks plausible demonstrates an example rollout. It does not by itself establish those distribution checks. Conversely, one convincing summary histogram cannot guarantee that every rare mechanism is modeled correctly. Think in terms of a validation matrix: normal behavior, rare mechanisms, interaction patterns and long-horizon stability.

[figure: av-validation]

reading.takeaway: Validate ordinary motion, rare events, mechanisms and rollout stability separately.

sections.title: D2RL concentrates learning on critical states
sections.body:
Proposal learning itself can suffer from rarity. Most natural trajectories may provide weak information about the safety-relevant objective. Dense deep reinforcement learning, or D2RL, addresses the information content of the learning process by editing its state-transition representation.

The mechanism identifies safety-critical states, removes uncritical states from the learning chain and reconnects retained states. “Dense” refers to concentrating useful information in the learning representation. It does not mean the simulated road becomes physically crowded, every timestep becomes a crash, or every discarded state stops existing.

The physical trajectory still contains the original transitions. A retained learning transition can span multiple original steps. Its effective transition law, accumulated rewards and any elapsed-time discount must be treated consistently. Arbitrarily deleting states and applying an unchanged one-step update would be a different, generally unjustified algorithm.

Criticality and outcome are also distinct. A near conflict can contain informative states even when the tested AV resolves it safely. The replay experiment computes a resolved-conflict trajectory and a collision trajectory from the declared traffic model. Both contain retained critical decisions. A quiet episode provides a contrasting trace with none under the same surrogate threshold.

The replay highlights the original indices, retained chain and elapsed time to the next retained state. It is a mechanistic illustration of state selection, not training the original D2RL neural agents. Its criticality comes from the transparent three-second surrogate rather than the full research risk assessment.

The [D2RL research description](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05732-2) verifies this edited-chain idea. To understand why such a change can improve learning, the next experiment uses a separately declared probability model where the mean and variance can be derived exactly. This keeps a research theorem distinct from a visual analogy.

[figure: av-critical-chain]

visuals.predict: Can the resolved-conflict episode retain useful states despite ending without a crash?
visuals.reflect: Compare original and retained indices and their elapsed times; then contrast the quiet and collision episodes.

reading.takeaway: Critical states can be informative in successful episodes; editing a chain also changes its learning contract.

sections.title: A variance calculation for concentrated information
sections.body:
A simple probability example makes the distinction between information density and unbiasedness concrete. Let B be an independent Bernoulli gate with probability ρ. Let Z be +1 or −1, with P(Z=+1)=a. The original contribution is G=BZ: most observations contribute zero when ρ is small.

Its mean is ρ(2a−1), and its variance is ρ−ρ²(2a−1)². If we can sample directly from the informative conditional population, a corrected contribution is H=ρZ. It has the same mean and variance ρ²[1−(2a−1)²]. For small ρ this can be substantially lower than the variance of G.

The factor ρ is essential. Averaging Z alone estimates the conditional mean 2a−1, not the natural mean of BZ. A dataset can become more informative and simultaneously become biased if its selection probability is ignored. The experiment displays this uncorrected mean alongside both correct ones.

There is also a computational caveat. Five hundred conditional contributions are not the same resource as five hundred unfiltered source observations. If obtaining each informative observation requires rejection from the original distribution, it costs about 1/ρ source draws on average. Lower variance per retained contribution is not automatically a free speedup per unit of original simulation cost.

The dense-learning theorem states preservation of an estimator's expectation and reduced variance under its construction. Its stronger reciprocal-prevalence statement additionally uses a second-moment factorization condition. The displayed condition is not equivalent to every possible state-filtering rule. At ρ=0 the reciprocal is undefined, so that limiting case needs separate treatment.

This independent-gate model is an exact teaching example, not proof that any red-node filtering scheme obeys the D2RL theorem. It helps you identify which correction, assumptions and computation budget a real claim would need.

[figure: av-dense]

visuals.predict: What happens to the uncorrected conditional mean as informative states become rarer?
visuals.reflect: Compare both exact variances, the sampled means and the stated source-draw budget.

reading.takeaway: Information concentration must preserve the target mean and account for sampling cost.

warnings.message: The stronger dense-learning variance factor uses a stated second-moment factorization condition and requires positive informative-state prevalence. It is not guaranteed for arbitrary state deletion or an uncorrected conditional sample.

sections.title: Keep target and behavior policies distinct
sections.body:
Learning a testing policy requires connecting the optimization objective to the data-collection policy. The target testing policy may change during training, while a behavior policy generated the stored trajectories. These are distinct distributions even when they occasionally coincide.

The displayed off-policy reward construction uses a crash indicator and two trajectory likelihood factors: r(X)=−I_A(X)W_target(X)W_behavior(X), where W_target=p(X)/q_target(X) and W_behavior=p(X)/q_behavior(X). This reward is a construction for the stated learning objective, not simply a count of crashes or a measure of the AV's everyday utility.

Why two factors? Under behavior sampling, taking its expectation cancels q_behavior and leaves a negative event-weighted second moment associated with q_target. In a deterministic finite event model, E_behavior[r]=−Σ_A p(X)²/q_target(X). Maximizing that negative quantity corresponds to reducing the importance estimator's second moment. This is different from encouraging an AV to crash as often as possible.

Correct support is needed for both denominators on relevant trajectories. A stored trajectory must retain the behavior probability that actually generated it. Replacing that probability with the newly updated target policy would generally change the calculation. This resembles the distinction between collection and current actor policies in the previous lecture, but the specific objective here concerns testing efficiency.

Critical-state identification can use behavior prediction, trajectory prediction and risk assessment. A proxy selects informative states, while a derivation specifies how learning uses them. A short TTC alone is not a complete learned testing reward, and an arbitrary heuristic reward cannot inherit this off-policy identity.

The browser's finite proposal experiment and gate example allow exact moment checks. They do not implement this full trajectory-level reward training, its off-policy replay machinery or the original neural policy. Keeping that boundary explicit protects the meaning of both the theory and the actual demos.

[figure: av-reward]

reading.takeaway: A testing reward derived from variance minimization differs from simply rewarding crashes.

sections.title: Read the later crash-rate comparison carefully
sections.body:
The later evaluation again compares corrected crash estimates and precision, then checks crash categories. Its plotted convergence and reported test totals belong to a particular testing setup. They should be distinguished from the earlier NADE highway result and from the browser's reduced experiments.

The caption compares 1.9×10⁸ NDE tests with an average 9.1×10⁴ tests for the proposed approach. Dividing gives approximately 2,088, matching the rounded statement 2.1×10³ fewer tests. The chart also labels one proposed-method threshold crossing as 4.96×10⁴. That is a different number from the caption's average; the distinction between a displayed run and the reported average is not resolved by the available evidence alone.

Use the caption totals for its reported average comparison and keep the separately labeled crossing distinct. Neither a displayed mean nor a shaded band fully specifies sampling uncertainty without its statistical definition.

Crash-type evaluation distinguishes rear-end, sideswipe, angle and head-on events. Unweighted proposal frequencies and weighted natural estimates are shown on different scales. Their shapes answer different questions: what challenging events the test generated, and what rates are estimated under the target model.

A zero head-on bar is an observed or displayed result for that evaluation, not universal evidence that head-on risk is absent. Domain, maneuver support, sample size and category definitions limit the interpretation. A total that agrees while one mechanism differs deserves investigation.

Compare efficiency only after matching the statistic, precision rule, sample aggregation and tested system.

[figure: av-later-evidence]

reading.takeaway: Keep separate evaluations, single-run labels and reported averages separate.

warnings.message: The chart labels a 4.96×10⁴ crossing, while its caption reports an average 9.1×10⁴ tests. The available material does not resolve that aggregation difference. The approximately 2.1×10³ comparison uses the caption’s 9.1×10⁴ value.

sections.title: World models and sensor fidelity
sections.body:
A testing world model connects physical road structure, observed driving behavior, interactive simulation and sensor observations. These layers have different fidelity requirements. A photorealistic scene can have incorrect traffic frequencies; a statistically useful traffic simulator can have simplified sensor appearance.

Road infrastructure and trajectory collection provide geometry and observed behavior. Logged data can support reconstruction and model fitting. Behavior modeling and interaction simulation generate traffic. An intelligent testing environment changes selected interactions to make rare cases more informative. A sensor-generation layer then renders what configured cameras or lidar would observe from the tested vehicle.

Camera number, placement, intrinsics, field of view and lens model influence the observations. Lidar placement, angular sampling and measurement properties matter too. Flexible sensor configuration is a modeling capability, not a guarantee that every synthetic measurement matches hardware. Occlusion, lighting, timing and calibration can affect the tested perception stack.

The visual examples motivate a connection between structured testing scenarios and generated sensor views. They do not provide a complete validation of every generated road, weather condition or sensor. Likewise, “anywhere and anytime” expresses an ambition to generate geographically flexible tests; it does not establish calibrated naturalistic probabilities for every location.

A robust interpretation asks which layer was validated and against what evidence. Was road geometry checked? Were joint interactions and event rates compared with observed data? Were sensor measurements calibrated? Was a physical AV in the loop? A result at one layer should not automatically be carried to another.

This lecture has two continuing quantities: p describes the modeled natural world, and q describes the deliberately informative test. A world model helps execute and observe both. It does not remove the need to define the endpoint, preserve relevant support, correct sampling and validate the natural target.

[figure: av-world]

reading.takeaway: Visual, dynamic, statistical and physical-loop fidelity require different evidence.

warnings.message: Geographic flexibility and photorealistic rendering do not establish validated natural event rates everywhere. New domains require relevant behavior data, model and sensor checks, and an explicit evaluation scope.

sections.title: Design an evaluation claim you can defend
sections.body:
Start an evaluation design by naming the driving feature and its operational domain. Specify the system version, the event endpoint, and the unit of exposure. A collision probability per eight-second scenario is a different claim from fatalities per mile. Do not let a compelling animation erase that distinction.

Next state the natural target. Describe where its data came from, which interactions and conditions it represents, and which assumptions factor its trajectories. Validate ordinary behavior, rare mechanisms and long-horizon rollout separately. If the model omits a relevant naturally possible event, no clever test proposal can recover its natural mass.

Then state the testing proposal. Explain which initial conditions or actions it changes, how principal decisions are selected, and how support is preserved. Record the actual proposal probability for every sampled decision. Compute the trajectory ratio from the complete changed law, including initialization or transition noise if those were altered.

Report actual sampled events and corrected contributions separately. Show precision appropriate to the weighted estimator and acknowledge finite-sample weaknesses. Evaluate crash categories as well as their total. Keep source-reported research numbers separate from teaching-model output, and test-count savings separate from runtime savings.

For learning, distinguish the tested driving policy, surrogate, natural behavior model and testing policy. Name the parameters updated, the boundary conditions and the objective. Critical-state concentration can be useful, but its mean-preserving construction and computation budget must be explicit. A resolved near conflict can teach something even when the final crash indicator is zero.

Finally identify which components the experiment reaches. Sensor injection, object injection, traffic-only simulation and physical–virtual testing exercise different portions of the loop. **The best evidence claim is specific enough that another reader can tell what would invalidate it.** The experiments in this lecture support conceptual and numerical understanding of those contracts; their invented traffic models do not validate a real vehicle.

[figure: av-synthesis]

reading.takeaway: A defensible claim ties the event, natural target, proposal, estimator and tested loop together.

questions.prompt: Why can a good image classifier still be part of an unsafe driving system?
choices: Localization, prediction, planning or control can fail in the closed loop.
Classification accuracy completely determines physical safety.
Every camera output directly sets the steering angle.
questions.why: Component performance does not determine the behavior of the complete interacting system.

questions.prompt: A level-4 feature is validated on a particular mapped urban domain. What does that establish about an unfamiliar rural domain?
choices: Its domain can be ignored because it has lidar.
Nothing automatic; the unfamiliar domain needs its own applicability and evidence assessment.
The higher level guarantees every rural road is safe.
questions.why: Level 4 specifies system responsibility within an ODD, not universal geographic competence.

questions.prompt: One disengagement per 10⁵ miles is compared with one crash per 10⁶ miles. What is the valid conclusion?
choices: The automated system has exactly ten times the crash risk.
The automated system has exactly one tenth the crash risk.
Those are different endpoints; their ratio does not establish a crash-risk ratio.
questions.why: A takeover is not the same measured event as a crash.

questions.prompt: Why is an event probability per variable-length test insufficient for a per-mile rate?
choices: The natural expected event count must also be related to natural exposure distance.
Miles are always identical to the number of tests.
A probability can be relabeled as a distance without a denominator.
questions.why: An episode denominator and an exposure-distance denominator are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A million ordinary cruising records contain no emergency-vehicle encounters. What remains uncertain?
choices: Rarity has been removed because cruising is frequent.
Behavior in that rare interaction may still be poorly learned or validated.
Dataset size proves every rare interaction is covered.
questions.why: More common observations do not ensure coverage of a specific infrequent mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which quantity expresses dimensionality rather than event rarity?
choices: The probability of the crash endpoint under natural traffic.
The number of crashes observed in one batch.
The number of joint road-user state and action configurations.
questions.why: Dimensionality describes the space; rarity describes probability or informative-signal prevalence.

questions.prompt: Does finding one adversarial crash estimate its real-world frequency?
choices: Yes, exactly.
No; exposure and sampling probabilities are also needed.
Only if the simulation looks realistic.
questions.why: Failure discovery and risk estimation are distinct tasks.

questions.prompt: Every agent matches its marginal speed histogram. Why can the joint simulator still be wrong?
choices: Any speed histogram guarantees correct crash frequency.
Their correlated responses and long-horizon interactions may differ from real traffic.
Marginal matching determines every joint distribution uniquely.
questions.why: Matching one-agent marginals does not determine dependence or trajectory statistics.

questions.prompt: At p=10⁻⁶, one million independent tests produce how many expected events?
choices: Exactly one guaranteed event.
One million.
One.
questions.why: Expectation np is one; the observed count can be zero, one or more.

questions.prompt: For a two-sided 95% normal approximation, what does α mean in z₁₋α/₂?
choices: The 0.05 significance level, so the quantile is 0.975.
The value 0.95 substituted into that formula.
The observed accident count.
questions.why: The confidence level is 1−α; α=0.05 gives z≈1.96.

questions.prompt: The proposal also changes the initial-gap distribution. What must the trajectory weight include?
choices: No initial-state factor because all roads have gaps.
The natural-to-proposal ratio for the initial gap as well as changed action factors.
Only the last action ratio.
questions.why: Every changed stochastic factor in the trajectory law contributes to its likelihood ratio.

questions.prompt: Why does oversampling dangerous scenarios require reweighting?
choices: To estimate the natural event rate despite a changed test distribution.
To remove all crashes from the dataset.
To guarantee the vehicle is safe.
questions.why: Raw frequencies under q generally differ from natural probabilities under p.

questions.prompt: A scenario has p = 0.01 and q = 0.2. What is its importance weight?
questions.why: The correction is p/q = 0.01/0.2 = 0.05.

questions.prompt: A testing proposal assigns zero probability to a crash-producing scenario that has positive natural probability. What follows?
choices: More testing under the same proposal will automatically recover its contribution.
The proposal misses relevant support, so the usual importance estimator cannot recover that contribution.
Its importance weight should be set to zero.
questions.why: A never-sampled natural crash contribution cannot be corrected by multiplying observed samples by p/q. Relevant target support must remain covered.

questions.prompt: Why can extreme oversampling be less efficient than a balanced event-focused proposal?
choices: Every valid proposal must have identical variance.
A raw event fraction above 90% guarantees zero variance.
It can neglect other event mechanisms and create highly variable weights.
questions.why: Efficiency depends on the full second moment, including rarely sampled event mechanisms.

questions.prompt: A batch observes zero events and reports empirical standard error zero. What follows?
choices: That sample contains no observed variation, but true uncertainty can remain positive.
The natural event probability is proven zero.
Every future batch must have zero events.
questions.why: Sample variance can miss rare contributions; it is not evidence that the true distribution has none.

questions.prompt: In the independent-bit example, what happens when each extra bit is sampled naturally?
choices: The event probability doubles per bit.
Its weight is one and it adds no extra second-moment factor.
Variance must grow exponentially just because a bit exists.
questions.why: The factor is exactly one when proposal and natural distributions agree.

questions.prompt: What assumption enables the product of per-bit squared-weight factors?
choices: The simulator has attractive road graphics.
All vehicle crashes have the same severity.
Independence of those extra variables under the stated factorized construction.
questions.why: The example deliberately factorizes the irrelevant bits; arbitrary dependent traffic does not inherit this calculation.

questions.prompt: For independent critical and noncritical variables, which natural distribution belongs to the unadjusted variables?
choices: p(X_−c), the natural law of the noncritical variables.
p(X_c), regardless of which variables are sampled.
The adversarial law q(X_c) copied without changing indices.
questions.why: Each variable group must be sampled from its own correctly indexed distribution.

questions.prompt: Which maneuver has higher criticality: h=0.9,p=0.001 or h=0.2,p=0.10?
choices: They are equal because each has two numbers.
The second: 0.020 exceeds 0.0009.
The first because only h matters.
questions.why: Criticality is the product of conditional challenge and natural exposure.

questions.prompt: A surrogate finds no critical maneuver. What does that prove about the tested AV?
choices: Every tested controller is safe in that state.
The natural exposure of every action is zero.
No safety guarantee; the surrogate may miss a failure mechanism.
questions.why: Surrogate judgments are model-dependent approximations.

questions.prompt: Why does the challenge experiment average future Q values instead of taking their maximum?
choices: It predicts risk under a fixed stochastic continuation policy.
Every risk calculation must choose the most dangerous action.
Averaging means no parameters are updated.
questions.why: Policy evaluation and optimizing action choice are different calculations.

questions.prompt: Why does NADE retain a positive naturalistic component in its defensive mixture?
choices: To preserve natural support even when surrogate criticality misses a maneuver.
To make all importance weights equal to one.
To prevent every crash.
questions.why: The mixture gives naturally possible maneuvers positive test probability. It mitigates surrogate errors but does not make every proposal efficient or the vehicle safe.

questions.prompt: What is the correct response when all maneuver criticalities sum to zero?
choices: Divide by zero and set every resulting probability to one.
Declare every possible action impossible in nature.
Use natural sampling rather than normalize a zero total.
questions.why: The normalized criticality proposal is undefined at C=0; no principal adjustment is warranted.

questions.prompt: Two unchanged background decisions have p=q. How do they affect the episode ratio?
choices: Each contributes one.
Each removes all previous weight factors.
Each contributes zero.
questions.why: A factor with unchanged conditional sampling probability cancels.

questions.prompt: Why check swept overlap rather than only end-of-step positions?
choices: Endpoint checks always detect every crossing.
A collision can occur between timestamps even if final positions are separated.
The graphic needs more colors.
questions.why: Continuous motion within the interval can contain an overlap missed at its endpoints.

questions.prompt: Why categorize lane changes by adjacent-vehicle configuration?
choices: Every lane change must have the same natural probability.
A category label removes all measurement error.
Different nearby gaps and relative speeds affect the conditional maneuver distribution.
questions.why: Conditioning on relevant neighboring traffic preserves differences lost in an unconditional histogram.

questions.prompt: About 1.5% of background maneuvers were adjusted. Does that prove the test joint distribution is natural?
choices: No; a small changed fraction can strongly alter rare-event statistics.
Yes; any adjustment below 2% leaves every probability unchanged.
Yes; sparse changes eliminate the need for weights.
questions.why: Sparsity and distributional identity are different properties.

questions.prompt: A method uses 6,000 times fewer tests at matched precision. What remains needed for a wall-clock speedup claim?
choices: No further information; every test has identical cost by definition.
The actual computation cost, hardware and parallelization of both methods.
Only the number of colors in the convergence plot.
questions.why: Test-count efficiency and computation time are different measurements.

questions.prompt: When do the category-specific weighted estimates sum to the total event estimate?
choices: Whenever the categories have appealing names.
When every category is assigned the same probability.
When the categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive for that event.
questions.why: The indicator of the total equals the sum of category indicators only under the stated partition.

questions.prompt: A rare crash type has zero observed count. What is established?
choices: No occurrence was observed in that sample; impossibility is not proven.
Its natural probability is exactly zero.
Its proposal probability must be one.
questions.why: Observed absence and structural impossibility are different claims.

questions.prompt: Virtual tracked objects are injected after perception. Which claim needs additional evidence?
choices: That the test contains simulated objects.
That the camera and perception pipeline handles those objects correctly.
That planning received any virtual object information at all.
questions.why: Injecting after perception bypasses some sensing and detection behavior.

questions.prompt: If q is corrected exactly to an inaccurate natural model p, what is obtained?
choices: A guaranteed real-world crash rate regardless of p.
No estimate of any kind is possible.
A model-based estimate for p, with real-world validity still uncertain.
questions.why: Importance correction removes the deliberate sampling shift; it does not validate the target model.

questions.prompt: Why can a simulator that prevents every collision be unsuitable as a naturalistic environment?
choices: It may remove genuine natural event mass and distort the target risk distribution.
Any collision-free simulator perfectly reproduces every human behavior.
Naturalistic means every vehicle follows a maximum-safety policy.
questions.why: A risk evaluator needs a representative distribution, including naturally occurring failures.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the discriminator in this modeling framework?
choices: The tested AV’s brake actuator.
A training signal for distinguishing generated from observed trajectories.
A proof that every safety statistic is correct.
questions.why: Adversarial training and final statistical validation are separate roles.

questions.prompt: Generated angle-conflict mass is zero while target angle mass is positive. Can acceptance-only fitting match it?
choices: Yes; a sigmoid greater than one will create it.
Yes; more rejection creates new angle conflicts.
No; it needs a generator or mechanism with support for that event.
questions.why: Accepting a subset cannot add mass to an absent group.

questions.prompt: What does a small speed-distribution distance directly establish?
choices: Agreement on that evaluated speed distribution, within its construction and data limits.
Perfect agreement on every crash mechanism.
Correct sensor appearance in every weather condition.
questions.why: One statistic does not establish all other aspects of the joint environment.

questions.prompt: Which episode can D2RL retain useful critical states from?
choices: Only an episode ending in a crash.
Only an episode with no other vehicles.
A near-conflict episode that ends without a crash.
questions.why: Criticality concerns informative states, not only the final binary outcome. The source diagram includes a non-crash trajectory with retained critical states.

questions.prompt: Removing uncritical states from a learning chain does what to the physical episode?
choices: It erases the vehicle’s intermediate motion from reality.
It changes every near miss into a collision.
Nothing by itself; the original dynamics and event still occurred.
questions.why: Representation editing is not physical time deletion.

questions.prompt: What does averaging Z without the ρ correction estimate in the gate example?
choices: The conditional informative-population mean, not E[BZ].
The identical natural mean for every ρ.
Always zero because B is rare.
questions.why: The selection changes the population; multiplying by its known gate probability restores this declared natural mean.

questions.prompt: Why is conditional sampling not necessarily a free computational improvement?
choices: The number of original trials is always identical to the retained count.
Obtaining an informative draw may require about 1/ρ original draws by rejection.
Smaller variance always means zero computational cost.
questions.why: Variance per retained contribution and cost per original sample are distinct budgets.

questions.prompt: Under behavior sampling, what does the two-factor reward expectation reduce to in the declared deterministic-event case?
choices: The negative unweighted crash count under every policy.
A guaranteed proof that the tested AV cannot crash.
The negative target-proposal event second moment, −Σ_A p²/q_target.
questions.why: Multiplying by p/q_behavior cancels the behavior density in the expectation; the other p/q_target factor remains.

questions.prompt: Which probability should a stored trajectory use for its behavior factor?
choices: The probability under the policy that actually collected it.
Whatever current policy is most recent.
The largest probability among all historical policies.
questions.why: Off-policy correction depends on the collection distribution, not a relabeled denominator.

questions.prompt: The caption uses 9.1×10⁴ average tests while a chart labels 4.96×10⁴ at one crossing. What should the reader do?
choices: Claim both values are identical after rounding.
Preserve and flag the difference unless the aggregation is verified.
Silently replace the average with the smaller number.
questions.why: The original evidence does not establish that these differently reported quantities are interchangeable.

questions.prompt: A photorealistic simulator reproduces individual trajectories well. Is its natural crash rate thereby validated?
choices: Yes; visual quality establishes statistical realism.
No; event frequencies and multi-agent long-horizon behavior require separate checks.
Yes, if enough screenshots are generated.
questions.why: Rendering quality and short-horizon trajectory fit do not establish the natural distribution of rare interactions or crash events.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the most defensible interpretation of a reduced browser simulation?
choices: It verifies the stated numerical mechanism under its declared model and assumptions.
It certifies every real autonomous vehicle.
Its attractive graphics establish all natural traffic frequencies.
questions.why: A teaching model can support a precise conceptual calculation without constituting real-world vehicle validation.

title: Simulation and AI for Critical Infrastructure
summary: Event-based control, simulation budgets, multiscale energy scheduling, occupant-aware buildings and safety constraints.

sections.title: Critical infrastructure is a coupled decision system
sections.body:
A building, data center or regional energy network must make decisions that affect a physical system. Those decisions have costs, constraints and delayed consequences. Turning on cooling changes temperature and electricity demand; scheduling electric vehicles changes both their readiness and the load seen by a grid. **A useful controller must connect information, decisions and physical outcomes.**

Cyber-physical energy systems combine several kinds of flow. Electricity, gas, heat and cooling move through physical networks. Measurements, forecasts and commands move through information networks. Prices, payments and contracts influence the economic decisions. These flows are linked but are not interchangeable: having a favorable market contract does not remove a line's power limit or a room's thermal dynamics.

The system can be described at regional, city and terminal-device scales. A regional energy balance coordinates large supply and demand. A city model adds local networks and resources. Terminal control chooses device actions in rooms, charging points and plants. A decision that is sensible at one scale can conflict with a constraint visible only at another.

Data centers make this coupling especially clear. Computation generates heat, cooling uses electricity, workload placement changes demand, and electricity supply or price can vary. A model that considers only the AI algorithm's prediction accuracy omits much of the operational problem.

The central challenges are a large policy space, dynamics at different scales, and uncertain supply or demand. This lecture follows those challenges through finite control models, simulation-based comparisons, energy schedules, occupant-aware buildings and constrained learning. Each method is useful only when its state, objective, information and physical assumptions are clear.

[figure: ci-system]

reading.takeaway: Connect the information and economic decisions to the physical system they control.

sections.title: Computation is itself an energy demand
sections.body:
Running an AI system consumes resources at several stages: data collection, model development, training, inference, storage and cooling. A critical-infrastructure controller can therefore change the energy system both through its physical decisions and through the computation needed to choose them.

Distinguish a measured electricity total from a scenario forecast. A graph extending to a future year expresses assumptions about growth, hardware efficiency, utilization and cooling. A historical projection can motivate an optimization problem while failing to establish current consumption. It should retain its time horizon and scenario definition.

The historical electricity graph used here projects information and communication technology toward roughly 21% of global electricity demand in 2030, with a large data-center component. Those figures are not a measurement that ICT currently consumes that share. The [underlying communication-technology study](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-1547/6/1/117) considers multiple growth and efficiency scenarios. This distinction matters because a controller should not be calibrated using a forecast relabeled as an observation.

For an AI task, a useful energy comparison specifies the task, system, workload, hardware, batch size and quality requirement. Energy per response depends on those conditions. A fixed multiplier between a chatbot query and a web search cannot be applied universally without matching them.

Optimization complexity also depends on the mathematical formulation. Discrete commitment decisions and network constraints can create difficult combinatorial problems. A simple continuous supply-demand balance is not automatically NP-hard. Millions of variables indicate scale; the structure of those variables and constraints determines which algorithms are appropriate.

Compare the value of better decisions with their computation cost, response time and feasibility.

[figure: ci-computation]

reading.takeaway: Separate workload-specific measurements, historical forecasts and mathematical complexity.

warnings.message: The roughly 21% ICT share and 3,000 TWh data-center figure are historical 2030 forecast claims, not verified current consumption. The forecast graph’s scenario and horizon must be retained.
A 3–5× energy comparison per AI request needs matched task, hardware, workload and quality. It is not a universal conversion between chatbots and searches.

sections.title: Why a policy search becomes enormous
sections.body:
A policy assigns decisions to situations. For a finite state set S and a common action set A, the number of deterministic stationary policies is |A| raised to |S|. With ten states and two actions, there are 1,024 such mappings. With one hundred states, there are more than a trillion trillion mappings.

If a system has N binary device indicators, it can already have 2ᴺ combinations before adding temperatures, occupancy histories or supply forecasts. A joint action can also grow exponentially when each device has an independent on/off choice. Exhaustively evaluating every policy against many stochastic simulation trajectories quickly becomes impractical.

That counting argument has a precise scope. It counts unrestricted deterministic stationary mappings over the declared finite states and common actions. Time-dependent policies, continuous actions, action masks and structured policy families have different counts. A threshold rule can be described by a few parameters without representing every mapping independently.

A smaller policy class trades expressive power for manageable search and implementation. A simple temperature threshold may be easy to evaluate and deploy but omit a load-dependent response. A richer policy may improve the objective while requiring more measurements, training or online computation.

Simplifying a policy can remove distinctions needed for low cost or feasibility. The experiments compare full-state and event-restricted decisions under a finite simulation budget.

The cardinality formula explains why representation and search strategy matter. It does not say that every problem requires an exhaustive policy search or that a neural network's parameter count measures the exact complexity of its behavior.

[figure: ci-policy-space]

reading.takeaway: Choose a policy representation that preserves useful decisions while keeping search manageable.

sections.title: States, actions, transitions and discounted cost
sections.body:
A Markov decision process makes a sequential control problem explicit. At state s, choose an allowed action a, incur cost c(s,a), and draw the next state from P(s′|s,a). A discounted objective adds current and future costs with powers of γ, where 0≤γ<1 in the infinite-horizon model used here.

The Markov property says that the current state contains the information needed for the future transition law, given the action. It does not say the physical system has no history. Temperature, stored energy and elapsed occupant stay can summarize relevant effects of that history. If they are omitted, the observation may no longer be Markov.

For a fixed policy, the value satisfies V(s)=c(s,π(s))+γΣP(s′|s,π(s))V(s′). Optimal planning instead minimizes over allowed actions. Costs are minimized in this lecture; changing to a reward-maximization convention requires changing the sign or interpretation consistently.

The cooling experiment has four states combining low/high workload with cool/hot condition, and two actions, Eco or Boost. Every transition row and immediate cost is available. Costs are charged before the transition. Bellman updates enumerate future states, so the visible value changes come from a complete calculation.

The discount controls how much delayed overheating matters relative to present energy. A cheap action can have a high total value when it frequently leads to an expensive hot condition. The exact reference is obtained from the declared finite model, not from a trained neural network.

For costs[4,4,4] and γ=0.5, the discounted total is 4+0.5×4+0.25×4=7. The first cost has exponent zero. This simple calculation is the same convention used in the larger Bellman equations.

$$V(s)=\min_a\left[c(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]$$

[figure: ci-mdp]

visuals.predict: Will the cheapest immediate action be optimal in every workload and temperature state?
visuals.reflect: Perform Bellman updates, inspect transition rows, then compare known-model planning with sampled Q learning.

reading.takeaway: A current action is evaluated through its immediate cost and its possible future states.

sections.title: Planning and sampled learning use different information
sections.body:
When the complete transition model is available, planning can sum over all possible next states. When only experience is available, a controller can estimate values from sampled transitions. Both can use a Bellman relationship, but their inputs and uncertainties differ.

Monte Carlo methods average returns from completed sampled episodes. Temporal-difference methods use an observed immediate cost and an estimated continuation value. A tabular cost-minimizing Q-learning target is c+γminₐ′Q(s′,a′). Only the sampled state-action coefficient is updated on that observation.

The cooling experiment implements both modes. Planning uses complete model probabilities. Sampled Q learning stores eight coefficients, explores with probability 0.25, and generates actual transitions from the declared model. Its learning rate decreases with the square root of the visited pair's count. Unvisited coefficients are not magically accurate because another state was observed.

A neural approximation can share statistical information across states through features and parameters. That can help generalization, but it does not guarantee correct action values for states never covered by training. Function approximation, exploration and model validation remain distinct issues.

The experiment's reference values provide an exact comparison because this small MDP is fully known. Sampled learning will fluctuate and may approach the reference slowly. Showing a finite training run does not establish convergence of every off-policy method, especially after introducing a nonlinear approximation.

Inspecting both modes makes a useful diagnostic possible: if the full transition model already predicts the wrong physical behavior, perfectly fitting its values does not repair the model. If the model is correct but important pairs are rarely visited, the learning problem can instead be coverage and sampling variance.

[figure: ci-learning]

reading.takeaway: A sampled TD target changes a visited coefficient; known-model planning enumerates possibilities.

sections.title: Events reduce observations and can hide decisions
sections.body:
An event-based representation replaces a detailed description with selected informative changes or categories. An event may be a set of state-transition pairs, such as entering a hot condition or a charging deadline becoming urgent. Events can also be used to organize a restricted policy's observations.

This can reduce the number of distinctions a controller handles. It can also lose information. If two full states produce the same observation but require different actions, an event-only policy cannot simply copy the full-state optimum. The resulting decision process may be partially observable.

The event experiment groups the four cooling states by temperature, by workload, or by their full identity. It exhaustively evaluates every deterministic stationary policy allowed by that grouping, under a uniform initial-state population. The costs are exact for the declared finite policy class.

Temperature-only grouping merges low-load/cool and high-load/cool. Their optimal actions differ in the full model. Moreover, the probabilities of next observable temperature groups can differ even at the same action. Thus the event label is insufficient to reproduce the original Markov transition law.

The display separates the restricted policy's loss from within-group transition disagreement. The first measures performance under a specified policy class and initial population. The second measures whether aliased hidden states induce the same next-event distribution. They are related but not the same diagnostic.

History, beliefs or a richer event can help recover useful information. That does not make every aggregation exact. Event-based methods should identify which distinctions can be safely merged for their task and which hidden variables still influence transitions, costs or constraints.

[figure: ci-events]

visuals.predict: Will a temperature-only controller choose the right action for both low and high workload?
visuals.reflect: Compare exact restricted-policy cost, full-state actions and next-event transition disagreement.

reading.takeaway: A smaller event space is useful only when its lost information is understood.

sections.title: Simple policies and a Pareto tradeoff
sections.body:
There are several meanings of policy complexity. The number of event categories, code size, online computation time, memory requirements and measured latency are practical quantities. They do not all measure the same thing, and none should be automatically equated with the shortest possible program describing a policy.

Kolmogorov complexity concerns the length of a shortest description on a fixed universal machine. It is not computable in general. Its relationship to undecidability does not make the complexity function literally identical to the halting problem; rather, general exact computation runs into an undecidability barrier.

For operational design, a tractable proxy can still be useful. Count event distinctions, measure the number of operations needed per decision, or benchmark controller response time. Then compare that proxy with a specified performance measure such as expected energy cost or comfort violations.

A policy is Pareto dominated when another policy is no worse in both complexity and performance and strictly better in at least one. A Pareto frontier contains policies for which improving one criterion requires sacrificing another within the considered set. Choosing a frontier point still requires operational priorities and constraints.

A crude complexity model and a noisy performance estimate can help screen designs. They do not prove that every selected policy lies on the true frontier. The quality of proxies, sample noise, policy-class coverage and evaluation assumptions matter.

A policy must compute an action before the physical deadline. Compare faster approximations against the coupled system’s cost and constraints.

[figure: ci-complexity]

reading.takeaway: Use declared practical complexity measures and compare them with the performance that matters.

warnings.message: Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable in general, but it is not literally equal to the halting problem. Event counts and runtime are usable complexity proxies, not exact Kolmogorov complexity.

sections.title: Ordinal optimization asks for a useful ranking
sections.body:
Precisely estimating every candidate's objective can be expensive. Sometimes the useful decision is which designs deserve further evaluation, rather than their exact costs to many decimal places. Ordinal optimization combines relative comparison with a softened selection goal.

**Ordinal comparison** asks which design appears better under a crude model. **Goal softening** asks for a good-enough design or several such designs instead of insisting on the exact global optimum. A top percentage of a defined candidate population is one possible good-enough set.

Let Θ be the design space, G the truly good-enough subset, and S the set selected by a noisy or crude evaluation. An alignment goal asks whether |G∩S| is at least k. The selection procedure can then be assessed by the probability of obtaining that overlap, under its stated distribution and noise assumptions.

Ranking can be easier than absolute precision when performance differences are sufficiently large relative to evaluation noise. It can be difficult when neighboring candidates are nearly tied, when the crude model has systematic bias, or when it misorders important mechanisms. Goal softening does not mean constraints can be ignored.

A crude screening stage also has a cost. Evaluating 200 candidates cheaply and keeping 12 for expensive validation can save downstream work, but the entire process includes both stages. Keeping only 12 does not itself imply the total computation was reduced from 200 evaluations to 12.

The experiment runs the 200-design ranking example. It reports both individual selections and empirical alignment across repeated runs.

[figure: ci-ordinal]

reading.takeaway: Use relative ranking to select candidates for further evaluation under a stated good-enough criterion.

sections.title: Run the 200-design noisy-ranking experiment
sections.body:
The numerical construction is deliberately simple. There are 200 designs, with true cost J(i)=i for i from 1 to 200. Smaller is better. The observation is Ĵ(i)=i+w_i, where the noises are independent Uniform[0, W]. Select the twelve designs with the smallest observed costs and count how many are truly among designs 1–12.

The noise is positive uniform. Replacing it with a centered Gaussian would change this particular experiment. Although its common positive shift does not systematically prefer an individual design, the random perturbations can change the ordering.
