At W=0 the top-twelve ranking is exact. At W=100, repeatable simulations show that several genuinely good designs tend to remain among the selected twelve. The original summary reports about five on average and at least three with probability at least 0.95 for that setup. The browser computes its own repeated-run mean and success fraction from actual draws; it does not insert the reported values into the results.

At W=10,000 the ranking is dominated by noise and approaches a blind selection. A uniformly random twelve-element subset of 200 has expected overlap 12×12/200=0.72 with the true top twelve. Saying “about one” is a loose description, not an exact mean or a guarantee that every run contains one.

A single selected set can look encouraging or disappointing. Repeated comparisons reveal that variability, but an empirical fraction still has sampling uncertainty. It is not a universal theorem about arbitrary policies, biased simulators or noise levels.

Reveal the complete true and observed table to inspect where the ranking changed. The selection uses the observed values; the exact costs are used afterward to evaluate its alignment.

[figure: ci-ranking]

visuals.predict: How much genuine top-twelve information survives when W changes from100 to10,000?
visuals.reflect: Run repeated comparisons and distinguish a particular ranking, empirical alignment and the blind-pick expectation.

reading.takeaway: A ranking experiment needs its actual noise law, selected set and repeated-run uncertainty.

sections.title: Selection guarantees have assumptions
sections.body:
A selection-size rule depends on how the candidates' true performances are distributed, how noisy the crude evaluation is, and how the selected and good-enough sets are defined. A steep performance curve separates leading designs more clearly than a flat curve with many nearly tied candidates.

The typical procedure begins by sampling candidates from a design space. Define the desired good-enough fraction and overlap k. Evaluate candidates with a cheap model. Estimate the relevant noise and problem type, then choose a selected-set size that targets the desired alignment probability. Finally perform detailed evaluation or refinement on that set.

Each stage introduces a contract. The candidate sample may miss entire policy families. The crude model's noise may not match the theoretical model. A table calibrated for one performance-curve type cannot be used as a guarantee for another. Constraints need screening or later validation rather than disappearing from the problem.

Statements about exponential convergence of observed order or alignment refer to specific mathematical conditions. They are not blanket assurances that arbitrary rough rankings quickly become correct. A biased simulator can converge very confidently to the wrong order as the number of observations grows.

Use cheap simulation to identify a promising set, then spend detailed simulation on uncertain comparisons. Report the candidate population, noise, set size and success criterion.

The 200-design experiment provides a transparent special case. It does not implement an unspecified published selection-size table, and its empirical success fraction should not be substituted for a theorem about a real infrastructure policy population.

[figure: ci-alignment]

reading.takeaway: A good-enough probability belongs to a candidate distribution, noise model and selection rule.

warnings.message: Exponential convergence and 0.95 alignment claims require their stated sampling, noise and problem-type assumptions. They are not guarantees for arbitrary crude simulators or every policy search.

sections.title: Allocate costly simulation where comparison is uncertain
sections.body:
After screening, the remaining designs may need different amounts of evaluation. A clearly poor design with small noise rarely needs as much attention as a noisy candidate close to the apparent best. Optimal computing budget allocation studies how to spend limited simulation effort to improve selection quality.

A useful signal-to-noise quantity compares an estimated performance gap with evaluation variance. Small gaps and large noise make comparisons uncertain. When simulation runtimes differ, counts alone do not describe the resource budget: ten expensive evaluations can cost more than many cheap ones.

The budget experiment uses six invented designs with hidden exact mean costs. Each noisy evaluation consumes one call and a declared number of seconds. Both strategies begin with five pilot evaluations per candidate. Equal allocation cycles through candidates. An observed-gap heuristic prioritizes estimated variance divided by squared observed gap and the current count.

The heuristic receives only observed means, sample variances and counts. It cannot read the hidden exact costs used by the teaching simulator to generate observations. The apparent best uses its nearest competitor gap rather than a meaningless zero self-gap. Candidate-specific noise streams make overlapping evaluations comparable across strategies.

This is a declared illustration, not the full named OCBA algorithm. It does not optimize varying simulation durations. Reveal exact costs after the comparison to inspect selection regret, while keeping the algorithm's information separate from the reference used to assess it.

Adaptive allocation can improve a particular selection, but it can also be misled by poor pilot estimates or a nearly tied noisy candidate. The displayed sample standard errors are descriptive; repeated adaptive selection changes the interpretation of naive confidence intervals. A finite computation budget makes that uncertainty part of the decision.

[figure: ci-budget]

visuals.predict: Which design will attract extra calls after a noisy pilot, and can equal calls have unequal runtime?
visuals.reflect: Compare observed rankings and counts, then reveal exact selection regret and computation seconds.

reading.takeaway: Budget allocation should use observed comparison uncertainty and account for the actual resource being spent.

sections.title: Cooling optimization needs more than a predictive model
sections.body:
A data-center optimization loop links workload, thermal state, cooling devices and electricity. A predictor can estimate quantities such as power usage effectiveness or future temperature. A controller must then choose actions under hardware and operating constraints.

Power usage effectiveness, or PUE, is total facility power divided by IT equipment power under a specified measurement boundary. It helps summarize overhead but does not identify every source of inefficiency. A change in IT utilization can change the ratio even when the cooling hardware's behavior is otherwise similar.

Correlation analysis over many control parameters can suggest influential variables. Correlation does not by itself identify causal effects of an intervention. Changing a control can alter workload or other conditions that were correlated in historical data. Those dependencies must be represented when the predictor is used for action selection.

A thermal surrogate can make repeated evaluation faster than a detailed physical simulator. Its usefulness depends on its operating range, errors and response to the proposed controls. A model that predicts familiar recorded states accurately can be unreliable when an optimizer finds unusual settings outside that range.

Modular optimization can separate parts of the system for tractability, but their coupling remains: workload generates heat, cooling capacity is shared, and electricity constraints affect the feasible operating point. Benchmark the full chosen control loop rather than assuming a good forecast automatically yields a good schedule.

The small cooling MDP establishes these roles without pretending to reproduce a full data center. Its cost and transition tables are declared examples. The research examples motivate richer thermal modeling and parameter analysis, while their particular datasets, hardware and performance remain separate evidence.

[figure: ci-data-center]

reading.takeaway: Prediction quality, causal action response and closed-loop constraints are different checks.

sections.title: Wind, charging and an energy balance
sections.body:
A microgrid combines local generation, controllable loads and a connection to a larger grid. Wind supply may be uncertain, while electric vehicles can shift some charging within their parking windows. The opportunity is to coordinate flexible demand with available supply without violating readiness requirements.

A power balance applies at each relevant instant or interval. An energy balance integrates that power over time. Supplying enough energy over a whole day does not guarantee that energy is available before an individual vehicle departs or within a feeder's instantaneous power limit.

Wind-turbine claims need a turbine specification, site conditions and a time basis. A mean wind speed alone does not determine annual energy: the speed distribution, power curve, operating limits and installation environment matter. A rooftop installation also differs from an unobstructed reference site.

The numerical feasibility claim about supporting 55,000 vehicles is not established by the adjacent building counts and 1,500 kWh turbine label alone. If each of 969 installations supplied 1,500 kWh over a year, the total would be 1,453,500 kWh. At 2,580 kWh per vehicle-year that would support about 563 vehicle-years. Supporting 55,000 would instead require about 146,440 kWh per building-year. These calculations identify the missing scale; they do not infer the intended turbine's actual yield.

The important control problem survives that uncertain motivation: renewable supply fluctuates, flexible charging has deadlines and rates, and grid procurement has costs. The next models declare their own wind profile, powers and time intervals so every energy quantity can be checked.

Avoid treating a large aggregate energy potential as a ready-made charging policy. An operational policy must specify when each vehicle receives energy and how it handles shortfalls.

[figure: ci-microgrid]

reading.takeaway: Energy potential must become a time-feasible power schedule with explicit units.

warnings.message: The stated 55,000-vehicle rooftop supply claim lacks a consistent verified turbine yield and time basis. Under an explicit 1,500 kWh per building-year interpretation,969 buildings support about 563 vehicle-years at 2,580 kWh each; the intended 22m turbine yield is not established.

sections.title: Day-ahead decisions constrain later choices
sections.body:
Energy scheduling often mixes decisions made before uncertainty is resolved with later corrective actions. A day-ahead purchase can be relatively cheap, while additional real-time energy can be more expensive. Renewable generation and demand forecasts affect how much to commit early.

A purchased amount is not the same as actual physical usage. An unused reservation can still carry cost under a stated contract. A shortfall can require additional procurement, but physical grid and charger limits still apply even if the operator is willing to pay more.

Electric vehicles introduce several event-driven constraints. They arrive, depart, undertake trips and return for another parking period. Stored energy carries consequences across those stages. The state should describe remaining charging need and available time, not only current aggregate load.

The decision is multistage because an early action changes the feasible choices later. Waiting for wind may save purchase cost but leave too little time to meet a deadline. Charging every available vehicle immediately may satisfy readiness while wasting flexible opportunities to use later renewable energy.

Uncertainty should be attached to a forecast horizon and error measure. A historical 20% wind-prediction-error statement does not define the error distribution for every site, hour or future scenario. An optimizer needs a declared stochastic or robust model rather than one unexplained percentage.

The teaching schedule uses finite known profiles to expose these mechanisms. Its overoptimistic forecast and actual wind are separate arrays. A perfect-forecast rolling comparator is explicitly labeled as an oracle, allowing a clear comparison without claiming that a real controller sees future weather.

[figure: ci-commitments]

reading.takeaway: An early commitment changes later costs and options; forecast uncertainty must be defined.

sections.title: Rollout improves a base policy under a model
sections.body:
Simulation-based policy improvement can compare candidate actions by simulating what follows them. Choose an action now, then continue with a base policy through the remaining horizon. Average the resulting costs across declared scenario draws to estimate that action's value.

The resulting quantity is an estimate of Q under the **base continuation policy**. It is not automatically the optimal Q*. Minimizing these estimated action costs gives a one-step rollout decision relative to the modeled base behavior. Approximation noise, model error and the candidate action set affect the improvement claim.

A simple example illustrates the distinction. A base policy charges every vehicle immediately. A rollout can test delaying one vehicle now while following that same greedy rule later. That is different from assuming every later decision is globally optimized. If the later rule is poor, the evaluated continuation remains limited by it.

Model predictive control instead repeatedly solves a finite future control problem, executes the current action and moves the planning window forward. Its value depends on the horizon, terminal treatment, forecast and solver. Replanning provides a chance to incorporate new information, but it cannot restore time already lost before a departure.

The browser's small charging planner enumerates a finite dynamic program rather than calling a large mixed-integer solver or implementing the original stochastic rollout. Its exact objective includes an explicit penalty for missed charging energy. The rolling comparator uses a known actual profile to isolate the value of correct future information.

When interpreting a policy-improvement result, identify which model supplies future scenarios, which policy supplies continuation actions, and what information the procedure receives at each decision. Those distinctions explain what “improvement” means.

[figure: ci-rollout]

reading.takeaway: A base-policy continuation value is distinct from the optimal value and from an oracle forecast.

warnings.message: A sampled rollout followed by a base policy estimates that base-policy continuation value. It is not automatically an approximate optimal value function without an additional optimization or approximation argument.

sections.title: Execute a schedule at its physical time scale
sections.body:
The charging experiment has a four-hour horizon divided into sixteen quarter-hours. Vehicle A needs 4 kWh before hour 2. Vehicle B arrives at hour 1 and needs 10 kWh before hour 4. Each vehicle can accept at most 4 kW, equivalent to one kWh per quarter-hour.

The wind profile supplies 0,4 or 8 kW. Grid power is capped at a declared 4 or 8 kW. Actions request a one-kWh quantum for each available vehicle. Actual delivery is bounded by supply and charging availability. When supply is scarce, the earlier-departing vehicle is served first. Every curtailed request and missed-deadline quantity is recorded.

A fixed schedule is computed from the initial planning forecast. An overoptimistic forecast can plan simultaneous charging that actual supply cannot deliver. The executed trace then contains a shortfall even though the nominal optimization thought its schedule was feasible. A lower purchase bill can simply reflect failed service.

The rolling actual-profile comparator replans from the current remaining energy using perfect knowledge of the future actual profile. It is an intentionally strong reference, not a realistic uncertainty model. Greedy charging supplies another contrast: charge immediately whenever vehicles can receive energy.

Day-ahead reservation and extra real-time purchase have explicit RMB-per-kWh prices. The optimizer adds an artificial 200 RMB/kWh missed-demand penalty, while the visible bill reports only purchased energy. Keep those measures separate: a policy cannot be called better merely because it spends less while missing the required charge.

This reduced finite model omits storage, conversion losses and travel energy dynamics. Its purpose is to make timing, procurement and forecast mismatch executable. The research cost tables later retain their own values and scope.

[figure: ci-scheduling]

visuals.predict: Will the optimistic fixed plan remain feasible when actual wind arrives late?
visuals.reflect: Step through requested versus delivered kWh, compare missed deadlines and cost, then use matched or oracle planning.

reading.takeaway: Compare delivered service and violations alongside cost at the actual execution scale.

sections.title: Action elimination needs the right conditions
sections.body:
A joint charging action can contain one binary choice per vehicle. With N independently selectable vehicles, there are 2ᴺ masks before constraints remove impossible choices. Structural rules can reduce that action space when their mathematical conditions apply.

The shortest-remaining-charging-load-first rule, or SELF, concerns vehicles with the same remaining parking time. It orders those vehicles by remaining required energy and prioritizes the shorter loads. The stated result is that at least one optimal policy has this property under the associated model assumptions.

That is narrower than a universal claim that every smaller battery should always charge first. Different departure times, charging powers, objectives or other constraints can change the relevant ordering. The browser's scarce-supply rule prioritizes an earlier deadline; it is not presented as an implementation of the original SELF theorem.

For a group of n vehicles with a valid prefix ordering, there can be n+1 choices: charge none, the first one, the first two, and so on. Several independent groups have a product of such counts. A group structure therefore matters when interpreting a complexity reduction.

The illustrated twelve-vehicle example has groups yielding 5×4×3=60 choices, compared with 2¹²=4,096 unrestricted masks. That is a substantial reduction. It does not by itself establish O(N) total action growth for arbitrary numbers and sizes of groups.

Action elimination is valuable when it preserves at least one useful optimum or has a quantified approximation effect. Verify the ordering assumptions before removing choices; otherwise a seemingly efficient controller can simply exclude the action needed for feasibility.

[figure: ci-self]

reading.takeaway: A structural priority rule reduces actions only within the assumptions that justify it.

warnings.message: A per-group prefix rule gives n+1 choices within a group. Across multiple independent groups their counts multiply; the illustrated 60 actions do not establish universal O(N) total growth. SELF also requires its stated equal-parking-time and model conditions.

sections.title: Interpret the reported charging results
sections.body:
The reported comparison separates day-ahead cost, real-time cost, total cost and a matching-degree measure. These are outcomes for particular methods and an experimental setup; they are not measured results of the small browser schedule.

Greedy charging has a reported real-time and total cost of 7,031.8 RMB, with matching degree 0.2969. The single-timescale method has 1,592.4 RMB day-ahead cost plus 3,671.3 RMB real-time cost, totaling 5,263.7 RMB, with matching degree 0.4148. The multi-timescale row shows 1,592.4 and 1,691.0 RMB components but a printed total 3,286.4 RMB. The components add to 3,283.4 RMB, leaving an unresolved 3 RMB inconsistency.

The corresponding charging-price figures are reported as 0.47,0.35 and 0.22 RMB. The available label does not specify the denominator, so it should not silently be rewritten as RMB per kWh. The reductions computed from those rounded values are approximately 53.2% and 37.1%.

Matching degree rises from 0.2969 to 0.5118, an increase of about 72.4% relative to the greedy entry. Relative to 0.4148, the increase is about 23.4%. Those computations describe the printed values. Understanding the statistic fully still requires its precise definition and experimental conditions.

Related extensions add storage, other renewable resources, shared vehicles, decentralized coordination or robust scheduling. Each extension changes the state, available actions and feasibility conditions. It cannot inherit the same reported savings merely because it uses a similar optimization idea.

The reported multiscale method improves the stated comparison measures. The inconsistent total and unspecified price denominator prevent a more precise cost claim.

[figure: ci-charging-evidence]

reading.takeaway: Keep reported components, totals, units and comparison scope distinct.

warnings.message: The reported cost row is inconsistent:1592.4 + 1691.0 = 3283.4 RMB, but the printed total is 3286.4 RMB. It is unclear which entry was intended, so that reported total should not be treated as verified.
The charging-price figures are labeled RMB without a denominator. Their unit must not silently be promoted to RMB/kWh; the cost table totals have separate RMB units.

sections.title: Aggregation upward, policy projection downward
sections.body:
A high-resolution simulation can expose short-lived constraints but be expensive to run. A coarse simulation can be fast while hiding the very mechanism that determines feasibility. Multiscale optimization links models rather than assuming one resolution is sufficient for every decision.

State and action aggregation carry information from a fine model to a coarser one. A macro model may describe daily energy and large regions; a meso model may describe hourly supply and local networks; a micro model may describe minute-level device behavior. The exact boundaries depend on the application.

Policy projection carries a coarse decision back to the more detailed system. A daily charging amount must become actions during actual parking intervals. An aggregate heating plan must become device commands in rooms. Projection should check rates, capacities, timing and couplings that the coarse optimization may have omitted.

A simple counterexample is supply[0,8]kW and load[8,0]kW over two equal intervals without storage. Their average powers match, but the first interval has an 8 kW shortage. A coarse average balance cannot repair that timing mismatch. Adding a battery introduces new state, power and energy bounds rather than making averaging automatically valid.

Large integrated examples include electricity, gas and heating networks with thousands of nodes and multiple resources. Their scale motivates coordination, but a quoted node count is not a proof of a particular algorithm's accuracy or runtime.

Choose the minimal spatial-temporal unit needed to preserve relevant dynamics, then validate the mappings between levels. The aim is to spend detailed simulation where it changes the decision while preserving the constraints that make a policy operationally meaningful.

[figure: ci-scales]

reading.takeaway: A coarse feasible balance still needs feasible projection through finer dynamics and constraints.

sections.title: Comfort feedback connects people and devices
sections.body:
Buildings serve people as well as energy objectives. Occupants generate heat, use equipment, open windows and communicate preferences. A timetable can miss actual presence or activity, so demand and comfort should be treated as measured or modeled quantities rather than fixed administrative schedules.

Integrated terminal control coordinates lights, blinds, ventilation, heating and cooling. Multiple-supply management coordinates resources such as photovoltaic generation, combined heat and power, batteries, grid supply and flexible vehicles. The first determines demand and comfort; the second supplies that demand at a feasible cost.

The iBuilding feedback loop distinguishes complaints, interpretation, setpoints and device control. A complaint about glare is not a direct actuator command. An interpreter converts it into an appropriate target or constraint; a controller chooses device settings; occupants experience the result and provide further feedback.

Different discomforts can interact. Closing blinds can reduce glare and solar heat while increasing the need for electric lighting. More fresh air can improve air quality while increasing thermal demand. A fan-speed adjustment can affect noise, airflow and cooling. Optimizing each subsystem independently may conflict with the shared experience.

A setpoint is also not a guarantee of the resulting physical state. Device capacities, room dynamics, sensor errors and delayed response determine whether temperature or air-quality bounds are actually achieved.

The reduced building experiment models two temperatures, occupancy heat gains and shared cooling. It deliberately omits humidity, illuminance and air-quality physics. The rebuilt feedback diagram teaches the larger architecture, while the live simulation keeps its limited physical variables explicit.

[figure: ci-feedback]

reading.takeaway: Translate occupant feedback into physical targets, then verify the device response.

sections.title: Elapsed stay changes a departure prediction
sections.body:
Two rooms can have the same current number of occupants but different likely future demand. If one group arrived recently and another has stayed a long time, a duration-dependent model can produce different departure predictions. Current occupancy alone loses that history.

The stay-time experiment uses a declared Weibull survival model with shape 2 and scale τ. Survival is S(t)=exp[−(t/τ)²]. Given that a person is still present after elapsed stay t, the probability of departure within the next Δ hours is 1−S(t+Δ)/S(t). This is a **conditional interval probability**, not the unconditional cumulative departure probability 1−S(t).

With shape 2, the conditional departure probability increases with elapsed stay for a fixed interval. A memoryless exponential comparison gives a probability independent of elapsed stay. These are different assumptions about occupants, not universal facts about every building.

The browser fits one log-scale parameter to eight explicitly invented completed stay durations. It performs actual gradient updates on the mean negative log density. An analytic maximum-likelihood solution, τ=√mean(t²), supplies a transparent check of the fitted value.

Complete, uncensored records make that likelihood simple. If occupants are still present when recording stops, those records are right-censored and need a survival contribution rather than a fabricated completed duration. Dependence between occupants or differing room populations can also require richer models.

The reported building framework uses stay-time information to improve occupancy estimates. The teaching model illustrates why that information matters; its tiny dataset does not reproduce the research estimator or justify the reported accuracy. Inspect both the learned scale and the resulting conditional predictions.

[figure: ci-stay]

visuals.predict: Will identical current occupancy imply identical next-hour occupancy for short and long stays?
visuals.reflect: Fit the scale, compare conditional departure probabilities, and explain what the memoryless model ignores.

reading.takeaway: Condition future departures on both current presence and elapsed stay under a declared model.

sections.title: Decouple calculations without deleting coupling
sections.body:
Partitioning a building by physical space can make simulation and optimization more manageable. Room models can be evaluated separately or coordinated through shared variables. The partition is useful because rooms have identifiable states, occupants and devices.

But room boundaries do not make the systems independent. Heat can move between neighboring rooms. A shared air-handling unit, chiller or electrical limit can constrain several zones at once. An action in one room can affect another room's temperature or available cooling capacity.

A cooperative optimization method should preserve those couplings in its coordination. It may exchange boundary conditions, shared-device usage or other aggregate information. A parallel computation that simply removes the coupling solves a different physical problem.

The two-room experiment makes both links explicit. Its thermal equation includes a conductance term proportional to the neighboring temperature difference. Its actions share a 4 kW cooling budget. Separate one-room recommendations can therefore be infeasible as a pair even if each looks sensible in isolation.

Occupancy-aware control adds another layer. An empty room can use wider temperature bounds, freeing capacity for an occupied room. That benefit depends on accurate presence information and the consequences of heat exchange. A false vacancy prediction can lead to discomfort in an actually occupied zone.

Assess a decoupling scheme by the information passed between subproblems and the error relative to the coupled system. Faster computation is valuable when the resulting actions still obey the shared constraints and preserve the performance measure of interest.

[figure: ci-coupling]

reading.takeaway: A computational partition must retain shared devices, boundary effects and coordinated constraints.

sections.title: Execute coupled temperature control
sections.body:
The thermal experiment models two rooms over six hours with fifteen-minute steps. Each room has a heat capacity, exchanges heat with the outside and the other room, gains heat from occupants, and receives cooling from a shared device. Electricity and temperature use distinct units.

The equation is T′=T+Δt/C[(Tout−T)/R+k(Tother−T)+g×occupants−COP×power]. The bracket is heat flow in kW. Multiplying by Δt in hours gives kWh; dividing by heat capacity in kWh per degree gives a temperature change. These units prevent a power command from being confused with an instantaneous temperature setting.

Cooling actions are nonnegative integer kW, totaling at most 4 across both rooms. Occupied comfort is 23–26°C; an empty room has a wider 19–30°C interval. The controller enumerates fifteen allowed actions and chooses a lowest-power one whose predicted next state satisfies the limits.

If no action is predicted feasible, the controller chooses a minimum-violation action and reports the failure. It does not label an impossible constraint as satisfied. A threshold rule provides a simpler comparison, while nominal and true-model filters isolate the effect of heat-capacity mismatch.

The nominal filter assumes C=2. Changing the actual C changes the physical response without changing that nominal assumption. A state predicted inside the comfort interval can then land outside it. The true-model filter receives the actual C deliberately, providing an oracle comparison within this small model.

Inspect predicted and actual temperatures, allocated power, electricity, cost and violations together. The system uses Euler time stepping and declared occupancy patterns; it is an educational control system, not a reproduction of a building's full thermodynamics or a real-world comfort guarantee.

[figure: ci-building-control]

visuals.predict: Will a filter using C=2 remain reliable when the actual room has C=0.8?
visuals.reflect: Run the coupled rooms, inspect predicted versus actual temperatures, and compare nominal, true-model and threshold rules.

reading.takeaway: A feasible action prediction must survive the actual coupled state transition.

sections.title: Read building cost, timing and accuracy separately
sections.body:
The reported event-based building comparison gives daily cost 1,501 RMB, computation time 4.1 s and response time 4.1 s. The one-minute time-based entry gives 1,496 RMB, computation time 165.5 s and response time 195 s. Other time-based entries use ten- and five-minute steps.

The cost difference relative to the one-minute entry is(1501−1496)/1496≈0.3342%. That is close to 0.3% when rounded, but the table's best listed comparator is not by itself a certificate of the global optimum. A global-gap statement needs an optimum or valid bound under the stated model.

Timing also has more than one meaning. The computation-time ratio is 165.5/4.1≈40.4; the response-time ratio is 195/4.1≈47.6. A rounded “about 50” description fits the latter more closely. It should not be silently substituted for every runtime measure or every building.

The occupancy application reports 94.5% estimation accuracy against 77% and 87% comparison values. The metric definition, population, evaluation horizon and error distribution are necessary to interpret those percentages. A high average occupancy accuracy does not establish that every rare vacancy or demand peak is correctly predicted.

Reported performance can motivate a method without becoming a universal guarantee. Separate the comparison's data, implementation and timing conditions from the mechanism the method teaches. The browser's tiny Weibull fit and thermal loop use their own invented parameters and measured values.

A good evidence statement identifies which cost was compared, which time was measured, and what accuracy means. That clarity is especially important when a faster approximate method is used inside an operational loop with hard response deadlines.

[figure: ci-building-evidence]

reading.takeaway: A comparison table establishes its own cost and timing differences, not universal optimality or speed.

warnings.message: 1501 versus 1496 RMB gives a 0.3342% comparison gap, not independently a gap to the global optimum. Computation and response ratios are about 40.4 and 47.6 respectively; a universal 50-fold speedup is not established.

sections.title: Model mismatch includes both scales and numerical dynamics
sections.body:
A controller can pass an offline evaluation and still fail after its policy is projected into a different model or deployed in a changing system. Mismatch can arise in state variables, timing, action interpretation, numerical integration or physical parameters.

Macro, meso and micro models represent different details. A daily decision can miss a minute-scale shortage. A state aggregation can hide a device limit. Privacy-preserving distributed observations can omit information used by a centralized training model. Each mapping should state what is preserved and what is approximated.

Time-driven, state-driven and event-driven simulation also use different update schedules. A coarse fixed step may miss a sharp transition or apply a control too late. Event-based updates need a well-defined trigger, event timing and treatment of what happens between events.

Stiff systems contain dynamics with widely separated rates. Power-system electromagnetic and electromechanical processes can require very different time resolution. A time step adequate for a slow quantity may be unstable or inaccurate for a fast one. A phasor representation and instantaneous three-phase values are different model descriptions, not interchangeable snapshots.

The two-room experiment isolates parameter mismatch rather than the full power-system problem. Its nominal heat capacity can differ from the physical one, making the same action change temperature at a different rate. The observed violation is a concrete reason to check the actual transition rather than only the nominal optimizer's output.

A model's lower resolution can be useful when its error is controlled for the decision. The task is to identify where detailed evaluation is necessary, preserve relevant constraints during projection, and update assumptions when physical or operating conditions change.

[figure: ci-mismatch]

reading.takeaway: Validate the model mappings and numerical evolution used by the actual controller.

sections.title: Rare fault data require class-aware evaluation
sections.body:
Physical knowledge and measurements provide different kinds of evidence. First-principles models can describe transients, faults and constraints as well as average behavior. Data can help estimate parameters, detect unfamiliar mechanisms and test predictions. Neither source of knowledge is sufficient for every rare failure.

The example data counts are 450,000 faulty records and 210,000,000 healthy records. Their healthy-to-faulty ratio is about 466.7, close to the roughly 468 figure quoted. If those labels formed one binary dataset, always predicting healthy would obtain about 99.786% overall accuracy while detecting no fault at all. This is why class-specific measures matter.

The reported maintenance comparison provides precision, recall and F-score for replaced and healthy classes. For replaced records, F-score changes from 0.808 to 0.981; for healthy records it changes from 0.896 to 0.979. Those are approximately 21.4% and 9.3% relative improvements from the displayed rounded values.

Precision asks how many flagged cases have the relevant label. Recall asks how many relevant cases were found. F-score combines them. These values are not automatically the same as a statement of 98% overall accuracy, and the class counts from one example should not be assumed to be the test population of another.

Early-warning claims also need a timing definition. A representative trajectory that rises before replacement can illustrate anticipation, but a fifteen-day lead-time claim across a population requires how the fault time, alert threshold and evaluation cases were defined.

Combine expert features with learned signals, then evaluate fault detection under the actual class imbalance. Aggregate accuracy can hide missed rare failures.

[figure: ci-fault]

reading.takeaway: Assess rare faults with class-specific metrics, timing and a defined population.

warnings.message: The displayed healthy F-scores imply about 9.3% relative improvement, whereas the text says 8%; its 98% accuracy claim is not the same metric. Class counts and evaluation populations must not be silently combined. First-principles models are also not restricted to averages.

sections.title: Combine models by their role and evidence
sections.body:
Large learned models, small learned models and structured physical solvers can contribute different capabilities. A broad model can suggest a decision or identify a pattern. A smaller model can specialize in a defined operating regime. A solver can enforce the constraints represented in its optimization problem.

Combining them requires clear interfaces. Which model supplies candidate actions? Which variables does it fix? Which model checks feasibility? What happens when they disagree or when a confidence signal is low? Calling the combination “hybrid” does not answer those questions.

Model development has real labor, data, hardware and energy costs, but unsupported model-size or training-cost estimates should not become specifications. The [GPT-4 technical report](https://cdn.openai.com/papers/gpt-4.pdf) explicitly does not disclose architecture size, training compute or dataset-construction details. Claimed precise parameter or token counts require independent evidence rather than being treated as official facts.

For unit commitment, a coarse model can predict some binary generator decisions while a finer optimizer solves the rest. Reducing the number of unfixed discrete variables can save search effort. Incorrect fixed decisions can instead remove every feasible solution or exclude a better one.

The model's usefulness therefore depends on selective retention and a recovery procedure. A specialized solver should verify the decisions under its actual constraints, and the workflow should permit uncertain or inconsistent fixed variables to be released.

This is a concrete way to relate broad learned representations to infrastructure optimization. It preserves their different roles rather than assuming that a fluent model output substitutes for a physical model, constraint checker or operating guarantee.

[figure: ci-hybrid]

reading.takeaway: Specify which model proposes, specializes, fixes variables and checks feasibility.

warnings.message: Precise GPT-4 parameter, token and training-cost figures are not established by its official technical report. That report does not disclose model size, training compute or dataset-construction details; speculative values should not be taught as specifications.

sections.title: Confidence needs calibration and a fallback
sections.body:
A proposal with a confidence score can help decide which variables to trust provisionally. But confidence is useful only when its meaning is tested. A model's expressed certainty is not necessarily a calibrated probability of correctness, and correctness of one variable is not the same as feasibility of their joint assignment.

A selective unit-commitment workflow can retain high-confidence binary predictions and send uncertain ones to a finer solver. It should also verify the retained choices, because several individually plausible commitments can jointly violate load balance, ramp rates or other restrictions.

The reported multiscale comparison uses 30-,118- and 300-bus cases. Its proposed-method time entries are 3.7134,80.7176 and 150.3085 s, against 12.216,381.5965 and 717.3248 s in the corresponding Gurobi columns. The ratios are about 0.304,0.212 and 0.210, respectively. The shown relative gaps are 0.0716%,0.0244% and 0.0317%.

Those are particular comparison values, not proof of a universal runtime fraction or independent global optimality. Solver tolerances, stopping conditions, hardware and how the gap was defined affect the interpretation. A plot of predicted and reference integer assignments provides another diagnostic but is not a feasibility proof by itself.

A fallback can unfix decisions, expand the search or return to a verified controller when a proposed assignment fails. Its cost should be included in evaluation. Otherwise the apparent speedup may omit the very recovery work that makes the system operational.

Think of confidence as a resource-allocation signal inside a checked workflow. It helps focus expensive computation when calibrated, while the actual solver and physical verification retain their own responsibilities.

[figure: ci-confidence]

reading.takeaway: Use calibrated confidence to allocate work, and verify retained choices jointly.

warnings.message: A reported confidence level is not automatically calibrated and does not certify feasibility. Retained integer predictions need a joint constraint check and a recovery path when they fail.

sections.title: Expected safety cost is not zero violation
sections.body:
A constrained learning objective can minimize expected discounted cost while limiting an expected discounted safety cost. If h is a violation indicator, the expected one-step h is the probability of that violation. An upper bound above zero can therefore permit positive risk.

The finite safety experiment has two actions. Cheap costs 1 and has a declared conditional violation probability p. Cautious costs 3 and has zero violation in this model. A policy chooses Cheap with probability π. Its expected cost is 3−2π and its one-step expected violation isπp.

For a budget C, the feasible interval isπ≤min(1, C/p). The browser performs actual projected updates: decrease cost by increasing π, then project back into that interval. The exact constrained optimum can still have a nonzero violation probability. At C=0, this declared model permits only the zero-risk action.

Repeated operation raises another question. Under twenty independent repetitions with the same one-step probability r, the chance of at least one event is 1−(1−r)²⁰. That cumulative chance is not the same quantity as the one-step expectation budget or an infinite discounted sum.

Rare-event testing can improve estimation efficiency by generating informative events and correcting their sampling probabilities. The experiment keeps the action probabilities fixed and changes only the conditional event distribution. It reports raw event frequency and a weighted natural-risk estimate separately, connecting to [importance sampling](#/lesson/transportation/transportation-3).

This illustrates a mechanism for feasibility evaluation, not a generative neural safe-RL algorithm. Pathwise physical constraints, chance constraints and expected costs require different claims and checks. An expectation constraint should never be relabeled as “no failures on any trajectory.”

[figure: ci-safety]

visuals.predict: Can the cheapest feasible policy still have positive natural violation probability?
visuals.reflect: Apply projected updates, then compare exact risk, raw proposal events, weighted estimates and repeated-operation chance.

reading.takeaway: Specify exactly which safety quantity is constrained and what positive budget permits.

warnings.message: An expected discounted violation-cost constraint does not generally guarantee zero violations on every trajectory. Rare-event generation also needs valid correction back to the target distribution; raw generated failures are not natural frequencies.

sections.title: A generator and a critic need separate validation
sections.body:
An actor produces actions or candidate outputs; a critic supplies an evaluation signal. Policy-based, value-based and actor-critic methods distribute these roles differently. Sharing parameters or using the same language model for both does not make the critic automatically correct.

A self-generated-data loop creates questions, generates answers, grades them and uses the results for further training. It can expand data coverage, but it can also reinforce a shared mistake. A generator that exploits its own critic may improve the internal score while worsening an independently measured task.

The reported comparison illustrates that concern. The discriminative accuracy chart begins at 83.3%. Subsequent CoEvol entries are 69.5%,69.0% and 69.6%, while the self-rewarding comparison falls to 54.4%,49.7% and 49.3%. Neither sequence supports a claim that the critic improved monotonically from its initial value.

Pairwise answer comparisons also depend on who judges. LLM-as-judge wins, ties and losses are different evidence from human judgments. Large tie fractions can limit what a small win-rate difference establishes. Without sample counts and evaluation definitions, percentages do not by themselves establish statistical significance.

Read the four iteration values alongside the evaluator’s role. A training-and-evaluation loop does not establish that repeatedly generating and assessing one’s own material guarantees improvement.

In infrastructure, this lesson applies to self-proposed policies too. Use an independent physical objective, feasibility test or held-out measurement to assess a candidate rather than relying only on the score of the model that proposed it.

[figure: ci-actor]

reading.takeaway: A self-evaluation loop needs independent task and feasibility evidence.

warnings.message: The discriminative-accuracy values decline from 83.3% in both displayed sequences. The self-generation loop and relative pairwise wins do not establish monotonic overall improvement, independent critic correctness or statistical significance without further evaluation details.

sections.title: Computation can be implemented in a different physical medium
sections.body:
Computation is a transformation of represented information. Digital electronics are one implementation; molecular systems can encode inputs and outputs in chemical states. This broadens the infrastructure question from how to schedule computation to how its physical implementation affects controllability and resource use.

The cited DNA study uses dynamic switching of nanostructures through toehold-free strand displacement. Blocking strands alter selected binding interactions, allowing controlled changes in preformed structures. The [research article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s 41467-021-25270-7) describes multi-input, multi-output Boolean examples, including four-input-bit/two-output-bit and sixteen-input-bit/eight-output-bit constructions.

A Boolean truth table describes the information mapping. It does not by itself describe the reaction time, error rate, preparation requirements or energy consumed by the complete implementation. Those physical quantities are essential when comparing a molecular computation with an electronic one.

Controllable molecular dynamics can be a meaningful research contribution without proving a general-purpose replacement for conventional computers. The proposed possibility of energy-efficient future computation remains a question unless a comparable workload and full resource accounting are supplied.

The reconstructed diagram separates input conditions, controlled binding changes and output readout. It teaches the role of the physical medium rather than copying molecular artwork or pretending to simulate reaction kinetics with invented rates.

[figure: ci-dna]

reading.takeaway: A demonstrated information mapping and a measured full-system energy advantage are different claims.

warnings.message: The DNA work demonstrates controlled molecular dynamics and Boolean computation. It does not by itself establish a quantified full-system energy advantage over comparable electronic workloads.

sections.title: Connect the decision, model, budget and constraint
sections.body:
Begin a control design with the actual system boundary. Name the states, observations, actions, transition timing, costs and constraints. Decide which history must be retained for the future law to be meaningful. An omitted elapsed stay or hidden workload can turn a seemingly Markov observation into partial information.

Next choose a tractable policy class. Full-state mappings, event-restricted policies and thresholds preserve different distinctions. Evaluate what the simpler class loses, using the physical and economic measures that matter. A small event count or neural parameter count is not a universal description of behavioral complexity.

Use computation deliberately. Cheap rankings can select promising candidates; repeated high-fidelity simulation can resolve close or noisy comparisons. Report call counts, actual runtime and the information available to the allocation rule. A reference true cost belongs to evaluation, not secretly to the candidate selector.

Carry coarse decisions into fine execution. Energy totals must become time-feasible power actions; local room requests must fit shared device capacities. Track actual delivered service, shortages and comfort violations alongside cost. A cheaper policy that failed its required service can be an operational failure rather than a saving.

Treat prediction and confidence as inputs to checked decisions. Nominally feasible actions can fail under model mismatch. High-confidence integer assignments can jointly violate constraints. A meaningful workflow includes error detection, verification and recovery rather than stopping at the proposed action.

Finally state the scope of safety. Expected violation cost, chance of any event and no-violation requirements are distinct quantities. Rare-event generation helps only when its relation to the natural target is valid. Independent evaluation is also necessary when actor and critic share a model.

The experiments tie these ideas to computed outcomes under declared finite models. Real systems need validated dynamics, data, hardware and operating scope. The same discipline scales from a two-room example to a network: **the model's decision must remain meaningful when the physical system executes it.**

[figure: ci-synthesis]

reading.takeaway: An operationally useful policy connects its information and computation to verified physical execution.

questions.prompt: Why can a cheap energy contract fail to make a device schedule feasible?
choices: Physical network and device constraints still apply.
Contracts eliminate every power and timing limit.
Economic prices fully determine room temperature.
questions.why: Cash flow and physical feasibility are related but different parts of the system.

questions.prompt: An electricity chart projects a share for 2030. What kind of evidence is it?
choices: A proof that all forecast assumptions will hold.
A scenario-dependent forecast, not automatically a current measurement.
A measured total for every present-day data center.
questions.why: The horizon and assumptions are part of the claim.

questions.prompt: Why does a large variable count alone not establish NP-hardness?
choices: Every large linear program is NP-hard by definition.
NP-hardness measures the electricity used by a computer.
Complexity also depends on the problem structure and discrete constraints.
questions.why: Scale and computational complexity are related but distinct.

questions.prompt: With four states and two allowed actions per state, how many deterministic stationary policies exist?
questions.why: Each of the four independent state assignments has two choices, giving2⁴=16.

questions.prompt: For costs [4, 4, 4] and discount 0.5, what is the discounted total?
Why can Eco have a higher total action value despite a smaller immediate cost?
choices: Discounting removes every future state from the objective.
Action values are just labels unrelated to transitions.
It can lead more often to expensive future hot states.
questions.why: Q includes immediate cost plus discounted expected continuation cost.

questions.prompt: What information does one sampled Q-learning update directly use?
choices: The visited state/action, observed cost, sampled next state and current continuation estimates.
The exact cost of every unobserved trajectory.
A guarantee that every state-action pair was visited.
questions.why: A temporal-difference update can operate from one actual sampled transition.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of aggregating detailed states into events?
choices: Losing information relevant to decisions.
Creating more perfect labels automatically.
Eliminating all uncertainty.
questions.why: A smaller event representation can make the problem partially observable.

questions.prompt: Two hidden states share a temperature event but have different next-event probabilities under Eco. What follows?
choices: The hidden states are automatically behaviorally identical.
An event label makes every transition deterministic.
That event label alone does not reproduce the full Markov state.
questions.why: A Markov aggregation requires the relevant transition behavior to agree within its observed groups.

questions.prompt: What does Pareto domination mean for cost and controller complexity?
choices: Another design is no worse in either and better in at least one.
Every design has the same cost and complexity.
The most complicated design is always globally best.
questions.why: Pareto comparison requires both objectives, not just the preferred one.

questions.prompt: What does ordinal optimization emphasize?
choices: Exact global optimization with no approximation.
Identifying good-enough candidates using useful relative rankings.
Ignoring every constraint.
questions.why: Approximate comparisons help allocate costly detailed evaluation to promising designs.

questions.prompt: What is the alignment event |G∩S|≥k?
choices: Every selected design is the unique global optimum.
The observed and true objective values must be identical.
At least k selected designs truly belong to the good-enough set.
questions.why: Alignment concerns overlap of the selected and truly good sets.

questions.prompt: For a blind twelve-design subset of200, what is the exact expected overlap with a fixed top-twelve set?
choices: Exactly12.
Exactly1 in every run.
questions.why: Each of the12 good designs is selected with probability12/200.

questions.prompt: Does an empirical alignment fraction from500 simulations prove the same probability for every design problem?
choices: Yes; positive noise cannot change rankings.
No; the construction and finite Monte Carlo uncertainty limit the claim.
Yes; five hundred draws validate all possible noise models.
questions.why: An empirical probability belongs to its declared simulation and sample size.

questions.prompt: Why can more observations fail to repair a systematically biased crude ranking?
choices: Every biased model becomes unbiased after100 samples.
Bias is just another name for a small standard deviation.
The mean observations can converge to the wrong ordering.
questions.why: Reducing sample noise does not remove model bias.

questions.prompt: Why may a noisy near-best candidate receive many evaluations?
choices: Its uncertainty can change which design should be selected.
Every candidate must receive exactly the same count.
A noisy candidate is known to have the best true cost.
questions.why: Small observed gaps and large variance can make additional comparison information valuable.

questions.prompt: Two methods use the same number of simulation calls. Must their computation times match?
choices: Only if they have different objective functions.
No; candidate runtimes and overhead can differ.
Yes; a call is always one second.
questions.why: A call budget and elapsed computation budget are different units.

questions.prompt: Why can a thermal model fail when an optimizer uses it outside its observed range?
choices: Optimization automatically validates every extrapolation.
A correlation matrix certifies every possible intervention.
The optimizer may select controls whose effects were not reliably modeled.
questions.why: A predictive surrogate needs validation over the controls and states the optimization actually explores.

questions.prompt: Why does a daily energy surplus not ensure every vehicle is charged on departure?
choices: Availability, deadlines and power limits determine when energy can be delivered.
Energy can always be moved backward in time.
Every vehicle has an unlimited charging rate.
questions.why: Aggregate energy balance omits timing and rate constraints.

questions.prompt: What can make waiting for cheap future wind fail?
choices: An optimistic forecast physically produces the promised wind.
The remaining charging window or power limit may become insufficient.
A later energy price removes an earlier departure deadline.
questions.why: A schedule must balance future supply opportunities with remaining feasible delivery time.

questions.prompt: What does a rollout that follows base policy πb after the first action estimate?
choices: The exact optimal Q* regardless of πb.
Only the current cost, with all later stages omitted.
The first action’s cost under that base continuation, Q^πb.
questions.why: The continuation policy is part of the value being estimated.

questions.prompt: A failed charging schedule has a smaller electricity bill. Why may it still be worse?
choices: It may have delivered less required energy and missed deadlines.
A smaller bill proves all service constraints were satisfied.
Every missed kWh has zero operational consequence.
questions.why: Cost and constraint satisfaction must be evaluated together.

questions.prompt: What information does the rolling actual-profile comparator receive?
choices: No information about charging deadlines.
The declared future actual wind profile, making it an oracle comparison.
Only a noisy forecast exactly like every deployed controller.
questions.why: Perfect future information isolates a mechanism but is not a real forecast guarantee.

questions.prompt: Three independent groups allow5,4 and3 prefix choices. How many joint choices remain?
choices: 2¹².
questions.why: Independent group counts multiply:5×4×3=60.

questions.prompt: What should be done with the inconsistent multi-timescale total?
choices: Report the component sum and flag which original entry is intended as unresolved.
Silently declare every printed entry correct.
Replace every method’s total by3,286.4.
questions.why: The component arithmetic is clear, but the intended source correction is not.

questions.prompt: Why can a feasible daily energy schedule fail when projected to minute-level control?
choices: A finer model always requires a different objective.
Aggregation may hide short-lived shortages or device constraints.
Daily schedules cannot include energy costs.
questions.why: The macro/meso/micro diagrams show aggregation and policy projection. A coarse balance can omit timing or constraints that become visible at a finer resolution.

questions.prompt: Supply[0,8] and demand[8,0] have equal mean power with no storage. Are they matched at both intervals?
choices: Yes; identical averages imply identical trajectories.
Yes; coarse models create storage automatically.
No; the first interval has an8-unit shortage.
questions.why: Timing can be lost by averaging, even when total energy agrees.

questions.prompt: Why should a glare complaint pass through interpretation rather than directly set every device?
choices: The appropriate targets and coupled device responses must be determined.
Every complaint always means maximum cooling.
Comfort feedback removes physical constraints.
questions.why: A complaint describes an experience; it does not uniquely specify a feasible actuator combination.

questions.prompt: Two rooms are both occupied now, but their occupants have stayed for very different durations. What does a stay-duration model add to a current-occupancy-only model?
choices: A stay-time-dependent departure estimate.
A guarantee that both rooms empty at the same clock time.
Proof that all occupancy estimation error is zero.
questions.why: The zonal stay-time curve relates departure probability to elapsed stay. Current occupancy alone loses that duration information; neither premise establishes error-free prediction.

questions.prompt: For a person known to remain at time t, which departure probability applies over the next Δ?
choices: 1−S(t) regardless of Δ.
Always one because t is positive.
questions.why: Conditional survival divides future survival by survival to the present time.

questions.prompt: Two rooms each request3kW from one4kW cooling plant. What is needed?
choices: A coordinated allocation that satisfies the combined limit.
Each room can receive3kW because its local request is valid.
Removing the plant from the model creates extra power.
questions.why: Local feasibility does not ensure feasibility of the joint shared-device action.

questions.prompt: Why can a nominal filter violate comfort when actual heat capacity is smaller?
choices: A model’s feasible label overrides physical evolution.
The same cooling energy can cause a larger actual temperature change.
Heat capacity has no role in temperature dynamics.
questions.why: Temperature change scales inversely with C in the declared energy balance.

questions.prompt: What should a feasibility filter report when no allowed action satisfies its predicted bounds?
choices: Guaranteed safety because it tried every action.
A new cooling capacity without changing the device model.
Infeasibility, with any fallback clearly identified.
questions.why: An empty feasible set is a physical or modeling limitation, not a successful constraint certificate.

questions.prompt: An event-based method has daily cost 1501 RMB and a one-minute time-based method has cost 1496 RMB. What can those entries establish on their own?
choices: The event-based controller costs about 0.334% more in this comparison.
The event-based controller is the global optimum in every building.
Every simulation method will run 50 times faster.
questions.why: (1501−1496)/1496 × 100 ≈ 0.334%. These are results for a particular comparison; the table alone does not prove a global optimum or a universal speedup.

questions.prompt: What does the1496RMB comparison entry establish about a global optimum on its own?
choices: It certifies all buildings have identical energy use.
It is a listed comparison value, not an optimality certificate.
It proves no possible policy has a smaller cost.
questions.why: A best reported comparator and a proven global optimum are different evidence.

questions.prompt: Why can a time step suitable for slow thermal dynamics be unsuitable for fast electrical transients?
choices: All physical systems share one exact time scale.
A larger time step always increases physical accuracy.
The fast rates can require finer or more stable numerical treatment.
questions.why: Separated dynamics create different resolution and stability requirements.

questions.prompt: Why can nearly99.8% accuracy still be useless for the stated imbalanced fault dataset?
choices: An always-healthy classifier can achieve it while recalling no faults.
The faulty class is the majority.
Accuracy always guarantees perfect recall.
questions.why: Large class imbalance can make majority prediction look accurate without detecting the rare class.

questions.prompt: The healthy F-score changes0.896→0.979. What is its relative improvement from those values?
choices: About83 percentage points.
About9.3%.
Exactly8% by definition.
questions.why: (0.979−0.896)/0.896≈0.0926; relative percentage and absolute points differ.

questions.prompt: Why can incorrectly fixing a predicted binary commitment decision hurt an optimizer?
choices: Every fixed variable makes every problem feasible.
A confidence label adds generating capacity to the grid.
It can remove feasible or better solutions from the remaining search space.
questions.why: Fixing a variable is a real restriction on the feasible policy set.

questions.prompt: Does high confidence on each predicted commitment guarantee joint feasibility?
choices: No; the combined assignment must still satisfy system constraints.
Yes; confidence probabilities add generating power.
Yes; each variable can be checked without any coupling.
questions.why: Joint constraints can fail despite individually plausible predictions.

questions.prompt: A one-step safety violation has probability 0.01. Does an expected violation-cost budget of 0.02 imply zero violations?
choices: Yes, any satisfied constraint guarantees every trajectory is safe.
Yes, if the policy is a neural network.
No; the expectation is within budget even though violations remain possible.
questions.why: For a 0/1 violation indicator, the expected cost is its probability, 0.01. An expectation constraint differs from requiring no violation on every trajectory.

questions.prompt: What does a positive expected violation budget permit in the two-action model?
choices: Every individual trajectory is guaranteed violation-free.
A simulator’s raw proposal frequency becomes the natural probability.
Some positive violation probability can remain feasible.
questions.why: An expectation constraint and a pathwise no-violation requirement are different conditions.

questions.prompt: Why can a policy improve its self-critic score without improving actual behavior?
choices: It can exploit or share errors in the proxy evaluation.
Every critic score is a verified physical measurement.
Generating more data automatically removes all bias.
questions.why: A proxy objective and independently measured quality can diverge.

questions.prompt: What extra evidence is needed to claim an energy advantage for molecular computation?
choices: Only the word DNA in the implementation.
A comparable workload and complete resource, timing and error accounting.
Only a correct Boolean truth table.
questions.why: Logic capability does not establish the full implementation’s energy efficiency.

questions.prompt: Which combination gives the most informative policy evaluation?
choices: Only the smallest electricity bill, even if service fails.
Only the critic’s score on its own generated actions.
Cost, delivered service, violations, computation and declared model scope together.
questions.why: The policy’s operational consequences and evaluation assumptions determine whether it is useful.
